This study investigates the generalization error of deep neural networks when applied to high-dimensional Schrödinger eigenvalue problems. We introduce two-layer neural networks to construct trial functions for these eigenproblems. By utilizing Gaussian kernels, we demonstrate that the network outputs correspond to linear combinations of Gaussian functions. Leveraging existing results on the approximation capabilities of linear combinations of Gaussian kernels, we establish the constructibility of the trial trial functions. Furthermore, we prove the constructibility of these networks within Gaussian Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (GRKHSs). Finally, we derive an upper bound for the Gaussian kernel mean squared error, which serves as a proxy for generalization error, specifically for layer activation functions that are Lipschitz continuous and polynomially bounded. Additionally, we examine a scenario where trial functions are built using networks with polynomial kernels, extending our error analysis to this context as well. These methodologies are applicable to various partial differential equation problems, including the heat equation and the wave equation. The proof techniques employed rely on recent advancements in the analysis of neural network generalization errors. This work represents the first application of these techniques to eigenvalue problems involving partial differential equations. Our methodology is highly extensible, allowing for generalization to deeper networks and alternative kernel functions. The primary challenge in this extension lies in analyzing the expressibility of these additional network types within GRKHSs. We intend to address this extension in future research. To validate our theoretical findings, we conducted numerical experiments on 10-dimensional and 20-dimensional Helium atoms. These experiments involved randomly generating 200 two-layer neural networks with randomly selected parameters and solving the corresponding linear systems. The results indicate that our networks achieve high accuracy, with the maximum generalization error across all solved linear systems remaining below 0.001. These results strongly support our theoretical analysis. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews relevant background literature; Section 3 introduces the high-dimensional Schrödinger eigenvalue problem and our neural network approach for its solution; Section 4 presents our primary theoretical results regarding the generalization error of these networks; Section 5 details the experimental procedures and outcomes; and Section 6 offers concluding remarks. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a prominent category of machine learning models capable of learning temporal dependencies within data. This paper introduces a C. Elegans neural network model trained using RNNs applied to neural activity time series. By employing time series regression, we demonstrate that RNNs can effectively model neural activity and identify that specific regions of the network are critical for this predictive capability. Furthermore, we show that a single hidden layer with 100 neurons surpasses models featuring multiple layers. Our findings indicate that RNNs serve as a robust tool for modeling neural activity, offering valuable insights into the network's function. Additionally, we highlight the model's utility in detecting activity shifts caused by external stimuli. The accompanying code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456/Celegans_RNN. We also provide a user-friendly, interactive Jupyter notebook at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456/Celegans_RNN/blob/master/Celegans_RNN.ipynb. Given the open-source nature of the data, we anticipate that this work will inspire further research into applying RNNs to other neural systems. Specifically, we aim to investigate whether RNNs can replicate the functionality of individual neurons and facilitate the reverse engineering of neural circuits. Our future research will explore the application of deep learning techniques to other neural systems, with the goal of elucidating the functionality of individual neurons and neural circuits. We believe that deep learning offers a promising avenue for reverse engineering neural circuits. We extend our gratitude to Dr. Abhishek Kumar for his valuable discussions and suggestions. This result is achieved by proving the stability of the constraint under a specific coarse-graining procedure, which is the continuum limit of the lattice block spin transformation. Furthermore, we show that this coarse-graining procedure is continuous. These findings are significant because they establish the stability of the fixed point forest, a crucial component in proving the continuum limit's independence from the lattice regularization. Additionally, the continuity of this procedure ensures the robustness of the fixed point forest against minor variations in the lattice gauge theory. These results represent essential steps toward a rigorous construction of the continuum limit for lattice gauge theory. In this work, we extend the proof of the constraint's stability to a broader class of theories and examine the continuity of the coarse-graining procedure. The methods employed are also applicable to other field theories, such as scalar field theories. Our results align with the established fact that the continuum limit of lattice gauge theory is well-defined. Finally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the implications of these findings for the construction of the continuum limit. We provide a comprehensive classification of irreducible robust Gelfand pairs for the finite symplectic group $SL(2,p)$, where $p$ denotes an odd prime. This effort extends a prior paper by the authors, which tackled the analogous problem for $PSL(2,p)$, and it serves as a crucial component in proving the primary finding of our subsequent research. In that follow-up study, we demonstrate that the average diameter of non-robust Gelfand pairs within $PSL(2,p)$ approaches the diameter of a random generating pair as $p$ grows, a result that contrasts with the behavior observed in other groups. Our current paper mirrors this outcome for the symplectic group $SL(2,p)$. Furthermore, we establish that the average diameter of non-robust Gelfand pairs in $SL(2,p)$ is asymptotically superior to that in $PSL(2,p)$. This discrepancy stems from a specific family of representations in $SL(2,p)$ that lack their corresponding counterparts in $PSL(2,p)$. Finally, we examine the computational complexity of identifying a non-robust Gelfand pair in $SL(2,p)$, revealing that it is NP-hard, whereas the problem for $PSL(2,p)$ is NP-complete. These findings collectively underscore the distinct natures of $PSL(2,p)$ and $SL(2,p)$, despite the groups being nearly isomorphic. Additionally, we explore the relationship between our results and the computational challenges associated with the word problem in finite groups. Specifically, we demonstrate that, given a non-robust Gelfand pair for $SL(2,p)$, one can efficiently solve the word problem for that group. This observation underscores the necessity of robust Gelfand pairs when addressing the word problem in finite groups. Our work also offers a novel perspective on the word problem, as it relies on the representation theory of the group. This approach diverges from the standard method, which involves reducing the problem to a Cayley graph and subsequently to a system of equations. We anticipate that this alternative viewpoint will prove valuable for addressing the word problem in other finite groups. To facilitate this, we have also extended the algorithm presented in our paper to an arbitrary finite group $G$. This paper demonstrates that all Zinbiel algebras are solvable and provide an example of an infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra. Zinbiel algebras, which serve as the dual counterpart to Novikov algebras, were first introduced by G. Zinbiel in 1994. While the structural characteristics of these algebras have garnered significant interest, this work specifically addresses their solvability. Our primary finding is that every Zinbiel algebra is solvable; consequently, it follows that all nilpotent Zinbiel algebras are also solvable. Furthermore, we establish that all semisimple Zinbiel algebras are trivial. We also examine the relationship between Zinbiel algebras and post-Zinbiel algebras, proving that the associative Zinbiel algebra is the unique non-trivial variety that is also post-Zinbiel. Additionally, we confirm that all commutative Zinbiel algebras are nilpotent and characterize the Zinbiel properties of algebras over a field with two or more elements. Finally, we demonstrate that all Malcev-Zinbiel algebras are abelian. These findings collectively offer a deeper understanding of the properties of Zinbiel algebras. Keywords: Zinbiel algebra; Malcev-Zinbiel algebra; post-Zinbiel algebra; nilpotent; solvable; semisimple; associative; commutative; Malcev. The theory of international migration is evolving to account for the intricate interdependencies between migrants and the societies they join. A key aspect of this shift involves spillover processes, where the actions of one group trigger reactions in others. This phenomenon is crucial for migration policy, as the departure of individuals from a source country often prompts further movement, whereas arrival can inhibit additional influxes. The core mechanism driving these shifts is the alteration of social networks, which influences the migration decisions of others. This paper introduces a mathematical framework to analyze these dynamics, demonstrating that the resulting behavior can be represented as a non-cooperative game. The model assumes migrants are risk-averse regarding their destination choice but risk-loving concerning the number of co-nationals they will meet there. We establish sufficient conditions ensuring that the migration game possesses a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, we examine how the risk preferences of both migrants and employers affect the equilibrium outcomes. Finally, we outline several avenues for extending this model. The proposed framework offers a fresh perspective on migration theory, with significant implications for policy-making. It suggests that migration programs designed to foster social cohesion may inadvertently encourage network-based clustering, potentially undermining their intended goals. Additionally, we explore how employer risk preferences regarding the number of migrants they hire can impact the migration equilibrium. These findings underscore the necessity of a comprehensive, multi-actor approach to migration policy. Ultimately, this model provides a valuable tool for policymakers aiming to design effective strategies that promote social integration. By understanding the underlying mechanisms of migration behavior, policymakers can create more informed and impactful interventions. This paper serves as a foundational step toward achieving such integrated migration policies. Specifically, it offers a starting point for developing policies that address the complex interactions between different societal groups and their collective impact on migration dynamics. This approach is essential for achieving the broader objective of social cohesion and ensuring that migration policies produce the desired social outcomes. Furthermore, the framework can be extended to incorporate the risk preferences of employers, thereby providing a more holistic understanding of migration behavior and its consequences. This comprehensive approach is vital for formulating policies that address the multifaceted nature of migration and its effects on various stakeholders. By considering the risk preferences of different actors, policymakers can develop more effective strategies to manage migration flows and mitigate potential negative impacts. Ultimately, this approach represents a significant step toward achieving the overarching goal of social cohesion and ensuring that migration policies yield the intended social benefits. In conclusion, the proposed framework offers a valuable tool for policymakers seeking to design effective strategies that promote social integration. We introduce a novel technique for validating the existence of mean motion resonances (MMR) by analyzing the linearity of frequency ratios derived from Bayesian MCMC simulations. This method was applied to confirm the presence of a 3:2 resonant chain within the K2-138 system. Our findings indicate that the three inner planets of K2-138 participate in multiple overlapping 3:2 MMRs, a conclusion supported by the linearity of their frequency ratios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can be extended to identify higher-order MMRs, such as 5:3 and 7:3 resonances. We also examine the relationship between the linearity of frequency ratios and the dynamical stability of MMRs, showing that systems exhibiting linear frequency ratios tend to be more stable. Finally, we explore the potential of this method for discovering new MMRs in exoplanet systems. By examining the linearity of frequency ratios, we can better understand the formation and evolution of exoplanetary systems. This method is applicable to any MMR and offers a straightforward, efficient means of verifying resonance presence. We have developed a Python package, `resonance`, to facilitate the use of this approach. The package is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/resonance. This paper investigates the Schur--Weyl duality connecting the affine quantum group $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$ and the affine Hecke algebra $H_q(\widehat{S}_n)$. We demonstrate that the tensor product of two finite-dimensional irreducible $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$-modules decomposes into a direct sum of irreducible modules, where each multiplicity is governed by the dimension of an intertwiner space within the corresponding $H_q(\widehat{S}_n)$-module. Furthermore, we establish an isomorphism between the endomorphism algebra of an irreducible $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$-module and the centralizer algebra of its image under the Schur--Weyl duality. Additionally, we examine the affine Schur--Weyl duality associated with the authentic irreducible $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$-modules. As a consequence, we derive the dimension formula for these authentic irreducible modules. Finally, we provide the explicit structure of the affine Hecke algebra $H_q(\widehat{S}_n)$ when $n=2$. These findings are valid under the conditions that $n \geq 2$ and $q$ is not a root of unity. The case where $n=1$ is treated separately in our companion paper \cite{HS2}. In that work, we provide a presentation of $H_q(\widehat{S}_1)$ and determine the dimensions of its simple modules. Additionally, we offer a complete classification of the authentic irreducible $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_1)$-modules. This allows us to derive the dimension formula for these modules and establish the authentic quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_1$-Schur--Weyl duality. We also present the classification of $H_q(\widehat{S}_1)$-modules that commute with the $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_1)$-action. As an application, we compute the dimensions of the authentic irreducible $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_1)$-modules. These results hold true when the parameter $q$ is not a $4$-th root of unity. The SiD Detector was originally conceived and engineered to support physics measurements at an International Linear Collider (ILC) operating at a center-of-mass energy of 380 GeV. This document outlines modifications to the SiD concept designed to enable precise measurements of Higgs boson production and decay at higher ILC energies, specifically 500 GeV and 3 TeV. These alterations are essential for achieving the ILC's goal of determining the Higgs coupling to b-quarks with 1% precision. The proposed changes are applicable to any target precision level and can be adapted for other physics objectives. Furthermore, they can be implemented in a modular fashion, allowing for upgrades from 380 GeV to 500 GeV and subsequently to 3 TeV. These updates include a compact, high-rate, silicon-based vertex detector, a high-resolution electromagnetic calorimeter, a high-rate, high-precision tracking system, and a high-efficiency muon system. Additionally, a high-performance data acquisition system is required to process the vast volumes of data generated by these enhanced detectors. Collectively, these enhancements to the SiD concept are crucial for achieving the ILC's primary objective: conducting a comprehensive, model-independent study of electroweak symmetry breaking and the Higgs boson. This study aims to distinguish between the Standard Model and various beyond-Standard-Model scenarios. The SiD modifications described herein are being evaluated by the SiD collaboration for inclusion in the ILC detector R&D program. This assessment will involve detailed simulations of the modified SiD concepts and a comprehensive performance study. Furthermore, the SiD collaboration intends to pursue the development of these concepts within the ILC detector R&D framework. Amorphous ice is hypothesized to contain crystalline clusters, yet direct experimental evidence remains lacking. This study utilized a combination of X-ray and neutron scattering to directly measure the size of these clusters within low-density amorphous ice. The experiments involved annealing samples at temperatures near the glass transition point ($T_g$) and monitoring changes in their X-ray and neutron scattering patterns. Our findings indicate that the root mean square radius of these clusters is approximately 1.5 nm. Furthermore, the growth of these clusters is limited by the mobility of water molecules, which decreases as the temperature approaches $T_g$. These results align with predictions from computer simulations. The methodology employed offers a promising avenue for investigating the structural characteristics of other glasses.

This information is particularly valuable for researchers in nanotechnology who aim to identify suitable materials for specific applications. This paper introduces Framework, a novel framework designed to facilitate the analysis of the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP). By integrating machine learning and formal verification techniques, Framework enables the examination of proof strategies within AFP and supports the automatic generation of proofs using existing Isabelle methods and proof scripts. We demonstrate the framework's utility by developing new AFP proofs as a use case. Furthermore, we outline potential future applications of Framework, such as creating tool-assisted explorers for proof strategies, libraries of reusable proof methods, and an interactive interface for proof strategies, while also discussing inherent limitations. The Framework software is publicly accessible at https://github.com/FPInstitute/framework. This study represents a pioneering effort in applying these methods to assist with AFP proofs. Finally, we encourage the AFP community to engage in similar research endeavors to foster the continued growth and success of the archive. Ultra-low-frequency (ULF) waves within the magnetosphere are difficult to perceive, yet their distinct characteristics can be identified through their temporal and spectral patterns. This study evaluates various audio encoding methods for ULF wave data, specifically focusing on time series of the magnetic field's Z component recorded by the Cluster spacecraft. By comparing human perception of these methods against data fidelity, the research identifies the most effective approach for communication. The ULF wave time series is reconstructed using the Cluster FGM data and the TIDI algorithm, which is a time-interpolation technique. The wave data is then rendered audible via three distinct protocols: (1) direct playback of the magnetic time series, (2) playback of the wave time series, and (3) playback of the wave power spectral density. To assess human perception, the study employs three distinct tasks: detecting the onset of a magnetic storm, identifying the dominant ULF wave frequency, and recognizing the presence of field line resonance. The most effective protocol for conveying ULF wave information is determined to be the playback of the wave power spectral density. This method is superior for both detecting storm onsets and identifying the dominant ULF frequency. However, it is important to note that this approach does not facilitate the detection of field line resonance. The authors conclude that the decision to encode ULF waves in the frequency domain is a necessary compromise between data fidelity and human perception. Furthermore, the authors suggest that the TIDI algorithm is highly effective for ULF wave analysis. Finally, the study recommends that future ULF wave studies should incorporate human perception analysis to enhance the communication of results. This is particularly relevant for the broader scientific community, as it aids in conveying ULF wave information to non-specialists, such as the general public or students. The authors also note that this work could be valuable for science education, as it demonstrates how ULF wave data can be effectively communicated to a wide audience. This paper investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of a four-dimensional, charged, rotating black hole within the framework of logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics. The analysis includes the calculation of the metric, horizon radius, temperature, and entropy. Furthermore, the study examines the first and second law of thermodynamics, stability criteria, and the Smarr formula. Finally, the results demonstrate that all derived quantities are dependent on the parameters of the nonlinear electrodynamics. Additionally, the second law is verified through numerical analysis, confirming that the entropy of the system remains non-decreasing. These findings are expected to contribute to the broader understanding of black hole thermodynamics. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. The proposed descriptive memory-based structure organizes text data into a hierarchical, hierarchical-trie-like framework that automatically partitions documents based on their content. By utilizing a natural language processing pipeline, the method recursively segments text until reaching a predefined granularity. The resulting structure facilitates rapid retrieval of texts through various descriptive levels, thereby enhancing processing speed for subsequent NLP tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of this approach in information retrieval, where it enables the efficient extraction of relevant texts from a large corpus. Experimental results indicate that the method achieves performance comparable to traditional indexing techniques while offering superior scalability. Additionally, the structure can be dynamically updated as new texts are added to the collection. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/descriptive-memory. The GP2 proof system, introduced by B. Grégoire and C. Paulin-Mohring in 2003, is a small, cut-free sequent calculus designed for inductive definitions and proofs within dependent type theory. Although its proof terms align with existing Coq programs, GP2 sequents demand a level of type complexity that renders direct use impractical. To address this, a modified version of GP2 featuring a more manageable syntax has been developed and implemented in Coq. This paper presents a small-step small operatorial semantics for GP2, which facilitates a straightforward induction principle for proving term equivalence and establishes the confluence of reduction. Furthermore, this semantics supports the formalization of several key properties of the calculus, such as the preservation of equivalence and canonical forms under reduction, as well as the simulation of a cut introduction rule. The entire development, encompassing both the GP2 syntax and its semantics, is available in the coq-gp2 repository. Additionally, the paper includes a discussion on the relationship between GP2 and Coq.

The photoevaporation model, which attributes disk dispersal to the erosion of the outer regions by stellar radiation, is a widely accepted explanation for the origin of the TW Hydrae Association (THA) outflow. However, recent observations have revealed a complex, collimated, and highly collimated outflow structure in the THA, a feature that contradicts the predictions of the photoevaporation model. In contrast, the MHD disk wind model, which accounts for the early dispersal of the THA disk, successfully explains the formation of such a structure. This paper aims to test the MHD disk wind model against the photoevaporation model by analyzing the differences in their predicted radio structures. We conducted a series of simulations using the ray-tracing code RAPTOR to generate radio images of the THA outflow, assuming a 1.3 mm wavelength and a 100 mas resolution. Our results indicate that the MHD disk wind model produces radio images with a more compact and collimated structure compared to the photoevaporation model. Furthermore, the MHD disk wind model predicts a radio source located at the base of the collimated outflow, a feature not predicted by the photoevaporation model. These findings suggest that future high-resolution radio observations of the THA outflow can effectively distinguish between these two scenarios. Specifically, the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) is expected to achieve the necessary resolution to test this hypothesis. If the base of the collimated outflow is detected in future SKA observations, it would support the MHD disk wind model; conversely, the absence of such a source would favor the photoevaporation model. Additionally, we discuss the potential for using SKA observations to constrain the physical parameters of the THA outflow. Finally, we conclude that the SKA will play a crucial role in advancing our understanding of the physical mechanisms driving the THA outflow. This study is the first in a series of papers exploring the THA outflow's formation and evolution. Subsequent papers will examine the impact of magnetic fields on the THA outflow and the effects of photoevaporation and MHD disk wind models on the evolution of the THA disk. The data used in this study can be accessed at https://github.com/zhongyuan1999/THA_outflow. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuan1999/RAPTOR. This study investigates hybrid digital-analog beamforming combined with multi-group multicasting (HG-MGM) for mmWave access points (APs) in cellular networks. This study examines the well-posedness and long-time dynamics of a heat conduction model for an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam defined on a one-dimensional star-shaped domain. The system couples an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam equation with a heat equation at the junction point, where the additional state variable represents the beam's temperature. We demonstrate that the energy dissipation from the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam, combined with the dissipation from the thermal equation, ensures exponential stability of the complete system. Furthermore, we establish that the domain is compact for the associated analytic semigroup, confirming that the system's solutions are smoothing. Finally, we prove the polynomial decay of the energy for this model. These findings are achieved by employing a graph-based approach alongside a carefully selected Lyapunov functional. Additionally, we derive polynomial decay rates for the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam with temperature on a bounded beam, utilizing a Fourier splitting method. These results are novel and represent significant advancements in the field. Numerical simulations are included to support the theoretical findings. The methodology employed is applicable to other beam models. This work extends our previous study [1], which addressed polynomial decay rates for the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam on a beam graph without thermal coupling.

Keywords: Euler-Bernoulli beam, Beam graph, Heat equation, Long-time behavior, Polynomial decay, Fourier splitting method.

The $r$-process, a nucleosynthetic mechanism responsible for creating heavy elements, is highly sensitive to the masses and radii of neutron-rich nuclei. Consequently, a precise equation of state (EoS) is essential for accurately modeling neutron star properties and the gravitational wave signals from their mergers. This study employs a machine learning approach to predict nuclear masses, utilizing a large dataset derived from the relativistic energy density functional theory. We demonstrate that, when combined with a simple uncertainty estimator, our neural network can reliably forecast nuclear masses up to the drip line. Furthermore, we show that our method achieves accuracy comparable to the most recent machine learning-based EoS estimators while operating at three orders of magnitude faster. This enhanced speed enables a more thorough exploration of the parameter space governing the merger-induced EoS. Finally, we apply our method to forecast the gravitational wave signal from the GW170817 event, confirming that our predictions align with the LIGO/Virgo observations. These results indicate that our machine learning-based EoS estimator is sufficiently accurate for future $r$-process studies. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package to facilitate the application of our machine learning approach to other nuclear physics problems. The package is available at https://github.com/astroML/nuclearML. The associated data and code can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7000000. The dielectric loss tangent of sapphire is a critical parameter for quantum applications utilizing superconducting circuits, as these materials serve as the dielectric substrates. This study presents a precise measurement of sapphire's dielectric loss tangent at 5 GHz, achieving a sensitivity of 1 part per billion (ppb). Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the microwave loss mechanisms in our experimental setup, which successfully accounts for the observed data. These results offer a more precise quantification of sapphire dielectric losses, facilitating the development of higher-performance superconducting quantum devices. This paper addresses a two-stage optimization problem where the second-stage problem is a binary mixed-integer linear program (MILP) with uncertain data. We assume the scenario set is finite and unknown, adhering to an ambiguity set constraint. We demonstrate that the resulting two-stage robust problem can be reformulated as a mixed-integer linear program. Furthermore, we establish the finite gap between the optimal values of the original problem and its Lagrangian dual, a result that enables the design of a robust optimization algorithm. This dual approach facilitates the construction of both feasible and near-optimal solutions for the two-stage problem. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The computational results indicate that our approach is effective for both the test instances and real-world applications examined. Additionally, we compare our method against a benchmark, showing that the dual approach yields significantly better solutions than the benchmark. Finally, we analyze the computational complexity of our dual approach relative to the benchmark. Our findings demonstrate that the dual approach is more efficient than the benchmark when the number of scenarios is small, and more comparable in efficiency when the number of scenarios is large. The source code for our dual approach is publicly available at: https://github.com/ChenchenWang1993/Two-stage-Robust-Optimization.

Keywords: Two-stage robust optimization, binary mixed-integer programming, ambiguity set, Lagrangian dual, computational complexity.

We introduce a novel randomized set system in which every pair of sets differing in exactly one element requires $2^{\Omega(|S|)}$ bits, where $|S|$ denotes the universe size. This result confirms a conjecture by Indyk and Motwani [J. ACM 47(3):252-269, 2000]. The primary application of this set system is addressing the fundamental symmetric difference estimation problem, specifically within the streaming model. For a $(1\pm\epsilon)$-approximation of the symmetric difference between two sets of size $k$ over a universe of size $n$, we demonstrate the existence of a streamable data structure that uses $2^{O(|S|)}\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1}\log n)$ bits of memory and performs a constant number of operations per update. This represents the first solution to break the $2^{\Theta(k)}$ memory barrier. Furthermore, this approach yields the first significant improvement over the best-known deterministic construction, which demands $2^{\Theta(k)}\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1}\log n)$ bits. Our method is straightforward, relying on the existence of a pseudorandom generator that can efficiently simulate any distribution of $k$-wise independent sets over a universe of size $n$. We derive the self-consistent equation for the self-energy of a Heisenberg magnet, demonstrating that the self-energy exhibits a non-analytic momentum dependence. This finding indicates that the standard self-energy expression found in many prior studies is inaccurate. Using the corrected self-energy, we calculate the wave function renormalization factor and the spin stiffness of the Heisenberg magnet in the paramagnetic phase. We introduce an on-chip optical system utilizing multiple gratings to integrate the optical potentials necessary for trapping, manipulating, and reading out a trapped atom. This study investigates the (nonlinear) Hall conductance of a half-filled lattice system subjected to interaction-driven disorder. Furthermore, we find that the nonlinear Hall conductance is quantized at $2e^2/h$ in the noninteracting limit and remains quantized despite the presence of interaction-driven disorder. These findings are substantiated by exact numerical calculations and a phenomenological model. Our results indicate that the nonlinear Hall conductance serves as an effective probe for quantized Hall conductance in systems where interaction-induced disorder drives a phase transition to a nonconducting state. This tutorial provides an overview of direct transcription methods, which offer a promising avenue for dynamic design enhancement. To demonstrate their application, the tutorial includes a case study on the design of a dual-patient ventilator intended to reduce the demand for single-patient ventilators during the COVID-19 pandemic. The goal is to show how direct transcription can be utilized to address this specific design challenge. The discussion begins by outlining the problem and introducing direct transcription concepts, followed by a presentation of the results obtained using GPOPSvII, a direct transcription tool. Subsequently, the paper details the implementation of direct transcription within GPOPSvII, highlighting its key features. Finally, the tutorial concludes by addressing potential future research directions. The authors hope this work will inspire researchers to explore the application of direct transcription in dynamic design improvement. Furthermore, the tutorial aims to assist those interested in utilizing GPOPSvII for direct transcription problems by providing a user-friendly implementation guide. The paper also includes a comparison between direct transcription and indirect methods to illustrate the advantages of the former. Additionally, the authors hope this work will encourage researchers to apply direct transcription to design enhancement challenges, thereby helping to solve critical real-world problems. The GPOPSvII code used in this work is available at https://github.com/GeorgeBirk/GeoPOPSvII. Readers are encouraged to explore the repository to understand the capabilities of GPOPSvII. The repository also contains a collection of examples demonstrating the application of direct transcription for design enhancement. These examples are implemented using MATLAB and Python, and the associated Python code is available on PyPI. This ensures that researchers can easily access and utilize GPOPSvII for their own work. The associated Python code can be installed via PyPI using the command: pip install geopops. For those interested in MATLAB, the code can be installed using: pip install geopops-matlab. The Python implementation of GPOPSvII is built on CasADi, a C++/Python algorithmic differentiation package, while the MATLAB version relies on GPOPSvII. Both implementations support a wide range of problems, including Mayer and Bolza formulations, pure and mixed continuous and discrete controls, pure and discrete states, pure and mixed path constraints, and both linear and nonlinear dynamics. Furthermore, the implementation supports various collocation schemes, including Gauss-Lobatto, Gauss-Radau, and both uniform and non-uniform Hermite-Simpson. A bicritical rational map $f:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ of degree $d\ge 2$ possesses exactly two critical points, denoted $\infty$ and $\beta$, each with local multiplicity one. The dynamics of such maps near the critical point $\beta$ are characterized by the existence of a local Fatou coordinate $\phi:\Delta\to\Delta$ satisfying $\phi\circ f\circ\phi = e^{2\pi i / \alpha}\phi$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\}$. This coordinate conjugates $f$ to the map $z\mapsto e^{2\pi i / \alpha}z$ within a neighborhood of $\beta$. We demonstrate that the Fatou coordinate $\phi$ is unique up to post-composition with a rotation, and the exceptional cluster $\mathcal{C}_\beta$ associated with $f$ is uniquely determined. Furthermore, we establish that the Fatou coordinate $\phi$ is unique if and only if $\alpha$ is an integer. The proof relies on a novel extension of the Riemann-Hurwitz formula, which computes the orbifold Euler characteristic of the Riemann sphere modulo $f$ for any bicritical rational map. This formula facilitates the calculation of the orbifold Euler characteristic for the local Fatou coordinate's domain, thereby yielding a formula for the number of preimages of $\beta$ under $f$. Additionally, we provide an explicit construction of the local Fatou coordinate for every bicritical rational map. Finally, we examine the stability of the exceptional cluster $\mathcal{C}_\beta$ under small perturbations of $f$. We show that the cluster is stable if and only if $\alpha$ is an integer, and we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the stability of the cluster when $\alpha$ is not an integer. These findings are derived from a general theorem concerning the stability of exceptional clusters in holomorphic germs possessing a Fatou coordinate. Our proof of this theorem utilizes the concept of the "modulus" of a family of annuli. Specifically, we demonstrate that the modulus of a family of annuli surrounding the exceptional cluster $\mathcal{C}_\beta$ is infinite if and only if $\alpha$ is an integer. This result is achieved by explicitly constructing a conformal map from the annular family to a family of annuli

Molybdenum and tungense dichalcogenides (MDMs) are emerging as viable two-dimensional (2D) alternatives to graphene in electron transport applications. However, their suitability for such devices hinges on their work functions, which are not fixed but vary with layer thickness. This study employs density functional theory (DPT) and the GW approximation to analyze how the work function of MDGs changes with the number of layers. Our findings indicate that the $d$-electron configuration of central atoms dictates this behavior: MDGs with a $d^0$ configuration exhibit a decreasing work function as thickness diminishes, whereas those with a $d^1$ configuration show an increasing trend. Additionally, we calculated the ionization potentials and electron affinities of MDGs to assess their electronic stability. We observed that ionization potentials for both $d^0$ and $d^1$ MDMs are significantly higher than electron affinities, suggesting that 2D MDMs are more prone to electron loss than to hole creation. Finally, we determined that the band gap of MDGs remains independent of the specific GW method used, provided the self-energy is derived from the Weyl approximation. These results offer valuable insights for the design and fabrication of MDG-based electronic components. Furthermore, the methodology utilized is broadly applicable to investigating the thickness-dependent properties of other MDGs and two-dimensional materials. This paper investigates uniform stationary phase approximation for phase functions that are merely $C^2$ in the uniform sense, yet potentially less smooth elsewhere. Specifically, we examine the phase $\psi(x,t) = tx^\alpha \sin(tx^\beta)$ where $\beta > \alpha > 0$, demonstrating that the order of approximation for this function is $t^{-1/2-\beta/2}$, which is less than $t^{-1/2+\alpha/2}$. This finding contrasts with the result established by R. Melrose and J. Sjöstrand in their 1987 study. Furthermore, we apply this finding to derive a sharp stationary phase approximation for the integral $\int_0^1 e^{itx^\alpha \sin(tx^\beta)} dx$. Additionally, we extend our findings to a broader class of functions characterized by a finite number of "jumps" in their smoothness. These findings differ from those of A. Erd\'elyi, who, in his 1939 work, derived an asymptotic expansion for $\int_0^\infty e^{ix^{\alpha}\sin(tx^\beta)} dx$ under the condition $\beta > \alpha > 1$. Erd\'elyi demonstrated that the expansion's order is $t^{-1/\beta}$, which is superior to the $t^{-1/2+\alpha/2}$ order we obtain for the related function $\psi(x,t) = tx^\alpha \sin(tx^\beta)$. We also provide an asymptotic expansion for $\int_0^1 e^{itx^\alpha \sin(tx^\beta)} dx$ when $\beta > \alpha > 1$, noting that this result aligns with Erd\'elyi's. Finally, we offer a concise proof of a theorem by S. Z. Ditzian and B. M. Levitan from 1975, which asserts that $\int_0^1 x^\alpha \sin(tx^\beta) dx = O(t^{-1/\beta})$ provided $\beta > \alpha > 0$. This conclusion is sharper than the $t^{-1/2+\alpha/2}$ order derived from our findings. Our approach to proving Ditzian and Levitan's result relies on a technique involving a specific contour in the complex plane. We also present an alternative proof of this result that avoids the use of complex numbers. In this alternative proof, the order becomes $t^{-1/\beta+\epsilon}$

This study introduces an adaptive multigrid method designed to efficiently calculate steady-state solutions for the Boltzmann equation in rarefied gas flows. The approach employs an adaptive strategy to accelerate the convergence of the Boltzmann operator and integrates a multigrid technique to rapidly converge the resulting linear system. Validated against the normal shock wave problem, the method demonstrates that achieving steady-state solutions within dozens of iterations is feasible. Furthermore, the proposed approach is applied to a more complex scenario: a rectangular channel featuring a single row of micro-pillars subjected to a pressure gradient. The results indicate that the adaptive multigrid method achieves the same level of accuracy in approximately 50 iterations as a conventional iterative method requires for 100 iterations. Finally, the computational efficiency of this proposed approach is benchmarked against a recent parallel domain-decomposition method. The findings suggest that the adaptive multigrid method offers superior computational performance, particularly when simulating complex flow configurations. Additionally, the method exhibits robust convergence, with the number of multigrid iterations required remaining independent of the initial guess or the grid resolution. These results underscore the method's potential for efficiently computing steady-state solutions across a broad spectrum of rarefied gas flow problems. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYuan1997/Adaptive-Multigrid. Keywords: Rarefied gas, Boltzmann equation, Multigrid, Domain decomposition.

The Horizon-10T experiment is designed to detect the axion-gamma conversion phenomenon, aiming to identify electromagnetic (EM) bursts generated by galactic and extragalactic axion dark matter nuggets. To identify the precise source of these EM bursts, we introduce a novel multi-modal clustering algorithm that integrates both time and frequency data. This method is anticipated to significantly enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of detected signals. Furthermore, the study examines the feasibility of this technique for observing EM bursts originating from axion nuggets. We also present initial findings regarding EM bursts from both galactic and extragalactic sources, demonstrating that the multi-modal clustering approach can effectively distinguish between these two categories of bursts. Ultimately, this research establishes a foundation for future EM burst source localization. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Multi-Modal-Clustering.

The CMS Collaboration reports a measurement of the production and decay of a Higgs-like boson with a mass of 125 GeV, utilizing a dataset of 5.02 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC in 2016. This analysis focuses on the exclusive channel where the boson decays into two photons. The study employs an event selection strategy requiring two photons with transverse momenta exceeding 25 GeV, an invariant mass within 120 to 130 GeV, and at least one photon possessing high pseudorapidity. The analysis is conducted across three distinct photon production categories: gluon-gluon fusion, vector boson fusion, and associated production with a W or Z boson. For each category, the observed signal significance is determined to be 4.1$\pm$0.3, 2.6$\pm$0.2, and 3.5$\pm$0.2 standard deviations, respectively. The results are compared against theoretical predictions for both the Standard Model and beyond-Standard-Model scenarios. Furthermore, a model-independent interpretation is provided, establishing lower limits on the signal strength relative to the Standard Model. Finally, the findings are integrated with prior CMS measurements from the same dataset and from 2012 and 2013 data, which were collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. This combined analysis yields a signal significance of 6.2$\pm$0.4 standard deviations, with a signal strength of 1.04$\pm$0.11 times the Standard Model expectation. Additionally, the study presents a measurement of the Higgs-like boson's mass, finding it to be 125.09$\pm$0.21 GeV. These results are consistent with the Standard Model Higgs boson predictions. The analysis also includes a study of the differential cross section as a function of the photon pair's transverse momentum. Furthermore, the study examines the differential cross section with respect to the transverse momentum of the Higgs-like boson, considering both the associated production with a W or Z boson and gluon-gluon fusion processes.

Using the theory of Siegel modular forms, we establish an infinite family of prime numbers $p$ for which the Fourier coefficients of any Siegel modular form with trivial Nebentypus are divisible by $p$ in a specific sense. Our approach relies on the existence of certain $p$-adic Lie group elements that act on these forms. The analysis is restricted to primes $p \geq 7$. We further demonstrate that the theorem holds for primes $p=5$ under an additional hypothesis and provide an example showing it fails for $p=2$. The findings are applied to Siegel modular forms of weight $k$ and level 1, yielding the following results: (i) For $k \geq 7$, the Fourier coefficients are divisible by 5 and 11; (ii) For $k \geq 10$, they are divisible by 7; (iii) For $k \geq 13$, they are divisible by 2, 3, and 17; and (iv) For $k \geq 17$, they are divisible by 3 and 5. Additionally, we offer an alternative proof of a result by Bringmann and Ono, which asserts that the Fourier coefficients of a Siegel modular form of weight $k$ and level 1 are divisible by a prime $p \geq k+3$. Finally, we present an infinite family of prime numbers $p$ such that the Fourier coefficients of a Siegel modular form of level $p$ are divisible by $p$. Furthermore, we show that the level of such a form must be at least $p+1$. These findings have implications for the level and weight of Siegel modular forms. The proofs utilize the existence of specific $p$-adic Lie group elements within the symplectic group. The paper also includes an appendix by the second author, which outlines the necessary background on Siegel modular forms and provides a detailed construction of the $p$-adic Lie group elements used throughout the study. This appendix is available as a separate publication. The precise sequence of the rigid fibrations of a surface with boundary is defined as the rigid fibration possessing the minimal possible number of components. This note establishes a criterion for determining when the precise sequence of a surface is rigid, deriving conditions based on the surface's Euler characteristic and boundary count. Furthermore, we present a general algorithm to construct the precise sequence for any orientable surface with a boundary and analyze the computational complexity of this construction. Finally, we offer illustrative examples of the rigid fibrations found on certain cosmological spacetimes. These examples demonstrate that the rigid fibrations of a specific space-like surface are not necessarily connected, and that the process of achieving the minimal number of components in the rigid fibration of such a space can be arbitrarily complex. Additionally, we examine the computational complexity associated with constructing the precise sequence for an orientable surface with boundary.

This paper presents a survey of the zeroing neural network (ZNN) approach, which addresses time-varying matrix problems through predictive calculations. Designed to serve as an introductory survey for researchers entering the field of neural computation, the work begins by defining the ZNN model and outlining its theoretical foundations. Subsequently, it details the algorithm for solving time-varying matrix problems using ZNN. The core of the paper focuses on applications, demonstrating how ZNN can address various predictive computation challenges by providing a unified algorithmic framework. These methods are shown to be effective for problems involving time-varying matrices, including matrix inversion, pseudoinversion, rank, and singular value problems. The discussion further extends to higher-order ZNN models, offering solutions for time-variant matrix inversion and singular value problems. Finally, the paper examines the solution of time-variant nonlinear matrix problems using ZNN, covering matrix power, square root, and matrix logarithm problems. The study concludes with an analysis of the ZNN algorithm's computational complexity. Throughout, the authors emphasize the predictive nature of ZNN solutions, their capacity to handle time-variant problems, and the model's unifying role in addressing a broad spectrum of matrix-related challenges. Additionally, the role of higher-order ZNN models in enhancing convergence performance is highlighted. The authors hope this survey inspires further research into ZNN models and neural computation. This paper introduces a new image classification approach utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with on-off center-surround (OOCSS) filters. The filters are organized into a bank that produces a feature map for each member, which are then fed into a fully connected CNN. The on-off terminology refers to the surrounding area of the filter's receptive field, while the center-surround distinction lies in the area of interest (AOI) immediately surrounding the center. The OOCSS filter is engineered to detect edges and corners with high precision and robustness, even under noise, geometric distortions, and illumination changes. We demonstrate the superior performance of this method on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. The results indicate that OOCSS filters serve as an effective feature extractor for deep learning classification tasks. Furthermore, the filters exhibit exceptional performance in identifying geometric distortions and illumination variations, surpassing other state-of-the-art techniques. This enhanced feature extraction capability is attributed to the filters' ability to maintain consistent AOI responses despite such transformations. Finally, we explore the application of OOCSS filters to medical imaging, specifically for classifying brain tumors in MRI scans. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the BraTS 2018 dataset. Our findings suggest that OOCSS filters are promising for medical image classification, potentially reducing the computational cost of deep learning architectures. Additionally, the strong feature extraction properties of OOCSS filters may contribute to more accurate diagnoses in medical imaging contexts. X-ray optics are currently being explored for advanced applications, including X-ray astronomy and microscopy. However, their use in these fields is often hindered by limited coverage and poor image quality. This review examines recent methods designed to broaden the coverage of both nested and open optics while simultaneously optimizing image contrast and resolution. These approaches involve modifying the traditional paraboloidal or ellipsoidal contours of mirrors to create new freeform shapes. Specifically, we will discuss the principles behind these techniques, their recent achievements, and the challenges they face. Our analysis indicates that these methods are highly effective at improving the performance of two-bounce telescopes, but they are less so for multi-bounce systems. Furthermore, we identify that the primary obstacle to their successful implementation is the requirement for freeform optics, which are difficult to fabricate and characterize. Finally, we outline the future prospects for these methods, emphasizing the need for new manufacturing and metrology techniques to bring these concepts to fruition. This work investigates the electronic structure of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) within a perpendicular magnetic field. By employing a continuum model for the system's Hamiltonian, we derive its analytical solution using magnetic Bloch states. Our findings indicate that at MATBG under a $2\pi$ flux, the system exhibits electronic band gaps at zero wavevector but displays complete band crossings throughout the Brillouin zone. Furthermore, we predict the existence of flat bands within these crossing regions, a phenomenon that persists across various twist angles and magnetic field strengths. These outcomes offer a comprehensive framework for interpreting recent experimental observations, including scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) data revealing incommensurate charge density waves and magnetotransport experiments detecting flat bands at finite momenta. Although steganography has been extensively researched for decades, particularly within the signal processing community, its application to natural language remains underexplored. This paper introduces a Stele\textit{LM}, a Steganographic Language Model built upon Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. We demonstrate that Stele\textit{LM} can successfully embed secret messages into text sequences. Furthermore, we show that the model can generate multiple distinct messages from the identical output when guided by different hidden inputs. Our experimental results indicate that Stele\textit{LM} achieves superior performance compared to prior methods in both embedding and extracting messages. Additionally, we find that the model's message capacity scales linearly with the input sequence length. Finally, we illustrate that Stele\textit{LM} can operate effectively with significantly fewer parameters than other Stele\textit{LM} variants or existing message-embedding approaches. Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge in power system operations that involves determining the optimal generation schedule for power plants over a specified horizon while minimizing costs. However, the high dimensionality of UC problems makes them difficult to solve quickly, especially when numerous scenarios must be evaluated. To address this, we introduce a learning-based cost model designed to rapidly estimate total system costs. This model is trained using data generated by the conventional UC model, enabling swift cost predictions for new scenarios. We then integrate this learned cost model into the UC formulation to replace the original, computationally expensive cost calculation functions. By substituting exact cost evaluation with learned approximations, we significantly reduce computational time. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach reduces the time required to evaluate UC costs by a factor of 100 to 1,000 compared to the conventional method. Furthermore, we show that this learned cost model can be effectively utilized to accelerate the evaluation of multiple UC scenarios. Specifically, we apply it to speed up scenario generation for stochastic UC and risk-constrained UC, achieving speedups of 2 to 3 times and 1.5 to 2 times, respectively. Additionally, the proposed model supports real-time scenario generation, a capability that the traditional cost model lacks. Finally, we demonstrate that scenarios generated using this fast cost model can be employed to enhance the solutions of the original UC problems. Overall, our method offers a promising solution for accelerating the evaluation of multiple UC scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/LearningCostModel. We report on the pressure-induced dimerization and the suppression of antiferromagnetism in the Kitaev material $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, as observed through neutron powder diffraction. At ambient pressure, the compound exhibits a long-range antiferromagnetic order below 25 K, characterized by a propagation vector of $(1/2,0,1/2)$ and a moment size of 0.35 $\mu_B$. Increasing hydrostatic pressure causes the unit cell to shrink without altering its symmetry until 1.5 GPa. Beyond this threshold, the unit cell volume doubles, indicating dimerization of the Li atoms, and the antiferromagnetic order is suppressed. The pressure-induced unit cell expansion is attributed to the breaking of the Li dimers. This study demonstrates that the long-range antiferromagnetic order in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ is fragile and can be suppressed by the displacement of Li atoms from their lattice sites. Furthermore, the persistence of the $(1/2,0,1/2)$ propagation vector during the dimerization process suggests that the magnetic structure is driven by the Kitaev interaction. These findings highlight the sensitivity of both the magnetic and electronic structures in Kitaev compounds to lattice distortions. Additionally, the observed dimerization in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ offers a potential explanation for the anomalous behavior previously reported in single crystals. Finally, the results indicate that the pressure required to induce dimerization in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ is comparable to that needed to drive the Mott transition in other Kitaev compounds. This underscores the critical role of lattice distortions in Kitaev materials, which can be manipulated via chemical substitution or external pressure. Ultimately, these findings provide a pathway to engineer the Kitaev interaction in these materials. The sample used in this study was generously provided by Prof. J. Ye. Synthetic control methods are widely used to create counterfactuals for treated units by combining multiple control units, yet their theoretical underpinnings remain largely descriptive. This paper presents a new, broader theory that unifies synthetic controls with other causal estimators, offering practical guidelines for both estimation and inference. Our approach integrates two key elements: a "synthetic" component that ensures the estimator remains consistent with observed data, and a "causal" component that defines the specific causal question being addressed. We demonstrate that our proposed estimator converges to the causal parameter of interest as the distance metric between the treated and pooled units increases. Furthermore, our theory facilitates inference by establishing the rate at which the estimator achieves the causal parameter, a capability that encompasses and extends previous findings. These insights are particularly valuable in high-dimensional settings, such as those encountered in many synthetic control applications. Additionally, we provide an implementation of our estimator and prove its finite sample performance through simulations. Finally, we apply this estimator to two empirical cases: the impact of the 1966 Elementary and Secondary Education Act on US school districts and the effects of the 2008 financial crisis on US states. In both instances, our estimator yields more reliable inferences than other methods. The Python code for this estimator is accessible at https://github.com/SeonghoLee1992/SyntheticControl. This paper introduces a privacy-preserving algorithm based on Gromov-Hausdorff distance to calculate the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy between two metric spaces. By integrating the Bregman-Max divergence, we develop a local differential privacy (LDP) framework that ensures privacy during both the empirical discrepancy computation and the corresponding hypothesis testing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed LDP GW test through simulations involving two-dimensional Gaussian distributions. Our method achieves a 30% reduction in variance compared to existing LDP-based tests for standard Euclidean distance, while maintaining the same significance level. Furthermore, we show that increasing the number of samples in the GW test results in a corresponding rise in the sample size required for the LDP hypothesis test. Finally, we apply our proposed LDP GW test to a real-world scenario: detecting communities in a distributed graph. In this application, we successfully identify two distinct communities within a social network using LDP-based graph data. The results indicate that our approach can achieve a 50% reduction in sample size for the LDP hypothesis test relative to other LDP methods. Additionally, we observe that the Gromov-Wasserstein distance is more sensitive to graph edge labels than the Euclidean distance between node features. A gas jet, pressurized to 100 Torr and extending 10 cm in length, is driven by a linearly polarized laser pulse with an energy of 100 J and a pulse duration of 100 fs. This process generates a plasma channel characterized by a density of $n_e/n_c=0.15$ and a radius of 1.5 mm. The channel's guiding properties are enhanced through the application of a second laser pulse, which induces self-steepening and self-focusing effects. When this second pulse, possessing 100 fs duration and variable polarization, strikes the front of the channel at a 30-degree angle, it creates a vacuum bubble that injects electrons from the jet into a laser wakefield. These injected electrons are subsequently accelerated to energies exceeding 1 GeV. The polarization of the second pulse is critical; it must be either linear or circular, whereas elliptical polarization fails to produce electron injection. Furthermore, the electron beam exhibits a high charge of 100 nC and a low emittance of 0.01 mm mrad. This research demonstrates that this injection and acceleration method is highly effective for generating intense, bright electron beams. Additionally, the study confirms that laser-plasma acceleration can achieve this using laser energies as low as 100 J, a level readily available in current laser laboratories. The renormalization of the flavor-singlet axial-vector current is examined within QCD using dimensional regularization. The analysis reveals that the renormalization constant linking the bare current to the fully renormalized one depends on the dimensional continuation parameter and exhibits a non-trivial scaling behavior with respect to the renormalization scale. Consequently, the renormalized current acquires an explicit dependence on the renormalization scale, a feature absent in other renormalization schemes. Furthermore, the evolution equation governing the renormalized flavor-singlet axial-vector charge is derived. This equation mirrors the evolution of the renormalized strong coupling, thereby confirming the non-trivial scaling of the strong coupling in dimensional regularization. As a result, the evolution of the axial-vector charge is determined by the evolution of the strong coupling, which is known to be independent of the dimensional continuation parameter. This evolution is subsequently applied to the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme. Finally, the connection between the renormalized axial-vector charge and the QCD anomaly is established. It is demonstrated that, unlike the bare charge, the renormalized charge does not vanish in the chiral limit; instead, it equals the sum of the bare charge and a finite, renormalization scheme-dependent term that scales with the renormalized strong coupling. This relationship ensures the consistency between the renormalized axial-vector charge and the QCD anomaly. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme. In this scheme, the renormalized flavor-singlet axial-vector charge is shown to be independent of the fictitious dimensional continuation parameter, a crucial point for the precise determination of the strong coupling's running. Specifically, the evolution of the renormalized flavor-singlet axial-vector charge in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme is derived up to the four-loop order. This result is essential for the next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (NNNLO) analysis of the strong coupling's running, which is currently being conducted. The four-loop order evolution equation is also utilized to analyze the QCD anomaly in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme. The findings indicate that the renormalized flavor-singlet axial-vector charge in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme adheres to the standard form, where it vanishes in the chiral limit. This outcome is consistent with the established understanding of the QCD anomaly. The results are also compared

This paper introduces a deep tinting method designed to align the color tones of surveillance footage from different cameras. Unlike prior approaches that depend on manual annotations or color bars, our technique leverages the inherent color relationships between cameras to determine the necessary tone adjustments. We frame this as a constrained optimization problem, where the known color relationships serve as equality constraints and the minimization of camera-specific image variance acts as the objective function. To address this, we developed a novel deep tinting network capable of iteratively solving for the optimal color transformations. We evaluated the method's efficacy using a synthetic dataset of multi-camera surveillance images and compared its performance against existing techniques. The results demonstrate that our approach effectively and efficiently solves the cross-camera color tone discrepancy, achieving superior outcomes compared to previous methods. Furthermore, we utilized this solution to enhance multi-camera surveillance imagery, successfully improving the performance of downstream computer vision tasks. This study examines the generalized three-dimensional Hamiltonian Ermakov system, extending previous work by examining its full Lie point symmetry algebra and associated Hamiltonian integrals. By applying the time-dependent Hamiltonian Noether theorem, the system's conservation laws are derived. The research demonstrates that this generalized system exhibits maximal symmetry, as its Lie point symmetry algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of all real $3\times 3$ matrices. Furthermore, the number of independent Hamiltonian preservation laws equals eight, matching the system's order. These findings generalize previous results specific to the three-dimensional harmonic oscillator and are applicable to arbitrary dimensions. The analysis reveals that the dimension of the symmetry algebra remains constant across all dimensions, while the number of preservation laws scales linearly with them. Additionally, the study establishes that the $n$-dimensional generalized system possesses maximal symmetry for any dimension $n$. The symmetry algebra for the $n$-dimensional case is isomorphic to the algebra of all real $n\times n$ matrices, and the count of independent preservation laws is determined to be $n(n+1)/2$. This count is shown to correspond to the number of second-order differential equations required to fully describe the system's dynamics. The results are supported by explicit calculations for the two- and four-dimensional systems. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the potential extension of these findings to the generalized $n$-dimensional Hamiltonian system. The symmetry structure and preservation laws for this generalized $n$-dimensional case are derived, with the number of second-order differential equations governing the dynamics identified as $n(n+1)/2$. The associated Lie point symmetry algebra is identified as the algebra of all real $n\times n$ matrices. The conclusion suggests that the symmetry algebra of the generalized $n$-dimensional Hamiltonian system may also be the algebra of all real $n\times n$ matrices. This hypothesis is substantiated by explicit calculations for the two- and four-dimensional cases. The authors anticipate that these findings will facilitate the extension of the results to the generalized $n$-dimensional Hamiltonian system. Additionally, the paper includes an appendix detailing the derivation of the symmetry generators for the $n$-dimensional system. The appendix confirms that the symmetry algebra of the generalized $n$-dimensional Hamiltonian system is indeed the algebra of all real $n\times n$ matrices. The authors anticipate that these findings will enable the extension of the results to the generalized $n$-dimensional Hamiltonian

A transit system's feed specification outlines the schedules, routes, and vehicle capacities of all constituent operators. While these documents are vital for analyzing system performance, they are difficult to interpret and yield no direct insights into how the system functions. Consequently, researchers have developed various metrics to quantify feed-specific attributes. However, because these metrics rely on specific assumptions, they can only indicate a feed's general characteristics rather than its precise parameters. This limitation stems from the fact that the underlying true parameters are unobtainable; multiple combinations of parameters can satisfy a given feed specification. This paper formalizes that concept and introduces a machine learning method to estimate these unobtainable parameters. By modeling the feed specification as a function of the hidden parameters, we trained a recurrent neural network to infer them. We validated this approach using vehicle-miles-of-service data from New York City's subway system. The results demonstrate that our model can accurately infer the unobtainable parameters and identify the underlying design principles of the feed specification. Ultimately, this model offers a promising avenue for future research into feed specifications. For instance, it can be utilized to evaluate the effectiveness of potential policy changes and to guide the design of new feed specifications. Furthermore, the model can be extended to analyze other aspects of a transit system, such as vehicle fleets and schedules. We have made the model publicly available to facilitate these and other applications. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/ashwinbhat/UnobtainableParameters. Few-shot learning aims to classify novel categories based on a very limited number of examples. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective framework that leverages class-level prototypes to achieve this goal. Our method relies on two core components: a feature extractor and a classifier. To create these components, we first train a class-level prototype network using a few-shot dataset. Subsequently, the prototypes are extracted from this network to define the classifier, while the feature extractor is retained. During inference, a new category is classified by calculating the distance between its features and the prototypes of existing categories. The advantage of this approach is that it establishes prototypes before encountering new categories, thereby eliminating the need for additional fine-tuning. Experimental results on the CIFAR100 and Mini-ImageNet datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our design, and a comprehensive analysis reveals the strengths and limitations of the proposed method. The code and models are available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Class-Prototypes. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.09500. Additionally, we show that these operators generate a non-local current whose two-point function remains finite at zero separation. This paper establishes a broad extension of the geometric foundation theorem regarding spherical subgroups within the B-type Coxeter groups $GL(n,R)$ and $O(n,R)$. Furthermore, this theorem facilitates the computation of the Euler-Poincaré characteristic for arbitrary spherical subgroups in $O(n,R)$. Specifically, the Euler-Poincaré characteristic of $GL(n,R)$ is determined as $n+1$, whereas for any spherical subgroup $H$ of $O(n,R)$, it is given by $\chi(H)=\frac{n}{2}+1$. Additionally, the theorem enables the calculation of the Poincaré polynomials and Hilbert-Poincaré series for spherical subgroups $H$ in $O(3,R)$ and $O(4,R)$. The necessary background and tools for these computations are provided in the accompanying section. The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SKU) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP) are two interrelated combinatorial optimization challenges. In both scenarios, the objective is to identify a subset of items with a total cost not exceeding a specified budget, such that the union of their associated elements maximizes a given profit function. This paper introduces two novel local search algorithms designed to address these problems. The first approach utilizes a standard swap-based strategy, while the second employs a more sophisticated technique grounded in set cover theory. We evaluate the performance of these new methods against existing state-of-the-art solutions using a comprehensive dataset of real-world instances. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed algorithms surpass current benchmarks, achieving superior solution quality within significantly reduced computational times. Furthermore, extensive experiments conducted on these instances enable a direct comparison between the two proposed algorithms, revealing that the swap-based local search consistently outperforms the method derived from set cover theory. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/fernando-ramos/SKU.

This study introduces a new approach to predicting customer churn for online gambling platforms. Churn prediction is a critical challenge for gambling operators, as retaining existing customers is generally more cost-effective than acquiring new ones. The proposed solution is a rule-based system that integrates various machine learning models, including decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting machines, and neural networks. The study's primary objective is to forecast whether a customer will remain active or stop playing within the next three months. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses both individual model performance and the accuracy of existing solutions found in current literature. Furthermore, the paper outlines several potential future enhancements, such as expanding the feature set, refining the prediction horizon, and implementing change prediction. These improvements would enable operators to proactively engage with at-risk customers before they churn, rather than reacting after the fact. The Ising model in two dimensions subjected to a magnetic field exhibits two distinct phases: a ferromagnetic phase and the Yang-Lee phase. This paper demonstrates that the critical exponents of the Yang-Lee phase are identical to those of the Ising model at zero magnetic field, thereby confirming that the Yang-Lee critical point marks the transition into this unique phase. Furthermore, the critical behavior near the Yang-Lee point is also equivalent to that of the three-dimensional $O(2)$ model. The study employs two methodologies: first, a numerical analysis of the Ising model on a $10\times10$ lattice using the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMG) to determine the Yang-Lee singularity; second, a derivation of the Yang-Lee Hamiltonian via the continuum limit of the lattice model, followed by the derivation of its critical exponents using the $\epsilon$-expansion. Both approaches yield consistent results. Finally, the critical exponents are compared against those of the Ising model and the $O(2)$ model in three dimensions. The research concludes that the Yang-Lee phase transition is of first order, with the Yang-Lee critical point situated precisely at the endpoint of this line. The Ising phase terminates at a critical point where the specific heat diverges, while the Yang-Lee phase displays a cusp in the specific heat. Additionally, the susceptibility diverges at the Yang-Lee point, and the correlation length diverges as the Yang-Lee singularity is approached. The correlation length exponent was calculated to be $\nu=0.632\pm0.005$. Finally, the critical amplitude of the specific heat was determined to be $C=0.49\pm0.02$. These findings align with the critical exponents of the three-dimensional $O(2)$ model. The study also examines the specific heat and susceptibility near the Yang-Lee point, noting that the specific heat remains finite, whereas the susceptibility diverges. The susceptibility exponent was found to be $\gamma=1.25\pm0.02$. The correlation length exponent is $\nu=0.632\pm0.005$, and the critical amplitude of the susceptibility is $\chi=1.2\pm0.1$. The critical exponents of the Yang-Lee point are thus identical to those of the Ising model and the $O(2)$ model in three dimensions. The Yang-Lee phase transition
