Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a powerful method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, recent research indicates that PINNs often suffer from spectral bias, meaning they struggle to capture high-frequency modes, which hinders their ability to learn complex functions. This study investigates the impact of spectral bias on PINNs and demonstrates that incorporating momentum into these networks can mitigate this issue. Our approach involves adding a momentum term to the first-order gradient descent update rule, creating a second-order optimization method. We validate the efficacy of this strategy through numerical experiments on both standard PDEs and real-world data-driven applications. Our findings indicate that networks utilizing momentum achieve faster convergence and produce more accurate results compared to those relying on standard first-order gradient descent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this momentum-based strategy enhances the performance of PINNs. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/Momentum-PINNs.

Although deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents excel at solving complex tasks, they function as black boxes, making their decision-making processes opaque and their behavior difficult to interpret. This paper introduces a novel hierarchical RL framework designed to enhance the interpretability of data-driven agents by integrating symbolic knowledge. We employ inductive logic programming (ILP) to derive task-relevant rules from historical data, which are then embedded into the agent's cognitive architecture. These learned rules serve as a prior for the high-level policy, while low-level policies are responsible for their execution. Our method demonstrates superior performance in terms of sample efficiency and total reward across three environments: a grid world, a car racing simulation, and a protein folding task. Furthermore, we show that our approach can adapt to novel tasks by leveraging the high-level policy's ability to generalize from prior experiences. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/ILP-HRL. A video demonstration of our method applied to protein folding can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1222222222. Asymmetry is a defining characteristic of many natural systems, often arising from the non-linear interactions between their components. In this study, we demonstrate that as a quantum non-linear effect, these interactions can be engineered, leading to a significant reduction in the squeezing of a specific quadrature component of a quantum field. This phenomenon, known as quantum squeezing-induced (QS-I) optical asymmetry, is observed in the output of a single-mode driven Duffing cavity under conditions of strong quantum squeezing. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of this asymmetry, supported by numerical results that illustrate its dependence on driving strength, squeezing level, and measurement precision. Furthermore, we show that QS-I induced optical asymmetry can be utilized to generate a robust, non-thermal asymmetric quantum state, thereby offering a novel method for quantum state preparation. Additionally, we highlight that this asymmetry can be effectively employed to enhance the performance of quantum sensors based on a single-mode driven Duffing cavity. Our findings suggest that QS-I induced optical asymmetry holds potential for diverse applications within quantum information science. Finally, we note that the QS-I phenomenon can be readily observed in current experimental setups. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into the quantum properties of nonlinear optics. To facilitate experimental verification, we have made our code available at \href{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/QS-I-induced-optical-asymmetry}{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/QS-I-induced-optical-asymmetry}. The source code for all figures can be found at \href{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/QS-I-induced-optical-asymmetry/tree/master/source_code}{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/QS-I-induced-optical-asymmetry/tree/master/source_code}. We introduce a direct, tabletop experiment designed to detect spin-dependent interactions with a proposed dark matter candidate known as "shadow matter." This substance, which may constitute a significant portion of dark matter, consists of fermions that interact with ordinary matter solely through spin-dependent forces. We demonstrate that our setup utilizes a $\sim$100 $\mu$g $\text{Li}^6$ target, leveraging its unique nuclear spin structure to achieve exceptional sensitivity to spin-dependent interactions. Furthermore, we show that a single year of data collection would surpass existing constraints, specifically improving limits on interactions with a dark matter candidate with mass $\lesssim 10$ GeV/$c^2$ by several orders of magnitude. The experiment is scheduled to commence operations in the coming months at the University of Geneva. We anticipate that the full setup will become operational by the end of 2022. The shadow matter hypothesis offers a promising avenue for direct detection experiments, as it circumvents the stringent limits placed on dark matter-nucleon cross sections derived from null results in traditional direct searches. Theoretical frameworks supporting this include the QCD axion model, which predicts a dark sector containing a fermionic axion partner; the Kaluza-Klein model, which features a fermionic zero mode; and the dark QED model, which posits a dark matter fermion interacting via a dark photon. Additionally, the shadow matter framework is compatible with the null results from the XENON1T experiment, which observed an excess in the electron recoil energy spectrum. This excess could be interpreted as evidence for dark matter interactions with electrons within the shadow matter framework. We demonstrate that a direct search for the shadow matter-electron coupling using $\text{Li}^6$ can constrain the parameter space of the dark QED model and the Kaluza-Klein model, as well as explain the XENON1T results. This paper serves as a proposal for the LISEKI detector, a direct dark matter search experiment based on the shadow matter hypothesis, which will be realized using $\text{Li}^6$ and will commence operations in 2023. Blind image restoration (BUR) is an inverse problem that seeks to recover original images from blurred observations without knowledge of the blur kernel. This study introduces a novel kernel mixture model designed to simultaneously estimate the blur kernel and reconstruct the original image. The proposed method is grounded in a nonparametric Bayesian framework, utilizing a Dirichlet process (DP) to define a nonparametric prior for an infinite kernel model. By applying a mean-field variational inference approach, the algorithm achieves efficient and rapid estimation of both the blur kernel and the latent image. Experimental results demonstrate that the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM). Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits robust performance across a diverse range of blur kernels. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/KernelMixture. Keywords: Blind image restoration, blur kernel estimation, kernel mixture model, Dirichlet process.

Nonuniform algebras serve as a generalization of associative algebras, designed to facilitate the study of discrete integrable systems. This paper investigates bialgebra structures on discrete integrable systems derived from nonuniform associative algebras, with a specific focus on the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. We present multiple examples of systems satisfying this equation, including the discrete Hirota three-wave interaction model, the discrete Toda lattice, and the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. Subsequently, we derive nonuniform analogues of the associative and R-matrix properties, which allow for the construction of solutions to the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. Finally, we establish the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation, a concept that extends the classical associative Yang-Baxter equation, and explore its relationship with the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. Additionally, we provide examples of solutions to the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation generated by the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation. This work represents a preliminary step toward developing a nonuniform version of the Drinfel'd-Sklyanin theory. This paper introduces natural Hoare logic, a new formalism designed for verifying the correctness of imperative programs specified in natural language. Our approach builds upon existing formalisms that bridge natural language and first-order logic with equality, utilizing syntactic validation to ensure type and usage correctness within the logical form. We demonstrate the proposed method through examples and provide a detailed illustration of the validation process. Furthermore, we extend natural language Hoare logic to accommodate data structures and their invariants, thereby enabling the verification of more complex imperative programs. The examples utilized in this study were gathered from various sources, including online forums, textbooks, and programming contests. These findings suggest that this methodology is particularly well-suited for educational contexts, such as teaching programming and logic. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. Given the foundational nature of this work, we have developed a prototype implementation available at https://github.com/fernando-garcia-garcia/Natural-Hoare-Logic. This tool allows users to input natural language specifications and programs, receiving either a formal validation or an informal explanation of errors. We believe this prototype will serve as a valuable foundation for further research into the formal validation of programs derived from natural language specifications. The implementation can be accessed at https://www.garcia-f.com/verificar.html. Additionally, we have prepared a supplementary video to illustrate the tool's capabilities, available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. This video was created in collaboration with the author's brother, Fernando Garcia Garcia, who specializes in video production. We hope this resource will be beneficial for researchers and educators interested in applying natural language specifications to program verification and education. Finally, we invite readers to explore the potential of natural language specifications in software development and education, and we look forward to collaborating with others to advance this field. Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus protocol designed for resource-constrained IoT devices, featuring a streamlined design that reduces message and round complexity. However, its straightforward architecture makes it vulnerable to a broad spectrum of protocol failures. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus that maintains the original protocol's simplicity while significantly improving robustness against protocol failures. The proposed improvements encompass: (1) a novel timeout mechanism to handle network delays and slowness; (2) a new leader election protocol to address leader failures; (3) refined message processing logic to mitigate message loss; and (4) refined quorum-based decision-making to prevent decision conflicts. Experimental results demonstrate that RCanopus outperforms the original Canopus by up to 100% in terms of round efficiency. Furthermore, the RCanopus implementation is provided as open-source software. The source code and documentation can be accessed at https://github.com/raunakgupta12/Robust-Canopus. Additionally, the paper includes performance evaluations to assess the impact of various protocol failures on RCanopus. These empirical findings confirm that the proposed improvements effectively safeguard RCanopus against diverse protocol failures. The code is available at https://github.com/raunakgupta12/Robust-Canopus. The paper's title is RCanopus: Making Canopus Robust to Failures and Byzantine Faults. We introduce a straightforward, classical approach to quantify the bending stiffness of lipid bilayers by analyzing their undulation profiles in the absence of cholate. This method is validated through molecular dynamics simulations of both pure and cholesterol-containing bilayers, which also facilitate the calculation of cholesterol's area modulus. The technique is subsequently applied to experimental data involving both experimental and simulated cholate, successfully reproducing the observed trends in undulation profiles and membrane area modulus. Furthermore, our findings align with recent measurements of the compressibility modulus for cholesterol fractions of 0, 0.25, and 0.5. The study concludes by outlining the limitations of this methodology. Ultimately, we contend that the undulation technique represents a valuable tool for investigating the mechanical properties of lipid bilayers. Additionally, we demonstrate that the previously reported reduction in stiffness due to the presence of cholate can be accurately replicated in experiments. Finally, we emphasize the necessity for further research to clarify the specific mechanisms driving these observations. To facilitate this, we have made our simulation data and analysis scripts publicly accessible. The scripts are available at https://github.com/andrewjames/ModulusAnalysis, and the corresponding data can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7100000. This study examines the Hamiltonian formulation of the loop quantum astrophysical (LQA) model previously derived via the Fock path integral method applied to the Hamiltonian constraint. By utilizing the ADM Hamiltonian, we derive the quantum constraint and solve it to obtain the quantum Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that the resulting Hamiltonian aligns with the earlier derivation, thereby establishing a direct link between the path integral and Hamiltonian approaches. Furthermore, we analyze the physical spectrum of the Hamiltonian, revealing that its eigenvalues are entirely real and bounded from below, ensuring the model's consistency. Finally, we investigate the physical implications of this quantum Hamiltonian. Our analysis indicates that the model successfully addresses the Big Bang singularity problem, predicting a Big Bounce scenario where the universe contracts before expanding. Additionally, we show that the quantum effects of the ADM Hamiltonian are identical to those of the LQA model formulated through the Fock path integral method. Consequently, we conclude that both methods yield the same physical results, thereby validating the consistency of the LQA model derived via the Fock path integral approach. These findings provide a foundation for future research into loop quantum gravity and the astrophysical models it generates. Additionally, this work offers a new perspective on the Hamiltonian formulation of LQA models, which can be applied to investigate other related models. To facilitate future investigations, we have included all technical details regarding the transition from the classical ADM Hamiltonian to the quantum Hamiltonian, as well as the eigenvalue analysis, within this paper. We hope these details will prove valuable to the community. This study presents the complete Phase I dataset from the Pierre Auger Observatory, encompassing all 152 recorded events with energies exceeding 10 EeV. The cataloged data includes the reconstructed energies and arrival directions of these ultra-high-energy particles. The event count rises steadily with energy up to 20 EeV before plateauing, a trend attributed to the energy threshold of the ground array. The distribution of event directions aligns with the isotropic sky, as anticipated for extragalactic sources, though a mild clustering is observed around the galactic plane. We also examine the potential for sources within the local group of galaxies and the existence of a dipole anisotropy in the arrival directions of these particles. Furthermore, we compare our results with prior publications and provide a comprehensive analysis of the energy spectrum derived from this catalog. Finally, we detail the data format and offer a Python interface to facilitate data access and analysis. The catalog is accessible via the Auger Web Portal, and the Python interface can be installed using PyAuger. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor John N. Capdeville, a pivotal figure in the development of the Auger project. The authors acknowledge the Exaunes and PyAuger collaborations for their contributions. Deep object detectors are widely used in computer vision, yet their inability to quantify prediction uncertainty hinders practical deployment. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, the first Bayesian approach designed for uncertainty estimation in deep object detectors. By integrating the concept of "objectness" with Bayesian inference, BayesOD effectively handles uncertainty in both object localization and classification. Evaluated on the COCO dataset, our method surpasses the baseline detector in both accuracy and uncertainty estimation performance. Furthermore, leveraging the predicted uncertainty, BayesOD successfully eliminates a substantial portion of erroneous detections, achieving a significant reduction in false positives with only a negligible impact on true positives. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyang1990/BayesOD.

This study introduces a traffic prediction framework designed to analyze traffic patterns using short video clips. We define these clips as "traffic moving snippets" and suggest employing moving snippet features as input for prediction models. To address the challenge of creating suitable feature representations, we propose the Traffic Optical Flow Network (TOFNet), which utilizes the frame-to-frame dynamics within the clips to generate informative moving snippets features. These features are then used to train Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for short-term traffic prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting traffic speed and volume. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/TOFNet. We introduce a novel concept of reversal for morphisms in an enriched category, initially examining it within presheaf categories. This concept aligns with existing definitions in enriched homotopy theory but offers distinct advantages in the context of presheaf categories. We subsequently extend the concept to general enriched categories, demonstrating that our definition facilitates numerous general coherency theorems. Specifically, we present two instances where this leads to combinatorial coherence results: one involving sheaves on a site and the other concerning presheaves on a small category. Furthermore, we establish that our definition of reversal is intrinsically connected to the Eckmann-Hilton duality. Finally, we show that this concept of reversal corresponds to the dual of suspension in simplicial sets. These findings suggest that our definition of reversal in enriched categories may hold significant relevance within combinatorial higher category theory. The technical groundwork for these outcomes is developed in the companion paper by the first author, which focuses on simplicial categories. Additionally, the second author's separate work provides a comprehensive set of examples and applications within various areas of combinatorics. This paper serves as a unifying framework that synthesizes these related but distinct bodies of research. Section 2 applies this to presheaf categories, yielding combinatorial coherence results. Section 3 explores the relationship between reversal and Eckmann-Hilton duality. Section 4 examines simplicial categories, a topic detailed in the companion paper. The paper concludes with an appendix providing a generalization of the Eckmann-Hilton duality. The authors believe that the findings in the companion paper regarding simplicial categories will be of significant interest to combinatorial higher category theorists. This study introduces a deep learning-based segmentation framework designed to isolate the hippocampus in 3D MRI scans from patients suffering from Alzheimer's disease or epilepsy. The process begins by extracting the hippocampus region using a 3D U-Net architecture, followed by a refinement stage that employs a 3D ResNet50 model to eliminate residual artifacts. The final output is a clean hippocampus segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that this two-stage approach surpasses the performance of individual deep learning models used in isolation. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/hippocampus-segmentation}. Additionally, the authors have released a pre-trained model trained on a dataset of 1,000 MRI scans, which can be downloaded from \url{https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/hippocampus-segmentation}. We re-examine the pigeonhole phenomenon. Originally, it was believed that two non-orthogonal quantum states could never be perfectly distinguished. However, we demonstrate that this limitation does not apply when utilizing transversal modes. Our findings indicate that these transversal modes enable perfect detection of a subset of photons, thereby surpassing the previously thought optimal success probability achievable with beam splitters. This superior performance is validated through both theoretical analysis and experimental results. Furthermore, this advancement holds significant potential for enhancing quantum communication protocols, such as quantum key distribution and quantum state teleportation. Additionally, we explore the connection between this breakthrough and the concept of nonlocality. Finally, our proposed method offers a more efficient solution for quantum bit commitment. This study presents a Monte Carlo simulation designed to evaluate the shielding capabilities of various Low Earth Orbit (LEO) spacecraft against trapped cosmic ray particles. The simulation incorporates a comprehensive model of Earth's radiation belts, including the inner Van Allen belt and the outer belt influenced by solar activity. Particle fluxes were computed for multiple LEO configurations, specifically analyzing the International Space Station (ISS) and the proposed Lunar Gateway station across different solar cycles. The results indicate that the probability of a particle penetrating a spacecraft is directly proportional to its mass. Furthermore, the simulation demonstrates that particle penetration is significantly higher for the Lunar Gateway than for the ISS. These findings are essential for accurately assessing the radiation exposure of astronauts and electronic systems in LEOs. Additionally, the research offers a method for predicting the radiation doses received by astronauts on the International Space Station. Future work will extend this model to simulate radiation doses for the Lunar Gateway and other LEO missions. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1234/CRAND. Keywords: Monte Carlo Simulation, Low Earth Orbit, Radiation Dose, Spacecraft Shielding, Cosmic Ray Particles.

The efficacy of Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) relies heavily on the interplay between deep neural networks and graph structures. However, current research lacks a systematic approach to designing these graph structures, often leading to suboptimal models. This paper introduces a novel framework that first shrinks the input graph's skeleton globally to a multi-scale pyramid-like structure and then rewires local topologies to optimize the DGNN framework. This design enables the model to capture multi-scale information and adaptively identify the most critical nodes and edges. Furthermore, we propose a graph pyramid shrinkage algorithm that eliminates redundant nodes and edges while preserving the graph's skeleton, and a node-edge selection algorithm that identifies and retains key graph elements. Experimental results on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing DGNN models. Additionally, we visualize the model's behavior to reveal its ability to extract multi-scale information and identify the significance of graph structures. Our framework is implemented in PyTorch and is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/GNN-Skeleton-Pyramid. Recent years have seen a significant rise in the adoption of differential privacy (DP) within real-world data collection and analysis. However, DP imposes substantial overheads on both computational resources and statistical power, often rendering many practical applications infeasible. This paper explores the application of DP to low-rank matrix completion, a widely used technique for filling missing values in large datasets. We examine the standard DP approach for this task, which involves adding Laplace noise to the missing entries of a low-rank matrix estimated via singular value decomposition (SVD) from the available data. We then introduce a new algorithm, DP-LIME, which integrates Huber loss into the DP framework. Our results demonstrate that DP-LIME achieves a marked improvement in utility compared to the Laplace-based method, while maintaining the same level of privacy guarantees. Furthermore, we show that DP-LIME exhibits robustness against hyperparameter selection, a critical advantage in practical deployments. We introduce a unified model that describes the extinction, emission, and polarization of the sparse interstellar medium (SISM) through the extinction and emission properties of cosmic dust. This approach relies on a three-component dust framework: astrodust, small polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (sPAHs), and large PAHs. The study outlines the physical and mathematical foundations of the model and demonstrates its application to the Galactic plane and the Cygnus OB2 association. By employing a novel parameterization of the fractional polarization fraction, the model achieves a significantly improved fit to extinction and emission data compared to the widely used Cardelli, Clayton, and Mathis (1989) law and the Draine model. Furthermore, the proposed polarization fraction formulation offers a more accurate description of polarization data in the SISM than the conventional linear law. The model predicts that astrodust constitutes 60% of the total dust mass, with a characteristic size of 0.25 microns and an oblateness of 0.1. The remaining 40% of the mass is attributed to PAHs, which are divided into sPAHs and large PAHs based on their ability to polarize light; this distinction is critical for explaining the observed dichotomy in extinction curves. Finally, the model forecasts that astrodust is responsible for 90% of the 100-micron emission, while sPAHs and large PAHs account for 10%. These findings suggest that astrodust serves as the primary constituent of the Galactic interstellar medium. The detailed model code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/astromd. We report the detection of a massive planet within the protoplanetary disk of CIDA 1, a young, low-mass star. By analyzing ALMA 1.3 mm continuum emission, we identified a prominent gap in the disk, which we modeled using the gap-opening framework. This analysis yields a planet mass of 10.5 (+1.8/-1.1) M_Jup at a semi-major axis of 10.5 (+0.5/-0.4) au. This system represents the lowest stellar mass known to host a massive planet, a finding that challenges current planet formation theories. Furthermore, the planet's mass is comparable to those found in disks around more massive stars, suggesting that the ability to form massive planets is not strictly limited by the host star's mass. The gap's size and position align with predictions from planet-disk interaction models, indicating that even around very low-mass stars, massive planets can significantly alter disk structures. Additionally, we observed a large, bright inner ring at 1.3 au, likely caused by a pressure bump resulting from dead zones or planet migration. The disk's overall morphology resembles those around higher-mass stars, implying that massive planet formation can occur around very low-mass stars. Finally, we present a tentative detection of CO emission in the disk's outer regions, which may be influenced by the planet. These observations suggest that the planet is driving the migration of both gas and dust, a critical factor for understanding the evolution of disks around low-mass stars.

This paper examines the Most Taps Problem, which involves determining the minimum number of button presses required to light all bulbs on an $m \times n$ grid, where each press toggles a row and a column containing the selected button. We demonstrate that this two-player game is never a draw and prove that the first player wins if and only if $m + n \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$. We also analyze the number of moves in a winning strategy for the first player. Additionally, we extend the game to an $m \times n \times k$ cuboid, where each move toggles a face passing through the selected button, and establish that the first player wins if and only if $m + n + k \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$. Furthermore, we investigate the scenario where players are restricted to pressing buttons only within the interior of the grid or cuboid. We establish that the game is never a draw in these scenarios and determine the winner based on the parity of the product of the dimensions. Finally, we consider a variant where the first player wins by being the one unable to move, providing a winning strategy for both sides when $m = n$. The paper concludes with several open problems. Abstract Interpretation (AI) is a method that approximates the semantics of programs to achieve decidable static analysis. It operates by maintaining an over-approximation of program semantics within a domain of abstract values. The standard AI workflow involves two primary phases: the *concretization* phase, which maps abstract values to programs, and the *fixpoint computation* phase, which determines the least fixpoint of the resulting semantic function. This paper introduces a novel technique to decouple these phases, allowing them to be executed independently. We demonstrate this method in the context of program termination analysis, showing that it enables the use of more precise abstract values during fixpoint computation compared to traditional AI approaches. Our experimental results indicate that this novel technique can enhance both the precision and efficiency of static analysis. Furthermore, we show that this approach extends beyond termination analysis to other scenarios, such as reachability analysis. Finally, we illustrate the method's applicability to various types of abstract values, including those based on polyhedra, intervals, and abstract interpreters utilizing SMT solvers. Topological materials have attracted significant attention due to their exotic physical properties and potential applications. While most oxide perovskites are topologically trivial, recent studies indicate that ultrafast laser irradiation can induce complex topological states in these oxides. This work demonstrates that ultrafast laser irradiation can generate topological phonons in bulk oxide perovskites. Specifically, we show that a single-phase perovskite material, strontium titanate (SrTiO$_3$), can host nontrivial phonon topological states. Furthermore, we predict the realization of these topological phonon states through ultrafast laser irradiation. Our findings provide a foundation for exploring and manipulating topological phonon states in oxide perovskites.

Identifying outliers is crucial across numerous data mining domains, including anomaly detection, fraud prevention, and change detection. However, existing outlier detection methods often fail to scale effectively within high-dimensional spaces, particularly when utilizing distance metrics like Euclidean, Manhattan, or Hamming. This paper introduces a novel, general, and highly efficient outlier detection framework based on proximity graphs, which are sparse representations of metric spaces. By integrating various outlier scoring mechanisms with proximity graphs, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both speed and accuracy. Furthermore, we validate the scalability of our solution for massive datasets by leveraging parallel and distributed computing architectures. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves up to 100 times faster anomaly detection performance compared to the best existing alternatives. The impact of a cavity wall on an excited atom is examined through two distinct approaches: a semiclassical model, where the atom is treated quantum mechanically and the wall classically, and a fully quantum model, where both the atom and the wall (modeled as a collection of quantum harmonic oscillators) are handled quantum mechanically. In both scenarios, cavity-induced modifications to the atomic dipole moment are calculated. These results indicate that within the near-zone, the atom experiences an oscillating electric field from the wall that drives a stimulated emission of the cavity field. Conversely, in the far-zone, the atom acts as a source of electromagnetic radiation stimulated by the wall. Additionally, the cavity influences the energy levels of the excited atom, causing a shift dependent on the cavity width. Finally, the quantum model predicts a spontaneous emission rate for the atom that varies with the cavity width. These findings are corroborated by the fully quantum model, which demonstrates that the atom's spontaneous emission is either inhibited or enhanced by the cavity. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these results. This paper addresses node classification on unlabelled graph-structured data, focusing on fairness within community structures. We introduce a novel framework for fair graph learning, which employs a latent variable model to capture community structures and integrates a new fairness constraint. This constraint ensures that community membership does not predict sensitive attributes across different demographic groups. We develop a scalable algorithm to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem and demonstrate its efficacy through node classification experiments. The results show that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and fairness. Furthermore, we apply this framework to a real-world social network to illustrate how the learned community structures can enhance community detection. This study presents a search for natural supersymmetry (nSUSY) and divided supersymmetry (DIV) models, analyzing proton-proton collision data from the CMS experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis targets events characterized by at least one jet with missing transverse momentum. A multivariate discriminant is employed to differentiate signal from background events, followed by a binned maximum likelihood fit to the data. The resulting 95% confidence level upper limit on the production cross section for the final state involving a chargino, gluino, and bottom squark is 0.11 fb. This limit corresponds to masses of $m_\chi^\pm = 950$ GeV, $m_\tilde{g} = 1950$ GeV, and $m_{\tilde{b}} = 950$ GeV for the nSUSY model, and $m_\chi^{\pm} = 950$ GeV, $m_{\tilde{g}} = 1950$ GeV, and $m_{\tilde{b}} = 950$ GeV for the DIV model. Additionally, a final state with two jets and missing transverse momentum is investigated. This paper introduces a new econometric framework designed to identify rational expectation asset price bubbles characterized by stochastic, mean-reverting termination times. We develop a general equilibrium model featuring a speculative bubble with a mean-reverting duration, alongside an asset generating a constant stochastic discount factor. The model's parameters are estimated using the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) applied to the joint distribution of asset returns and consumption growth. Subsequently, we propose a suite of econometric tests to evaluate the unit root hypothesis, determine the mean-reverting nature of the bubble's lifetime, and estimate its duration. We also introduce a novel test for the constancy of the stochastic discount factor, which relies on a non-linear test statistic. Finally, we apply this methodology to detect bubbles in the S&P 500 and the German DAX 30 indices. Our empirical analysis confirms the presence of speculative bubbles in both markets, with the S&P 500 exhibiting a higher probability of mean-reverting bubble behavior compared to the DAX 30. Furthermore, our diagnostic approach successfully identifies the onset and offset of the 2000–2002 and 2008–2009 financial bubbles. The study concludes by discussing the limitations of this methodology and suggesting avenues for future research. We present a straightforward numerical approach to compute time-dependent correlation functions for quantum harmonic oscillators subjected to arbitrary time-dependent drives. This method utilizes the path integral formulation, where the quantum mechanical path integral is approximated through an importance sampling technique based on Monte Carlo integration of Euclidean time paths. Although the approach was developed for driven harmonic oscillators, it is extendable to broader classes of systems, such as many-body systems, provided the driving force remains independent of the system's dynamical variables. The study demonstrates the method's efficacy by calculating the time-dependent position and momentum correlation functions for a single driven harmonic oscillator. Additionally, we report results regarding the oscillator's response to different driving protocols, including square pulses, linear ramps, and superpositions of Gaussian pulses. Our findings indicate that the method yields accurate and reliable correlation functions within a reasonable computational time frame. The accompanying code is written in Python and can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/abhishekdatta1999/QHO}. User reviews offer rich, detailed insights into item attributes that algorithms can leverage to enhance recommendation quality. However, existing review-centric models struggle to effectively extract and utilize this information. To address this, we introduce the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which integrates user ratings with item attributes through a feature extraction module and a sentiment analysis module. The latter combines sentiment classification and aspect-based sentiment analysis to generate review embeddings. These embeddings are then fused with item attributes via a multi-layer interactive fusion mechanism to produce final representations. Experiments on two large-scale e-commerce review datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Data augmentation serves as a potent method for enhancing Neural Machine Translation performance, particularly for code-switched multilingual data, which remains a challenging and under-researched area. This study examines two lexical subtititution techniques—Synonym Replacement and Word Substitution—applied to Arabic-English code-switched data, evaluating their impact on Neural Machine Translation. We introduce a novel, data-driven Word Substitution model that leverages a pre-trained Word2Vec ensemble to generate and filter high-quality translations. Furthermore, we propose a straightforward yet effective code-switching detection algorithm to identify and extract code-switching words for substitution. Experimental results on the ArEnCST dataset demonstrate that both substitution models significantly boost Neural Machine Translation quality, with improvements ranging from 1.1 to 2.1 BLEU points. The findings indicate that the Word Substitution model yields a greater average performance gain than Synonym Replacement. Additionally, we present an open-source code-switched corpus, the ArEnWiki, derived from Wikipedia, which complements the existing ArEnCST dataset. The complete code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/AmrKhaled/ArEnWiki. The paper can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.00222. Given the scarcity of research on code-switching, this work holds significant potential to advance the field. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/AmrKhaled/ArEnWiki. We demonstrate that any Roelcke-precompact collection of homeomorphisms acting on degree $d \geq 2$ surfaces must possess a uniform modulus of continuity relative to the spherical metric. This finding offers a negative response to a query by M. Gromov concerning whether non-constant maps on degree $d$ surfaces can have an infinitesimal that is infinitesimally close to their modulus of continuity when measured against the hyperbolic metric. Furthermore, we establish that the modulus of continuity relative to the spherical metric serves as a Roelcke invariant for groups of surface homeomorphisms. These findings generalize earlier work by M. Gromov and J. Lohkamp specifically to the context of surfaces. Additionally, we present a self-contained proof of the fact that the modulus of continuity with respect to the hyperbolic metric is the largest sharp asymptotic invariant for surface homeomorphisms. Finally, we extend our findings to include spherical manifolds. The paper concludes with several open questions. We introduce a new class of sigma-model solutions, extending Generalized $\lambda$-deformations to include membranes. These models arise from Poisson $\sigma$-models whose dual frames exhibit specific membrane symmetries. We demonstrate that if the Poisson structure of the dual frame adheres to certain constraints, the resulting membrane solutions are well-defined. Applying this framework, we construct novel integrable membranes within symmetric spaces and group manifolds. Additionally, we establish the existence of non-trivial current algebras for these membranes, confirming their integrability. Finally, we examine specific examples where the membranes represent self-dual strings in superstring solutions. Notably, in the case of $AdS_5 \times S^5$, these membranes correspond to self-dual strings found in $\lambda$-deformations. Furthermore, we identify a new membrane solution on the deformed five-sphere $S^7_\delta$ that corresponds to a self-dual string in a $G_2$-deformation. This solution is characterized by a non-vanishing M2-charge, distinguishing it from previously known self-dual strings in $AdS_5 \times S^5$ and $AdS_4 \times S^7$ backgrounds. Consequently, this represents the first self-dual string solution with a non-vanishing M2-charge in a $G_2$-deformation. The construction of similar solutions in other $G_2$-deformations is currently under investigation. This paper serves as a foundation for a subsequent study, which will detail the explicit form of these membranes and their associated charges. We introduce a new algorithm for solving the hex board game Hex on boards featuring regular hexagonal grids of hexahedra, commonly known as hex meshes. This approach, termed Hex-Mesh, leverages the mesh structure to achieve exceptional performance, reaching speeds of up to 58 Tets/Hex on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X CPU. By utilizing tetrahedralization to bypass the traditional "convergence theorem" found in Hex-Mesh literature, the method accelerates both the simulation of random games and the evaluation of winning positions. Furthermore, the algorithm offers a clear victory path for completed games and provides specific move suggestions for active ones. Relation extraction (RE) is a critical NLP task focused on identifying relationships between entities within a given sentence. This paper introduces a new approach that integrates knowledge graph link prediction with relation extraction. We leverage the connection that entity relations are essentially links in a knowledge graph, thereby utilizing extensive, readily available data to enhance RE performance. Our proposed framework, Knowledge-enhanced Relation Extraction (KE3), employs a two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, a self-supervised link prediction task is used to pre-train the RE model, generating synthetic data for rare RE triples. This allows the model to learn generalizable patterns from abundant knowledge graph data before fine-tuning on a specific RE task. In the second stage, we further refine the model by leveraging the training data from the first stage. Experimental results on three public RE datasets demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, ablation studies and analyses of the generated synthetic data reveal that our model effectively transfers knowledge from the knowledge graph to the RE task. This work investigates the robustness of reinforcement learning (RL) agents, a critical factor for their practical deployment. We introduce a metric-based framework that quantifies robustness in two dimensions: policy similarity and regret. Our primary contribution is the concept of coarse-grained continuity, which generalizes established continuity metrics from continuous domains to the metric space of policies. We demonstrate that this property ensures uniform policy continuity and provides a regret bound that scales linearly with the policy's distortion. Furthermore, we establish a regret bound for agents exhibiting Lipschitz continuity and propose an empirical study to assess the computational feasibility of estimating policy noise. These findings offer a novel perspective on the relationship between policy noise and regret, with implications for future RL research. This paper introduces a new numerical structure-preserving filter designed for finite element simulations in multiple dimensions. The method employs a convex optimization framework to enhance noisy simulation data by eliminating filtering artifacts, such as spurious oscillations and ripples, while maintaining the original solution's geometry. The filter is grounded in a convex optimization model that balances the preservation of the solution's non-convex geometry with the minimization of total variation. We provide a rigorous analysis proving the existence of a solution and demonstrating its stability regarding the noisy input. Numerical experiments across various multidimensional scenarios confirm the filter's effectiveness in both 2D and 3D environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the filter can recover the underlying noise-free function from noisy data generated by high-order numerical methods. The proposed approach is applicable to diverse hyperbolic and parabolic problems, including those in fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and image processing. This work extends our recent research on the structure-preserving filter originally developed for 1D simulations. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/CMF. Additionally, we have released a user-friendly Python package, ConvexMultiFilter, which implements the filter and includes a collection of examples for 2D and 3D applications. The package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install ConvexMultiFilter. The package documentation is available at https://chenyi-1997.github.io/CMF/. Finally, a comprehensive report detailing the structure-preserving filter and its implementation is forthcoming in a separate publication. Keywords: structure-preserving filter, convex optimization, finite element method, total variation minimization, high-order numerical methods. This study employs the high-energy spectrometer of Insight-HXMT to investigate the evolution of the corona in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571, which is currently in a low/hard state. We identified type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) within the 2–10 keV band, which were analyzed using the disk reflection model. Our results indicate that the corona's physical properties varied during the observation, with the corona becoming more compact and less distant from the disk as the source's luminosity declined. This behavior aligns with the inverse correlation between corona size and luminosity observed in other low/hard state black hole X-ray binaries. Furthermore, the QPO frequency in the 2–10 keV range exhibited a decline as luminosity decreased, a trend that may be attributed to the decreasing corona size. Additionally, the disk inclination angle was determined to be $37.0^{+1.4}_{-1.1}$ degrees. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of these findings for the phenomenological models of type-C QPOs. Identifying materials from visual data is a critical challenge in fields like remote sensing and robotics. While current deep learning methods excel at recognizing materials within their training datasets, they fail in real-world scenarios where materials may appear in unfamiliar environments or remain unseen during training. To address this, we introduce a framework designed to identify any material from anywhere. This is achieved through a two-stage process: first, a physics-based renderer generates a diverse range of synthetic images to train a contrastive learning model; second, a learned image-to-image translator adapts these synthetic features to match real-world conditions. This approach enables the reliable identification of materials across new environments and includes previously unseen items. We validate the framework's effectiveness across three distinct datasets spanning different modalities and domains: a remote sensing dataset of vehicles captured via satellite, a synthetic dataset of fruits rendered in various lighting conditions, and real-world robotic data featuring cluttered objects. Our results demonstrate that the framework successfully identifies materials across all three datasets and performs effectively on real-world test cases. Furthermore, we have released an interactive web application allowing users to explore material representations and test the framework on real-world images. This application is available at https://material-representation.net. Finally, we have made our synthetic dataset and pre-trained models publicly available at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/CP-RLE. We hope this resource will inspire future research in this area. We introduce a new end-to-end model for robust keypoint detection and descriptor matching, designed to generate sparse matches even in highly cluttered scenes. Our approach relies on two distinct geometric attributes—local features and descriptors—and addresses them through two specialized sub-networks. Unlike traditional methods that depend on keypoint detectors, our fully end-to-end framework eliminates the need for separate keypoints by using LoFTR, a transformer-based model. This model generates dense feature maps from input images and performs cross-matching to establish dense matches. To extract descriptors, we utilize global attention features derived from the cross-matching process. Furthermore, we introduce a novel feature normalization technique to enhance the robustness of our descriptors. Experimental results demonstrate that LoFTR outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a 1.5x improvement in local feature matching accuracy and a 2.5x increase in correct matches per image pair. This study examines the bias inherent in the Inferred Diffraction Method (IDM), a prevalent technique for reconstructing solar magnetic fields. We identify two primary sources of bias in IDM: first, the specific choice of a magnetic field model, and second, the selection of a diffraction model. To mitigate these biases, we introduce two strategies: (1) employing a magnetic field model that avoids overfitting, and (2) utilizing a diffraction model that accounts for the finite size of point spread functions (PSF). We validate these approaches using synthetic data generated from various magnetic field distributions and diffraction point spread functions. Our results demonstrate that these methods effectively reduce the biases associated with different field models and diffraction characteristics. Furthermore, we apply these improvements to analyze the emergence of a bipolar active region in the sunspot region NOAA 10486, utilizing high-resolution observations from the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) and the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS). We find that the emerging bipolar region exhibits asymmetry, characterized by a stronger magnetic field in the leading polarity compared to the trailing polarity. This conclusion is supported by both the reconstructed magnetic field maps and the observed magnetic flux transport across the region's boundary. Additionally, we observe that the magnetic flux within the region expands at a rate of approximately $10^{11}$ Mx s$^{-1}$, a rate comparable to the photospheric horizontal flow speed of roughly 1 km s$^{-1}$. These findings suggest that the asymmetry in the emerging bipolar region is established during its formation and persists as it rises through the convection zone. Finally, we conclude that the proposed methods are essential for accurately reconstructing solar magnetic fields. Specifically, the magnetic field model should be selected to prevent overfitting, and the diffraction model must incorporate the finite size of the point spread function. These approaches are particularly critical for high-resolution observations, such as those from DKIST, where the diffraction model plays a significant role in the inference process. We anticipate that these methods will facilitate more accurate reconstructions of solar magnetic fields in the future. This paper introduces a new demand-side management framework that combines consumption scheduling with instantaneous load billing. To foster short-term demand response, the utility incentivizes consumers to reduce their energy usage, while consumers aim to minimize both their energy costs and disutility arising from deviations from scheduled consumption. The proposed consumption scheduling and instantaneous load billing mechanism ensures that consumers and the utility reach a Nash equilibrium, achieving Pareto-optimality and fairness among consumers. Furthermore, we develop an aggregative game to characterize the consumers' best responses to the utility's supply strategy. This approach facilitates the analysis of the game's existence, uniqueness, and Pareto-optimality, with a best response dynamic providing a practical method for reaching the unique equilibrium. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the mechanism. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly benefits both the utility and consumers compared to traditional consumption scheduling strategies. Additionally, the study confirms the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and verifies the convergence of the proposed dynamic. Notably, the proposed mechanism outperforms the utility's supply strategy in terms of both economic and social welfare. Consequently, this framework offers a promising solution for demand-side management, particularly for smart grids utilizing smart meters. It holds significant potential for future smart grid applications, including real-time pricing, dynamic demand response, and load management. The proposed approach is applicable to various market structures, such as wholesale markets, retail markets, and direct load control schemes. Moreover, it can be extended to other scenarios, including the design of demand response programs and the development of new business models for third-party demand response aggregators. In this scenario, consumers act as both suppliers and demanders, while the utility serves only as an aggregator. This extension is expected to yield substantial economic and social benefits for all participants. The results of this study can serve as a foundation for future research in these areas. This work examines the rate of convergence for von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, $\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T U(t)\rho \,dt \to \sum_\alpha \hat{\rho}(\lambda_\alpha)P_\alpha$, by analyzing the spectral properties of the underlying generator $-\mathrm{i}L = -\mathrm{i}\frac{d}{dt}$. We demonstrate that the asymptotic convergence speed is contingent upon the spectral gap of the operator $\mathbb{I} - E_0$, where $E_0$ represents the orthogonal projector onto the kernel of $L$. Furthermore, we establish that this gap remains of a constant order with respect to $T$, as it is bounded below by $\frac{2\pi}{\lambda_{\mathrm{max}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}}$, where $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}$ denote the maximum and minimum eigenvalues of $L$, respectively. Additionally, we investigate the convergence of spectral measures, $\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T e^{-\mathrm{i}tL}\rho \,dt \to \sum_\alpha \hat{\rho}(\lambda_\alpha)P_\alpha$, and prove that the error term decays at a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)$. These findings are applicable to the linear advection equation, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0$, and the linear Schrödinger equation, $\mathrm{i}\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = 0$, on the unit circle. Finally, we validate these theoretical results through numerical experiments. The study underscores the critical role of spectral characteristics in the long-term behavior of linear evolution equations and offers a quantitative assessment of the convergence rate for von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. This analysis is particularly pertinent to scenarios where the spectrum of the generator is bounded away from zero, such as in the linear advection equation, and holds significance for understanding the asymptotic dynamics of various physical systems. The Gaia mission's Blue Photometer and Red Photometer/Radial-Fogging Spectrographs (BP/RP) are anticipated to generate low-resolution spectra for approximately 100 million stars, offering a unique chance to investigate stellar populations. However, the sheer volume of data presents significant challenges for analysis. This study introduces a novel method to efficiently identify metal-poor stars within the Gaia EDR3 BP/RP spectral catalog. The technique relies on a supervised machine learning algorithm utilizing a Support Vector Machine (SVM), trained on a sample of 1,000 stars with known metallicities from the LAMOST survey. We applied this approach to the Gaia EDR3 catalog, successfully identifying 10,000 metal-poor stars. Our results indicate that the SVM accurately classifies stars with [Fe/H] < -1.5, achieving a contamination rate of only 0.01% and a completeness of 99.9%. For stars with -1.5 < [Fe/H] < -1.0, contamination remains below 10%, though completeness drops to 70%. We further demonstrate that the method's accuracy is highly sensitive to the quality of the training sample, with a minimum of 1,000 training stars required for optimal performance. Finally, we compare our findings with other selection methods and discuss the scientific potential of these newly identified metal-poor stars. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of global blaze severity data from 1983 to 2018, utilizing the GARCH model to examine temporal and cross-sectional patterns. We demonstrate that while the distribution of global severity exhibits fat tails, neither the global frequency nor individual country-level frequencies show this characteristic. Furthermore, we find that global and national-level severity displays strong long-memory, with the Hurst parameter indicating a tendency toward persistence. Our results also reveal that global and national severity figures are highly positively correlated. Finally, we develop a forecasting model for annual global severity and provide predictions for the subsequent five years. Additionally, we explore methods to enhance forecast accuracy by incorporating historical forecast errors. The implications of these findings for fire insurance are discussed. Given the increasing frequency and severity of wildfires driven by climate change, our research offers valuable insights for both the insurance sector and policymakers. Specifically, our ability to forecast global severity and the associated correlations with country-level data could significantly aid insurers in managing their portfolios. For policymakers, the correlation analysis may assist in identifying nations likely to experience high severity in the coming years, thereby guiding resource allocation for fire prevention and mitigation strategies. This study investigates the correlation between two corpus-derived metrics designed to assess morphological complexity in natural languages. We observe a strong positive correlation between the measures, indicating that they largely evaluate the same underlying property. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both metrics align with established findings regarding the relationship between morphological complexity and the count of productive affixes. However, the second measure proves more robust, as it remains robust even when the inflectional affix inventory is empty. These findings suggest that the second measure is particularly well-suited for evaluating morphological complexity across a broad spectrum of typological categories. Finally, we examine the implications of these results for the ongoing debate concerning the existence of a universal measure of syntactic complexity. Specifically, we argue that the existence of a syntactic complexity measure is less probable than that of a measure for morphological complexity. This conclusion stems from the fact that syntactic complexity is not consistently associated with high word length, whereas such a relationship is consistently observed in morphological complexity. Additionally, we note that a measure for typological word order complexity exhibits a correlation with mean word length that is the inverse of what is expected. These observations collectively support the view that mean word length serves as a reliable indicator for identifying morphologically complex languages but is a poor predictor for morphologically simple ones. Consequently, we contend that a measure based on mean length of surface forms is more effective for distinguishing morphologically complex languages than for distinguishing simple ones. Finally, we explore the consequences of these results for the debate surrounding the universality of complexity measures. We conclude that the debate is most productively framed as a question of whether a single measure can capture complexity across all languages, rather than whether complexity itself is universal. We argue that the evidence strongly favors the latter perspective. Specifically, we posit that morphological complexity is universal, whereas syntactic complexity is not. This conclusion is supported by the fact that mean sentence length correlates positively with syntactic complexity in some languages but negatively in others. In contrast, mean word length consistently correlates positively with morphological complexity, as evidenced by the robustness of the link between this feature and the number of productive affixes. We contend that the universality of complexity measures is best understood as the universal presence of complexity, with the specific nature of that complexity varying across languages. We further propose that the universality of morphological complexity is more robust than that of syntactic complexity, a hypothesis that warrants further investigation. Our analysis employs the convergence power spectrum, $P(\ell)$, to characterize this substructure. We demonstrate that the amplitude of $P(\ell)$ at high multipoles ($\ell$) is highly sensitive to the nature of dark matter. Specifically, we find that self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models fail to reproduce the observed high-$\ell$ power spectrum amplitudes, whereas both cold dark matter (CDM) and fuzzy dark matter (FDM) models align well with the data. Furthermore, we observe that the amplitudes of $P(\ell)$ at high $\ell$ are more strongly influenced by satellite galaxies than by dark matter subhalos. Finally, we note that the $P(\ell)$ signal is particularly sensitive to the concentration of subhalos. Our results indicate that SIDM models tend to produce more concentrated subhalos compared to CDM, a distinction that is clearly reflected in the high-$\ell$ power spectrum. These findings suggest that gravitational lensing offers a complementary approach to dwarf galaxy kinematics for probing dark matter properties. Additionally, we show that high-$\ell$ lensing data can effectively constrain dark matter models, especially in galaxy clusters where dwarf galaxy contributions are minimal. Model simplification is a critical technique for reducing the computational demands of model-based control in large-scale systems. This paper introduces a new approach that reduces a discrete-time linear system with discrete inputs and outputs to a smaller equivalent system using only local input-output data from the original system. The proposed method relies on a novel concept called the generalized annihilating polynomial, which extends the traditional annihilating polynomial used in continuous systems. Model reduction is achieved by identifying the generalized annihilating polynomials for the reduced system's state and input spaces based on this local data. The resulting reduced system is derived using the coisotropic realization technique. Simulation results demonstrate the method's effectiveness across various scenarios, including cases where input data is unavailable or where local output data is contaminated with noise. Furthermore, the approach is extended to handle scenarios where output data is accessible only at specific time instants. Additionally, the method yields a finite-dimensional reduced system for finite-time systems and generates an infinite-dimensional reduced system for time-varying systems. Finally, the relationship between this proposed approach and the annihilation-based subspace identification method is examined. The method is implemented in MATLAB, and the source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/model-reduction. The accompanying video, illustrating the method with a simple example, can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. Keywords: model reduction, model simplification, model-based control, large-scale systems, local data, generalized annihilating polynomial, subspace identification.

This paper introduces a novel method for autonomous Component Analysis, designed to identify and extract features from datasets without requiring prior knowledge of the target features. The proposed M-ar-K-Fast Component Analysis (M-KFCF) algorithm is engineered to deliver rapid extraction of components that are both highly discriminative and interpretable. The core concept involves iteratively decomposing a data matrix into a set of features and a residual matrix, where the residual is progressively down-weighted to prioritize the extraction of specific components. The paper provides a theoretical foundation for M-KFCF, establishes its convergence properties, and demonstrates its effectiveness through various numerical examples. Furthermore, the method is applied to a real-world dataset to extract features that facilitate the classification of different types of lung cancer. The results indicate that M-KFCF outperforms other component analysis techniques in terms of classification accuracy, feature interpretability, and computational efficiency. Additionally, the study confirms the algorithm's robustness by showing that it successfully extracts features from datasets with varying dimensions and sample sizes. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/M-KFCF. This study introduces a real-time incident detection framework utilizing spatio-temporal processing of geotagged social media. The system's performance was evaluated using Twitter data collected during the 2015 Paris terrorist attacks. Results indicate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms traditional traffic monitoring systems in terms of detection latency and accuracy. Furthermore, the experimental outcomes demonstrate that the real-time processing of geotagged social media is a highly effective method for identifying incidents. The accompanying Python code can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/RT-GT-Traffic-Monitoring. This paper establishes new findings regarding the equivalence between $E$-capacity and the $L^q$-norm of a measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $q>1$ and $E$ denotes an arbitrary separable Banach space. Specifically, we analyze the case where $\sigma$ is an elliptic surface measure defined on a non-tangentially accessible (NTA) domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$. We derive sufficient conditions for the equivalence between $H^{1,p'}(\Omega)$-capacity and the $L^q$-norm of $\sigma$, with $p'$ being the conjugate exponent of $p \in (1,\infty)$. Furthermore, we examine this equivalence within the context of the $p$-Laplace equation. As an application, we demonstrate that the $p$-Laplace equation admits a unique $\sigma$-solution under the condition that $q' < \frac{n}{n-p}$, where $q'$ is the Hölder conjugate of $q$. Additionally, we explore the relationship between $\sigma$-solutions and generalized $\sigma$-solutions for the $p$-Laplace equation. Finally, we address the existence and uniqueness of $\sigma$-harmonic functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. These results extend and complement prior work by authors such as Fabes, J. Jones, S. A. Telia, M. A. Pinsky, and others. Notably, our findings are applicable to the study of the $p$-Laplace equation in the critical dimension. Our approach relies on the theory of function spaces, capacity, and the properties of the $p$-Laplace equation. This study employs evolutionary search, a global optimization technique, to identify cobalt-abundant compounds within the Y-Co-B system. Risk-aware bidding is a critical capability for automated display ad platforms, enabling advertisers to optimize campaign performance while adhering to budget constraints. However, accurately estimating the risk of overspending remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a novel adaptive budget allocation framework designed to enhance performance under limited budgets. Within this adaptive system, we propose a new adaptive risk estimation algorithm that dynamically calculates real-time spending risk using historical data, ensuring robustness against distribution shifts. Furthermore, we develop a new regret analysis to demonstrate the regret bounds of this adaptive risk estimation method. Extensive experiments conducted on both real-world and synthetic datasets confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/ABA.

Wigner negativity is a fundamental characteristic of Wigner functions that enables quantum states to surpass the capabilities of classical probability distributions. This study investigates how Wigner negativity influences quantum guidance within the Wigner-Wheeler-Newton (QGW) framework, a semiclassical approach that incorporates quantum corrections into the semiclassical Newton equation via the Wigner distribution. We demonstrate that these corrections rely on the Wigner density and Wigner flow, both of which can exhibit negativity. Furthermore, we establish that while pure states always produce negative Wigner terms in the QGW equation, mixed states do not necessarily exhibit Wigner negativity. Finally, we analyze the impact of Wigner negativity within the QGW framework on the quantum behavior of a particle subject to a harmonic potential. Our findings indicate that Wigner negativity within the QGW formalism can generate non-classical phenomena, such as double-peaked probability distributions and non-classical current flows. Additionally, we observe that Wigner negativity enhances the accuracy of the Wigner equation, allowing it to better approximate the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. These results highlight the significance of Wigner negativity in the Wigner distribution for developing quantum corrections in semiclassical theories. The methodology and insights presented here can be extended to other quantum corrections in semiclassical frameworks. All numerical computations were performed using the open-source Python package QGrip, which is available at https://github.com/QuantumGuidanceResearchInstitute/QGrip. The Python code for this research can be found at https://github.com/QuantumGuidanceResearchInstitute/QGrip/blob/master/examples/wigner_negativity.ipynb. This study presents a limit analysis of quantum key distribution security by employing the arithmetic mean and a non-uniform random seed for privacy amplification. We demonstrate that the entropy of this non-uniform seed exceeds the standard uniform seed used in conventional security analyses. Furthermore, we establish that the entropies associated with both the uniform and non-uniform seed methods are optimal. Our numerical results indicate that applying privacy amplification with a non-uniform random seed enhances the final key rate. Consequently, the theoretical security analysis of QKD utilizing the limit analysis method offers greater generality and flexibility compared to existing security analyses that rely on the randomizer method. This research provides a theoretical foundation for future QKD applications, particularly in scenarios with low photon transmission probabilities. Additionally, the limit analysis method developed in this work is applicable to other cryptographic systems, such as secret sharing and authentication. This paper explores the theory of timelike F-Bertrand curves within a semi-metric space. We examine the relationship between two such curves sharing a common principal vector and establish that multiple timelike F-Bertrand curves cannot lie in the same osculating plane. Furthermore, we derive general necessary conditions for their existence and provide a sufficient condition applicable to arc-length parameterized curves. Finally, we demonstrate that both necessary and sufficient conditions hold true for timelike F-Bertrand curves parameterized by any function. As an application, we explicitly construct the timelike curve corresponding to a given timelike F-Bertrand curve and provide a practical example. Additionally, we explore the relationship between timelike F-Bertrand curves and timelike helices of the first kind, demonstrating that multiple such helices can share the same principal null vector. We also present two examples of timelike F-Bertrand curves parameterized by a function other than arc-length. Finally, we generalize these findings to higher dimensions by defining F-Bertrand curves in an n-dimensional semi-metric space and investigating the relationship between two n-dimensional timelike F-Bertrand curves with a common principal vector. In this context, we prove that multiple n-dimensional timelike F-Bertrand curves may share the same principal vector, and we provide an example of two such curves whose principal vectors are linked by a linear relationship. The necessary conditions for the existence of these curves are also addressed. Notably, this work represents the first investigation into the existence of F-Bertrand curves in a general semi-metric space. Consequently, the necessary and sufficient conditions derived herein are novel and hold significant value for future research in this area. Furthermore, the results are readily extendable to space-like and time-like surfaces, offering a foundation for extending these findings to higher-dimensional manifolds. This research holds potential for applications in theoretical physics, particularly in the study of space-time surfaces and their associated geometric structures. Overall, the paper contributes to the advancement of differential geometry and its applications across various disciplines. Specifically, it offers a new perspective on the study of F-Bertrand curves in general metric spaces and provides a basis for further research into their properties and applications. This paper investigates the sampling distributions of equidimensional coalescing particle systems defined on $[0, \infty)$ with non-negative, non-decreasing, non-degenerate, and non-defective absorbing barriers. We demonstrate that for any Feller process, the $n$-dimensional marginal distribution of the first coalescence time for an initial $2n$-mer is identical to the sampling distribution of an order statistics process derived from the corresponding one-dimensional marginal. This finding provides a practical method for calculating the distribution of the first coalescence time for Feller processes, as the order statistics sampling distribution for the one-dimensional marginal is generally more accessible. Furthermore, we establish that the coalescence time distribution for a Feller process is uniquely determined by its mean and variance. Finally, we extend the coalescence time distribution for the $X^2$-process, originally derived by Takacs (1967), to the $\chi^2$-Feller process. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we offer a novel proof of the uniqueness of the Feller process on $[0, \infty)$ with respect to its sampling distributions, utilizing a recent result by Baccelli and Broutin (2015). This proof relies on the distribution of the first order statistic from an i.i.d. sample from a Feller process and the relationship between the coalescence time for an initial $2n$-mer and the first coalescence time for an initial $n$-mer. We also provide an alternative proof of the coalescence time distribution for the $\chi^2$-Feller process, which was previously established by Takacs (1967) using a different approach. The methodology employed in this proof is subsequently utilized to derive the coalescence time distribution for the $\chi^2$-Feller process with degrees of freedom $d \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$. Finally, the study concludes with an analysis of the coalescence time distribution for a Feller process characterized by a linearly increasing mean and variance. These results are validated through numerical simulations.
