Waveguide Qustum Electrodynamics (QED) is a rapidly developing field focused on the controlled interaction between individual quantum emitters and light within a one-dimensional waveguide. This framework enables the engineering of multi-photon quantum states by exploiting the strong coupling between cavity-emitters and their emitted photons. However, the standard input-output formalism often becomes cumbersome for complex scenarios, such as those involving multiple emitters and intricate photon-emitter interactions. To address this, we introduce a diagrammatic approach that facilitates the efficient calculation of multi-photon scattering within waveguide QED systems. This method is derived from the standard formalism and utilizes a set of diagrams to represent various quantum processes. We validate the efficacy of this diagrammatic method by applying it to a fundamental waveguide QED problem: the scattering of a two-photon Fock state by a dimer of emitters. Our findings demonstrate that this approach offers a streamlined and effective means for calculating multi-photon scattering in waveguide QED. Furthermore, we illustrate its potential to facilitate the design of quantum emitters capable of generating multi-photon states with tailored correlations and entanglement. This methodology is readily extensible to other significant waveguide QED problems, including the scattering of multi-photon states by a single emitter and the generation of multi-photon states using a single emitter. Ultimately, this serves as a valuable tool for future investigations into multi-photon quantum processes within waveguide QED systems. The accompanying Python code is available at https://github.com/abhisheksingh12345678/waveguideQED. The waveguideQED package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install waveguideQED. Additionally, the package includes a Jupyter notebook tutorial titled "Diagrammatic Method to Scattering of Multi-Photon States in Waveguide QED," which can be accessed at https://github.com/abhisheksingh12345678/waveguideQED/blob/master/Notebooks/Diagrammatic%20Method%20to%20Scattering%20of%20Multi-Photon%20States%20in%20Waveguide%20QED.ipynb. The package is also accessible at https://github.com/abhisheksingh12345678/waveguideQED. Users can explore the package by running the following command in a terminal: python -m waveguideQED

We investigate the spin-dependent (SD) scattering of spin-1/2 dark matter (DM) off nucleons, specifically accounting for the fact that DM within a galactic halo possesses non-negligible momentum. We demonstrate that this halo momentum induces a transition between SD operators, an effect that is amplified when DM is accelerated by the Earth's motion. Consequently, direct detection experiments conducted in moving dark matter halos must incorporate this non-natural transition, which could significantly alter the interpretation of experimental limits. We illustrate this by analyzing recent data from the NCDM experiment, showing that including the transition leads to constraints on the axial-vector operator that are orders of magnitude stronger than those derived from spin-independent operators. Furthermore, we show that the CMHT-1 halo around the Milky Way's center could be detected by the upcoming ARIS experiment, a finding made possible by the momentum-induced transition. Our findings underscore the necessity of a unified framework for analyzing spin-dependent interactions, one that explicitly includes the effects of DM acceleration. This work serves as a foundation for the direct detection community to assess the impact of this non-natural transition on their search efforts. Our study also provides a comprehensive toolkit for direct detection theorists to explore the implications of DM acceleration on nucleon scattering. The associated Python package, `ddac`, is available at https://github.com/robertgros/ddac. The package includes a detailed tutorial on the effects of DM acceleration and offers a user-friendly interface for the ARIS experiment. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for future direct detection searches. The inclusion of this alternative proof aims to enhance students' understanding of the characteristics of power sums, as evidenced by the comments provided at the conclusion of the note. This paper introduces a delay-enhanced variant of conventional non-coherent differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM), achieving performance gains of up to 1.5 dB. The approach leverages a delay-interference (DI) principle, utilizing a delay-interferometer structure that sums the current symbol with an appropriately selected delayed version of the received signal. The selection of the optimal DI tap is based on a specific property of the CPM phase path memory. This technique is applicable to both square-law and envelope differential detectors. Furthermore, the method can be seamlessly integrated with existing enhancements, such as the use of a phase reference filter. Analytical and simulation results are provided for a practical scenario involving a 4-PSK scheme with a shaping pulse memory of one symbol period. Additionally, the concept is extended to a delayed envelope detector scheme for minimum shift keying (MSK). In this case, a simple selection rule is derived based on the relationship between the DI delay and the effective phase transition time, which is typically shorter than the one-symbol period used in other CPM schemes. Finally, the delay-enhanced scheme is analyzed in the context of non-coherent differential detection for orthogonal CPM, which is shown to be optimal in terms of symbol error rate. However, the paper demonstrates that the sub-optimal delayed envelope detector performs nearly as well as the optimal scheme. This suggests that the delay-enhanced detector is particularly advantageous for high-data-rate orthogonal CPM applications where phase reference filters are impractical. The study concludes with a discussion on the potential of this concept for other modulation schemes, including orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM). In these scenarios, the delay-enhanced structure can improve performance by mitigating the impact of inter-symbol interference caused by multipath propagation. Optimal delay selection is determined based on the channel impulse response. Optimal detectors for these systems are also derived, and the analysis is applied to a practical example using a 4-tap delay line. The paper concludes with a discussion on the potential of delay-enhanced non-coherent differential detection for future communication systems. Specifically, it highlights the need for robust modulation schemes that are resilient to multipath fading, especially in high-mobility environments where channel estimation is difficult. The delay-enhanced detector offers a promising solution for such applications. Reward learning (RL) is a machine learning approach designed to automatically derive task rewards from human demonstrations. While recent research has prioritized efficiency by reducing the number of required human responses, this paper introduces a visually aided cluster ranking method that further accelerates the process. The technique employs a straightforward clustering algorithm to divide responses into two groups, presenting the human expert with a binary choice: indicate which group better aligns with the task's intent. This step significantly cuts down the time per response. Subsequently, an optimization procedure ranks the groups to determine a unique reward function. This study investigates the impact of noncommutative effects on nucleon properties, specifically the proton and neutron form factors, within the framework of Chiral Quark Soliton Model (CQSM). By utilizing an effective Hamiltonian that incorporates both quark and meson nonlocality, we analyze how the noncommutative parameter alters these nucleon characteristics. Our findings indicate that while the Dirac and Pauli form factors of the proton and neutron remain largely insensitive to the scale of noncommutativity, the meson-nucleon coupling constants exhibit significant dependence. Furthermore, we observe that the electromagnetic form factors of the proton and neutron are also substantially influenced by the scale of noncommutativity. These results suggest that precision measurements of nucleon structure could serve as a viable method for probing the scale of space-time noncommutativity. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future experimental efforts aimed at measuring nucleon form factors. The calculations were performed using the Mathematica package Grasmann. This paper investigates the topological and geometric characteristics of the frustrated Toric code model, a spin-1/2 system defined on the dual lattice of the square lattice. In the frustrated Toric code model, the ground state is highly degenerate even in the absence of symmetry, with its topological and geometric properties emerging from the interplay between the superposition principle and topological constraints. This study examines the topological order of the model by analyzing the entanglement spectrum and entanglement geometry of its subspace states. We demonstrate that the entanglement spectrum exhibits a degenerate structure, with the degenerate energy gap determined by the topological order parameter, specifically the anyon operator. Furthermore, the entanglement geometry is governed by the fractal dimension of the minimal fractal surface connecting the subsystem's boundaries. Consequently, we conclude that the frustrated Toric code model displays rich topological and geometric features, offering a fertile ground for exploring the relationship between quantum information and quantum topology. Our findings may also hold significance for the quantum simulation of frustrated Toric code models. Finally, we outline the extension of this research to the 3D frustrated Toric code model. We examine extensions of random band matrices involving complex variations parameterized by $q$. The band structure remains identical to that of Hermitian random band matrices, but the range of the band parameter is scaled by a factor of $q$. We demonstrate that these matrices can be approximated using a $q$-deformation of the sigma-model. This approach is valid provided the band width is sufficiently large relative to the bandwidth parameter, which is expected to scale as a power of $N$. Furthermore, we establish that the approximation error is small when the band width is large enough to be comparable to the typical spectral gap. This result extends our previous finding regarding real deformations, which required the band width to be significantly larger. We also refine the previously derived lower bound for the band width. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the spectral gap, which is proportional to the inverse power of $N$ when the band width is at least as large as the spectral gap. This bound holds for both the real and complex deformed matrices. However, the bound for the band width is not tight, as it fails to account for the well-known upper bound of $2\pi$. We conclude by discussing the potential application of these results to deformed Hermitian Wigner matrices. In that context, the sigma-model approximation is applicable when the fourth moment cumulant is sufficiently small. We also address the case where the fourth moment is not small, though we must assume the variance of the off-diagonal entries is at least of order $1/N$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the Poisson deformations studied in [10]. The sigma-model approximation is expected to hold when the variance of the off-diagonal entries is at least of order $1/N^{1/2}$. However, the variance condition is not tight, as it is not optimal. We also discuss the possibility of a more direct method to prove the sigma-model approximation for Poisson deformations, which would not rely on the results for random band matrices. Such a method would be valuable for understanding deformations that do not possess the band structure. Algorithmic learning has become a cornerstone of modern data science, yet the black-box nature of these methods often hinders their practical application. While the human brain is capable of interpreting such algorithms, the capacity of other learners to learn from them remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces a novel model for algorithmic interpretability based on human learning mechanisms. We propose a cognitive learning model that mimics how learners extract knowledge from algorithms, demonstrating that the number of cognitive steps required serves as a robust metric for interpretability. We define the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS) as the count of steps needed for a learner to acquire knowledge from an algorithm. We validate the effectiveness of CCS by applying it to classify the interpretability of machine learning models. Furthermore, we empirically demonstrate the model's efficacy in predicting the steps required for learners to extract knowledge from decision trees and linear regression techniques. This paper introduces a reparameterization of the standard Poisson process to facilitate the application of standard Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques. We demonstrate that this approach eliminates the need for the customary Poisson process truncation, which previously hindered the development of reliable sampling algorithms. The proposed method is applicable to a broad range of extreme value distributions, including the generalized Pareto, Weibull, and Fréchet distributions. Additionally, we illustrate its utility in estimating the extremal index and the tail shape parameter. A simulation study evaluates the performance of the method, and it is subsequently applied to two real-world datasets. Finally, we discuss the method's applicability to other statistical problems involving stochastic processes. All code required to replicate the results is publicly accessible. This work extends the findings of [1].

This paper investigates the relationship between the average cross section and incident energy for a sequence of 40 spherical nuclei, utilizing the double-folding potential within the optical model. The analysis reveals distinct energy zones where the average cross section remains nearly constant; within these regions, it shows weak dependence on incident energy and nuclear mass, with variations of less than 10%. These findings are compared against predictions from the optical model potential and the semi-empirical formula proposed by Kaul and Singh. Additionally, the study examines the influence of energy and nuclear mass on the average cross section within these specific regions. The results indicate that the double-folding potential offers a more accurate description of the system's behavior in these regions compared to the semi-empirical formula. Our approach involves employing BERT to generate event descriptions from the ATOMIC knowledge graph, which are subsequently fine-tuned using event descriptions as labels to establish a correlation between commonsensical knowledge and question answering. Furthermore, we show that fine-tuning BERT using neural commonplace knowledge graphs derived from BERT itself also yields a substantial performance improvement. Additionally, our analysis of the ATOMIC knowledge graph reveals that question answering performance is closely tied to the specific type of commonsensical knowledge being queried. The Hi-GAL survey utilizes the Herschel Space Observatory to investigate star formation within molecular clouds across far-infrared wavelengths (70, 100, 160, and 250 $\mu$m). To facilitate the analysis of Hi-GAL data, a pipeline was developed to perform data compression, thereby reducing the volume of data required for storage and transfer. This pipeline employs the N2D2 software, which implements the NEMESIS data compression algorithm originally created by the NEMESIS consortium. Following the release of the Hi-GAL survey, the pipeline was refined to accommodate the survey's expanded wavelength range and to enhance the quality of the resulting compressed data. The study presents the characteristics of the newly generated compressed data and compares it against the original uncompressed versions. Results indicate that the compression pipeline achieves a 99% data reduction at the 70 $\mu$m band and 80% reduction at the 160 $\mu$m band, while maintaining a signal-to-noise ratio loss of less than 1%. Furthermore, the impact of compression on the survey's primary scientific objectives is assessed. Finally, the paper details the availability of the Hi-GAL survey data in both uncompressed and compressed formats. The latter is accessible via the Hi-GAL archive at http://www.higal-archive.org/ and the Hi-GAL website at http://www.higal.org/. The pipeline itself is distributed as a standalone executable and can be downloaded from http://www.higal.org/software.html. Additionally, a Python interface is available for users to modify the pipeline and generate custom compressed data. This interface is hosted on the Hi-GAL website at http://www.higal.org/software.html and can be installed via pip using the command: pip install higal. The required dependencies are: numpy, scipy, scikit-image, scikit-learn, and astropy. **Context.** The presence of a metallicity spread within a single stellar population (SSP) is a critical indicator of the early universe's star formation history. However, determining precise metallicity spreads in metal-rich SSPs is challenging due to the degeneracy between metallicity and age in stellar evolution models.

**Aims.** This study aims to precisely determine the abundances of iron and $\alpha$-elements in the metal-rich globular cluster NGC 2808.

**Methods.** We conducted a high-resolution spectroscopic analysis of 10 blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars in NGC 2808, utilizing the MILES spectrograph on the 3.6 m William Herschel Telescope. We employed a self-consistent method to derive abundances, which were subsequently compared to values from the literature.

**Results.** Our findings indicate a metallicity spread of $\Delta$[Fe/H] = 0.12 dex among BHB stars in NGC 2808. Additionally, we observed a significant spread in the [O/Fe] ratio, with $\Delta$[O/Fe] = 0.25 dex.

**Conclusions.** Our results confirm the existence of a SSPP in NGC 2808. The observed spread in [O/Fe] suggests that the cluster's metal enrichment was driven by massive stars with masses exceeding 20 $M_{\odot}$. These findings are consistent with the cluster's two-population structure, where the second population exhibits lower metallicity and an older age. Our analysis reveals a significant spread in the [Mg/Fe] ratio, with $\Delta$[Mg/Fe] = 0.2 dex, though this cannot be definitively attributed to the presence of a second population. Finally, we demonstrate that the spread in [O/Fe] is more accurately reproduced by a scenario involving two distinct star formation episodes rather than a single, continuous episode. This implies that NGC 2808 may also host a second population characterized by a different $\alpha$-element abundance pattern. These results are also consistent with the cluster's blue loop morphology.

This study investigates single-file particle diffusion within a channel featuring two asymmetric walls, each possessing a position-dependent entropy profile. By employing large deviation theory, we characterize the temporal and spatial characteristics of particle displacement during the first exit times. We demonstrate that the entropy profiles of the confining walls generate an effective entropic force, which governs the macroscopic transport of particles. Furthermore, we establish that the moments of the first exit duration diverge at a moment index equal to the spatial dimension of the domain. These findings are validated through extensive Monte Carlo simulations. Our results offer a rigorous theoretical framework for analyzing nonequilibrium transport phenomena in single-file systems. Additionally, the methodology is applicable to a broader range of constrained diffusion scenarios, including biological transport processes. Finally, our work provides a comprehensive analysis of the temporal and spatial properties of first exit times for general single-domain diffusion processes. These insights are essential for characterizing the time-dependent behavior of first passage times, a critical factor in understanding the dynamics of single-file systems. Our findings are supported by rigorous mathematical proofs. This research was conducted as part of the 2022 Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) program at the University of Notre Dame. In the context of inferences drawn from measurements in quantum mechanics, we establish the application of quantum Bayes' rule within probability amplitudes. This approach clarifies the rule's role in the quantum formulation of the Bayes' theorem, which governs inferring the quantum state based on measurement outcomes. Additionally, our findings demonstrate the inherent consistency of inferences resulting from sequential measurements. The methodology and conclusions presented are applicable to the broader domain of quantum information. Furthermore, as an illustrative example, we examine the quantum Bell key distribution protocol, which serves as a practical application of quantum measurement inference. We show that the Bell key distribution rate can be expressed as the difference between the mutual informations associated with two quantum measurement inferences. This relationship offers a new perspective on the connection between the Bell key distribution rate and quantum mutual information. Specifically, it indicates that the Bell key distribution rate is constrained by the mutual information between the quantum state and measurement outcomes, thereby establishing a novel lower bound for the quantum key distribution rate. This result extends the previously established lower bound for quantum key distribution, which was limited to classical key distribution. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Bell key distribution rate can be expressed as the difference between two quantum conditional entropies. This expression is analogous to the expression for the classical secret key rate in one-way secret key agreement, which is defined as the difference between two classical conditional entropies. Consequently, this suggests that the quantum Bell key distribution rate is also bounded by the quantum conditional entropy. These findings provide valuable insights for the development of quantum key distribution protocols. Finally, we discuss the relationship between quantum measurement inference and quantum channel capacity. We observe that the quantum mutual information between the input and output of a quantum channel can be interpreted as the difference between two quantum measurement entropies, analogous to how the mutual information between classical random variables is defined as the difference between two conditional entropies. This observation implies that the quantum mutual information of a quantum channel can be viewed as the quantum equivalent of classical measurement channel capacity. Furthermore, we note that the quantum mutual information of a quantum channel is also constrained by the quantum conditional entropy, a relationship that extends the corresponding classical relationship. These results offer valuable insights for the study of quantum channel capacity. In conclusion, we believe that the framework of quantum measurement inference will prove valuable for future research in quantum information theory. Specifically, we anticipate that this framework will facilitate the development of new quantum information theories and provide new perspectives for investigating quantum measurement, quantum communication, and quantum key distribution. This Letter reports initial findings from a systematic investigation into the thermodynamics of small systems, specifically focusing on the equation of state. We introduce a finite-volume lattice Monte Carlo framework designed to calculate the energy density of hot QCD. Our results demonstrate that significant thermal fluctuations persist even at volumes corresponding to the transverse dimensions of the LHC. Furthermore, we observe that small systems fail to adhere to QCD thermodynamic relations derived for the infinite volume limit, such as those linking energy and pressure density to temperature. These deviations are quantified using the concept of thermalization volume, which marks the scale at which small systems begin to exhibit bulk-like properties. Our analysis indicates that the thermalization volume is approximately 1 fm. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the thermal model, which has been widely applied to analyze hadron yields in high-energy collisions. In this context, the thermalization volume serves as a lower bound for the physical systems examined. We further discuss how the scale of this thermalization volume influences the interpretation of the thermal model's parameters. Additionally, we show that finite-volume effects can be mitigated by employing an improved lattice action that more accurately represents the continuum limit. This approach enables the extraction of thermal properties from significantly smaller systems, thereby reducing statistical uncertainties. Ultimately, we conclude that the finite thermalization volume of QCD must be accounted for when investigating the thermodynamics of small systems. This insight is crucial for understanding the formation of the quark-gluon plasma in small systems and for determining the thermalization mechanisms in high-energy collisions. The code utilized in this study is publicly accessible. Let $H^*(E_*)$ represent the Ext-groups of the Steenrod algebra over the mod-$p$ Cohen-Macaulay algebra $E_*$, where $E_* = \mathbb{F}_p[\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots]$ is a polynomial algebra in the mod-$p$ Steenrod algebra's generators. We demonstrate that for any non-negative integers $a$, $b$, and $c$, the group $H^*(E_*)_{a, b, c}$, defined as the subspace of $H^*(E_*)$ with degree $(a, b, c)$, is non-zero if and only if $a = b = c = 0$. Furthermore, we establish that the group $H^*(E_*)_{a, a, c}$ is finite-dimensional for all $a, c \geq 0$. These findings extend a theorem by Adams and are derived from the structure of the dual of $H^*(E_*)$. Additionally, we provide the explicit form of this dual and a characterization of its generators. We also present an algorithm to identify the dual's generators, which we have applied to the case where $p = 2$ and $a = b = 1$. Finally, we offer a conjecture regarding the dual's generators. The Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) line at 1216 \AA\ serves as a critical tool for studying the early universe, yet observing it is challenging because Earth's atmosphere blocks it completely, and ground-based telescopes cannot reach the required 100 \AA\ wavelength resolution. A potential solution involves space-based instruments equipped with on-orbit repair capabilities. However, the high cost of such systems stems from the need for complex optical designs and extensive wavelength coverage. To address this, we propose a more economical approach: a small Ly$\alpha$ filter combined with a standard optical telescope. This paper presents the design and initial laboratory test results for a prototype filter featuring a 100 \AA\ full width at half maximum (FWHM) centered at 1216 \AA\, utilizing a plasma-based thin-film stack. We demonstrate that this filter can be manufactured with high precision, achieving a final thickness variation of less than 1 \AA\ across a 10 cm diameter. Furthermore, we confirm that the filter meets the design specifications, exhibiting a 100 \AA\ FWHM, a peak transmission of 80%, and a rejection ratio of 1:1000. These findings indicate that a filter of this type is feasible for future Ly$\alpha$ space missions. Additionally, we outline the next steps needed to fully characterize the filter and validate its performance in an actual space environment. This development represents a significant step toward enabling Ly$\alpha$ photometry, spectroscopy, and spectroscopy-imaging in the Lyman ultraviolet region. The filter design and fabrication techniques described here are applicable to other narrowband filters in the vacuum ultraviolet and soft X-ray ranges. This paper introduces a new image indexing approach designed for large, dynamically updated collections of images. The proposed method, called Dynamic Image Pyramid (DIP), is built upon a recent technique known as Quantized Gabor Histograms (QGH). QGH has demonstrated superior performance compared to other indexing methods by effectively balancing image discrimination and compactness. However, QGH is computationally intensive, requiring significant time to calculate the index for each image. To address this, DIP incorporates a pyramid structure that enables the rapid computation of QGH indices. Experimental results indicate that DIP outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, such as QHOG and QHOF, in both discrimination and compactness. Furthermore, the method is highly efficient, allowing for the quick retrieval of the top-10 relevant images from a growing dataset of 100,000 images. This paper introduces a keyless physical layer authentication scheme designed for the Gaussian channel, utilizing a random process characterized by its mean vector and covariance matrix. The transmitter and receiver jointly select a specific set of parameters, known as the identity, which is then encoded into a sequence of mean vectors and covariances. This sequence is transmitted over the air and received with noise. The receiver then calculates the likelihood of the observed noisy sequence under each candidate identity. An identity is deemed authentic if its likelihood exceeds that of every other candidate. We demonstrate that this verification method is reliable and that the probability of false acceptance diminishes as the channel's signal-to-noise ratio increases. Furthermore, we establish that the number of reliable identities grows exponentially with the transmission time, with the exponent determined by the channel's SNR. Finally, we apply this framework to the additive white Gaussian noise channel and provide an information-theoretic analysis of the achievable set of identities. The results indicate that reliable keyless verification is feasible for Gaussian channels when the identity distribution is uniform, with an exponential growth rate in transmission time that is linearly proportional to the SNR. Additionally, we prove that the capacity of the Gaussian channel for this problem is unbounded. These findings are supported by simulations. Our work represents the initial step toward developing a practical physical layer authentication system for the Gaussian channel. The proposed keyless verification approach eliminates the need for a shared secret key, thereby simplifying key management and enhancing system security. Moreover, the identity can be derived from natural random processes, such as channel fluctuations, which are readily available in wireless environments. This enables authentication in scenarios where traditional key-based methods are infeasible, such as when the transmitter and receiver are located in different countries. Finally, the identity can be dynamically updated as transmission time grows, allowing the system to adapt to varying conditions. The paper concludes with a discussion of open research questions. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first attempt to achieve keyless verification in the Gaussian channel. Our findings hold significant potential for practical applications, including the authentication of remote sensors and the secure transmission of data from distant sources. The proposed framework is expected to facilitate the development of more robust and efficient wireless communication systems. We believe that the results presented in this paper will inspire further research in the field of physical layer security. The paper also addresses several open issues, such as the impact of non-Gaussian noise and the possibility of achieving better performance through non-linear processing. We hope that the insights gained from this work will contribute to the advancement of secure wireless communications.

This study examines the dynamics of a Brownian particle within a washboard potential, highlighting the existence of two distinct stationary states: a localized Brownian particle (LBP) and a moving particle (MP). The LBP emerges at low temperatures and high noise levels, whereas the MP is driven by weak thermal fluctuations or noise. The transition between these two regimes is governed by the balance between thermal noise and the particle's self-dispersion noise, which arises from interactions with other particles. This noise-induced motion shares characteristics with deterministic hopping dynamics observed in similar systems. Furthermore, the research identifies conditions under which a third stationary state, termed the bound state (BS), can exist. These findings are validated through both analytical methods and numerical simulations. The proposed model offers a framework for understanding the operation of Brownian motors and could facilitate the design of new devices capable of rectifying fluctuations. Additionally, the insights gained may inform the development of novel sensors and contribute to a deeper understanding of fundamental stochastic processes. Finally, this work holds relevance for both classical and quantum domains, as well as for systems involving active particles. This study presents a flexible local projection framework designed to estimate dynamic responses to impulse shocks. The approach comprises two components: first, a flexible regression method utilizing Bernstein polynomials to model projection coefficients; second, a spectral deconvolution technique applied to the resulting coefficient series to recover impulse responses. We establish both frequentist and Bayesian asymptotic theories to ensure the consistency and asymptotic normality of impulse response estimates. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the proposed method delivers superior finite-sample performance compared to standard alternatives. Finally, we apply the methodology to various economic datasets to examine the impact of monetary and fiscal shocks. The findings indicate that the impulse response estimates are robust across different estimation techniques. Specifically, the impulse purchase power parity (PPP) shock reveals a significant negative short-term effect on output, whereas the impulse government spending shock shows a positive short-term effect on output. Additionally, the impulse tax shock produces a negligible short-term effect on output. These results remain consistent regardless of whether the projections are linear or nonlinear. Finally, we observe that the impulse PPP shock exerts a more pronounced effect on inflation than the impulse government spending shock. These conclusions hold true for both linear and nonlinear projection scenarios. Finally, we conclude that the impulse purchase tax shock has a more significant impact on inflation than the impulse government spending shock. We calculate the angular Casimir torque exerted on a point electric charge within a Landau level by utilizing the difference in the dielectric susceptibility of the Landau plasma between parallel and perpendicular orientations relative to a magnetic field. This phenomenon, known as the angular Casimir effect, arises due to the anisotropy of the plasma's response to electromagnetic fluctuations. Our findings indicate that the angular Casimir torque is proportional to the square of the magnetic field and diminishes rapidly as the Landau level index increases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the angular Casimir force vanishes, thereby confirming the conservation of angular momentum. Additionally, we observe that the angular Casimir torque is significantly smaller than the Ohmic torque generated by an external drive. Finally, we discuss the potential experimental feasibility of detecting this angular Casimir effect. These results offer new insights into the unique response of a Landau plasma to quantum vacuum fluctuations and suggest that the angular Casimir effect could be observed in laboratory settings. Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves identifying and categorizing entities within sentences. While existing methods have achieved significant progress, they often struggle with fine-grained NER due to the high confusion between similar entities. To address this, we introduce FGNET-RH, a novel approach that leverages the inherent properties of hyperbolic space to enhance the discrimination of similar entities. Specifically, we first map word embeddings from a Euclidean space into a hyperbolic space using a transformation network. Subsequently, we propose a refinement network that iteratively updates entity span boundaries by iteratively sampling and aggregating refined embeddings. Finally, we employ a contrastive learning strategy to further optimize the model, ensuring that entities of the same type remain close while those of different types are pushed further apart in hyperbolic space. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-grained NER datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. We introduce a new category of forecasting networks designed to model dynamic systems where the equilibrium depends on exogenous exogenous variables. Leveraging the fact that the equilibrium of a continuous dynamical system constitutes a fixed point of its transition function, we develop Fixed Point Networks (FPNs) capable of forecasting equilibria from regressors. We evaluate FPNs against baseline models on two continuous dynamical systems with regressors: a discrete-time logistic growth model and a continuous-time Lotka-Volterra model. FPNs achieve performance comparable to or superior to the baselines, demonstrating that this approach can effectively forecast equilibria in such systems. Additionally, we extend FPNs to handle the continuous extension of regressors and show that they can accurately predict these extensions. Finally, we apply FPNs to discrete-time economic models, specifically the Solow and Swan growth models, where parameters represent equilibria. The results indicate that FPNs can accurately forecast these parameter values. Overall, FPNs offer a promising method for forecasting equilibria in both mathematical and economic models. The implementation details and experimental code are available at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/Fixed_Point_Networks. For instance, in economics, the steady state of the Solow growth model represents a long-term equilibrium where capital and output stabilize; similarly, in biology, the coexistence equilibrium of the Lotka-Volterra model describes the stable population levels of interacting species. Accurately predicting these equilibria is crucial for understanding system behavior and guiding decision-making. However, many dynamical systems are too complex for analytical solutions, and existing machine learning methods often fail to account for the inherent structure of dynamical systems. This paper aims to address these limitations by proposing a novel approach that respects the underlying structure of the systems being forecasted. Specifically, we consider dynamical systems where equilibria are functions of exogenous parameters. This paper introduces novel upper and lower bounds for causal influence measures defined through do-expressions, a framework for manipulating variables in structural causal models. These bounds rely exclusively on the marginal distributions of the involved variables, remaining independent of the specific causal mechanisms. The methodology is highly general, facilitating the derivation of bounds for various influence metrics, including those based on total variation distance, the Hamming metric, and influence on expectation. Furthermore, the technique is highly scalable, enabling the calculation of these bounds for total variation distance and the Hamming metric across high-dimensional datasets. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to provide bounds without the need to estimate the densities of high-dimensional random variables. The findings are demonstrated through several examples, and a Python library implementing these bounds is made available. The authors intend to utilize this library for feature selection tasks. Additionally, the paper presents a new lower bound for the Hamming metric that is also scalable to high dimensions, which can be applied to assess the stability of random forests. The study concludes with a discussion on the applicability of causal influence measures to high-dimensional data. The authors' intention is to facilitate the development of methods for estimating these bounds within high-dimensional settings. This paper introduces a new algorithm for monitoring linear time-invariant systems against stealthy attacks, designed to operate with minimal computational overhead. The core concept involves modeling the system as a time-varying linear system with unknown inputs, where these inputs are predicted using an extended Kalman filter. A residual is then generated by comparing the system's actual measurements to those estimated by the filter. The authors provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's performance and demonstrate its application as a supplementary monitoring layer alongside traditional Kalman filtering. This additional layer remains undetectable by the attacker while simultaneously offering superior performance in specific scenarios. Finally, the paper validates the proposed method through a numerical case study. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm effectively detects attacks that remain undetected by standard Kalman filters. Furthermore, it highlights that the algorithm's performance is highly sensitive to the initial error covariance matrix, suggesting that adaptive tuning of this parameter could lead to further performance improvements. The case study specifically illustrates how adjusting this parameter can be utilized as a tuning mechanism to enhance detection capabilities. Finally, the study confirms that the algorithm is capable of detecting attacks that do not significantly alter the system's state. Overall, the proposed approach offers a promising solution for monitoring linear time-invariant systems while maintaining stealthiness. Future research will focus on developing methods to adaptively tune the initial error covariance matrix to maximize the algorithm's performance. Additionally, the authors intend to extend this work to time-varying and nonlinear systems, as well as to scenarios involving multiple attackers. The latter extension will require the use of a multiple hypothesis testing framework to identify the specific attack locations. Finally, the paper will explore the application of this algorithm to systems with nonlinear dynamics that are not well-approximated by linear models. In such cases, the residual calculation will need to be modified to account for nonlinearities, potentially by incorporating a nonlinear uncertainty term into the residual definition. This approach will ensure the algorithm's robustness in handling nonlinear systems. The authors will also investigate the use of nonlinear filters to estimate the unknown inputs in these scenarios. Finally, the paper will examine the potential for distributed implementation of the algorithm, which could reduce computational complexity and enable real-time monitoring of large-scale systems. This will involve developing a distributed residual calculation method that combines local measurements from multiple sensors to generate a global residual for attack detection. The authors will also investigate the use of distributed Kalman filters to estimate the unknown inputs in a distributed manner. Summarization is a widely researched task, yet it remains underexplored for low-resource Indian languages. To address this, we introduce GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised, graph-based framework designed to generate summary translations across multiple Indian languages. This approach leverages the cross-lingual capabilities of the pre-trained Graph Attention Encoder (GAE) to derive topic representations from various language encodings. By modeling the relationships between these topics across different languages, we generate summary translations using a topic-based graph. We evaluated our framework on SummEval datasets in Indian languages, demonstrating that it effectively learns to produce summary translations that align with the original English summaries. Furthermore, we show that these generated translations aid the GAE model in summarizing the remaining languages within the graph. Our experiments confirm that GAE-ISumm produces summary translations that maintain high coherence and relevance across all languages in the graph. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Deepak-1998/GAE-ISumm.

The concept of Cohen-type S-rings is introduced, extending the notion of Cohen-type group rings developed by G. Navarro and J. P. Robinson. Robinson finding regarding the order of Cohen-type group rings is generalized to apply to Cohen-type S-rings. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that S-rings of Cohen type represent a strict subset of both metric and locally metric S-rings. The paper concludes with a survey of examples and a series of open questions. A related article will address the automorphism groups of these S-rings. Keywords: S-rings, group rings, Cohen type, metric type, locally metric type, automorphisms. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are a type of generative model that approximate the posterior distribution of latent variables using a variational lower bound. This study introduces a least squares VAE (LS-VAE) that substitutes the standard KL divergence lower bound with a least squares approximation. The LS-VAE is trained via stochastic gradient descent to minimize the squared error between the approximate posterior distribution and the true posterior distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that the LS-VAE achieves superior performance compared to conventional VAEs. Furthermore, the paper investigates the regularization effects of the least squares lower bound, noting that it can mitigate overfitting and enhance the model's generalization capabilities. The authors conclude that the LS-VAE is a potent tool for generating high-quality data and uncovering informative data representations. This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to Gray-coded modulation, leveraging a multi-layer perceptron to assign l-bit long codes to Q-ary symbols. The primary advantage of this method is its ability to enhance the error performance of Gray-coded modulation relative to traditional Q-PAM. Furthermore, the long codes facilitate a reduction in the number of parallel branches required in the demapper, thereby lowering computational complexity. We demonstrate that maintaining the error performance of the system is feasible without increasing the branch count. Additionally, we analyze the impact of the deep learning-based assignment on the branch probabilities within the demapper. Finally, we evaluate the trade-off between error performance and computational complexity by examining the relationship between the code length and the demapper's branch count. Our results indicate that the deep learning-based assignment outperforms conventional Gray coding, particularly when using short codes. However, the advantage diminishes as the code length increases, as shorter codes allow for more effective learning. We also show that the performance gain of the deep learning-based assignment over conventional Gray coding is inversely proportional to the demapper's branch count. Furthermore, we observe that the computational complexity of the demapper is directly proportional to the branch count. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the deep learning-based assignment achieves superior error performance compared to conventional Gray coding while simultaneously reducing the demapper's branch count. These findings suggest that the proposed deep learning-based assignment is particularly advantageous for short codes and low branch-count demappers. Finally, we illustrate that the deep learning-based l-bit code can be derived from an (l+1,n,k,d) cyclic code with d=2. This paper examines the parameterized complexity of the UPWARD PLANARITY problem, which involves determining if a directed acyclic graph can be drawn without edge crossings under a specific geometric constraint. We present a novel parameterized algorithm that runs in $O((k+1)^{O(k)} \cdot n)$ time for UPWARD PLANARITY, achieving $O(n)$ complexity when the number of crossing edges is fixed. Additionally, we develop a straightforward $O(n^{1+1/\Omega(\log\log n)})$-time algorithm for the problem. Finally, we demonstrate that UPWARD PLANARITY is para-NP-complete with respect to the number of upward paths passing through any single vertex. Our para-NP-completeness proof relies on a straightforward para-NP-completeness result for the UPWARD HAMILTONIAN PATH problem, a variant of UPWARD PLANARITY where every edge is assigned a weight of one, and the goal is to decide if a directed acyclic graph contains an upward Hamiltonian path with a total weight not exceeding a given threshold $k$. We establish that UPWARD HAMILTONIAN PATH is para-NP-complete even when the graph is already upward planar. This result contrasts with the fact that UPWARD PLANARITY is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number of crossing edges. Consequently, we conclude that UPWARD HAMILTONIAN PATH is para-NP-complete for UPWARD PLANARITY, thereby resolving a question posed by Bodlaender et al. [BODAENDER ET AL., 2019]. Furthermore, we show that the para-NP-completeness of UPWARD HAMILTONIAN PATH holds even under the stronger condition that the input graph is an upward planar DAG with a maximum degree of three. This finding is particularly striking because UPWARD HAMILTONIAN PATH is solvable in polynomial time for UPWARD PLANAR DAGs with a maximum degree of two. Our para-NP-completeness proof is based on a straightforward reduction from the most general version of 3-SAT. This reduction is also utilized to establish the para-NP-completeness of FEEDBACK VERTEX SET for UPWARD PLANARITY, a problem that is known to be fixed-parameter tractable. This study introduces a novel framework for analyzing noisy, crowdsourced datasets, a method that avoids the need for pre-filtering or post-filtering of individual responses. We propose a technique that assigns a probability distribution to each respondent, thereby quantifying their uncertainty. These distributions are subsequently utilized in an ensemble model to determine the true labels of the items within the crowdsourced data. We have applied this approach to two datasets: a collection of 1,000 emoji items with 1,500 respondent labels, and a collection of 1,000 animal images with 2,000 respondent labels. The ensemble modeling was implemented using a Bayesian approach, which propagates uncertainty from the crowdsourced responses to the final item labels. We demonstrate that this methodology outperforms a baseline that assumes all respondent labels are equally likely. Furthermore, we show that the uncertainty metrics derived from the distribution model can be employed to identify high-quality respondents and to detect and mitigate the impact of specific response patterns. The entire approach is fully non-deterministic, ensuring that the distribution of estimated item labels remains independent of the specific realization of the respondent population. The code required to replicate these results is accessible at https://github.com/brandonjg/emoji-hmm-ensemble. This work introduces a streamlined proof-optimized version of the fractional transfer operator concept, originally developed by Baladi and Gouëzel, to establish spectral properties for semiflows. Specifically, we introduce a novel norm tailored for families of transfer operators associated with semiflows exhibiting sufficient mixing characteristics. This new norm facilitates the spectral gap analysis of semiflows by demonstrating a robust norm decline for the transfer operator family. Furthermore, we apply these findings to the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius theorem for semiflows. As an illustrative example, we examine the Birkhoff-Sinai shift semiflow on the space of measures, proving the spectral gap for the Riesz potential kernel of the transfer operator family. The proof relies on the established exponential mixing property of the shift semiflow and the norm decline of the transfer operator family. Additionally, we outline a general strategy for analyzing the spectral gap of semiflows by decomposing the norm decline of the transfer operator family into two components: the norm decline of the operator family and the singularities of the kernel. This approach is demonstrated through an analysis of the transfer operator kernel for the shift semiflow. Finally, we discuss the spectral gap of the shift semiflow on the space of measures, deriving it from the norm decline of the transfer operator family and the Riesz potential's transfer operator kernel. This methodology extends the norm decline concept to general semiflows and offers a foundational framework for investigating the spectral gap of semiflows. The paper concludes with a discussion on the spectral gap of the shift semiflow. Notably, the shift semiflow's transfer operator kernel is the Riesz potential, whose transfer operator kernel is the Riesz kernel. We demonstrate that the norm of the transfer operator family for the Riesz potential does not decline, thereby implying that the shift group lacks a spectral gap when acting on measures. This result aligns with the well-established fact that the shift group is amenable. Consequently, our findings offer a novel approach to studying the spectral gap of semiflows by analyzing the norm decline of their transfer operator families. This research was inspired by the norm decline of transfer operators for hyperbolic semiflows, as detailed in the author's prior work. The paper also addresses the norm decline of transfer operator families for geodesic flows on hyperbolic surfaces and the linearized Poincaré map of geodesic flows on negatively curved manifolds. A decision problem is classified as local if it can be resolved by examining only a bounded subset of the input. This paper investigates the locality of specific problems concerning nonlocal games, defined as scenarios where two parties, Alice and Bob, utilize shared randomness and a quantum state to maximize their winning probabilities in a challenge posed by a third party, Charlie. We demonstrate that for a broad class of games involving noisy maximally correlated states, there exists a finite subset of strategies sufficient to determine optimality; consequently, these games are local. Our approach relies on a general theorem establishing the equivalence between the local nature of a problem and the finiteness of a specific set, which we apply to the games under consideration. Furthermore, we extend this result to a more general category of noisy states, provided they do not asymptotically approach a maximally correlated state. Finally, we contrast these findings with recent research indicating that localism in nonlocal games is undecidable in general, thereby highlighting the unique properties of the specific class of states addressed in this work. The methods employed are also relevant to other decision problems within quantum information theory. Additionally, our proof technique offers an alternative derivation of the nonlocality of the PR box. As a corollary, we establish that determining the optimal value for the CHSH game is local, and more broadly, that local optimization is feasible for all nonlocal games based on maximally correlated states. This confirms a conjecture by Bravyi, which posits that the local nature of a decision problem is contingent upon the quantum state employed. Our findings also imply that the local nature of such problems remains invariant under small perturbations of the state. In the appendix, we explore the implications of these results for the local nature of the $k$-local separability problem. Specifically, we show that for noisy maximally correlated states, $k$-local separability is local, whereas for noisy Bell diagonal states, it is undecidable. This resolves an open question regarding the local nature of this problem. The paper also addresses the local nature of the NCS problem, which involves maximizing the expectation value of noisy maximally correlated states over separable states. We prove that $k$-local optimality in the NCS problem is equivalent to $k$-local separability. Additionally, we establish that $k$-local optimality in the NCS problem is undecidable, even when the input is restricted to noisy Bell diagonal states. This study aims to validate the efficacy of Genetic Algorithms (GA) in crash reproduction. To achieve this, we performed a guided GA-based automated crash reproduction on Jupyter Notebook applications, utilizing the same application, crashes, and GA implementation from the original paper. Our findings indicate that GA effectiveness is contingent upon the specific application and crashes under investigation, as well as the efficiency of the fitness function and the quality of the guiding information provided. Additionally, we observed that GA performance can be enhanced by increasing the population size and the number of generations. However, these improvements are not guaranteed for all scenarios, as they may be hindered by the specific GA configuration, the fitness function, or the application's inherent characteristics. Consequently, we recommend that future research explore alternative methods for automated crash reproduction, such as symbolic execution, to further evaluate their utility. This partial replication is intended to assist researchers in assessing the reproducibility of the GA-based approach and to facilitate the investigation of other techniques in automated crash reproduction. We present the initial direct visualization of the vortex lattice within a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductor, specifically YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.95}$, utilizing scanning SQUID microscopy. By examining the vortex arrangement across various magnetic fields, we identified experimental proof of a square-square grid transition, a phenomenon previously documented only in underdoped cuprates via indirect methods. This study marks the first observation of such a transition in an optimally doped cuprate through direct imaging. Furthermore, the measured vortex densities align with London theory predictions, and the detected vortex mobility offers new insights into the nature of vortex interactions. These findings collectively indicate that the vortex-vortex interaction in optimally doped YBCO follows a $1/r$ potential, consistent with a square grid. Additionally, the observed transition is corroborated by the shift from a single vortex row to two rows as the vortex density increases. These results suggest that the emergence of the second vortex row serves as a direct indicator of the square-square grid transition. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the mechanism driving the square-square grid transition. Our analysis suggests that the transition is not a manifestation of the nematic phase, which is typically associated with the pseudogap phase in underdoped cuprates. Instead, we propose that the transition is governed by the competition between elastic and magnetic energies of the vortex lattice. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the transition occurs at a magnetic field of approximately 0.15 $H_{c2}$, a value consistent with theoretical predictions. We also address the potential impact of substrate-induced strain on the vortex grid and the associated vortex row transition. Overall, our findings suggest that strain does not play a significant role in the square-square grid transition in YBCO. These conclusions are reinforced by the direct imaging of individual vortices and the identification of the second vortex row. The successful direct observation of the square-square grid transition in optimally doped YBCO provides valuable insights into the mechanism behind this transition. We conclude that the vortex grid transition in YBCO is driven by the competition between elastic and magnetic energies, rather than the pseudogap phase or strain effects. This conclusion is consistent with the nematic phase, which is typically observed in underdoped cuplates. Our findings provide a deeper understanding of the vortex grid transition in YBCO and offer new insights into the mechanisms driving this transition. We investigate the anisotropic flow of thermal photons generated during the hadronization and subsequent thermalization of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) as it expands. Our findings indicate that the photon anisotropy coefficient $v_1$ exhibits a distinct dependence on transverse momentum $p_T$ compared to hadrons, offering a unique signature for future experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the photonic $v_2$ signal is particularly sensitive to the QGP's shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio $\eta/s$, with the optimal $p_T$ window for this analysis lying between 1 and 2 GeV. This research is especially pertinent to the ALICE detector at the LHC, which is scheduled to upgrade its photon detection capabilities. The new system will feature an extended acceptance and enhanced energy resolution, enabling the precise study of $v_2$ at low $p_T$ for the first time. Additionally, we examine the potential for detecting a momentum gap in the $v_2$ signal, a phenomenon predicted by theoretical models. Such a gap would serve as a critical test of thermalization models and could help differentiate between signals originating from the QGP and those from hadronization. Our results underscore the necessity of simultaneous measurements of both photon and hadron flow coefficients to achieve a precise extraction of the QGP's $\eta/s$. This study is part of the Photon RHIC Initiative (PPI), a collaborative effort between the ALICE collaboration and the USPHINCS community. The PPI aims to develop a theoretical framework for interpreting photon measurements from future high-energy heavy-ion collisions, thereby advancing our understanding of the QGP's transport properties. The framework will be implemented using the open-source THERMINATOR3 event generator. We have also made our code publicly available to support the PPI's objectives. We conducted a comprehensive study of magnetic ordering in three-dimensional triangular and kagome lattices using the continuous spin Ising model, which is defined by the constraint that the sum of squared components of interacting spins equals a constant. Our analysis of the kagome lattice revealed that the 120-degree antiferromagnetic state, previously identified in the fully symmetric $D_6$ phase, remains stable across a broad range of other symmetries. Furthermore, we identified additional distinct magnetic states, including a novel 60-degree antiferromagnetic phase and two unique ferromagnetic configurations. In contrast to the rich variety found in the kagome lattice, the dimensional reduction of the cubic triangular lattice to a two-dimensional triangular form yields only two distinct magnetic states: the aforementioned 60-degree antiferromagnet and a ferromagnetic phase. These findings are supported by exact numerical simulations and the Landau expansion of free energy. Additionally, we examined the influence of the constant in the spin component square sum on the magnetic phases of the triangular lattice. Our results indicate that the fully symmetric ferromagnetic state is unstable under the constraint, and we observed a first-order phase transition between the 60-degree and 120-degree antiferromagnetic phases. Finally, we demonstrated that applying a weak external magnetic field can induce transitions between these various magnetic states. This research holds significant potential for the study of magnetic phases in triangular and kagome lattices. Keywords: Dimensionality reduction, continuous spin Ising model, triangular lattice, kagome lattice, Landau expansion. PACS numbers: 75.10.Hk, 75.40.Mg, 75.45.-j, 75.10.b.

This paper introduces a new framework for the large-scale identification of treatment effects, grounded in a historical dataset that includes experimental units receiving various treatments alongside some controls. We establish a nonparametric model for the joint distribution of outcomes and covariates across all units, leveraging historical observations of units with the same treatment-covariate profiles to identify the distribution of treatment effects for units sharing those profiles. This approach enables a data-driven selection of units with potentially significant effects while maintaining a false discovery rate (FDR) below a pre-specified threshold $\alpha$. We provide an asymptotic error rate guarantee for the proposed selection procedure and demonstrate its application in identifying personalized treatment effects within large-scale educational experiments. Furthermore, we extend this method to allow for FDR control under weak dependence among selected units, a condition that encompasses both independence and mild dependence scenarios. Our simulation study illustrates the utility of this proposed approach. Finally, we apply the method to identify units with potentially significant treatment effects using data from a large-scale online advertising experiment. The analysis reveals that units with a higher propensity to click on the control advertisement are more likely to exhibit a positive treatment effect. Additionally, we show that the proposed FDR control method remains valid even when the number of covariates is large. These findings underscore the value of historical data in large-scale experiments for enhancing future experimental designs and enabling more precise inferences regarding treatment effects. This study examines the type-X two-Higgs-doublet model as a potential explanation for both the muon $g-2$ anomaly and the $W$ boson mass discrepancy. We derive the constraints imposed by the Fermi constant measurement, muon $g-2$, and $W$ boson mass, alongside the condition that the scalar mass matrix remains positive definite. Our analysis reveals that while the $W$ mass constraint is stringent, it can be relaxed by incorporating a tree-level contribution from charged scalar particles to the Fermi constant measurement. Furthermore, we identify a viable region satisfying all constraints, with best-fit parameters yielding a charged scalar mass of approximately 100 GeV and a scalar mixing angle of about 0.1. This scenario predicts a Higgs boson mass near 125 GeV, consistent with LHC observations. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this scenario for branching ratios and production cross-sections at the LHC, as well as the production cross-sections for heavy scalars at a future muon collider. Finally, we present the most significant implications of this scenario for various flavor physics observables. Notably, the type-X 2HDM accommodates a large enhancement in $B \to D^{(*)}\tau^+\tau^-$ decays, driven by a large $\tau$ Yukawa coupling, a feature also present in type-I and type-II 2HDMs. However, this model predicts a substantial suppression in $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$, a prediction that conflicts with current experimental data. Consequently, we conclude that the type-X 2HDM is disfavored as a unified explanation for the muon $g-2$ and $W$ mass anomalies. Nevertheless, if the $W$ mass anomaly is disregarded, the model remains a promising candidate for explaining the muon $g-2$ anomaly. Software developers frequently encounter requirements to restructure software, a process that is both costly and time-intensive. Consequently, there is a significant demand for automated techniques that can reduce these expenses and the effort required. This paper introduces QUICKAR, a novel approach that automatically reformulates inquiries to leverage crowdsourced knowledge for locating concepts. QUICKAR utilizes a two-stage pipeline: the first stage employs a neural network to extract semantic features from inquiry text, while the second stage utilizes a neural sequence-to-sequence model to generate reformulated queries based on these features and crowdsourced data. We evaluated QUICKAR's capability to accurately reformulate inquiries using a newly developed dataset, QuickarQ, which comprises over 1,000 inquiries along with their reformulations and effectiveness labels. Our results demonstrate that QUICKAR significantly surpasses baseline methods in accuracy, thereby laying a foundation for future research aimed at integrating these reformulations into automated concept location systems. The QuickarQ dataset will be made available to support further research in this domain. The source code for QUICKAR can be accessed at https://github.com/quickar/quickar. Entrainment represents a vital social-communicative mechanism where speakers subtly mimic one another's vocal qualities, such as pitch, speaking rate, and lexical choices, to foster rapport. This paper introduces a novel, unsupervised deep neural network-based metric designed to quantify the likelihood of entrainment. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the metric's performance across multiple dimensions, including speaker consistency in various acoustic features, speaking speed, and conversational turn-taking. Furthermore, we validate the metric's efficacy by assessing its ability to distinguish between natural and artificially constructed dialogues. Our findings indicate that the proposed metric achieves state-of-the-art results in detecting entrained behavior within conversational speech. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Entrainment-Metric}. Our results demonstrate that this metric offers a robust and effective approach for measuring entrained vocal behaviors in spoken dialogue systems. Additionally, we suggest that the metric's robustness and effectiveness make it a promising tool for evaluating conversational abilities in large language models. We anticipate that this metric will be a valuable resource for researchers studying entrained behavior in conversational speech. The source code can be found at \url{https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Entrainment-Metric}. We hope this tool will assist researchers in analyzing entrained vocal behaviors within conversational speech. Imaging spectroscopy is a powerful technique for analyzing the chemical and physical characteristics of materials. The growing availability of spectral imaging data has created a demand for web-based tools that allow researchers to interactively visualize both spatial (imaging) and spectral dimensions. This paper introduces the second version of the Remote-sensing Community Driven Image Visualization Tools (RCSEDv2), a suite of open-source web applications built using the OpenSeadragon and D3.js libraries. These tools enable the visualization of spectral data cubes, offering users control over spectral axes, spectral intervals, and the selection of specific spatial locations. Additionally, RCSEDv2 includes a tool for exploring two-dimensional spectral data sets, where users can select specific wavelengths. The software is freely accessible online at http://rcsed.org. The source code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/RCSED, and the project is managed via GitLab at https://gitlab.com/RCSED. Contributions, including bug reports and feature suggestions, are welcome. Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is a critical computer vision task that involves identifying and segmenting temporal boundaries for various actions within videos. While deep learning has driven significant advancements in TAS, it remains dependent on annotated data. To address this limitation, we introduce SSCAP, an unsupervised TAS framework designed to learn representative features and segmentations without annotations. SSCAP utilizes a self-supervised representation learning module alongside a self-supervised co-occurrence action analysis module. The representation learning component captures video features through a contrastive loss function, while the co-occurrence analysis module derives action knowledge from these features to generate predictions. We evaluate SSCAP's performance on two public datasets, UCF101-24 Frames and HMDB51-24 Frames, under both single-label and multi-label settings. Experimental results demonstrate that SSCAP achieves competitive performance compared to supervised methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/SSCAP. Additionally, our dataset can be found at https://drive.google.

Furthermore, we examine the decay $\Sigma_c^{(*)} \to P_{cJ} \, D^{(*)}$, which offers a pathway to access these states. We predict that the pentaquark multiplet will be observable in the decays of $\Sigma_c^{(*)}$ baryons at LHCb. Additionally, we estimate the production cross sections for these states in the reaction $\gamma^*\, p \to P_{cJ} \, \bar{D}^{(*)}$, suggesting that the resulting signal could be detected at the EIC. Finally, we address the issue of mixing between the pentaquark multiplet and the conventional baryon decuplet. This study represents the initial attempt to investigate pentaquark production and decay within the current algebra formalism. Consequently, our findings should be considered preliminary, and we hope they will inspire further research into pentaquark states using this approach. This study introduces a new pedagogical approach for teaching software testing, termed Inquiry-Based Conceptual Feedback (IBC), which utilizes the same testing techniques as traditional methods but differs in how it delivers results to students. Unlike conventional tools that provide detailed, line-by-line feedback on specific issues, IBC offers high-level, conceptual guidance on the overall quality of the testing strategy. This research reports on an empirical study comparing the learning outcomes of these two feedback mechanisms. The study involved 120 undergraduate students divided into three groups: one receiving IBC, another receiving traditional detailed feedback, and a third with no feedback. Participants were tasked with developing test cases for a provided Java program. The findings indicate that IBC is as effective as traditional detailed feedback in teaching software testing concepts. Furthermore, the authors hypothesize that IBC offers additional benefits, such as fostering independent learning and reducing student stress. The paper concludes by outlining potential future applications of IBC within the software testing education curriculum. IBC is currently being utilized in the Java Testing Lab, an online environment designed to facilitate testing education. This lab is publicly accessible at http://www.cs.technion.ac.il/~davidg/testinglab/ and is available for download. The authors invite researchers and educators to explore the tool's potential for enhancing software testing education. Additional details regarding the tool and its application can be found in the paper's supplementary materials. The authors thank the students who volunteered for this study. David Grossman's work was partially funded by the Technion V.P. of Research and Administration Research Fund. Finally, the authors extend their gratitude to the anonymous reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions.

Domain adaptation is a widely adopted strategy for addressing label scarcity across different source and target domains. However, most existing methods rely on a fixed source domain, a constraint that limits their applicability in real-world scenarios where access to the source data is often restricted. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) framework that utilizes unlabeled datasets from both the source and target domains. Specifically, we propose a novel framework termed Shifted Semi-Supervised SFDA (HSS-SFDA), which leverages hypothesis shifts to guide domain alignment. This approach employs domain alignment losses to minimize distribution shifts between domains and employs a hypothesis shift operator to enhance feature discrimination. Furthermore, we develop a domain-invariant feature learning method that integrates both local and global information from both domains. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art SFDA methods across various datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1998/SFDA.

This paper outlines the fundamental concepts of a gas core engine, detailing its core architecture and control mechanisms. We demonstrate that this system offers superior specific impulse compared to solid-core engines while maintaining a dry mass only marginally higher. Furthermore, we illustrate that the dry mass of a single-stage-to-orbit vehicle utilizing a gas core engine is nearly identical to that of a chemical rocket with a high specific impulse. The analysis concludes by emphasizing the critical need for high-temperature materials and the potential for nuclear fusion to serve as the engine's power source. Additionally, we highlight that the feasibility of this concept hinges on advancements in high-temperature materials, specifically requiring a material capable of withstanding approximately 3000 K. Finally, we note that the concept was originally proposed by General Electric in the 1950s. We also present a preliminary estimate of the specific impulse for a fusion-based gas core engine, which is roughly 1000 seconds. This paper is intended to provide a foundational understanding of the concept and to outline the technical challenges associated with its realization. We believe this study will inspire further research and development efforts aimed at bringing the gas core concept to fruition. Neutrino and cosmic-ray observatories are rapidly expanding, necessitating the precise localization of particle interactions to facilitate data analysis and background rejection. This study introduces a domain-informed neural network architecture designed for interaction positioning, utilizing only reconstructed charged particle tracks captured by optical sensors. The method's efficacy is evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations of optical signals generated by 300 keV electron excitations from 6 GeV neutrino interactions within the IceCube experiment's detector volume. The proposed approach surpasses recent machine learning methods by achieving a 30% reduction in position uncertainty. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this domain-informed framework can be readily extended to analyze experimental data. Specifically, we apply the method to publicly available OpenData from the IceCube 2014A live data period, achieving a 20% improvement in interaction positioning accuracy compared to the reconstruction software's default performance. These findings indicate that domain-informed neural networks constitute a highly effective tool for future observatory analysis pipelines.
