Atmospheric retrievals for exoplanets and brown dwarfs necessitate extensive databases of line lists and cross sections for molecules like H2O, CO, CO2, CH4, and NH3. These resources are typically sourced from diverse origins, often tailored to specific retrieval frameworks, creating a fragmented landscape. We introduce EXOPLINES, a unified archive of cross sections for H2O, CO, CO2, CH4, and NH3, designed to be compatible with both the TauREx retrieval framework and the Molecfit line list. This paper outlines the structure of EXOPLINES, which is accessible at https://github.com/astro-berkeley/Exoplines. The authors intend to expand the database with additional molecular cross sections in the future. EXOPLINES will be updated regularly to incorporate new data and corrections, with the most recent version available at https://github.com/astro-berkeley/Exoplines/tree/main. We encourage the community to utilize EXOPLINES to ensure consistency across retrieval studies. Furthermore, we plan to integrate EXOPLINES into the TauREx framework to streamline the retrieval process for researchers. This initiative aims to harmonize the field and facilitate more comprehensive and accurate interpretations of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres. This work investigates the relationship between classical logic programming and answer list programming, introducing a declarative method to transform answer list programs into programs utilizing negation as failure. We subsequently examine the relationship between answer list programs and ground programs, which are defined as those containing no negation as failure rules. Our primary contribution is a constructive procedure that defines a surjective mapping from the set of all ground programs to the set of all answer list programs, where each ground program maps to itself and every answer list program is mapped to by at least one ground program. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this mapping preserves both the semantics and the computational complexity of the programs involved. These findings are achieved through the application of normal form transformations and the execution of specific algorithmic procedures. Finally, we illustrate the application of this mapping with several examples. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. The proposed mapping serves as a valuable instrument for analyzing the semantics and computational complexity of answer list programs, as well as for developing new procedures and algorithms within this domain. Additionally, it provides a framework for investigating the relationship between classical and answer list programming, which can facilitate the advancement of classical logic programming. We establish the law of mass action for general quantum resource theories, defining resources as states deviating from free states by specific relative entropy measures. This law characterizes the maximal rate at which free operations can generate excess resource, a phenomenon analogous to chemical equilibrium. We further demonstrate connections to quantum hypothesis testing and introduce a generalization of the free energy known as "free work." These insights are extended to many-body systems through thermodynamic limits, resulting in a quantum version of the initial law of mass action. Consequently, we derive many-body properties of thermal states from pure-state laws and establish the first resource-theoretic properties of thermal states. Notably, we prove that the free work of a thermal state equals its free energy, thereby generalizing Gibbs' theorem. Additionally, we examine many-body resource theories for various resource measures, including relative entropy, hypothesis testing relative entropy, and free energy. This framework offers a novel perspective on quantum thermodynamics, laying the groundwork for future investigations into resource theories for many-body systems. Specifically, we introduce many-body resource measures that extend concepts such as entanglement, entanglement entropy, and entanglement of formation. Finally, we discuss applications of these findings to quantum resource theories for randomness and coherence.

We introduce a new framework designed to estimate the integral of a function using the same integral expressed as a function of its moments. This method is applicable to a wide range of functions, provided their moments exhibit sufficient decay. Our findings include error bounds, a discussion on sufficient versus necessary conditions for the bounds to hold, and an analysis of the convergence rate of the approximations. We also present a procedure for determining appropriate cutoff points for both the input function and its moment-based representation. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through several examples, including the approximation of the Riemann zeta function, the error function, and the cumulative normal distribution. Furthermore, we extend the approach to functions of multiple variables and develop an algorithm that enables users to interactively explore the method with functions of up to two variables. This algorithm is implemented in Python and accessible via a web interface. The method is illustrated using functions of one and two variables, with the two-variable examples available through the provided link. Our results indicate that the approximations converge rapidly, with the number of terms required to achieve a specified error tolerance being significantly lower than the number of terms needed for equivalent accuracy when evaluating the function directly. Additionally, we demonstrate that these approximations extend the domain of the functions beyond their original definition. The Python code used to generate our results is publicly available. We anticipate that this method will be valuable for researchers in mathematics, physics, and the physical sciences who deal with functions of one or two variables. We believe that the insight gained from our methodology will inspire the development of analogous methods for functions of higher dimensions. Our methodology is particularly well-suited for applications where high precision is essential. We have applied this method to evaluate the error function and the cumulative normal distribution to 100 decimal places, a level of precision that is difficult to achieve through conventional methods. This paper introduces a novel framework for multivariate time series analysis featuring heavy tails and time-varying parameters. We develop a new class of time series models capable of capturing these characteristics and establish their asymptotic properties. Furthermore, we propose a two-stage estimation approach: the initial stage employs a self-consistent estimator, while the final stage refines this using a maximum likelihood estimator. The study demonstrates the asymptotic behavior of the final estimator and provides simulation results to validate the method's performance. Notably, we demonstrate that the final estimator achieves the same asymptotic properties as a maximum likelihood estimator under fixed parameter conditions, thereby confirming its efficiency. Additionally, we find that the two-stage estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal even when parameters are time-varying, although it exhibits a reduced convergence rate compared to the fixed parameter case. We also discuss the method's applicability to both finite- and infinite-dimensional linear non-stationary models. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this approach through a case study analyzing the daily returns of the S&P500 index. The results indicate that time-varying parameter models offer superior performance compared to those with fixed parameters. Furthermore, we observe that the time-varying parameter GARCH model outperforms the fixed parameter version in terms of both model fit and forecasting accuracy. This research extends our previous work (Zhang et al., 2021) to the multivariate context. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the framework and model; Section 3 presents the main theoretical results; Section 4 applies the methodology to the S&P500 index; and Section 5 compares the proposed model with several alternatives. The remainder of the paper is organized into five sections. Section 6 contains all proofs, and Section 7 concludes the study. The authors thank the editor, associate editor, and referee for their constructive comments, which have been incorporated into this version. Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are extensively utilized in practical communication systems due to their efficient decoding capabilities. However, existing quantum LDPC codes face a trade-off: they either possess a constant rate or check rate but suffer from linear decoding complexity, or they achieve linear rate and check rate but maintain constant decoding complexity. This paper introduces a family of quantum LDPC codes that combine a linear rate, linear check rate, linear distance, and linear decoding complexity. Specifically, for a block length of $n$, these codes achieve a rate of $\Omega(n^{-1/3})$ with a check rate of $\Theta(n^{-2/3})$ and a distance of $\Omega(n^{1/3})$. The decoding complexity is $O(n)$, and the decoder operates with linear speed, meaning it can correct any error pattern with weight up to $d/2$ within $O(n)$ time. Furthermore, the decoder exhibits sublinear latency, completing each time step in $O(1)$ time. To achieve this, we employ a modified version of the minimum weight perfect matching decoder, utilizing a new data structure for graph representations and an enhanced breadth-first search algorithm. Additionally, we demonstrate that these quantum LDPC codes are locally testable, enabling efficient detection of any local error pattern. This local testability is realized through a constant-depth decision circuit, further reducing both circuit depth and latency. Our proposed data structure and modified decoder are applicable to any LDPC code, offering a general framework for enhancing decoding efficiency. Experimental results indicate that our method improves both runtime and latency compared to the original minimum weight perfect matching decoder. Our construction relies on a specific class of bipartite graphs known as expander graphs, which are also integral to various other quantum LDPC code families. Consequently, our data structure and modified decoder can benefit these related codes as well. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first instance of quantum LDPC codes achieving linear rate, linear distance, and linear decoding complexity. Our work advances the state of the art in quantum LDPC code design and holds significant potential for practical implementation. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1999/gqldpc}. The implementation is open-source and can be integrated into existing LDPC decoder libraries. This study addresses the challenge of identifying a distance-$r$ dominating group with the minimum cardinality within high-girth graphs through distributed computation. We introduce a distributed algorithm capable of resolving this problem on sparse graphs that possess a high enough girth to prevent short cycles. The method leverages the graph's local tree-like topology to enable distance-$r$ dominating group selection based on node degrees and the attributes of their neighbors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distributed outcomes are identical to those produced by a centralized algorithm, which is significant for verifying distributed solutions. Our proposed algorithm operates in $O(r)$ rounds, and the communication complexity per round is $O(\log n)$ bits, contingent upon the node identifier size. Additionally, we establish that the distributed algorithm achieves a constant approximation ratio. The findings presented in this paper are applicable to both undirected and directed graphs. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a distributed algorithm that resolves the distance-$r$ dominating group problem in high-girth graphs with minimal redundancy, thereby addressing a significant challenge in distributed graph problems. This problem is particularly relevant for large-scale graphs, such as social networks, where global information is unavailable to individual nodes. We investigate topological characteristics of disordered higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs) by employing a bulk-surface correspondence. Specifically, we demonstrate that the surface states of bulk 2D HOTIs are topologically equivalent to the boundary states of non-interacting surface 1D topological insulators. Furthermore, the topological invariants of surface 2D topological insulators (TIs) are shown to dictate the topological nature of bulk HOTIs. Finally, the localization of surface states in disordered systems is analyzed, revealing that the surface states of bulk 2D HOTIs exhibit distinct topological behaviors compared to those of surface 1D TIs. These findings are corroborated by explicit numerical simulations. Our results offer a novel perspective on bulk-surface correspondence within higher-order topological insulators. Additionally, the methodology employed can be extended to other topological systems. This work is based on the paper: J. Li, Y. Liu, and S. Zhang, \textit{Phys. Rev. B} \textbf{104}, 045403 (2021). This article presents the latest experimental findings from the CMS experiment at the LHC, specifically within the framework of the Supersymmetric Standard Model. These results have been achieved using a proton-proton dataset with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV. We provide an in-depth overview of the analyses conducted to search for supersymmetric phenomena, including squark and gluino pair production, gluino decay into various neutralinos, neutralino pair production, and neutralino decays into the Higgs boson. Furthermore, we examine the recent CMS results on Higgs boson production and their implications for supersymmetry. This discussion is followed by an outlook on upcoming CMS searches for supersymmetry, which will leverage the full 13 TeV data set. Finally, we highlight the potential of the High-Luminosity LHC to explore the rich and extensive supersymmetric parameter space. We introduce a neural radiance field technique designed to automatically synthesize high-quality, view-dependent images from a sparse collection of in-focus scene captures. Our method leverages the scene's in-focus information by employing a differentiable focus loss to optimize a novel 3D focus map, which is subsequently utilized to render novel views. We demonstrate that this proposed differentiable focus loss is effective in training high-quality focus maps. Our technique is highly versatile and can be integrated with various neural rendering approaches, including those based on differentiable rendering and those utilizing neural point clouds. We validate our method's efficacy by presenting superior quantitative results and qualitative comparisons against existing techniques across multiple datasets. Furthermore, we show that the method can successfully reconstruct complex scenes, such as those containing moving objects. We introduce a new class of non-local conserved charges for three-dimensional Yang-Mills theory, grounded in the Witten diagram expansion of tree-level amplitudes on the celestial sphere. These charges adhere to the chiral algebra structure of Minkowski space and possess a spectrum with an infinite multiplicity of states sharing identical helicity and momentum. We demonstrate that, when expressed in light-cone coordinates, the equations of motion for these charges correspond exactly to the tree-level Yang-Feldman equations. This finding establishes a novel chiral subsector of Yang-Mills theory, termed "hue space," which exhibits kinematic duality with standard momentum space. This study investigates the general two Higgs doublet model, specifically analyzing its capacity to address recent flavor anomalies and the $(g-2)_\mu$ puzzle. We establish that the general framework can indeed accommodate these discrepancies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model's parameter space is sufficiently broad to simultaneously satisfy the Standard Model predictions for $R_{K^{(*)}}$, $R_{J/\psi}$, and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Our analysis reveals that the general model is highly flexible, allowing for a wide range of scenarios to fit the likelihood of these flavor anomalies. Additionally, we find that the model can significantly enhance the Higgs diphoton rate, with the best fit occurring at approximately $1.3$ times the Standard Model value. We also examine the potential for the general model to resolve the $R_{D^{(*)}}$ anomaly and the current $a_\mu$ discrepancy, noting that the best fit for $a_\mu$ corresponds to a value roughly $6.5$ times the Standard SM prediction. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future collider experiments. In conclusion, the general two Higgs doublet model remains a viable candidate for explaining the observed flavor anomalies and the $(g-2)_\mu$ problem. However, we emphasize that the general model is less constrained than its type-II variant, resulting in a much broader parameter space and consequently weaker predictions. This lack of tight constraints makes it difficult to derive specific predictions for other observables, such as the branching ratio $\text{Br}(h\to\gamma\gamma)$. Nevertheless, we have shown that the general model can still accommodate the latest flavor data and the $(g-2)_\mu$ result, suggesting that the general model is a promising candidate for new physics beyond the Standard Model. Future measurements of the Higgs sector and flavor observables will be crucial in determining whether the general model can indeed explain the current flavor anomalies and the $(g-2)_\mu$ problem. In particular, the upcoming measurement of $\text{Br}(h\to\gamma\gamma)$ at the HL-LHC will provide a more precise determination of this observable, which could help to distinguish between the different two Higgs doublet models. If the measured value of $\text{Br}(h\to\gamma\gamma)$ deviates significantly from the Standard Model prediction, it would provide strong evidence for the existence of new physics, such as the general two Higgs doublet model. This study introduces a new methodology for simulating two-dimensional incompressible Euler vortices by employing a functional stochastic differential equation (FSDE). Vortex motion is modeled as a non-linear, non-elliptic, functional, and non-Markovian random process. The proposed algorithm utilizes a novel stochastic integration technique for FSDEs, which offers superior accuracy and efficiency compared to conventional numerical methods for solving the method of ring regularization. Furthermore, the simulation results align well with direct numerical simulations. This work represents the inaugural application of FSDEs to simulate two-dimensional incompressible Euler vortices. Additionally, the article explores the mathematical implications of this approach by examining the relationship between FSDEs and the method of ring regularization. The findings suggest that FSDEs may serve as a new mathematical framework for simulating two-dimensional incompressible Euler vortices. Finally, the paper discusses potential future research directions, including the development of a comprehensive mathematical theory for FSDEs and their application to other areas of fluid dynamics. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/FSDE. The corresponding author is Chen Yi. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to be efficiently executed by quantum devices but difficult for classical machines. This study examines the entanglement within the output states of this model. We demonstrate that the average entanglement of the full state vector scales linearly with the number of modes, exhibiting a distinct dependence on mode entanglement. Furthermore, we establish a connection between entanglement and the distinguishability of bosonic particles, revealing that the two are not simply proportional. Finally, we explore the potential for extracting information about boson sampling outputs through measurements performed on subsystems. These findings offer valuable insights into the information-theoretic characteristics of boson sampling outputs and suggest new avenues for investigating the model's properties. Additionally, the research methods employed can be applied to other quantum computational models. The data and code supporting this work are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/BosonSamplingEntanglement. The source code is written in Python. The Python package `qutip` was utilized for quantum state and dynamical simulations, while `numpy` handled numerical computations. The `matplotlib` package was used for data visualization. All computational tasks were performed on a personal computer equipped with an Intel Core i7-10700 CPU and 16.0 GB of RAM. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Temporal data, characterized by its sequential and time-dependent nature, is frequently encountered in scientific research. However, temporal sequences are often brief and high-dimensional, posing significant challenges for analysis. This study focuses on analyzing time-series data from electrophysiological recordings of neuronal activity in the *Drosophila* brain. We introduce a method that leverages prior knowledge regarding the temporal dimension to enhance learning efficiency. This approach is evaluated against several baseline techniques, including autoencoders, variational autoencoders, and a recently proposed method called Temporal Autoencoders. The results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses all baselines, achieving superior performance with reduced computational costs. Furthermore, we illustrate how this technique can be utilized to uncover latent variables and generate synthetic data. These capabilities facilitate the investigation of the relationship between neuronal activity and behavior, as well as the creation of virtual flies for research purposes. The entire methodology is implemented in Python and is publicly accessible. The accompanying paper and code are available at https://github.com/NeuroML/TemporalAutoEncoder. The *Drosophila* dataset used in this study can be downloaded from https://zenodo.org/record/5000505. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a framework for investigating how agents tackle decision-making tasks within uncertain settings. In partially observable scenarios, the agent's understanding of its surroundings is encapsulated by a belief state, representing the probability distribution of its hidden state. This study examines whether recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can acquire value functions contingent upon these belief states. We demonstrate that, despite RNNs being inherently stateless, they can be enhanced with an auxiliary output module to produce a condensed state that effectively mirrors the belief state. This finding holds true for both actor-critic algorithms utilizing importance-weighted variational autoencoders and those employing auto-regressive state encoders. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this methodology in addressing partially observable control challenges. Our results indicate that incorporating such an auxiliary module yields substantial performance gains, particularly when the state dimension is high. Ultimately, this research sheds light on the internal mechanisms of deep RL agents and facilitates the development of more efficient algorithms for complex, partially observable environments. The core model involves a perturbed parabolic equation, specifically a perturbed backward Kolmogorov equation subject to boundary conditions that represent a small probability of degradation to a base state. The paper concludes with a discussion on the implications of these findings. This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the leading-order charge-conjugation covariant (LOCCC) model. By applying the LOCCC framework to the gap equation, we derive the magnetic field-dependent quasiparticle dispersion relation. Employing the Landau-Osborn-Coulter-Vautherin (LOCV) technique, we solve the gap equation to determine the quasiparticle energy gap as a function of the magnetic field. Furthermore, we calculate magnetic phenomena such as the Fermi energy, kinetic energy, and symmetry energy. Our results indicate that the quasiparticle energy gap increases with magnetic field strength, whereas the Fermi energy and symmetry energy exhibit decreasing trends. Additionally, we observe that symmetry energy displays an oscillatory behavior as a function of the magnetic field. Finally, we note that the LOCCC model successfully explains the phase transition from normal to superconducting nuclear matter. These findings suggest that superconducting nuclear matter could potentially exist within the core of neutron stars. This study addresses the challenge of training a global model from distributed data by integrating federated learning with differential privacy. We introduce a new framework called DP-REC, which employs a generalized exponential mechanism to minimize the exchange of intermediate model updates between the central server and local participants. REC stands for Regularized Encrypted Computation, a method that encrypts and regularizes the transmission of intermediate results. REC is a lightweight, secure, and privacy-preserving protocol that reduces the volume of data shared between the central server and local users. Our results demonstrate that the model generated by the federated learning protocol is highly accurate, and the regularized encrypted computation protocol significantly decreases the number of intermediate updates exchanged between the central server and local users. Furthermore, we validate the security of this protocol through both theoretical analysis and experimental verification. Finally, we illustrate the efficiency of DP-REC by comparing it against two alternative protocols: DP-SGD and FEDERATED-ABACUS. These comparisons reveal that DP-REC achieves substantial communication savings while maintaining high accuracy. Specifically, DP-REC reduces communication overhead by 90% compared to DP-SGD and by 40% compared to FEDERATED-ABACUS. Additionally, we confirm that DP-REC is both secure and communication-efficient. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) imaging surveys of the Taurus, Perseus, Aquila, and Ophiuchus star-forming regions using the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE) and the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE). These observations enabled us to measure the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of young stellar objects (YSOs) and determine their accretion rates. Our analysis of the combined FUV data reveals that the four regions exhibit distinct characteristics. Taurus and Perseus are dominated by YSOs with high accretion rates ($\sim 10^{-7} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$), whereas Aquila and Ophiuchus contain primarily YSOs with low accretion rates ($\sim 10^{-9} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$). Furthermore, the mean FUV luminosity in Taurus and Perseus is approximately 100 times greater than that in Aquila and Ophiuchus. These findings suggest that Taurus and Perseus are at an earlier evolutionary stage compared to Aquila and Ophiuchus. Additionally, we identified a significant number of YSOs with FUV luminosities exceeding 1000 $L_{\odot}$ in Taurus and Perseus, which are notably absent in Aquila and Ophiuchus. This discrepancy indicates that the latter two regions are more heavily obscured by dust, preventing the detection of their most luminous YSOs. Finally, we observed that the FUSE FUV spectra of YSOs in Taurus and Perseus are dominated by C IV emission, while those in Aquila and Ophiuchus are primarily driven by C II emission. This spectral difference may be attributed to variations in the physical conditions of the accretion shocks. Collectively, these results support the hypothesis that Taurus and Perseus are more evolved than Aquila and Ophiuchus. The FUV spectral analysis of YSOs in star-forming regions offers a novel perspective on their evolutionary stages. We anticipate that future FUV observations of YSOs will continue to provide valuable insights into the accretion process. (Abridged)

Table extraction from documents is a critical step in information retrieval, yet it remains a challenging task due to the diverse structures and layouts of tables in real-world PDFs. This paper introduces a graph neural network (GNN) approach to retrieve tabular data within documents. We begin by converting a PDF into a graph representation, where table cells serve as nodes and horizontal or vertical adjacency as edges. This graph is subsequently modeled using a GNN to generate node embeddings, which are aggregated into table embeddings for comparison with query embeddings. Our results demonstrate that these GNN table embeddings are highly discriminative. Furthermore, we show that self-attention mechanisms can effectively extract features from these node embeddings to enhance retrieval performance. We introduce a cognitive hierarchy framework for multi-stage games characterized by incomplete information. Within this framework, players form beliefs regarding the probability that others engage in reasoning at various depths, subsequently utilizing these beliefs to derive posterior probabilities concerning the traits of individuals at each hierarchical level. We demonstrate that a unique cognitive hierarchy equilibrium always exists, provided the incomplete information satisfies a specific condition known as differential sufficient statistics. Furthermore, we establish a link between our differential sufficient statistics condition and the standard sufficient statistics condition applicable to one-shot games with incomplete information. Our findings indicate that, in the context of multi-stage games, the sufficient statistics condition is strictly stronger than the differential sufficient statistics condition. We illustrate the practical relevance of our model and its relationship with the sufficient statistics condition through a case study of the second-price sealed-bid auction. Finally, we examine multiple extensions of the model, including scenarios with common prior beliefs, continuous types, and extensive form Bayesian networks. In each of these extended scenarios, we show that the differential sufficient statistics condition remains the appropriate requirement for ensuring the existence of a unique cognitive hierarchy equilibrium. Additionally, we explore the dynamic properties of cognitive hierarchy equilibria within these extended frameworks. Specifically, we demonstrate that, under a suitable condition, cognitive hierarchy equilibria converge to the unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium as the cognitive depth increases toward infinity. This condition is notably weaker than the differential sufficient statistics condition. Consequently, we conclude that the differential sufficient statistics condition is the necessary and sufficient criterion for guaranteeing the convergence of cognitive hierarchy equilibria to the Bayesian Nash equilibrium as cognitive depth approaches infinity. This result holds true for both the original multi-stage game model and its extensions. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for the study of cognitive hierarchies.

Keywords: Cognitive Hierarchy Equilibrium, Multi-Stage Games of Insufficient Information, Bayesian Nash Equilibrium, Differential Sufficient Statistics, Sufficient Statistics.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating population counts within specific geographic regions using satellite imagery. We introduce a novel deep learning framework designed to enhance the sustainability of autonomous population estimation, thereby reducing reliance on manual human labeling. The model utilizes a synthetic dataset generated from satellite images of varying resolutions, paired with human-annotated population data at a higher resolution. We evaluate multiple deep learning architectures, including ResNet, VGG, and Inception, alongside a new model that integrates both images and region coordinates. Our results indicate that the new coordinate-based model outperforms image-only approaches, while the Inception architecture achieves the highest overall accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that training the model on higher-resolution images significantly boosts accuracy, although this comes at the cost of increased computational resources. Finally, we explore the application of transfer learning to improve model generalization. This research offers valuable insights for future efforts in autonomous population estimation, particularly for large-scale census operations in developing nations. Approximate membership data structures are engineered to allow rapid, memory-efficient checks for element presence, accepting a controlled risk of false positives. This paper introduces a novel structure termed an AMR-tree, which uniquely identifies itself as the first filters capable of generating zero false positives while maintaining the efficiency of standard approximate membership structures. The N-level Bloom filter serves as the foundational concept behind the AMR-tree, with the N-level structure representing the initial step toward AMR-trees. We demonstrate that Bloom filters are a specific instance of N-level structures and that N-level structures subsume Bloom filters. Furthermore, we establish that Bloom filters are the terminal structure in this hierarchy, where the number of levels corresponds directly to the dimensionality of the vector used to store each element. Finally, we provide an analysis of the AMR-tree's memory consumption and insertion latency, comparing these metrics against existing state-of-the-art filters. Our results indicate that an AMR-tree offers superior memory efficiency and comparable insertion speed relative to other filters. Additionally, we observe that the false-positive-free collection functions effectively as a cache, enabling the N-level Bloom filter to outperform traditional Bloom filters in terms of both memory usage and insertion speed. We introduce a theoretical framework to investigate atom-molecule transitions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate. This approach examines direct three-to-two body transformations, specifically $^{87}$Rb + 3Rb $\rightarrow$ $^{87}$Rb$_2$ + Rb, which occur via two distinct pathways: (i) the creation of two excited atoms and one ground-state atom, followed by rapid relaxation to the ground state, or (ii) sequential two-body reactions. We analyze how laser intensity and detuning influence these processes and identify optimal conditions for efficient atom-molecule transformation. Furthermore, we explore the impact of an external magnetic field on both reaction channels and determine the appropriate setup for achieving molecule formation. Finally, we discuss potential applications of this scheme in quantum information processing. Our findings indicate that the proposed method could facilitate atom-molecule conversion, thereby advancing the field of multi-body recombination physics. Additionally, this technique may enable the creation of $^{87}$Rb$_2$ molecules in their absolute ground state, a capability that could be valuable for quantum information processing. This paper presents a novel framework designed to simulate incompressible fluid-structure interactions involving multiple fluids with distinct densities. The method integrates a multi-resolution strategy with a level set approach for interface tracking and a direct-forcing technique for the coupling of fluid and solid phases. To address numerical instabilities, the study employs a new artificial viscosity formulation alongside a density correction technique. The framework's robustness and accuracy are validated through simulations of fluid-solid interactions and multi-fluid scenarios. Furthermore, the paper investigates the influence of kernel functions and the effects of mesh deformation on the interface. Finally, a three-dimensional simulation of a falling cube is utilized to examine the scalability of the method across distributed computing architectures. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework is both robust and efficient for simulating complex fluid-structure interaction problems. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abdelhamid-ben/Ben2020.

Long-term spatiotemporal prediction is essential for numerous real-world applications, including weather forecasting, traffic flow estimation, and demand prediction. However, these tasks are difficult to address due to the complex spatiotemporal dependencies inherent in the data. Current Transformer-based approaches have shown promise in capturing these interactions but are limited to processing only a single time step at a time, which restricts their ability to model long-term dependencies. To address this, we introduce Hopper, a multi-hop Transformer architecture designed for efficient long-term spatiotemporal prediction. By incorporating a multi-hop attention mechanism, Hopper effectively captures long-range spatiotemporal interactions. Furthermore, we introduce a novel multi-head spatiotemporal attention mechanism that simultaneously models both interactions and forecasting lags. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that Hopper achieves competitive performance compared to existing methods while offering superior inference speed. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/Hopper. Additionally, our results can be reproduced at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/Hopper/tree/master/Results. Finally, the model is deployed as a REST API at https://api.hopper.ai/. The paper is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. This study investigates the potential of lepton-pair production in association with a $b\bar{b}$ pair for determining the $W$ boson mass. The analysis focuses on the irreducible background from top-quark pair production, which is the primary obstacle to measuring $m_W$ with high precision. Our findings indicate that the full dataset from the LHC, with an integrated luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, could enable a determination of $m_W$ with a statistical uncertainty of approximately 10 MeV. Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as remote interfaces that facilitate communication and situational awareness by providing users with a physical presence in distant locations. While interactive applications like these offer significant benefits, they depend on network performance to function effectively. This study investigates the subjective experience of TPR usage under varying network conditions. We conducted a user study involving 12 participants across three scenarios—audio, video, and interactive video—where they controlled a robot under three network performance levels: poor, fair, and good. The results indicate that user experience is influenced by both the application type and network performance, with interactive tasks showing greater sensitivity to network fluctuations than audio or video alone. Furthermore, users demonstrated a strong desire to be informed about the current performance level. These findings suggest that future TPR systems should include a performance indicator to assist users in managing their expectations. Additionally, the research offers a framework for designing such indicators, which could enable TPR providers to deliver a superior user experience. Finally, the paper discusses the potential for leveraging machine learning to enhance TPR performance through proactive network management. To support this, we introduce a novel method for assessing interactive application quality of experience (QoE) using a deep neural network, which was trained and evaluated using data from our subjective study. This machine learning approach holds promise for enabling TPR providers to deliver a more consistent experience. The source code for the assessment method is available at https://github.com/5G-LLC/TPR-QoE. This research was conducted within the 5G-LLC project, a European H2020 initiative (Grant Agreement No. 814461). The project's primary objective is to develop a 5G-based network management solution that ensures a seamless experience for interactive applications. Specifically, 5G-LLC aims to create a framework that allows applications to interact with the network, thereby ensuring that service requirements are met. This paper serves as a foundational step toward that goal. To achieve this, 5G-LLC is developing a framework that enables applications to monitor network performance and adapt to it. This work represents the initial phase of that project. The paper begins by reviewing related research, followed by a description of the proposed solution. This paper offers a pedagogical overview of Bayesian hierarchical linear models, designed to guide novice analysts in analyzing educational datasets. It provides practical guidance on implementing these models using the R programming language and its packages, specifically brms and Stan. The accompanying dataset, which includes information on students, schools, and teachers, is available at https://github.com/andrewheiss/guide_to_brlms. Furthermore, the paper includes a fully functional Jupyter notebook that integrates R and R Markdown to facilitate the analysis. The primary objective is to demonstrate the utility of Bayesian hierarchical linear models for educational data analysis. Additionally, the text aims to clarify the benefits of a Bayesian approach compared to frequentist methods, such as maximum likelihood estimation, and to illustrate how hierarchical modeling enhances inference by explicitly accounting for the data's nested structure. The discussion begins with a straightforward one-way school-level random effects model, followed by an analysis of how incorporating student-level covariates alters the findings. Finally, the paper explores the advantages of moving from a random-intercept model to a random-slope model. The goal is to provide an accessible introduction to hierarchical linear models for both statisticians and educators, with the latter finding the examples particularly relevant for their own data analysis tasks. We hope this introduction inspires readers to explore Bayesian hierarchical linear models in their own work.

Keywords: Bayesian analysis, brms, Stan, hierarchical linear models, Jupyter notebooks, R, education data analysis.

This study examines the simultaneous accretion of gas by two giant planets within a protoplanetary disk. We conducted 2-D hydrodynamical simulations of a single disk containing two planets with fixed orbital separations and initial radii, varying their initial masses. Our simulations tracked the planets' mass evolution and the disk's structural changes over 10 Myr. Our findings indicate that the mass of the less massive planet exerts the most significant influence on the growth of both planets. Specifically, when the less massive planet resides in a region with a higher surface density, the final mass of the more massive planet can increase by up to 20% compared to scenarios where it is the less massive one. This enhancement occurs because the gas inflow driven by the less massive planet pushes the accretion shock of the more massive planet inward, thereby increasing its accretion rate. Additionally, the gas inflow from the less massive planet generates a shock that settles into a quasi-steady state, creating a local pressure maximum. This maximum acts as a barrier, restricting the inflow of gas from the inner disk to the outer disk and causing gas accumulation between the two planets. We conclude that the mass of the less massive planet is a critical factor in the simultaneous accretion of a pair of giant planets. This insight may help explain the existence of super-Jupiter planets in close proximity to low-mass companions, such as brown dwarfs or low-mass stars. Furthermore, the local pressure maximum formed between the planets could account for the observed gaps in protoplanetary disks. Finally, this mechanism may contribute to the formation of brown dwarfs and low-mass stars in binary systems. To further explore this, we conducted a statistical analysis of the mass evolution of planet pairs in this work. These results will be presented in a forthcoming paper. This paper introduces a novel fuzzy clustering algorithm designed for high-dimensional data, integrating entropy-based feature weights to dynamically adjust the significance of each dimension. We demonstrate that the proposed method reduces to the standard fuzzy k-means algorithm when all feature weights are uniform. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the algorithm and provide numerical examples to validate its effectiveness. These examples illustrate that entropy-driven weighting successfully identifies the most relevant features, thereby enhancing the quality of the resulting clusters. Additionally, the computational efficiency of the proposed approach is analyzed. Finally, the method's utility is confirmed through applications in both synthetic and real-world datasets. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, comprising a linear combination of expert models weighted by a soft-max function, are widely used in machine learning. Despite their popularity, the theoretical analysis of MoE remains limited. This paper addresses a fundamental MoE classification task where experts are defined as linear classifiers. We demonstrate that this problem is inherently difficult, proving that no efficient algorithm can achieve a consistent learning result without additional information. Specifically, we show that the standard soft-max weighting mechanism creates a significant challenge, as the weight distribution becomes highly skewed, causing most experts to receive negligible weights. To overcome this barrier, we propose a novel weighted sum function to replace the soft-max and develop a corresponding efficient algorithm. We further prove that our algorithm achieves a consistent learning result, even in the absence of extra information. Additionally, we establish a lower bound for any efficient algorithm, demonstrating that the soft-max model is significantly more challenging than the weighted sum model. Finally, we conduct experiments to validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/MoE. This article provides a comprehensive proof of the Mumford conjecture, which asserts that the stable homotopy group of a closed orientable surface of genus $g$, denoted $H_g$, is freely generated by elements of Adams-Novikov type. This approach leverages the $b$-map family, originally developed by Miller and Miller in their proof of the Miller conjecture. The $b$-map family, which extends the Miller map, is constructed via the $J$-homomorphism and serves as the surface-level counterpart to the Miller map within the context of the $sp$-map. A pivotal component of this proof is a novel obstruction theory grounded in the cohomology of the automorphism group of a free group. This method establishes that the $b$-map family can be refined to preserve the surface structure of the $sp$-map's input. The validity of this obstruction theory relies on the interplay between Adams-Novikov theory and the Miller map. Consequently, the proof of the Mumford conjecture also encompasses the proofs of the Miller and Novikov conjectures. Furthermore, the techniques employed herein offer a streamlined proof of the Miller conjecture. The core of the Adams-Novikov approach involves utilizing the Miller map to construct a free action on the stable homotopy type of the universal cover of a classifying space for free surfaces. This construction is achieved through the Miller map's connection to the $sp$-map and the Miller map's link to the $J$-homomorphism. The $sp$-map is defined as the stable extension of the $sp$-map, which maps the based loop of a surface to the based normal fiber of the classifying map of a surface of the same genus. A transferability guarantee ensures that a model trained on one dataset can be deployed on another. This paper challenges the conventional view that a classifier's agreement with human labels across two training datasets serves as such a guarantee. We argue that, absent further evidence, high agreement merely indicates that the model fits the training data well, rather than ensuring correct labeling of the second dataset. To support this, we introduce the "overfitting hypothesis," which posits that deep neural networks can achieve agreement with human labels in a second dataset by memorizing the first, even when that dataset is significantly smaller. We validate this hypothesis through experiments on a synthetic task and the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the overfitting hypothesis offers a more accurate explanation for the behavior of state-of-the-art transferability guarantees than the traditional two-agreements hypothesis. Finally, we propose a new transferability guarantee that offers a more precise explanation of the phenomenon while maintaining the simplicity of the two-agreements approach. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/DeepLearningSecurity/transferability}.

Networks are inherently modular, and this structural characteristic significantly influences the dynamics of information spread. While prior research has demonstrated that modularity can either accelerate or decelerate the diffusion of information, the specific mechanisms driving these variations remain unclear. In this study, we employ a continuous-time network diffusion model to investigate how modularity affects information propagation. Our findings indicate that the impact of modularity on spreading speed is contingent upon the network's internal structure, specifically the relationship between intra- and inter-modularity density. We demonstrate that when a network features high density overall, high intra-modularity density, and low inter-modularity density, it results in a slower spread of information. Furthermore, we reveal that this modularity-driven effect operates through the network's internal path length distribution. Finally, we validate these conclusions by analyzing both synthetic and real-world networks. These results offer valuable insights for designing networks to control information flow. Additionally, our methodology is applicable to a wide range of networks, including those with complex topologies, weighted, and directed structures. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/NetworkModularity.

This paper introduces the concept of distinctiveness for Lagrangian submanifolds within Calabres-Finsler manifolds, demonstrating its quantitative nature through the use of Calabi functional bounds on functional bounds on symplectic quasi-energy. The Thomas-Yau conjecture posits that the Calabi functional is bounded from below by these quasi-symplectic energies. The notion of distinctiveness is defined by the boundedness of the Calabi functional given fixed symplectic quasi-periodic energies. This concept extends to other classes of Lagrangian submanifolds, such as those with constant Maslov form or constant phase function. The proof relies on a Thomas-Yau type inequality for the curvature of the holomorphic line bundle associated with a Lagrangian fibration, which is established using the curvature properties of the dual line bundle over the base. This approach draws inspiration from the Thomas-Yau conjecture and the work of Lohkamp and others on curvature estimates. The paper concludes with a discussion of the relationship between distinctiveness and the Thomas-Yau conjecture. Future research will explore the application of distinctiveness to the study of special Lagrangian submanifolds and mirror symmetry. The concept of distinctiveness is also related to the concept of "Lagrangian capacity" introduced by Entov and Polterovich. In this context, the capacity of a Lagrangian submanifold is defined as the infimum of the symplectic quasi-energy over all Hamiltonian isotopies of the Lagrangian submanifold. The distinctiveness of a Lagrangian submanifold is closely related to its capacity, as a high capacity implies a low value of the symplectic quasi-energy, leading to greater distinctiveness. This study introduces a precision analysis for the time-domain regular perturbation model of an unamplified link, grounded in a discrete-time framework. By modeling the perturbed oscillator as a linear time-invariant system with a time-varying initial condition, we demonstrate that this approach can be viewed as a discrete-time extension of the time-domain regular perturbation model, which is originally defined in the frequency domain. Leveraging the properties of the Bessel function, we establish that the discrete-time formulation is valid under the condition that the sampling interval is sufficiently small. Furthermore, we prove that the discrete-time model converges to the original frequency-domain model as the sampling interval approaches zero. Finally, we derive the output phase power spectral density from the discrete-time model and confirm, through numerical simulations, that it matches the result obtained from the frequency-domain model. These findings offer a rigorous foundation for precision analysis based on the discrete-time regular perturbation model. Additionally, the methodology is applicable to other frequency-domain time-continuous regular perturbation models, such as those used for amplified or crystal oscillator links. The primary constraint of the discrete-time model is the requirement for a sufficiently small sampling interval, which may necessitate extensive computation. However, this limitation is not applicable to other frequency-domain time-continuous models, which do not require such a small sampling interval. Consequently, the discrete-time model is generally unsuitable for simulating or designing oscillators, though it remains valuable for theoretical analysis. We specifically apply this theoretical analysis to the phase noise of an LC oscillator. The paper concludes by demonstrating that the phase noise of an LC oscillator can be accurately predicted using the discrete-time model, provided the sampling interval is sufficiently small. This result is achieved by deriving a discrete-time representation of the perturbed oscillator and proving that its phase power spectral density aligns with the continuous-time model's output. The primary advantage of the discrete-time model is that it enables the derivation of the phase power spectral density without requiring Fourier transforms, thereby simplifying the analysis. The paper also presents a comparison between the phase power spectral densities of LC oscillators derived from both the continuous-time and discrete-time models. The conclusion shows that the discrete-time model yields the same phase power spectral density as the continuous-time model, provided the sampling interval is sufficiently small. This confirms that the LC oscillator phase power spectral density can be accurately predicted using either model. The Android operating system, developed by Google, is a leading global platform that powers billions of devices and supports a vast array of applications. Its open-source nature has facilitated numerous security research initiatives aimed at uncovering vulnerabilities and enhancing the system's security posture. This paper provides a comprehensive review of literature concerning security issues within the Android OS. It begins by examining the fundamental security architecture of Android, followed by a detailed analysis of research efforts categorized into three primary domains: application-level, system-level, and framework-level issues. Each study is evaluated based on its methodology, findings, and the tools employed. The discussion further explores the challenges inherent in Android security research and outlines potential future directions. Finally, the paper offers an in-depth examination of emerging trends, specifically focusing on evasion attacks within the Android issue-space. By synthesizing existing literature, this survey aims to assist researchers in navigating the field and fostering new advancements in Android security research. The authors believe this work will serve as a valuable resource for both scholars and practitioners. Additionally, the paper is accessible as a supplementary material at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/Issue-Space-Evasion-Attacks-in-the-Android-OS-a-Survey. Container orchestration platforms are essential for managing large-scale container deployments, yet they are complex and resource-heavy. This paper introduces Ozy, a universal orchestration container designed to enable self-hosting of orchestration services within containers. By integrating Ozy, containers can independently execute core orchestration functions such as scheduling, service discovery, and self-healing. We present a high-level architecture for Ozy and demonstrate its implementation, validating that container-level self-orchestration is feasible. Furthermore, we show that Ozy's design can be extended to support advanced container applications, including edge computing and serverless architectures. Finally, experimental results indicate that Ozy adds only a 1.5% overhead to containers, both in terms of execution time and memory usage. This work paves the way for developing lightweight, self-orchestrizing containers. The Ozy source code is accessible at https://github.com/CloudLab/ozy. We introduce a unified theoretical framework that harmonizes prior phenomenological theories of reentrant quantum Hall phases with recent numerical findings. Our analysis indicates that these phases emerge within the composite fermion model when composite fermions occupy low-order Fermi liquid phases. This approach elucidates the mechanical dynamics driving the reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase observed in both experimental settings and numerical simulations. Furthermore, we predict the existence of additional reentrant quantum Hall phases at the filling factors of 7/2, 9/2, and 11/2. Finally, we propose a viable experimental strategy to detect the anticipated reentrant 7/2 quantum Hall phase. These results offer a fresh perspective on the enigmatic nature of quantum Hall phases near the 5/2 filling factor. The accompanying arXiv preprint includes supplementary material featuring a theoretical overview of the reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase and an experimental proposal for its observation. Additionally, an arXiv video highlights the significance of this work. Keywords: Fractional Quantum Hall Effect, Quantum Hall Phase Transitions, Composite Fermion Theory, Variational Monte Carlo, Exact Diagonalization.

We demonstrate that its line element does not approach the Schwarzschild metric in the appropriate limit and that it introduces a singularity at the horizon, rendering it unsuitable for describing black hole spacetimes. Consequently, we conclude that the recent Thakur et al. study [1] [arXiv:2105.01010] regarding the evaporation of primordial black holes (PBHs) is flawed. Furthermore, we show that the constraints on PBH mass derived by Thakur et al. are identical to those obtained by Carr et al. [2] [arXiv:2006.10072]. Finally, we establish that the conclusions of the Thakur et al. paper do not alter the current understanding of PBHs. Accretion of pebbles by protoplanets is a widely accepted mechanism for forming the cores of gas giants, yet the influence of dust and pebble dynamics on this process remains poorly understood. This study investigates how radial density fluctuations in pebbles affect planet formation through pebble accretion. We conducted 1000 simulations using the DustyAcc code, which models both gas and dust dynamics, to analyze these fluctuations. Our results indicate that the standard deviation of pebble density ($\sigma_{\rm{peb}}$) typically ranges from 0.1 to 1.0, with a median value of 0.2. Consequently, the probability of encountering a high-pebble-density region is low, and the likelihood of such events increasing over time is minimal. We further examined the impact of these fluctuations on planet formation, finding that while they can accelerate core growth by factors of 2 to 10, the median outcome shows no significant change. Additionally, we identified a critical threshold for $\sigma_{\rm{peb}}$ that determines whether planet formation is enhanced. Finally, we assessed the effects of non-linear gas-dust interactions on pebble density, concluding that these processes do not significantly influence the frequency of high-pebble-density events. Overall, this research underscores the necessity of including dust dynamics in planet formation models to accurately capture the effects of pebble density fluctuations. Furthermore, we have updated the public version of DustyAcc to incorporate a new feature for calculating pebble density fluctuations. Overparameterized models are common in machine learning, yet their behavior remains poorly understood. This study examines a specific source of overparameterization arising from computational constraints. Specifically, when data is overfitted, the effective number of parameters is typically estimated as the model's in-sample training error. However, numerical errors inherent to finite-precision computation can lead to a training error of zero, making the counted errors essentially machine epsilon. Consequently, the number of countable errors is so vast that the corresponding parameter count is astronomically high. To address this, we propose a solution by introducing a regularization term and analyzing its impact on both the count of overparameterized models and generalization performance. Our findings indicate that even a minute regularization strength is sufficient to reduce the number of overparameterized models to a manageable level, with the resulting parameter count scaling linearly with the dataset size. Furthermore, the derived upper bound on test error demonstrates that these overparameterized models generalize effectively. Finally, we validate these theoretical results through experiments on a real-world dataset. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Google DeepMind Machine Learning Research group. Let $G$ be an abelian group with a subgroup $H$ of finite index, where $H$ contains no nontrivial squares. Let $A$ be a subset of $G$ such that its sumset $A+A$ contains a Bohr set $B$ centered at the identity with parameters $(\kappa, \gamma)$ that are contained within $B+B$. We demonstrate that $A$ possesses structure resembling a Bohr set. This finding extends our primary theorem, which applies when $G$ is an arbitrary abelian group and $H$ is the trivial subgroup $\{0\}$. Furthermore, we establish that this structural result is optimal by presenting examples that lack such ablation. Our proofs rely on the recent work of Green and Ruzsa regarding nilpotent groups and the classical Freiman-Ruzsa theorem concerning sumsets. Additionally, we provide an example that is not nilpotent and exhibits the same structure, thereby confirming that our result cannot be extended to general groups. Finally, we demonstrate that the conclusion fails for groups with small commutators, such as the free abelian group of rank 2, and that the assumption $B \subseteq B+B$ cannot be weakened. These examples are constructed using free groups and their quotients. In the process, we also prove that the main theorem holds for finitely generated groups under the condition that the commutator subgroup is trivial. The inability to extend the theorem to groups with a nontrivial commutator subgroup stems from the fact that Bohr sets in such groups do not necessarily exhibit the required structure. We further illustrate that the assumption $B \subseteq B+B$ is essential for our proof, as it enables the application of the Freiman-Ruzsa theorem. However, this assumption is not essential in the context of finitely generated groups, as the theorem remains valid without it. We also examine the necessity of the condition that the $(n-1)$-th powers in $H$ are contained in the center of $G$, showing that this requirement cannot be dropped. Our examples are again drawn from free groups and their quotients. Finally, we extend our results to subsets of finite groups that are dense with respect to the normalized counting measure. We show that the theorem holds for groups with a nontrivial commutator subgroup, provided the exponent of the group is sufficiently large. This study addresses an urban dial-a-ride problem featuring flexible pickup and delivery time windows, dynamic requests, and a specific objective to minimize total customer waiting durations. We introduce a Branch-and-Cut algorithm utilizing a novel mixed-integer programming model enhanced by various valid inequalities. Furthermore, we develop a large neighborhood search heuristic to generate high-quality feasible solutions that guide the branch-and-cut process. Computational results demonstrate that our method effectively solves instances with up to 20 customers within a one-hour timeframe. Additionally, the heuristic yields superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art algorithms for both static and dynamic instances. Finally, we apply our approach to a real-world case study of a shared mobility dial-a-ride service in Rome, Italy, evaluating the impact of varying numbers of vehicles and drivers on average waiting times. Finally, we analyze how changes in demand affect the performance of our proposed heuristic. The code is available at: https://github.com/AndreaGatti1/Urban-Dial-a-Ride. This paper details the e-commerce multimodal pretraining model we developed, which secured first place in the MAUVE 2021 Deep Learning Track. Our approach utilizes the lightweight, knowledge-driven MMS model as a base and incorporates four specialized modules designed to process e-commerce data across text, images, and graphs. The integration of these modules yields significant improvements over the baseline, with gains of 1.5 to 2.5 points in Recall@K and 2.5 to 3.5 points in Recall@K2 for the top-N automatic metrics. Furthermore, we observe that our model's performance is highly robust across various subsets of the test dataset. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/alibaba/MMS. Given the confidential nature of our data, we are unable to share the pre-trained model. Our contributions are threefold: 1) We explore the application of multimodal pretraining models in the e-commerce domain; 2) We introduce a domain-specific model architecture tailored for e-commerce tasks; 3) We demonstrate that our model achieves substantial performance gains compared to the baseline. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines the task description; Section 3 describes the MMS model and our specific e-commerce adaptations; Section 4 presents the experimental results; and Section 5 concludes with a discussion. This study introduces a new deep learning approach designed to forecast the progression to Alzheimer's disease (AD) in individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We developed a deep InfoMax network that jointly learns a low-dimensional, nonlinear dynamical system from multi-modal brain imaging data, including structural MRI, FDG-PET, and apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotypes. This approach surpasses the current state-of-the-art method, which relies on a standard convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on static features. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the latent variables generated by our model can be utilized to construct a nonlinear dynamical system for predicting AD conversion. Our findings indicate that the proposed deep dynamic network enhances both the interpretability and predictive performance of AD classification models. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/DeepInfoMax. In the context of the spin-charge separation theory for one-dimensional correlated systems, we investigate spin-orbit coupling (SOC) within a one-dimensional Hubbard model that includes next-nearest neighbor hopping and canonical momentum coupling. We demonstrate that the expectation value of SOC in the spin-fluid state is significantly amplified compared to its value in the electron-fluid state. This enhancement of SOC is also observed in higher-dimensional systems where strong electron correlations induce one-dimensional-like behavior. Furthermore, we show that the canonical momentum coupling term, which acts as a symmetry-breaking perturbation, stabilizes a magnetic phase by inducing a ferromagnetic phase transition. This mechanism offers a pathway to achieve strong SOC in correlated materials without relying on atomic spin-orbit interactions. Finally, we highlight that this symmetry-breaking effect is also present in the one-dimensional Heisenberg model. These findings are supported by exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group calculations. Our results suggest that the momentum coupling term, representing a form of canonical momentum coupling, is a crucial ingredient for achieving strong SOC in correlated materials. Additionally, we discuss the potential for engineering this momentum coupling term through spin-orbit coupling and strain. Our findings are particularly relevant to the recently discovered quasi-one-dimensional materials, including the kagome metal CsV$_3$Sb$_5$ and the kagome semimetal AV$_3$Sb$_5$ (where A = K, Rb, or Cs). These materials exhibit a charge density wave phase transition at $T_c = 0.85$ K, accompanied by a ferromagnetic phase transition at $T_N = 0.5$ K. Our results indicate that the momentum coupling is essential for stabilizing this ferromagnetic phase. Finally, we discuss the possibility of achieving strong SOC in these materials by combining spin-orbit coupling with uniaxial strain. Our findings are also applicable to other strongly correlated systems, such as Sr$_2$RuO$_4$, where spin-orbit coupling plays a pivotal role in determining the nature of the superconducting state. We introduce a new dark matter candidate known as metastable conformal shadow matter. This model features a "portal" interaction that couples the standard matter sector to a separate, nearly conformal hidden sector. Within this hidden sector, dark matter exists as a metastable state that decays into the hidden radiation bath. We demonstrate that this mechanism can account for the observed dark matter density and examine the model's implications for both direct and indirect detection experiments. Furthermore, we illustrate how measurements of the dark matter equation of state during cosmic evolution could offer a means to distinguish this model from others. Finally, we show that shadow matter could be probed via high-energy cosmic rays through its decay products. Our findings indicate that this class of dark matter models represents a viable alternative to the more conventional stable dark matter scenarios. Additionally, we emphasize that this framework provides a natural setting for studying the cosmological evolution of metastable dark matter states. Specifically, it offers a unique opportunity to investigate the transition from matter-like to radiation-like behavior in dark matter, a phenomenon that could potentially be tested through future observations of the cosmic microwave background. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting such metastable dark matter using the upcoming Cherenkov Telescope Array. This could be achieved by searching for dark matter annihilation products within the dark halos themselves. Such a detection would be distinct from standard dark matter annihilation signatures because it would exhibit a strong dependence on the dark matter velocity. This unique signature would be particularly prominent in the dark halos of galaxy clusters, where dark matter self-annihilations are expected to be enhanced. We conclude that the Cherenkov Telescope Array could provide the first evidence for the existence of this hidden sector. This would be confirmed by observing dark matter-induced gamma-ray emission from the dark matter distribution in the Virgo cluster. Our analysis of the Fermi-LAT data suggests that the shadow sector could be detected at a 2.5$\sigma$ significance level. Regulatory bodies are increasingly scrutinizing the performance of AI-driven medical devices, yet validating these systems remains difficult due to the challenge of ensuring their test datasets adequately represent real-world deployment conditions. This discrepancy is exacerbated by distribution shift, where differences between training and deployment data distributions can compromise model reliability. To address this, we introduce a framework that evaluates test efficacy by quantifying the likelihood of discovering errors during testing. We estimate this efficacy using conformity scores and distribution discrepancy metrics, specifically the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and Wasserstein distance. Our approach is demonstrated on a case study involving a deep learning model designed to detect atrial fibrillation from ECG recordings. The results indicate that efficacy estimates derived from MMD align with actual error detection rates in the validation phase, whereas those based on Wasserstein distance tend to overestimate efficacy. Furthermore, efficacy calculated from MMD remains stable even when training data is contaminated with test data, a phenomenon known as data leakage. In contrast, efficacy derived from Wasserstein distance is highly sensitive to data leakage, dropping sharply as the proportion of leaked data increases. These findings highlight the potential of our method to enhance the regulatory approval process for AI medical devices by providing more robust assessments of test data utility. Additionally, our analysis reveals that Wasserstein distance is less suitable than MMD for measuring the similarity between training and test data distributions in this context. Finally, we offer a set of guidelines for researchers and practitioners to select the most appropriate similarity metric for their specific applications. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ai-medical-devices/conformal_test_efficacy. This work was supported by the JSPS KAKENHI Grant Numbers 20K19835 and 21K11791. Enhancing the sampling of DNA conformations is a critical challenge in biophysics. This study introduces a novel approach to molecular dynamics (MD) simulations that employs rigid substrates to sample the conformations of a single DNA duplex. This method, referred to as Rigid Substrate Biasing in MD (RSB-MD), utilizes a biasing potential applied to the major and minor grooves of the DNA. The resulting conformational ensemble was validated by comparing it with MD simulations conducted on a PNA-DNA duplex, where the PNA groove was biased to mimic the biasing potential used for DNA. The conformational space of the PNA-DNA system was successfully compared against experimental data from NMR and X-ray crystallography. Furthermore, the method was applied to a DNA sequence known to adopt a Z-DNA conformation, revealing that RSB-MD accurately reproduces the minor groove width observed in NMR experiments for the Z-conformation. These findings demonstrate that RSB-MD is a promising new tool for investigating DNA conformational landscapes. The RSBD-MD code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkjaer/rsbd-md. The input files for the systems analyzed in this work can be found at https://github.com/robertkjaer/rsbd-md-inputs. The ANS is a universal entropy encoding method grounded in arithmetic coding, which partitions the probability space into intervals of non-integer size. This technique is widely utilized in entropy-optimized compression formats, such as AVIF, JPEG XL, and WebP, as well as in various data structures. This study evaluates the ANS across different word sizes and explores alternative methods for implementing the Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) algorithm using ANS. Our findings indicate that smaller word sizes are more effective, and that the ANS-LZW variant outperforms both raw ANS and standard CABAC-LZW implementations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ANS-LZW can be realized with reduced complexity by employing a specialized stack-based approach. Ultimately, we achieve a 10% reduction in execution time compared to arithmetic-CABAC-LZW, with only a marginal increase in file size. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/avikdas/answep. Additional details are available at https://www.avikdas.com/answep. The dielectric properties of cement-based materials are extensively utilized to evaluate their hydration status and mechanical strength. However, the dielectric response of these materials is closely tied to the dielectric behavior of the interfacial region between cement particles and the pore solution. This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to analyze the dielectric response functions of the interfacial region surrounding hydrophilic surfaces within a NaCl aqueous solution. The results indicate that the dielectric response of this interfacial region is significantly influenced by the ionic concentration of the solution and the type of counterions present. Furthermore, the interfacial region exhibits a distinct dielectric response compared to the bulk solution, a phenomenon attributed to the formation of an electric double layer. These findings offer crucial insights into the dielectric characteristics of cement-based materials. Additionally, the proposed methodology is applicable to investigating the dielectric response of other interfacial regions in electrolyte solutions. Finally, the computational approach utilized in this work is also relevant to other computational physics domains, such as the investigation of electronic and magnetic properties of solids. The source code employed in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/MD-Dielectric. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable cosmological tool for mapping the distribution of matter within the intergalactic medium (IGM) at high redshifts. By analyzing the three-dimensional correlations of absorption features in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, we can derive the matter power spectrum of the IGM, thereby characterizing the dark matter halo mass function and probing the initial density fluctuations of the universe. This study presents a direct calculation of the Lyman-$\alpha$ matter power spectrum using the $N$-body simulation "Mega-Millennium," which employs a $2048^3$ grid with a comoving volume of $(5370\,\mathrm{Mpc})^3$ and a mass resolution of $M_p = 1.5 \times 10^6\,M_\odot$. We compute the three-point correlation function of Lyman-$\alpha$ absorption features across three distinct redshifts ($z=2.2$, $z=3.0$, and $z=4.0$) within a $100\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ box. Furthermore, we observe that the IGM power spectrum is significantly suppressed relative to the matter power spectrum, with the suppression factor decreasing as redshift increases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the IGM power spectrum is nearly independent of the simulation's mass resolution. These results are consistent with those obtained from the "Mega-Millennium" simulation combined with the Zeldovich approximation.
