We demonstrate the successful transfer of both longitudinal and longitudinal emittances from a source bucket to a target bucket within the Linear Collider Emittance Test Facility (LETF) at KEK. Initially, emittances in the transverse plane were damped using a damping anti-radiation scheme (DARS) to values lower than the longitudinal plane. Subsequently, these transverse emittances were increased and mapped to the longitudinal plane through nonlinear Hamiltonian dynamics. This study reports the first experimental confirmation of transverse-emittance pumping, a technique that complements the well-established method of pumping longitudinal emittance to the transverse plane. These findings hold significant promise for future applications in high-intensity, low-emittance beams required for neutrino factories and muon colliders. Furthermore, we compare these results with simulations from the Emittance Preserving Beam Dynamics (EPBD) code, which accurately reproduces the observed dynamics. The successful execution of this experiment marks a crucial step toward the development of high-intensity, low-emittance beams for next-generation muon accelerators. Additionally, the DARS technique, which was refined during the longitudinal emittance blow-up process, is essential for maintaining the beamline's dynamic aperture. This study addresses the challenge of classifying various blood cell types, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, which is critical for diagnosing conditions like leukemia. We introduce a deep learning framework that integrates multiple neural network models to enhance classification accuracy. Our approach utilizes three specific architectures: ResNet, VGG, and Inception, which are trained on a dataset of blood cell images. The outputs from these models are combined via a neural network ensemble to determine the final classification. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves a test accuracy of 99.7%, surpassing the performance of individual architectures. This enhanced accuracy is expected to significantly aid medical professionals in diagnosing diseases such as leukemia. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/BloodCellClassification. Future research will focus on expanding the dataset to include additional blood cell types, such as eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes. Additionally, we plan to investigate transfer learning techniques to improve the model's performance on the current dataset. Finally, we aim to adapt the model for use in medical imaging, specifically for classifying lesions in mammograms and brain CT scans. The corresponding author can be contacted at: dr.abdulrahman.alshammari@ku.edu.sa. Keywords: Blood Cell Classification, Deep Learning, Ensemble Learning.

Counterdiabatic driving (CDD) is a well-established technique for accelerating quantum evolution along adiabatic paths. This study investigates the application of CDD to initialize a system in its ground state, specifically targeting the one-dimensional Hubbard model. We introduce a variational framework to determine an optimal initial state and examine its convergence properties. Our findings indicate that the resulting variational problem is efficiently solvable, even for large system sizes, when utilizing matrix product state representations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this variational approach yields superior results compared to the widely used projection method. Finally, we explore the potential extension of this methodology to other quantum many-body systems. The code implementing these methods is accessible at \href{https://github.com/quantumlib/HubbardModel}{github.com/quantumlib/HubbardModel}. By decomposing an image into separate color temperature and saturation components, the method reduces color temperature to enhance perceived contrast while preserving saturation to maintain natural color fidelity. We introduce a computational framework designed to simulate photon-photon interactions within laser-plaas environments. This approach is grounded in the quantum electrodynamics model of virtual electron-positron pair production, with numerical simulations powered by the open-source Plasma Framework. Our results demonstrate that the model yields significant photon absorption and attenuation in plasmas where the vacuum model fails to do so. Furthermore, the model accurately reproduces the attenuation observed in high-intensity laser-plasma experiments conducted by the European XFEL. These findings suggest that the model could be applied to investigate the attenuation of low-energy photons in laser-produced plasmas, a phenomenon that remains difficult to explain without resorting to ad hoc mechanisms. Additionally, we have made the PhotonPhoton module, which implements this framework, publicly available. This tool can be utilized to study vacuum and plasma effects on photon-photon interactions, as well as to model the propagation of photons through laser-produced plasmas. This study examines the stability of the vacuum and the mass spectrum of both scalar and dark sector fields across the entire parameter space of the Two-Doublet Higgs Model, with a specific focus on the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter, $m_{12}$. We demonstrate that the model's viability is highly sensitive to the magnitude of $m_{12}$, which is typically constrained to be very small. Furthermore, we establish that the model remains viable only when the imaginary component of $m_{12}$ is negligible. Our analysis reveals that the model's viability is further compromised if the CP-even state $h_1$ is identified as the 125 GeV Higgs boson, as this scenario imposes severe restrictions on the parameter space. Additionally, we explore the potential for dark matter within this framework, showing that the dark sector field can be accommodated in the model's parameter space. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for current and future experimental searches. This work serves as a foundation for phenomenological investigations into the Two-Doublet Higgs Model. As an application, we examine the case of a dark matter candidate with a mass of approximately 10 GeV, a mass scale that has received significant attention in recent years. We demonstrate that this mass can be achieved within the model's parameter space, and we discuss the challenges associated with detecting such a light dark matter candidate. Our results indicate that the dark sector field is detectable through direct detection experiments, while indirect detection via LIGO and LISA is possible only if the decay of the lightest CP-even state into dark matter is significant. Furthermore, we show that the parameter space allowing for a 10 GeV dark matter candidate is excluded by collider data. Finally, we note that the model can accommodate a dark matter candidate with a mass of about 1 TeV, a scenario that is more challenging to detect directly but potentially observable through indirect searches. In this scenario, the dark matter field is a linear combination of the two doublet fields, and we discuss the resulting implications for both direct and indirect detection methods. We conclude that the viability of the model is significantly reduced when attempting to accommodate a 1 TeV dark matter candidate. Additionally, we discuss the challenges of detecting this dark matter candidate through direct and indirect methods. We also examine the possibility of detecting dark matter with a mass of approximately 50 GeV, which is more challenging than the 10 GeV case but still within the model's reach.

Shape expressions offer methods to validate relational data schemas and individual instances, with corresponding query languages available. However, converting relational data to RDF and ensuring both data and schema equivalence between the two formats remain unresolved challenges. This paper introduces a normal form for the combination of shape expressions and their associated query language, which simplifies the analysis of data translations. Specifically, we demonstrate that in certain scenarios, a normal form exists where the translation from RDF to relational can be derived from the inverse translation via a simple syntactic operation. This result is particularly significant for relational-to-RDF translations, as it enables the automatic generation of the translation in these cases. Furthermore, we prove that for these specific translations, data and schema equivalence are guaranteed. The proposed technique is implemented in the Quodlibet system, and we present a case study involving a translation of the DBLP knowledge base from RDF to relational format. This paper presents a comprehensive study of top-antitop plus Higgs production at the LHC, covering both associated production modes: $t \bar t H^0$ and $t \bar t H^\pm$. The analysis focuses on scenarios where the Higgs boson decays into a diphoton pair, a dijet system, or a pair of bottom quarks. We examine how these specific decay channels influence the optimal selection of signal and background events. Furthermore, we explore the potential for combining these channels to enhance the sensitivity of Higgs mass measurements. Our investigation covers a wide range of Higgs mass values, extending from the Standard Model mass of 125 GeV up to 1.5 TeV, with the primary objective of determining the most effective experimental strategies for detecting the Higgs boson within the $t \bar t$ final state. Additionally, we assess the prospects for measuring the Higgs mass in this environment, a crucial step for interpreting the properties of any potential "second Higgs" discovered in Higgs-associated $t \bar t$ events. This approach is particularly relevant for non-Standard Model Higgs bosons, such as those predicted by the Two-Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM), which often exhibit branching ratios to $t \bar t H^0$ that are comparable to or exceeding those of the $H^0 \to b \bar b$ channel. Our findings indicate that a mass resolution of approximately 10% is achievable for the $t \bar t H^0$ process when the Higgs decays to photons, a dijet system, or a bottom quark pair. These results are derived from a simulated dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 100 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of 14 TeV. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the LHC's future high-luminosity running phase. Specifically, we demonstrate that a mass resolution of 5% can be attained for the $t \bar t H^0$ process if the Higgs boson possesses a branching ratio to the $b \bar b$ channel that is at least 10% greater than that of the Standard Model Higgs. This study investigates the application of pretrained language models (PLMs) in few-shot and zero-shot learning. We examine various PLMs, optimization strategies, and prompt designs to evaluate their effectiveness across different tasks. Our approach is systematic, offering a straightforward method to analyze and compare PLMs without relying on task-specific components. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive framework that facilitates the easy comparison of PLMs, optimization techniques, and prompt engineering. The experiments were conducted across eight datasets spanning classification and generation tasks. Our findings indicate that unsupervised few-shot learning performance is primarily driven by the PLM's in-context few-shot capabilities, while the selection of the PLM is secondary to the design of the prompting context. Additionally, we observe that the advantages of fine-tuning diminish as the number of training examples increases. Finally, we demonstrate that the benefits of using task prompts are more pronounced in generation tasks than in classification tasks. This study evaluates the current state of automated speech recognition (ASR) for German. We present a new English-German comparative analysis based on the latest versions of ESpeech and Mozilla's ASR systems. The source code, along with pre-trained models for German, is accessible at https://github.com/kaheeriga/german-asr. Our top-performing model achieves a word error rate (WER) of 12.1% on the TIMIT-DE test set, compared to an average ASR worker performance of 20.5%. Additionally, we provide a German ASR demo (https://speech.cs.cmu.edu/demo/german-asr/) that matches the capabilities of the ESpeech demo available at https://speech.cs.cmu.edu/demo/english_asr/. Finally, we offer practical insights into training English-German ASR models using both systems. The ESpeech section covers training on the German-TIMIT dataset using both TIMIT-DE and English data, while the Mozilla section details training on the German Common Voice dataset. This work aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers interested in developing English-German ASR models. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across various machine learning domains, yet their decision boundaries often lack realism and robustness. Recent studies indicate that DNN outputs can be modeled as functions within reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs), offering a promising avenue for analyzing DNN behavior. However, existing methods typically model DNNs using non-Exchangeable Tangent Kernels (NTKs) and employ empirical risk minimization (ERM) for training, which overlooks the regularization effects inherent in the NTK-based loss function. This work addresses that limitation by explicitly accounting for such regularization. We demonstrate that the gradient of the empirical loss under NTK is equivalent to regularizing DNN training with NTK-based gradient descent (GD). Extensive experiments reveal that NTK-GD enhances the generalization performance of DNNs, yielding more realistic predictions and greater robustness. This paper presents an experimental investigation into the acoustic characteristics of talker variability within the VALL-E 2 text-to-speech system. Our primary objective is to assess how effectively VALL-E 2 can generate speech mimicking the vocal qualities of unseen speakers. Our findings indicate that while the system successfully reproduces general talker traits, it fails to capture certain acoustic features, particularly those related to pitch. Furthermore, we observe that the degree of similarity to a target voice is influenced by the specific phonetic content of the utterance. Finally, VALL-E 2 demonstrates a tendency to overfit during zero-shot cloning, resulting in speech that sounds more similar to the training data than to the desired target voice. These limitations suggest that current text-to-speech models require further refinement to achieve more faithful and diverse voices. To address this, we propose a new approach for generating synthetic speech by synthesizing multiple utterances from the target voice and averaging them. Our results show that this technique produces speech that is more similar to the target than the individual cloning attempts, thereby offering a viable solution to the identified issues. This study examines the impact of a quantum gravitational effect, represented by a minimal length, on the collective motion of triaxial nuclei. Utilizing the algebraic framework, we derived expressions for energies and eigenstates corresponding to three distinct collective behaviors: gamma-softness, beta-softness, and spherical symmetry. Our analysis reveals that the minimal length effect is most pronounced in the gamma-soft case, where it induces splitting in the energy spectrum. Conversely, under beta-soft and spherical conditions, the effect is significantly weaker. Furthermore, we observed that both eigenstates and wave functions are substantially influenced by this effect. These findings suggest that the minimal length phenomenon is more readily observable in gamma-soft nuclei. Additionally, the calculated energies align with experimental data, confirming the validity of our theoretical results. Finally, we demonstrate that the minimal length effect is more prominent in heavy nuclei compared to light ones. These conclusions are supported by graphs and tables. The research was conducted using the ALIEN-1000 supercomputer at the Supercomputing Center for Simulation (SCS) of the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (MIPT). Polyphase Golay complementary arrays (PGCA) have recently attracted significant research interest due to their ability to produce a single-sided array response pattern (ARP) and a closed-form closed-loop ARP. This paper introduces the design of PGCA using three methods: (1) constructing a new type of PGCA through the combination of polyphase Golay complementary sequences (PGCS) and orthogonal arrays (OA); (2) developing a step-by-step construction method for PGCA based on polyphase array (PA) and OA; and (3) proposing a direct construction method for PGCA utilizing generalized PA. The performance of the proposed designs is evaluated through peak sidelobe level (PSL) analysis, which demonstrates that the proposed methods yield lower PSL values compared to existing approaches. Additionally, the computational complexity of these methods is assessed, revealing that the proposed schemes require fewer operations than previous methods. Finally, the practical application of PGCA in array processing is illustrated by designing radar waveforms with PGCA structures, which exhibit lower peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) and higher peak compression ratios (PCR) than traditional methods. Furthermore, these radar waveforms offer superior range resolution and reduced range sidelobes. Numerical simulations confirm the validity of the proposed designs. Detecting changes in remote sensing imagery is a critical yet difficult task, particularly when dealing with multispectral and hyperspectral data. This paper introduces a new approach to the challenging problem of unsupervised change detection in hyperspectral images, where only pre- and post-event image pairs are available and no change masks exist for training. We propose a novel feature fusion architecture that integrates two distinct neural network models: a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that processes spatial-spectral features and a 1D CNN that analyzes spectral features extracted from spatially aligned pixels. This design is intended to enhance the detection of subtle, low-contrast changes. We evaluated the proposed architecture on two real-world datasets, the ROSE and Pavia University scenes, and compared its performance against several baseline methods. The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed architecture significantly outperforms the baselines. Furthermore, we conducted ablation studies to assess the contribution of each component, and the findings confirm the validity of our proposed architecture. This study examines the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in molecular fluids, as well as molecular liquids and model potentials. The entropy-entropy scaling law, which connects residual entropy to viscosity, is evaluated using kinetic theory, the Vogel-Fulcher-Tamman (VFT) equation, and the Adam-Gibbs equation. For molecular fluids, the correlation between residual entropy and the Bernal-Hindley free volume is also investigated. Results indicate that while kinetic theory accurately describes the residual entropy-viscosity connection for non-quantum atomics, molecular fluids, and classical molecular potentials, it fails for quantum atomic and molecular potentials. Conversely, the VFT equation consistently correlates residual entropy with viscosity across all fluid types. Furthermore, the Adam-Gibbs equation demonstrates a strong correlation between free volume and viscosity in these systems. Finally, the VFT equation is applied to determine the configurational entropy of all molecular fluids and potentials examined. The study concludes that residual entropy serves as a universal state variable for describing the viscosity of molecular fluids and model potentials. We outline a cyclical cosmology grounded in the $\Lambda CDM$ model, where each cycle comprises an expansion phase followed by a contraction. The universe's fate hinges on the Hubble constant and the density parameter; if the product remains below unity, contraction halts and reverses into expansion, initiating a new cycle. Conversely, if this product exceeds unity, the universe undergoes recollapse. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dark matter and dark energy can be interpreted as residual radiation and dark matter remnants from the previous cycle's death, respectively. This framework offers a novel perspective on the nature of dark matter and dark energy, potentially opening new avenues for their investigation. Additionally, we show that the entropy generated during each cycle's collapse and subsequent Big Bang increases, resulting in a non-increasing entropy across the cyclical process. This outcome aligns with the second law of thermodynamics, thereby resolving the entropy problem typically associated with the Big Bang theory. Ultimately, we contend that our cyclical model represents a more robust foundation for understanding the universe's evolution compared to the standard Big Bang framework. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future research. (arXiv:1909.03004v2 [astro-ph.CO])

This study investigates the superdeterministic hypothesis, which posits that Bell's theorem is circumvented by a violation of statistical independence between the choice of measurement and the state of the particles. The analysis begins with a classical model of particle polarization, where the correlation of measurement outcomes is governed by a shared hidden variable, $\theta$, which dictates the polarization state for both Alice and Bob. The paper then reviews the Invariant-set theory proposed by Florin Iorga, a deterministic, superdeterministic hidden-variable framework. In this theory, the hidden variable $\theta$ is selected from an invariant set, $\Theta$, a subset of the total set of all possible $\theta$ values, $\Theta_{all}$. The theory posits that only the elements within this invariant set evolve forward in time. Iorga demonstrates that this theory is consistent with the predictions of quantum mechanics. Subsequently, I examine the conditions required for superdeterminism to function within the context of Bell's theorem. My analysis reveals that for the superdeterministic explanation to hold, there must be a correlation between the hidden variable $\theta$ and the measurement choice, $\phi$, such that the distribution of $\theta$ in Alice's and Bob's experiments is restricted to a specific subset of the invariant set, $\Theta_{all}$, determined by the choice of measurement. I show that the Invariant-set theory fails to meet this condition, as the choice of measurement is determined by a random process that is independent of the hidden variable. Consequently, the Invariant-set theory cannot explain the violation of statistical independence in Bell's theorem. Furthermore, I argue that any superdeterministic theory must adhere to the following conditions: 1) The distribution of $\theta$ must be limited to a subset of the invariant set, $\Theta_{all}$, dependent on the measurement choice $\phi$. 2) The selection of $\theta$ from this subset must be independent of the measurement choice $\phi$. 3) The selection of $\theta$ must be independent of the measurement results. I demonstrate that the Invariant-set theory violates the first condition. Additionally, I outline a testable experiment that could distinguish between the Invariant-set theory and quantum mechanics. This experiment involves measuring the polarization of entangled photons at angles $\phi_A$ and $\phi_B$ that are not standard quantum settings but are instead determined by the specific measurement choice $\phi$. Automated keyphrase spotting involves segmenting audio streams and classifying them to detect phrases matching a specific set. This task is computationally intensive, making it unsuitable for deployment on IoT devices with restricted processing and memory capabilities. To address this, we introduce a novel neural network architecture designed to minimize the number of operations and memory usage. We evaluated this model against existing approaches on the AudioSet dataset and validated its efficacy on real-world data using a speech recognition system. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model reduces both processing time and memory consumption compared to state-of-the-art solutions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexeykolesnikov/nn-keyphrase-spotting. Furthermore, the model's inference time on Raspberry Pi 400 is competitive with other state-of-the-art methods, such as Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks (CRNN) and Deep Audio Convolutional Neural Networks (DANet). We anticipate that this model will facilitate the development of new, efficient speech processing applications for IoT devices. Additionally, we intend to release a Python package on PyPI in the near future to streamline the deployment of the model on these devices. Finally, we plan to explore the potential of keyphrase spotting for enhancing speech processing systems on IoT hardware. Specifically, we aim to investigate whether a speech recognition system can be made more efficient by first detecting the presence of speech and then processing only the relevant segments. This strategy could significantly improve the overall efficiency of speech processing systems on IoT devices. We will present the results of our experiments regarding this approach in future publications. The code for these experiments can be found at https://github.com/alexeykolesnikov/speech-detection-and-recognition-on-IoT-devices. Our findings indicate that detecting speech presence before processing yields a 2x speedup in recognition time on IoT devices. This represents a significant improvement over current state-of-the-art methods, which do not account for the presence of speech. We expect this approach to substantially enhance the efficiency of speech recognition systems on IoT devices. The proposed method is particularly beneficial for applications such as voice assistants, where it is crucial to minimize processing time and energy usage. We believe this approach will enable the creation of more efficient voice assistants for IoT devices. Group lasso methods are widely utilized for analyzing high-dimensional data, yet they face challenges when dealing with categorical variables due to an excessive number of distinct levels. This paper introduces the sparse contingency table model, a novel approach designed to enhance group lasso for high-dimensional categorical data. By employing a tailored loss function, the method effectively manages the interaction effects between categorical variables. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed model maintains the same computational complexity as group lasso. Simulation studies indicate that the proposed model outperforms group lasso in both prediction accuracy and variable selection. Embedded systems are increasingly vital across numerous sectors, yet they face a scarcity of resources and a lack of flexibility. Hardware virtualization offers a solution by enabling the concurrent execution of multiple operating systems on a single platform. However, current hypervisors are tailored for general-purpose computing and fail to address the specific needs of mixed severity embedded real-time environments. To overcome this limitation, we present T-Visor, a novel hypervisor designed specifically for such embedded real-time systems. T-Visor facilitates the simultaneous operation of a critical real-time OS and a non-critical general-purpose OS. We have validated its efficacy through extensive testing, demonstrating that it maintains the deterministic performance of the critical OS while successfully executing the non-critical OS. Furthermore, T-Visor is lightweight, occupying less than 10KB of flash memory and consuming under 1KB of RAM. Our findings indicate that T-Visor introduces a maximum overhead of 1.5% on the critical OS and 1.2% on the non-critical OS. These results confirm that T-Visor is highly suitable for mixed severity embedded real-time applications. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SeoulNU-T-Visor/T-Visor. This study examines a system of two populations, where each individual is modeled as a phase oscillator with uniformly distributed natural frequencies and irregular, randomly varying coupling phases. We establish conditions for the emergence of complete synchronization, chimera states, and incoherence within both coherent and random coupling frameworks. Our findings indicate that as coupling intensity rises, a sequence of transitions occurs: starting from incoherence, the system moves to a chimera state, and finally to complete coherence. Notably, the synchronization threshold is lower than previously reported in the literature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the periodic switching characteristic of chimeras can be derived from the system's Fokker-Planck equation. These results are validated through numerical simulations. Additionally, we show that the observed transitions are qualitatively similar to those found in systems with constant coupling phases. The approach used here is applicable to networks of oscillators with irregular or random couplings. This model is particularly relevant for describing biological systems, such as neuronal networks, where synaptic connections exhibit irregularity and randomness. We anticipate that this model will prove valuable for investigating chimeras in biological contexts. Finally, we discuss the potential of this model for analyzing incoherence and chimeras in networks featuring both strong and weak oscillators. This study addresses the robust regulation problem, which involves designing a controller to minimize the probability of a cost function exceeding a specific threshold. We introduce a model-based probabilistic regulator, capable of solving this task when the probability distribution of disturbances is known. Our approach utilizes a linear dynamical system to forecast future states and state-dependent functions to estimate the likelihood of cost violations. We propose a gradient ascent algorithm to optimize regulator parameters, ensuring convergence to a local optimum that guarantees a specified cost satisfaction level. Furthermore, we extend this method to handle disturbance uncertainties by formulating a distributionally robust probabilistic regulation problem. We subsequently develop a novel model predictive control (MPC) algorithm that leverages the aforementioned probabilistic regulator to address this regulation under uncertain disturbances. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1997/learning_robust_regulators. Additionally, the probabilistic regulator serves as a foundational component for the next-generation safety-critical autonomous driving system at Uber. We examine the asymptotic behavior of reflected information within random tensor networks, demonstrating that it scales linearly with the network's size. This contrasts with the von Neumann entropy, which exhibits reflected information that grows at most logarithmically. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the asymptotic reflected information serves as a gauge for the network's degree of tree-likeness. We also present applications of these results to models involving random tensors with fixed ranks. Finally, we establish that the reflected information spectrum can be interpreted as a quantization rate for a source of reflected information. These models represent novel examples where the reflected information spectrum is non-trivial, displaying a kink at a rate proportional to the network size. Additionally, we illustrate that these models can be realized through networks of quantum channels. Finally, we propose a method for constructing tensor networks with a prescribed reflected information spectrum. Our results suggest that such networks can be built from random tensors possessing ranks drawn from a specified distribution. This approach extends the framework of tensor network ensembles, which are typically defined by the rank distribution of individual tensors. We also show that this construction enables the modeling of reflected information within quantum channels. Tensor networks with quantum channels can be generated by taking the direct sum of tensor networks composed of quantum channels with randomly selected ranks. Our methodology relies on a novel technique for analyzing the asymptotic behavior of reflected information in random tensor networks, which we term the "tensor network method." This approach is applicable to a broad class of random tensor networks, including those formed by networks of quantum channels. We anticipate that the tensor network method will prove useful for investigating the asymptotic behavior of reflected information in various other random tensor network models. We investigate heritable information within non-equilibrium dynamics, defined as the mutual information between a specific initial state and a future pattern of activity, normalized by the pattern's spatio-temporal span. This metric quantifies how much future behavior can be predicted based on the initial condition. We demonstrate that in a broad category of stochastic dynamics, this measure is governed by a universal scaling law determined by the space-time diffusion constant and the correlation time of the process. Furthermore, we show that this information content can be computed using a variant of the two-point function. We apply this framework to various physical systems, including Brownian motion, active matter, and specific random field theories. Additionally, we examine a computational model of self-replicating patterns in the cellular automaton Rule 110, revealing that the automaton's ability to encode and transmit information is intrinsically linked to the persistence of heritable information across its different sectors. These findings suggest that the concept of heritable information offers a universal characterization for non-equilibrium dynamics and may facilitate a more fundamental understanding of information processing in both physical and computational systems. Finally, we outline potential directions for extending this framework to quantum systems. The technical derivations are detailed in an accompanying supplementary material. This work expands upon the study by B. D. Smith, A. M. Somoza, and A. J. Bray, published in Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 060601 (2020). Moreover, this approach may facilitate a deeper comprehension of how information is processed in non-equilibrium physical systems, such as those exhibiting self-organized criticality. We demonstrate that the gravitational holonomy, which encodes the parallel transport of a spinor field along a closed loop within spacetime, constitutes the unique copy of a nontrivial holonomy in general relativity. This implies that any theory aiming to generalize gravitational holonomy—such as one that assigns a gravitational holonomy to every open path or one that incorporates non-geometric or non-gravitational information—must include additional fields or structures beyond the metric. Such additions would manifest as new degrees of freedom in the theory's equations. Consequently, this finding establishes a limit on the potential forms of theories that extend Einstein's equivalence principle. We further illustrate the significance of this result by applying it to theories designed to generalise Einstein's equivalence principle. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for both fundamental and phenomenological physics. This study introduces a novel clock mechanism for tunneling, termed the Larmor clock, which relies on fluctuations in spin within the tunneling region. By analyzing the spin's precession in a magnetic field, we identify variations in the Larmor frequency caused by these local spin changes. The associated tunneling time is then defined as the product of the number of precessions and the Larmor period. We demonstrate that this duration exhibits significant fluctuations contingent upon the tunneling particle's spin state, a phenomenon that can be observed through quantum interference effects. Furthermore, we illustrate that this spin-dependent tunneling time can be experimentally verified by measuring the spin polarization of the transmitted particle. Finally, we show that this polarization can be accurately predicted using the newly introduced spin-based time. Our findings indicate that the proposed Larmor clock offers a fresh perspective on characterizing tunneling times, potentially resolving the longstanding debate in the field. Additionally, the method for measuring spin-dependent tunneling times holds promise for applications in quantum information processing. This research investigates the leading-twist distribution amplitudes (DAs) of P-wave mesons within the nonrelativistic framework. Utilizing the Dirac equation, we establish a system of integral equations governing the DAs. By applying a perturbative approach to P-wave mesons, we solve these equations to express the DAs in terms of the meson's wave function, thereby clarifying the internal quark dynamics of P-wave mesons. Our findings indicate that, at leading order, the leading-twist DAs for P-wave mesons are directly proportional to their wave functions, with the proportionality constant varying based on the specific meson type. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the leading-twist DAs for nonrelativistic P-wave mesons exhibit universality across different meson varieties. Finally, the leading-twist DAs derived in this study can be integrated into the light-cone sum rules approach to calculate the form factors of P-wave mesons. We introduce a method for constructing polynomials of field operators that maintain bosonic commutation relations. This approach is demonstrated using the standard Gross-Pitaevskii Hamiltonian for a Bose-Einstein condensate. In this example, we develop a bosonic set of Hamiltonian-like operators and provide the unitary transformation connecting it to the standard formulation. This set offers a convenient framework for analyzing low and high occupation number regimes. Additionally, we suggest a generalization of the Hamiltonian set that includes terms for kinetic, potential, and nonlinear fields. We also examine the commutation relations between bosonic field operators and the generalized non-linear field, demonstrating that they are not vanishing and are not simply proportional to the fields themselves. These findings suggest that the non-linear field is not entirely spurious and can be treated as a bosonic degree of freedom. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of these results for Bose-Liquid theory. We examine the BMS phase space of four-dimensional gravitational scattering and demonstrate that the associated BMS charges correspond to conformal primary gamma-ray operators (CPOs) defined on the celestial sphere. This correspondence enables the reformulation of both the asymptotic symmetry group and the scattering matrix into the language of CPOs. By utilizing the concept of "dressed states," we show that the Barnich and Glorioso soft theorem, which characterizes the gauge invariance of the S-matrix, is equivalent to the conformal soft theorem, which involves the insertion of a CPO within correlation functions. Furthermore, we prove that the Barnich and Glorioso soft charge generates the subleading soft graviton charge, thereby establishing an equivalence between the Barnich and Glorioso and Strominger soft theorems. Finally, we extend the Barnich and Glorioso analysis to the case of double soft gravitons. In this scenario, the gauge invariance of multi-particle states yields the equivalence between the Barnich and Glorioso double soft theorem and the conformal double soft theorem, which involves the insertion of two CPOs. Consequently, the Barnich and Glorioso super-soft charge emerges as the product of two conformal soft charges, each carrying a distinct conformal dimension. These findings rely on the soft expansion of the S-matrix up to the second order. Additionally, we investigate the implications of these results for the CPO operator product expansion and the Barnich and Glorioso Ward identity. Our findings suggest that the Barnich and Glorioso Ward identity can be derived from the operator product expansion, provided that the double soft graviton charge is interpreted as the commutator of two CPOs with specific conformal dimensions. This approach offers a novel perspective on the Barnich and Glorioso soft theorem, as it bypasses the need for an explicit characterization of the S-matrix under asymptotic symmetries. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our results and the recent findings of Kapec, He, and Strominger. In summary, we establish a new framework for understanding the Barnich and Glorioso soft theorem and its connection to the conformal soft theorem, which is based on the CPO operator expansion. This framework is expected to facilitate further research into the structure of the Barnich and Glorioso soft theorem. Addressing the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and overfitting in continual learning is crucial for the widespread adoption of deep neural networks. Ensemble methods offer a promising solution by maintaining multiple networks with varied initializations to enhance performance. However, traditional online ensemble approaches are often computationally intensive and require storing a large volume of parameters. This paper introduces a novel method for online ensemble learning that utilizes a single network architecture. The proposed model employs a dynamic learning rate strategy to automatically adjust the contribution of each sub-network based on the data stream's distribution, thereby minimizing both computational costs and the number of stored parameters. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance across various subfields of continual learning, including class incremental, task incremental, domain incremental, and input-output incremental scenarios. Furthermore, the model is computationally efficient, requiring only the storage of a single network's parameters. The paper introduces a novel class of generalized Calabi-Yau forms, denoted as $\Gamma_k$, which encompasses the standard Calabi-Yau form as a specific instance within the spectrum. It demonstrates that these forms satisfy a suite of properties analogous to those of Calabi-Yau forms, including parallelism under all associated connections, unimodularity relative to a specific metric, and nullity across every Chern curvature tensor. Furthermore, the study establishes the existence of non-Kähler manifolds populated with such forms and investigates the structure of the associated metrics, highlighting the presence of several novel metrics that are neither flat nor Ricci-flat, despite being conformally flat. The analysis concludes by examining the curvature characteristics of these metrics. Additionally, it is noted that the generalized Calabi-Yau form remains parallel under the first Chern connection, and the paper provides a complete characterization of this form based on the curvature properties of said connection. Finally, the study examines the holonomy groups of the metrics under consideration, revealing that they are contained within $SU(n)$. The paper concludes with an outline of the authors' future research directions. This work extends the findings presented in [10]. This paper investigates the structure of total permutation polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$, where $q=p^{n}$ and $p$ is an odd prime. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for a polynomial of degree $m(q+1)$ to be a total permutation polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$, provided $m \equiv 1 \pmod{q+1}$ and $m-1$ is square-free. Additionally, we present several new permutation polynomials and rational functions defined over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Furthermore, we examine and characterize total permutation polynomials of the form $(x-a)^{2}(x-b)^{2}(x-c)$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$, where $a, b, c \in \mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Finally, we analyze and characterize these same polynomials when the degree is reduced to $m(q+1)-2$. Our findings extend and complement existing results by Li and Li [J. Number Theory 130 (2010) 1492–1507] and Wang and Li [J. Number Theory 132 (2012) 1003–1013]. Additionally, we offer some remarks and open problems.

Intestinal parasites are a significant cause of illness and death globally, particularly in developing nations, where they are transmitted through contaminated food and water. Accurate diagnosis is essential for administering appropriate treatment, which requires the correct identification of the specific parasite involved. However, distinguishing between different species can be challenging for pathologists due to the visual similarities among parasites. This study introduces a classification system for intestinal parasites utilizing Deep Belief Networks (DBN). The proposed model was evaluated using the publicly available ISIC 2013 dataset, which includes three categories: Eosinophil, Giardia, and Cryptosporidium. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves an overall accuracy of 91.67%, with individual class accuracies of 91.67% for Eosinophil, 91.67% for Giardia, and 91.67% for Cryptosporidium. These findings indicate that the proposed system is effective for classifying these specific parasites. Additionally, the study addresses the limitations of DBNs regarding feature extraction by integrating them with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for feature extraction. This hybrid approach yielded an overall accuracy of 95.83%, representing a 4.16% improvement over the standalone DBN system. The enhanced performance of the hybrid model is attributed to the CNN's superior ability to extract relevant data. The source code for this work is accessible at: https://github.com/raufkhan123/Intestinal-Parasites-DBN-CNN. Future research will explore other neural network architectures to further refine the proposed system. The dataset used in this study can be downloaded from: http://www.isic-archive.com/datasets/2013-parasites. This study addresses a non-zero-sum stochastic differential game involving two insurers aiming to optimize their investment and reinsurance strategies. The jump-diffusion dynamics of each insurer are governed by a Markov chain, creating a piecewise hybrid system. We establish the existence and uniqueness of a viscosity solution for the associated nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs (HJB) system. Furthermore, we derive numerical approximation methods for these nonlinear HJB equations and employ them to compute nearly optimal controls. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our numerical approach through simulation experiments. Notably, this work represents the first instance of approximating stochastic HJB equations for Heston-type investment-reinsurance models featuring regime-switching jump-diffusion dynamics. Additionally, the proposed numerical scheme is applicable to a broader class of Heston-type investment and reinsurance problems with regime-switching jump-diffusion. This framework can be extended to various other Heston-type nonlinear HJB systems, including those involving interest rates, stock prices, and commodity prices. The paper concludes with a discussion on the extension of these findings to such scenarios. This research is particularly relevant for applications in economics, finance, and commodity markets. To demonstrate the practicality of our numerical method, we apply it to several other Heston-type investment and reinsurance models with regime-switching jump-diffusion, including interest rate models, stock price models, and commodity price models. These applications are also significant for economists, financial analysts, and commodity market analysts. This paper introduces a novel control algorithm designed to enhance the smoothness and stability of quadrotor flight. The proposed Probabilistic Dual Simplex Algorithm (PIDA) integrates the dual simplex method with probability theory to create a smooth, stable controller. By imposing a specific cost function, PIDA regulates the angular velocity of the quadrotor. To address the non-stationary nature of the vehicle's dynamics, a genetic filter is employed to estimate the parameters required for the PIDA cost function. Simulation results demonstrate that PIDA outperforms the traditional Proportional-Integral (PID) controller in terms of angular velocity response, settling time, and control effort. Furthermore, a statistical analysis of the parameters generated by the genetic filter confirms the accuracy of the estimated model parameters. Finally, experimental data from an actual quadrotor validates the efficacy of the PIDA controller. We present a low-energy model for pion-nucleon interactions that adheres to chiral symmetry and its spontaneous breaking, while also incorporating local vector meson dominance. This framework is demonstrated to be highly effective in describing low-energy phenomena, including pion production off the nucleon, low-energy pion scattering, and the pseudoscalar meson-baryon octet. Furthermore, the model offers a straightforward explanation for the existence of the sigma meson. The primary findings are: (i) the pseudoscalar meson-baryon OMEs are accurately reproduced, (ii) the masses of the scalar and vector mesons are determined, (iii) the scalar meson is identified as a local rho meson, (iv) the scalar meson mass is fixed at 550 MeV, (v) the coupling constant $g_{\sigma NN}$ is established as 4.8, (vi) the coupling constant $g_{\sigma \pi \pi}$ is set to 1.5, and (vii) the mass of the sigma meson is calculated to be 800 MeV. Additionally, the model successfully replicates the low-energy pion-nucleon phase shifts and the $p + p \to \Delta + \Delta$ cross section. The implications of these results are also examined. Keywords: Chiral Symmetry, Pion-Nucleon Interactions, Vector Meson Dominance, Sigma Meson. PACS: 12.10.-g, 11.10.-w, 11.80.+m, 13.40.-g.

The Large Hadron Collider (LBNL-HEP-CMS-P1P) Phase-1 Pixel Pilot Blade Detector, situated within the CMS experiment at CERN, is designed to identify charged particles and measure their transverse momentum. This paper presents the initial performance analysis of the detector, which was installed in December 2019 and utilized during the 2020 LHC run. The study details the data analysis workflow and evaluates the system's efficiency and spatial resolution. Results indicate a tracking efficiency of approximately 90% for particles with a transverse momentum ($p_T$) of 1 GeV, with a measured spatial resolution of 10 $\mu$m. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates the detector's capability to reconstruct tracks with a $p_T$ of 1 GeV. These findings confirm that the pilot blade is fully operational and ready for data-taking. The paper concludes by outlining future prospects for the system.

This study employs machine learning to analyze the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide (HSC-W120) survey dataset, which comprises 1.2 million galaxies with redshifts $z<1$. We utilize a convolutional neural network (CNN) to estimate the fraction of active galactic nuclei (AGN) hosts within this sample. The analysis reveals that AGN hosts are predominantly found in the red sequence, with a median stellar mass of $10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$ and a median redshift of 0.2. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between AGN activity and host galaxy properties, including stellar mass, star formation rate, and color. Our results indicate that AGN hosts exhibit higher star formation rates and stellar masses compared to non-hosts, though these differences diminish at higher redshifts. Additionally, AGN hosts are observed to be redder than non-hosts, a characteristic that becomes more pronounced at lower redshifts. Finally, we compare our findings with those from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Strategic Program on the Galaxy Evolution (HSC-SPRING) Wide Area Galaxy Evolution Survey (WAGE), which covers a smaller area ($1.5$ deg$^2$) but offers deeper imaging. Our findings suggest that AGN hosts in the WAGE survey are more massive and redder than those in the HSC-W120 survey, a trend that is consistent with the HSC-W120 results at overlapping redshifts. These observations align with the expectation that AGN hosts are typically more massive and redder than non-hosts. Overall, the HSC-W120 survey provides a statistically significant sample of $z<1$ AGN hosts, enabling a more robust characterization of their host galaxy properties. This large dataset will facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of AGN host properties and their evolution across cosmic time. Nuclear short-range correlations (SRCs) are traditionally defined using one- and two-particle densities integrated over momentum. This study introduces a novel framework for examining SRCs across phase space by leveraging the Wigner distribution. The paper demonstrates that this distribution can be derived from the two-particle density integrated over a momentum variable, specifically within a Gaussian window that mirrors the Gaussian profile of the one-particle density. Furthermore, it is established that integrating the two-particle density over either coordinate or momentum yields the same one-particle density, regardless of the window function used. Finally, the distribution is applied to analyze the SRC structure of a realistic SRC state. These findings pave the way for future investigations into SRCs within nuclei using various nuclear Hamiltonians. Additionally, the methodology is extended to the three-particle density, with an analysis of its associated distribution for a realistic three-particle SRC state. These results are expected to be valuable for interpreting three-body correlation data. The distribution is constructed using the SRC ansatz proposed by Hen et al. [Phys. Rev. C 81, 074001 (2010)] and Hen et al. [Phys. Rev. C 85, 034001 (2012)]. The one- and two-particle densities utilized in this work were computed by the SRC collaboration. Complex numbers are frequently encountered in mathematics, science, and engineering, yet they are rarely utilized in Machine Learning. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework designed for complex-valued data, featuring a new activation function and an implementation of complex equality within the PyTorch ecosystem. Additionally, we provide a demonstration applying our equality function to the domain of radio signals. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/complexdl/complexdl. We hope this work inspires further research into activation functions and loss functions that adhere to the unique algebraic and geometric properties of complex numbers. Our goal is to expand the application of complex-valued neural networks across various fields, including Radio Frequency (RF) signals, neuroscience, and quantum computing. For instance, complex equality serves as a critical component in our RF signal denoising application, where it enables the training of a deep learning model to distinguish between noisy and clean signals. We anticipate that our contributions will facilitate and inspire future research in these areas. For more information, please visit https://complexdl.org. The saturation of the gluon distribution within target hadrons and nuclei is a fundamental concept in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) that has garnered significant interest over the past few decades. This saturation phenomenon is closely linked to the gluon gluon merging process, which causes geometrical scaling in the deep-inelastic scattering of lepton beams off hadronic and nuclear targets. Additionally, it plays a crucial role in explaining the suppression of particle production at low transverse momenta in heavy-ion collisions. In this work, we review the saturation scale, its relationship to the QCD coupling constant, and its implications for hadron production in both proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, we examine the parton distribution functions (PDFs) of the proton and nuclear modified factorization, along with their experimental verification. Finally, we explore the potential for using the saturation scale as a probe to investigate the gluon-glass phase of QCD matter. This review is based on a plenary lecture delivered at the International Conference on High Energy Physics in Chicago, 2019. Amplitude variations in young stars are frequently linked to the presence of a hot Jupiter, yet this relationship is not always straightforward. This study investigates the sources of amplitude dispersion in young stars by analyzing the Kepler-290 and Kepler-102 systems, which host a hot Jupiter and a hot Neptune, respectively. We developed a forward model to simulate the light curves of both systems, incorporating a spot-tracking algorithm to account for spot evolution. Our results indicate that the dispersion in amplitude values observed in low-metallicity stars stems from two primary factors: the evolution of spots over time and the distribution of spot parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dispersion in amplitude is inversely proportional to the number of observed transits. Finally, we conclude that the variability seen in the light curve of Kepler-290 is primarily driven by the evolution of spots. These findings suggest that the correlation between amplitude and planet radius is not universal and that the current understanding of how spot parameters influence amplitude dispersion requires refinement. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of observing young stars for extended periods to accurately characterize the impact of spot evolution on amplitude variability.

This study introduces a new R package, "sensitivity," designed to assess how robust machine learning models are to variations in their input features. The package utilizes a novel approach grounded in statistical learning theory, offering superior scalability and accuracy compared to existing methods. It includes a comprehensive suite of tools for calculating sensitivity metrics across various feature types, such as numerical, categorical, and textual data, alongside an intuitive visualization module. We validate the package by reanalyzing data from the Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), a global survey on adult skills and knowledge. Our analysis reveals that financial literacy models are highly sensitive to specific attributes within both categorical and textual features, including political orientation, country of residence, and language proficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the "sensitivity" package can effectively identify these nuances in textual data, a capability that surpasses the performance of current sensitivity analysis techniques. This Letter introduces a SQUID machine, representing the inaugural hardware implementation of a quantum machine capable of universal computation. By utilizing a quaternary question interface, the SQUID machine demonstrates superior performance compared to both classical binary and quantum question interfaces. We constructed a SQUID machine comprising four quaternary questions and validated its computational capabilities through experimental measurements. These findings establish a robust foundation for the broader field of quantum machine intelligence. Our SQUID machines are scalable, and we have already developed a two-squid system; this approach offers significant advantages for the mass production of quantum hardware. Furthermore, we have designed a control system that enables the execution of multiple machines sequentially on a single hardware unit, thereby enhancing resource efficiency. This work marks the first experimental realization of quantum hardware capable of performing computational tasks, paving the way for the development of larger-scale quantum machines. We anticipate that the creation of these quantum machines will play a pivotal role in advancing quantum machine intelligence. The PALEOCCENE experiment aims to achieve a mass sensitivity of 100 g and a volume sensitivity of 1000 cm³ for low-energy nuclear recoil events. This goal is pursued through the use of color centers within synthetic diamond, which can be read out via near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence. These color centers are generated by implanting nitrogen-vacancy (NV) complexes with a single phosphorus atom. The specific type of color center targeted is the $^{129}$I-NV-P center, formed by implanting an NV center with a single phosphorus atom alongside iodine. This specific center was selected because the $^{129}$I nucleus possesses a nuclear spin ($I=1/2$), which creates a hyperfine structure in the NIR fluorescence spectrum. This spectral feature enables the detection of nuclear recoil events. The experiment is designed to operate at a temperature of 4 K and is scheduled to commence in 2024. This paper outlines the scientific objectives of PALEOCCENE and reviews the current status of the technology. Furthermore, it presents initial results from a proof-of-principle study involving a 100 mg diamond sample doped with an NV center and implanted with 100 ng of iodine. Finally, the paper details the planned production of a 100 g diamond target and a 1000 cm³ volume of doped diamond. Ultimately, PALEOCCENE is expected to advance the field of nuclear recoil detection and contribute to the next generation of low-mass, low-threshold, large-volume detectors for dark matter and neutrino research. Additionally, it will serve as a novel detector for nuclear forensics and a potential tool for detecting nuclear explosions. Our predictions align with experimental data obtained from particles in a self-propelled colloidal suspension under a sedimentation force. Specifically, we demonstrate that these colloidal molecules can self-assemble from monomers and disassemble into individual colloids through a hysteresis loop. Furthermore, we illustrate that the lifetime of these molecules can be tuned by adjusting the sedimentation strength and the active noise intensity. These findings offer valuable insights into the stability of synthetic colloidal molecules and establish a pathway for their potential applications. Additionally, our results provide a quantitative understanding of the impact of activity gradients on colloidal molecules, thereby expanding the scope of the sedimentation model. Finally, we suggest that this framework could be utilized to design and fabricate a wide range of complex colloidal structures. This study investigates the quantum states of interacting electrons confined to a two-dimensional plane under a strong perpendicular magnetic field. By employing the generalized lowest Landau level (GLLL) approach, we demonstrate that magnetic flux quantization can occur at values other than $h/e$. This framework enables the calculation of exact ground and excited states for arbitrary electron counts at these non-$h/e$ flux quanta. Our findings reveal multiple magnetoroton states within a single magneton, a phenomenon we term "multiple magnetorotons." Furthermore, we observe that the spectral rule established by Jia and Zaikin for $h/e$ extends to all rational magnetic fluxes. We also provide a theoretical explanation for this spectral total rule, which holds significant potential for advancing quantum simulation research. Finally, we explore the implications of multiple magnetorotons for understanding the fractional quantum Hall effect. These results suggest that non-$h/e$ flux quantization could be utilized to engineer novel quantum phases, such as a magneton-induced fractional quantum Hall state. Additionally, we propose that this mechanism may explain the enigmatic six-fold degeneracy observed in the lowest energy state at $5h/2e$. The theoretical methods developed herein are broadly applicable to a wide range of quantum Hall problems. Furthermore, we outline a feasible experimental protocol for detecting multiple magnetorotons. This paper introduces a geometric framework designed to identify network regions with high outbreak risk by analyzing the interplay between their size and internal connectivity. We derive both a precise mathematical definition of these regions and an efficient algorithm to locate them within large networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these identified regions align with the outbreaks predicted by the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model, as well as the more permissive Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) and Susceptible-Infected-Dead (SID) models. The study concludes by discussing the potential applications of this approach. Our method is implemented in an open-source Python package available at https://github.com/andreafelici/epi_networks. Additionally, we provide a Jupyter notebook that includes a simulation of the aforementioned models on the resulting networks. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. This work was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the goal of offering a theoretical basis for the policy of isolating highly connected network regions to mitigate virus spread. We hope this approach can inform the design of similar policies in the future. To our knowledge, this is the first work to establish a theoretical link between high-risk network regions and outbreaks in both the SIS and SIR models. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature; Section 3 presents the geometric approach; Section 4 establishes the connection between high-risk regions and outbreaks; Section 5 details numerical experiments; and Section 6 concludes the study. This study presents a straightforward method for avoiding 2D Gaussian kernel convolutions at the locations of Galactic foreground residuals, specifically X-features, which may obscure point sources in CMB maps derived from maximum likelihood estimators. We demonstrate that the likelihood can be reformulated to exclude these regions without requiring interpolation. This approach is particularly advantageous for future experiments, such as CMB-S4, where X-features are anticipated to be more pronounced due to the inclusion of additional foreground tracers. We illustrate the technique using a Planck-like simulated map and show that it enables the creation of CMB maps with significantly reduced X-features. Furthermore, we confirm that point sources can be recovered with minimal bias and substantially lower variance compared to standard methods that rely on interpolating likelihood values across X-features. Finally, we establish that this procedure is applicable to any map generated via maximum likelihood estimation. We conclude that this method offers a viable strategy for mitigating the impact of X-features on point source recovery in future CMB experiments.

Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) has recently gained significant attention for its potential to reduce the need for manual task specification. Instead of requiring explicit rewards, policies are guided by descriptions of desired states, such as "reach the red cup." However, these statements often contain ambiguous references; for instance, "reach the red cup" could refer to either the red cup or the blue cup. This paper addresses the challenge of integrating GCRL with language-driven policies to create agents capable of handling such ambiguities. We introduce a novel method that enables agents to acquire the ability to resolve referential ambiguity through interaction with an external source of common knowledge, such as a robot operator or a natural language question-answering system. Our results demonstrate that this approach allows agents to effectively learn to resolve ambiguous references. Furthermore, we show that agents trained on ambiguous goals generalize more effectively to novel tasks compared to those trained on unambiguous ones. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our method in a simulated kitchen environment. The code is available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/ambiguity.

We introduce a shadow procedure tomography method designed to characterize quantum channels. Our approach relies on preparing a comprehensive collection of diverse input states, executing the quantum channel on each, and subsequently analyzing the resulting output states. We demonstrate that this methodology can efficiently and precisely determine the parameters of a channel's Kraus representation. Furthermore, we establish that the technique is universally applicable to any quantum channel, irrespective of its specific properties. Additionally, we extend this procedure to identify an unknown channel embedded within a known one, a capability that proves valuable for detecting deviations from theoretical expectations in experimental settings. Finally, we present a numerical analysis of the method's performance, including an assessment of the number of parameters that can be accurately reconstructed. Our findings indicate that the method remains effective for channels with a substantial number of parameters, provided the count does not surpass the number of available data points. This offers a promising avenue for the efficient analysis of quantum channels that are difficult to simulate. The code accompanying our study can be found at https://github.com/QuantumAIResearch/Shadow-Tomography-of-Quantum-Channels. Keywords: Quantum process tomography, quantum machine learning, quantum parameter estimation. PACS numbers: 03.67.Lx, 03.67.Pp, 03.67.Mn.

This paper establishes precise bounds for the relationship between a convex body's Cheeger constant and its isoperimetric ratio, with the analysis revealing distinct behaviors when comparing a domain to half-spaces versus domains enclosed by closed curves. Additionally, we introduce a new geometric inequality: for any planar convex body, the product of the Cheeger constant and the square root of $(4\pi - I)$ does not exceed 2, where $I$ represents the isoperimetric ratio. We also formulate and explore related conjectures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sharp constants in these inequalities correspond to specific convex bodies, notably disks and rectangles. Finally, we examine the convergence of sequences of convex bodies and the continuity of the Cheeger constant within this context. In this regard, we prove that the Cheeger constant varies continuously with respect to the Hausdorff distance metric. We also address the convergence of Cheeger domains, demonstrating that a subsequence of these domains always converges to a limiting domain, even when the Cheeger constants themselves do not converge. The paper concludes with several open problems. Notably, we conjecture that the product of the Cheeger constant and $\sqrt{(4\pi - I)}$ is bounded above by 2 across all dimensions, and we propose that the sharp constants in our main theorem are attained by ellipsoids in higher dimensions. Finally, we examine the monotonicity of Cheeger constants under linear maps and establish that for a convex body with non-zero volume, there exists a linear map that either strictly increases or strictly decreases the Cheeger constant, depending on whether the body is ellipsoidal or not. Additionally, we demonstrate that the set of all linear maps preserving the Cheeger constant of a convex body is either a singleton or forms a connected set. Finally, we show that the limit of a sequence of convex bodies, under the assumption that their Cheeger constants converge, possesses a Cheeger constant equal to the limit of the sequence's values. These findings are derived from and supported by various examples and conjectures. The study of this problem was inspired by a question posed by Professor Shoshichi Kobayashi. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly utilized for diverse applications, including surveillance, search and rescue, and military operations. This paper introduces a new optimization framework designed to enhance the efficiency of UAV paths for time-sensitive tasks. The study begins by reviewing the fundamental concepts of UAVs and their associated challenges. Subsequently, it defines the core problem and outlines the methodology, which comprises three key components: a novel ovoid curve, an ovoid curve optimization algorithm, and an ovoid curve search algorithm. The ovoid curve optimization algorithm employs a genetic approach to refine trajectories, while the search algorithm utilizes a hill-climbing strategy to generate superior ovoid curves. These methods are integrated into a complete path search algorithm that constructs initial paths using straight lines and refines them through iterative improvements. The proposed algorithm is benchmarked against existing path planning techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating optimal trajectories. Furthermore, the paper includes a case study applying the algorithm to a specific scenario to validate its performance. The results indicate that the proposed approach yields efficient paths characterized by shorter durations and reduced energy consumption. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits robustness, as evidenced by its ability to successfully plan paths for scenarios involving multiple UAVs. Ultimately, this research offers a novel and effective solution for optimizing UAV path planning. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abdulrahimk/OUVIA. Keywords: Path Planning, UAV, Optimization, Genetic Algorithm.

The renormalization group (RG) approach is employed to investigate the instability of a Coulomb-interacting bilayer system at low temperatures. The model, formulated in momentum space, incorporates two anisotropic Fermi velocities and electron-electron interactions mediated by the background dielectric medium. By integrating out high-energy modes, the analysis reveals that the low-energy effective model exhibits three distinct types of instability, contingent upon the relationship between the Fermi velocities and interaction parameters. Specifically, the instability of the diagonal channel drives a Mott transition, while the instability of the anti-diagonal channel induces a metal-insulator transition. Furthermore, the RG analysis demonstrates that the low-energy effective model remains unstable against the generation of a non-zero mass term. This instability signifies a metal-semiconductor transition, which is more accurately described as a band inversion, as the resulting gap closes when the mass term vanishes. The study confirms that the critical dimension, above which these instabilities occur, is governed by the combined effects of the dielectric interaction and the anisotropic Fermi velocities. Additionally, the RG approach elucidates the competition among these various instabilities. Finally, the analysis indicates that the low-energy effective model is unstable toward the generation of a non-zero hopping term, a phenomenon that can be interpreted as a finite-temperature instability. These findings are consistent with previous research. The results suggest that the low-energy properties of bilayer systems are highly sensitive to the interplay between Fermi velocities and interaction parameters, a factor that must be carefully considered in the design of electronic devices. Furthermore, the RG analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of the phase diagram of the model, which is essential for interpreting experimental data. This work is anticipated to stimulate further research into the low-energy properties of bilayer systems. The findings may also offer valuable insights for the design of novel electronic devices and the development of advanced materials. Ultimately, the results underscore the critical role of anisotropic Fermi velocities and dielectric interactions in determining the low-energy properties of bilayer systems. This understanding is crucial for the design and characterization of next-generation electronic devices and materials. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of the RG approach and potential avenues for future research. These limitations include the inability of the RG method to capture strong correlation effects, the necessity of a more rigorous treatment of dielectric interactions, and the need for further investigation into the interplay between different instabilities. The findings may also offer valuable insights for the design and characterization of next-generation electronic devices and materials. The paper concludes with a discussion

The structural and electronic characteristics of endohedral fullerenes are significantly influenced by the nature of their internal atoms. This study employed scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to examine the interaction between Sc2TbN@C80 and an C80/Ir(111) system. Our findings indicate that the off-center conformation of the Sc2TbN@C80 molecule is stabilized by the hybridization between the C80 shell and the substrate. Furthermore, the STM results reveal that the molecule transitions from an off-center to a centered conformation as the temperature rises. These observations are well-reproduced by DFT calculations, which demonstrate that the off-center state corresponds to the ground state, whereas the centered state is an excited state with a low energy barrier. Consequently, thermal energy at elevated temperatures is sufficient to overcome this barrier, facilitating the transition to the centered conformation. This research offers valuable insights into the interplay between the internal atoms, the C80 shell, and the substrate in these advanced molecular systems. Additionally, the findings provide a deeper understanding of the conformational behavior of endohedral fullerenes, which is crucial for their potential applications. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of considering temperature-dependent effects when utilizing these molecules in nanotechnology.
