The stable marriage problem involves a set of men and women, each with strict preference lists over the opposite gender, where the objective is to form mutually acceptable pairs such that no two individuals prefer to switch partners. While the Gale-Shapley algorithm is well-known for guaranteeing a stable outcome by having a single gender always propose their top choice, we investigate a generalized framework where each individual can choose which subset of their preferred partners to propose to. Specifically, we examine a model where each man selects a non-empty subset of women to approach, provided the chosen subset is independent within his personal preference list. We demonstrate that a stable matching is guaranteed if and only if every man's proposed subsets satisfy this independence condition relative to his preferences. Furthermore, we present a straightforward greedy algorithm that efficiently finds such a matching and prove its optimality. Finally, we extend these findings to the many-to-one setting, where multiple positions are available for each role. In this scenario, each job listing proposes a subset of independent candidates to interview, while each candidate chooses which listings to apply to; we establish that a stable matching exists precisely when the number of applications from each candidate does not exceed a fixed integer $k$, and we again show that a greedy approach yields an optimal solution. These findings contrast sharply with the classical Gale-Shapley method, where stability is achieved simply by having one gender always propose to their first choice, regardless of the number of available slots. Our results hold for both finite and infinite sets of men and women. Additionally, we explore a related problem concerning the "best" stable matching—one that maximizes the number of men matched to women—and prove that this problem is NP-hard even when the number of slots per woman is limited to two. To address this, we introduce a novel algorithm that, given a stable matching, iteratively improves it by identifying and executing augmentations. We analyze the algorithm's performance, showing that it converges to the optimal solution in polynomial time for finite instances and within polynomial time per individual for infinite instances. Finally, we extend these findings to many-to-one matchings and examine a variant where individuals can reject proposals, proving that this version is also NP-hard. We further develop an algorithm to find the best stable matching in this context, which converges in polynomial time for finite instances and polynomial time per individual for infinite instances. In both extensions, we establish that the algorithm is optimal. The paper concludes with a comprehensive discussion of the underlying combinatorial structures. LiDAR and camera sensors are extensively deployed in autonomous driving systems, yet their fusion remains difficult due to complementary yet distinct data modalities. This paper introduces BEVFusion, a straightforward yet powerful fusion framework that aligns LiDAR and camera features within a common bird's-eye view representation. The approach begins by projecting camera features from their original space into the BEV plane using a two-layer convolutional network, followed by a 2D convolutional fusion module that integrates camera and LiDAR features. Experiments on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art techniques for object detection and keypoint localization. Furthermore, we apply BEVFusion to the nuScenes dataset to evaluate its performance in complex scenarios, including rain, fog, and nighttime conditions. This study examines the dissipation range in incompressible hydrodynamic turbulence, focusing on the fundamental characteristics of the most energetic fluctuations at the smallest scales. We derive exact analytical formulas for the one-point one-time probability density function (PDF) of velocity and temperature, as well as their respective Fourier spectra. Our findings indicate that these dominant turbulent fluctuations are primarily governed by the cumulative effects of all scale interactions up to that point, rather than the interactions occurring at that specific scale. Consequently, the self-similar scaling of small-scale turbulent fluctuations is determined by the total accumulated turbulent energy dissipation rate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the one-point one-time velocity and temperature PDFs are nearly identical, implying that the temperature field is essentially dragged along by the velocity field. These results offer a comprehensive understanding of the structure function and scaling exponents of small-scale turbulent fluctuations. Finally, we compare our theoretical predictions with direct numerical simulation (DNS) data for the inertial and dissipation ranges, showing excellent agreement. Our theory provides a complete and accurate description of the energy cascade and scaling behavior in the turbulent dissipation range, thereby resolving the longstanding debate regarding the origin of the Kolmogorov scaling law. Additionally, our findings suggest that the previously proposed local inertial law is inaccurate. We also address the issue of the anomalous intermittency exponent in the dissipation range, revealing that the intermittency correction to Kolmogorov's 1941 (K41) scaling is linear and identical to that in the inertial range. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that the inertial range intermittency correction is a linear function of the Reynolds number. Our theory thus offers a complete and accurate explanation of the anomalous intermittency in fluid turbulence. Finally, we show that the intermittency correction in the dissipation range is directly linked to the anomalous intermittency in the inertial range, establishing a direct relationship between intermittency in the inertial and dissipation ranges. This relationship is derived from the one-point one-time PDFs of velocity and temperature in the dissipation range, which are determined by the energy cascade and the intermittency of the inertial range. Our theory provides a complete and accurate explanation of intermittency in the turbulent dissipation range, thereby resolving the longstanding debate regarding the Kolmogorov-Obukhov intermittency correction. Overall, our theory offers a complete and accurate description of the energy cascade and scaling behavior in the turbulent dissipation range, effectively resolving all open problems concerning intermittency in fluid turbulence. Our results demonstrate that the intricate patterns observed in interferometric images of these liquids stem from the non-linear relationship between temperature and the refractive index. Furthermore, the complex diffraction patterns result from the interaction between this non-linearity and the competition between thermal diffusion and elastic stress propagation. We show that both water and ethanol can transition between conducting and elastic regimes depending on the laser pulse duration. Additionally, the ratio of the thermal diffusion time to the stress wave propagation time is shown to be a critical parameter in determining the thermal profile. Finally, we provide a comprehensive numerical analysis of the factors influencing the thermal profile. These findings are validated by numerical simulations of laser-induced interferometry experiments performed on water and ethanol. Our analysis reveals that the thermal profile is governed by the competition between the thermal and elastic regimes, as well as the non-linear dependence of the refractive index on temperature. We also establish that the temperature gradient at the laser spot is proportional to the absorbed energy density and the laser pulse duration. These insights enable the prediction of thermal profiles under various conditions. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that the thermal profile is highly sensitive to the laser pulse duration, with both water and ethanol exhibiting distinct behaviors across different regimes. Software design discussions are frequently documented in source code comments, serving as a valuable resource for maintenance tasks such as change impact analysis. However, manually interpreting these comments is labor-intensive and time-consuming. This paper introduces a text extraction approach that leverages natural language to identify the evolution of software features from design discussion comments. The method employs a conclusion stability strategy to ensure the stability of the text extraction process. Furthermore, the study validates the effectiveness of the conclusion stability measure through an ablation study. The findings indicate that the text extraction technique is effective for the specific task of design discussion comments, and conclusion stability provides a more accurate solution for NLP-based text extraction than feature-based stability. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as the leading method for knowledge base (KB) linkage, surpassing traditional hand-crafted approaches. However, current NMT models for KB elements fail to leverage entity sharing within KBs, resulting in inefficient translations. This paper introduces a new NMT architecture designed to handle repeated KB elements by implementing a global memory mechanism. This system enables the model to retain information about previously translated elements and utilize this historical context during decoding. We assess our approach using the MultiDialog corpus, which features high entity repetition, and demonstrate that global memory significantly enhances translation accuracy. Furthermore, we find that incorporating this global memory into existing NMT models for KB elements offers performance benefits. Our comprehensive analysis reveals that the global memory model boosts recall by 10.5% and improves overall performance by 3.5%. The code is accessible at https://github.com/SeongJinLee1997/copy-NMT.

We introduce a citation-free methodology for assessing research quality, which relies on modeling the temporal evolution of a venue's reputation. This approach yields venue scores that can substitute for journal or conference-specific citation metrics. The proposed model is straightforward, requiring no assumptions regarding the underlying data generation process, and is straightforward to implement. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness through a case study focused on the AI field. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of the method, available at https://github.com/ashwinb/venue_analytics. The accompanying code includes a demonstration of the method applied to the AI domain, with the model trained on papers published from 2000 to 2019 in proceedings spanning 1950 to 2019. The output consists of venue scores for all papers within the specified timeframe. We also present preliminary findings from analyzing these scores, which can be found in our arXiv paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01000. This paper addresses the challenge of validating neural networks employed in nonlinear control systems. While recent literature has established methods for verifying neural network models, there remains a significant gap in validating networks designed for control applications. We introduce and evaluate strategies to enhance validation efficiency by leveraging the inherent structure of neural networks. Furthermore, we apply these proposed strategies to control-relevant neural networks to demonstrate their effectiveness. Our results indicate that these approaches yield substantial improvements in validation efficiency, with speedups of up to 1000 times. Additionally, we illustrate the necessity of these methods by presenting examples of neural networks that are difficult to validate using traditional techniques. The code required to replicate our experiments is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1997/nnet-validation. Our findings suggest that the efficiency gains from these validation techniques can be extended to other control-relevant neural networks. Ultimately, we contend that rigorous validation is essential for the safe deployment of control networks in real-world applications. This work was conducted while the first author was a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford.

We introduce a method for grouping objects based on pairwise similarity, where the hierarchical structure is generated through a functor that maps between categories of object collections and their pairwise relationships. This approach offers several benefits: it naturally incorporates overlaps, facilitates parallel computation, and produces output structures that are stable against minor fluctuations in similarity scores. The paper demonstrates the method's applicability and illustrative value within metric spaces, simplicial sets, and sets. Additionally, we establish that the procedure is stable when similarity scores are perturbed, provided these perturbations satisfy a mild contractive condition. Finally, we sketch an extension of the method to handle similarity data represented as weighted graphs. The technique is implemented in Haskell, with the code available at https://github.com/rgueno/functorial-grouping. A tutorial is provided in the companion paper, "Parallel and functorial data grouping with overlaps," which also details the method's extension to weighted graphs. Both papers are accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.00020. The current arXiv version includes an updated reference and the corrected arXiv id. Streaming tensor completion addresses data recovery in streaming systems by leveraging the multi-way structure of online data. While this approach is vital for numerous streaming applications, current methods often suffer from high computational costs and memory usage, rendering them impractical for many real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel loop completion strategy that exploits the inherent loop structure within streaming data. Specifically, we partition online streaming tensors into patches and model the loop structure by tracking these patches over time. This proposed loop completion framework is demonstrated on visual data recovery, where streaming video data is segmented into patches that maintain a temporal loop structure. Our method achieves superior computational efficiency and visual quality compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, we validate the framework's effectiveness across diverse datasets, including both synthetic and real-world cases. The experimental results confirm that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of computational cost, memory requirements, and visual performance. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1999/PatchTracking. This work was presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM). We present numerical simulations of two-dimensional, randomly forced and damped nonlinear Schrödinger turbulence. Our results confirm the presence of a Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) cascade within the inertial interval, characterized by a $k^{-7/3}$ spectral slope. This ZK cascade is driven by the resonant interaction of wave packets, which are initially generated by the forcing mechanism. Furthermore, we observe that the energy dissipation rate within the inertial interval adheres to the scaling law derived from the ZK equation. These findings provide compelling support for the validity of the ZK scaling law in the inertial range of turbulent wave systems. Additionally, we investigate the impact of forcing and damping on the spectral slope across various forcing and damping wave number bands. Our analysis demonstrates that both forcing and damping can generate Kolmogorov-like spectra, with slopes of $-5/3$ and $-2$, respectively. These outcomes are consistent with scaling laws established in the context of turbulent wave turbulence. Finally, we show that the spectral slope in the forcing or damping region is contingent upon the relative intensity of the forcing and damping waves. This phenomenon is explained by the existence of a critical intensity threshold, above which the forcing wave intensity surpasses that of the damped waves. This threshold is derived from a simplified model incorporating only forcing and damping terms. We also examine the influence of the forcing and damping wave number cut-offs on the spectral slope, revealing that the forcing and damping intervals shift toward higher wave numbers as these cut-off values increase. These observations are also consistent with the proposed scaling law. Our findings are corroborated by existing experimental and numerical data. We conclude that the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum is a prevalent feature in turbulent wave systems. This study presents the first low-frequency radio observations of the binary system CR Draconis, a young, active star exhibiting electron-cyclotron maser emission. We conducted a 10-year monitoring campaign using the LOFAR Low Band (LB) and Low Band Edge (LBE) instruments, supplemented by a single observation at the GBT's 1.4 GHz band. Our LB/LBE data revealed 10 maser outbursts lasting between 10 and 100 minutes, with peak flux densities reaching up to 100 mJy. These outbursts were detected at a mean frequency of 170 MHz, with a median of 160 MHz, and exhibited a mean spectral index of -1.1. The LB/LBE observations identified maser activity during 10% of the time, while the single GBT observation at 1.4 GHz detected no emission. We propose that the maser emission originates from a hot, dense coronal region on the stellar surface, heated by flares. The detected 10-minute outbursts likely represent the longest duration of electron-cyclotron maser emission ever recorded from a flare star. The spectral index of -1.1 suggests a maser mechanism operating in a low-density environment, consistent with a coronal origin. The absence of emission at 1.4 GHz may be attributed to the maser's narrow bandwidth or a lack of maser activity during that specific observation. Our findings indicate that maser emission from CR Draconis is driven by flares occurring on a timescale of approximately 100 minutes, which is significantly longer than the typical 10-minute flare duration observed in other active stars. This suggests that maser emission from CR Draconis is driven by a large-scale coronal structure rather than localized magnetic reconnection. Furthermore, the low-frequency properties of maser emission from CR Draconis differ from those of solar masers, highlighting the need for future low-frequency observations of other active stars to better understand the nature of maser emission from young stars. Humans and machines often interpret the same image differently, particularly after severe transformations. While algorithms typically struggle with these changes, humans are remarkably resilient. This paper investigates how humans and machines respond divergently to significant image transformations. We demonstrate that this discrepancy is substantial and can be quantified using a novel metric termed "Human-Machine Discrepancy" (HMD). Our findings indicate that humans are far more effective than machines at maintaining consistency across heavily transformed images. Furthermore, we show that the HMD can be leveraged to enhance machine performance, yielding substantial improvements when trained with human data. Finally, we explore how specific image properties and transformation types influence this human-machine disparity. The HMD metric and associated code are publicly available at https://github.com/abhishekkrishna/Human-Machine-Discrepancy. The source code for all experiments can be found at https://github.com/abhishekkrishna/Severe-Image-Transformations-Affect-Humans-and-Machines-Differently.

We compute the Chern-Simons link invariant for the Hopf link by evaluating the path integral in three dimensions. The resulting calculation yields the $q$-deformed Askey-Wilson norm as the final outcome. This connection serves as a physical justification for the appearance of the $q$-deformed Askey-Wilson norm within the context of the colored Jones polynomial. Furthermore, this relationship aligns with the three-dimensional duality between M5-branes and M2-branes. Specifically, the Hopf link can be represented as the intersection of two M5-branes or as the world-volume of two M2-branes embedded within the M5-brane. The M5/M2 three-dimensional duality thus unifies the link invariant and the $q$-deformed Askey-Wilson norm. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $q$-deformed Askey-Wilson norm corresponds to the two-point function of a specific operator in a three-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ Chern-Simons-Matter theory. This correspondence further supports the link between the Chern-Simons link invariant and the $q$-deformed Askey-Wilson norm.

This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of two-dimensional trimer antiferromagnets (TAFs) using the cluster quantum Monte Carlo method. The TAF model consists of strongly interacting triangular units (trimers) linked by weak interactions. We present the results for the Heisenberg model with nearest-neighbor interactions on a square lattice, specifically analyzing the $J_1$-$J_2$ model where $J_1$ and $J_2$ represent respectively the strong intra-trimer and weak inter-trimer coupling strengths. Our analysis covers the temperature ranges $0.05 \leq J_1 \leq 0.15$ and $0 \leq J_2 \leq 0.05$. We compute the specific heat, magnetic susceptibility, and correlation length, employing finite-size scaling techniques to determine critical temperatures and the crossover temperature separating the $J_2=0$ and $J_2 \neq 0$ regimes. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of $J_2$ on the specific heat peak's height and width, as well as on the magnetic and correlation length scales. Finally, we discuss the phase diagram of the system and the nature of its phase transitions. Our findings indicate that the specific heat exhibits a sharp peak at the crossover temperature, which marks the transition from a $J_2=0$ trimer antiferromagnet to a $J_1$-$J_2$ trimer antiferromagnet. Additionally, the crossover temperature aligns with the onset of the second peak in specific heat. We also observe that the magnetic length scale diminishes as $J_2$ increases. These results are compared with existing literature. Finally, we note that the cluster quantum Monte Carlo method proves effective for studying TAFs. This approach is also applicable to other frustrated models, including the $J_1$-$J_2$ model on a square lattice involving triangular and tetrahedral units. The methodology can be extended to investigate the phase diagrams of various spin models, such as the $J_1$-$J_2$ model on a square lattice with both triangular and tetrahedral units. Additionally, the cluster quantum Monte Carlo method is suitable for investigating the phase diagrams of $p$-trimer antiferromagnets, where $p$-trimer units are polygons with $p$ sides. Zero-shot learning (ZSL) represents a significant advancement in NLP, enabling the prediction of labels for unseen examples based solely on textual descriptions. This study introduces ZSL-MDA, a straightforward yet effective framework that adapts large language models for zero-shot learning through meta-tuning on dataset assemblies. To enhance ZSL performance, we propose a novel approach called dataset assembly, which involves training on multiple datasets to acquire generalized linguistic knowledge. Furthermore, we introduce prompt assembly, a technique designed to meta-tune models on automatically generated prompt examples. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the ZSL task of identifying languages from descriptions, demonstrating that our prompt assembly technique can identify languages with an accuracy of 60.5%, surpassing prior methods by 10.5%. Additionally, we show that ZSL-MDA generalizes effectively to new datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhinavrao123/ZSL-MDA. This work is presented at the 49th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval. This paper examines the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) within the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) under a $Z_3$-invariant framework. We analyze the stability of a first-order phase transition and the conditions necessary for it to proceed strongly, while simultaneously investigating the implications of recent LHC data and constraints derived from dark matter searches. Our analysis reveals that achieving a strong EWPT while maintaining a dark matter candidate compatible with LHC limits is highly challenging. Furthermore, we note that the dark matter mass falls below $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$, rendering it undetectable by the LUX and XENON1T experiments. Finally, we discuss the potential for observing gravitational waves generated by this electroweak phase transition. To facilitate this, we have developed a dedicated code capable of calculating both the gravitational wave spectrum and the EWPT characteristics. We conclude that the strong EWPT scenario is viable only in a narrow parameter region, and we provide a detailed examination of the resulting gravitational wave signals. Additionally, we have included a comprehensive discussion on the computational complexity associated with these calculations. Our findings indicate that the gravitational wave spectrum is detectable by LISA, with a peak frequency situated between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. We have also provided an in-depth analysis of the parameter space yielding detectable signals and demonstrated that the dark matter mass is typically below $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$. Finally, we have compared our results with those from the CosmoMicrOMEGAs code. We introduce a new diagnostic tool designed to assess the robustness of submillimeter redshifts, drawing a deliberate analogy to the well-known Sudoku puzzle. This instrument is particularly effective for distinguishing between redshifts secured by the 3.4$\mu$m line and those relying on multiple lines. By applying this method to the existing literature, we demonstrate its utility in clarifying the redshifts of (sub)mm sources at $z>4$. Furthermore, we illustrate how Sudoku can be utilized to evaluate the redshifts of newly identified sources, thereby aiding in the prioritization of targets for future spectroscopic confirmation. Ultimately, we show that Sudoku serves as a straightforward yet effective means to identify the most robust redshifts within the (sub)mm wavelength range. This approach is especially valuable for the upcoming ALMA Large Program "Cosmic Dawn" and the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope, both of which will employ (sub)mm and IR spectroscopy to investigate the early Universe. The Sudoku code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ALMACOSD/High-z-Sudoku. We welcome any comments or suggestions.

We investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of a $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo simulations. By analyzing specific heat, magnetic susceptibility, and the specific heat susceptibility, we identify distinct signatures of the 120-degree ordered ground state. Furthermore, we detect clear indicators of a recently proposed spin-liquid phase at elevated temperatures, evidenced by anomalies in these same thermodynamic quantities. Our results demonstrate that both the 120-degree ordered phase and the spin-liquid phase exhibit discernible thermodynamic signatures. Additionally, we observe that the specific heat susceptibility displays a broad peak near the critical temperature $T_c$ associated with the transition to the 120-degree ordered state, a feature that may serve as a useful metric for estimating $T_c$ in future studies. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of these findings for experimental investigations of the kagome lattice. This work is based on arXiv:2009.00001. This study investigates the confinement-deconfinement transition within $3+1$ dimensional $SU(3)$-Higgs theory, which serves as a simplified model for deconfinement scenarios in QCD. The theory is formulated in the continuum using an $SU(3)$-invariant action that couples a compact $SU(3)$ gauge field to a non-interacting adjoint Higgs field. Monte Carlo simulations were conducted to determine the deconfinement deconfinement shift relative to the deconfinement transition in pure $SU(3)$ gauge theory, a quantity that can be interpreted as the energy required to create a static quark-antiquark pair. The analysis utilized $12$ lattice volumes ranging from $4^3\times 8$ to $8^3\times 16$ and an average of $1.5\times 10^5$ configurations per gauge coupling. Results indicate that the confinement-deconfinement shift is approximately $1.5$ times larger than the deconfinement energy in pure $SU(3)$ gauge theory. This finding aligns with the potential model proposed by Gross and Suleiman, which predicts that the confinement-deconfinement energy equals the potential energy of a static quark-antiquark pair. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that this result can be accurately reproduced by analyzing the energy spectrum of static quark-antiquark pairs in the deconfined phase. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for the deconfinement transition in QCD. Keywords: QCD phase transition, deconfinement, QCD string tension. PACS: 12.38.Gc, 11.15.Ha.

Cr2Al crystallizes in a tetragonal structure with space group I4/mcm, where the Cr atoms occupy two distinct sites: the special 2a position at the origin and the general 4c position along the [110] direction. This magnetic arrangement was determined using the small-angle neutron diffraction method. The magnetic moment at the 2a site measures 1.7(1) μB, while the moment at the 4c site is 1.3(1) μB. The 2a moments align antiparallel to the c-axis, whereas the 4c moments form an angle of 35(2)° with the ab-plane. The observed magnetic structure corresponds to the propagation vector (1/2, 1/2, 1/2). Exchange interactions were calculated using the simulated annealing method, revealing that nearest-neighbor interactions along the [100] and [010] directions are ferromagnetic, while those along the [001] direction are antiferromagnetic. The strongest interactions occur between the 2a and 4c sites along the [111] and [1-11] directions. These findings are consistent with a superexchange mechanism mediated by Al atoms. Additionally, the study examines the relationship between the magnetic structure and the electronic band structure. Finally, the results are compared with existing data on the related compound Cr2Ge. (Note: The notation Cr2X refers to a tetragonal structure derived from the AuCu3-type lattice.) Keywords: antiferromagnet, Cr2Al, small-angle neutron diffraction, electronic structure.

This study introduces a kinetic model that incorporates a velocity-dependent collision frequency to capture the nuances of intermolecular potential in rarefied gas flows. Utilizing the Chapman-Enskog expansion, the collision operator is decomposed into two components: the first drives the gas toward a Maxwellian distribution, while the second accounts for deviations caused by the specific intermolecular potential. The free-streaming term and the second component of the collision operator are discretized via the velocity-rectangular rule and the spectral element method, respectively. Numerical experiments are conducted to assess the model's performance, with results demonstrating strong agreement against the Boltzmann equation. We introduce a straightforward yet effective framework for semantic parsing that surpasses state-of-the-art methods requiring extensive supervision. Our approach employs a two-stage training strategy: initially, a self-training phase enables the model to produce accurate translations even without a syntax bias, which are subsequently refined by a model guided by syntax bias. This technique is broadly applicable and yields significant gains across various domains, including single and multi-modal tasks. Furthermore, our fully natural-language-trained model achieves superior performance compared to models incorporating syntax bias, demonstrating that rich semantic interpretations can be trained with minimal data. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will function as a high-energy, high-luminosity machine designed to investigate the internal structure of protons and nucleons, as well as the properties of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) in their vicinity. Powered by a 10 GeV electron beam and a 250 GeV proton beam from the RHIC collider, the EIC will utilize a fixed-target configuration to achieve a center-of-mass energy of approximately 10–20 GeV. To ensure precise event reconstruction and effective background suppression, the proposed EIC detector will incorporate a forward silicon tracking system positioned near the interaction point. This system is engineered to deliver high-precision measurements of charged particle trajectories, enabling the identification of protons, pions, and kaons with transverse momenta ($p_T$) below 1 GeV/$c$. This article outlines the EIC's forward silicon tracking concept and presents recent R&D advancements in sensor design, fabrication, and readout technologies. Furthermore, it details the progress of the EIC test-beam experiment, which is currently underway at CERN's North-South Extractor (NSE) test-beam facility. This initiative aims to validate the performance of the silicon tracker and its sensors under conditions mimicking the expected environment at the EIC. The experiment has already been conducted at the NSE, with a second test-batch scheduled for the upcoming year. Additionally, the paper discusses the EIC's development timeline and the anticipated commissioning of the collider in the 2020s. Finally, the text addresses the EIC's role in the global high-energy physics community and its potential to drive innovation in computing and data science. EIC development is a collaborative international effort spearheaded by Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) in the United States, with the physics design report expected for release in 2022. The project involves over 1,000 physicists and engineers from more than 30 countries, supported by a broad coalition of funding agencies. Specifically, the forward silicon tracker development is a joint venture between the EIC Collaboration and the Silicon Tracker Collaboration, which was established in 2019 to advance the tracker technology. This group includes institutions from Europe, Japan, and the United States, such as the University of Jyväskylä, INFN, KEK, and UC Berkeley. We report on the discovery of a new, highly variable low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (LM-AGN) located in the galaxy SDSS J092847.97+002120.0 (z=0.011). This source was identified through a systematic search of the 10-year Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) Legacy Survey, which revealed a significant increase in brightness between 2018 and 2020, followed by a sharp decline in 2021. We analyzed the source's spectral energy distribution (SED) using archival data from the ZTF Legacy Survey, the Catalina Real-time Transient Survey (CRTS), the Catalina Real-time Survey (CATS), and the ZTF Main Survey. Our analysis indicates that the source's luminosity is approximately $10^{42}$ erg/s, with a black hole mass of $10^5$ solar masses, yielding an Eddington ratio of roughly $10^{-3}$. We propose that the observed brightening is caused by an eruption from the black hole, while the subsequent dimming results from the reprocessing of this energy within the accretion disk. This finding is significant because it demonstrates that low-luminosity AGN can exhibit substantial luminosity variations, a phenomenon previously thought to be exclusive to high-luminosity counterparts. Furthermore, this source may represent a rare instance of a low-luminosity AGN undergoing an eruption, a class of objects that has historically been difficult to detect. Our results suggest that the ZTF Legacy Survey is a valuable resource for identifying such rare and elusive objects. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this discovery for the broader population of LM-AGN. Finally, we highlight the importance of conducting follow-up observations to better understand the nature of this unique object. Our findings underscore the necessity of a comprehensive, systematic search for LM-AGN to fully characterize their population and behavior. HD58260 is a rapidly rotating, metal-poor star that exhibits a large-scale magnetic field with a dipolar geometry. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD58260 conducted at the Dunn Solar Telescope, utilizing the Stokes Q and U signals to map the magnetic field across the stellar disk. The observations were performed at two phases of the stellar rotation, employing high-resolution spectra of the Ca II H&K lines. By applying the spectropolarimetric inversion method known as SPINFOR, we successfully reconstructed the magnetic field maps of HD58260. Our findings indicate that the magnetic field strength is highest at the poles, reaching approximately 1.5 kG, and decreases toward the equator, suggesting a negative radial slope. This observation confirms the presence of a radial field slope in HD58260, a feature previously predicted by numerical models. Furthermore, we determined that the magnetic field is predominantly located in the photosphere, with a mean strength of about 1.1 kG. Finally, we compared our results with existing observations and models of HD58260. These results support the hypothesis that the star hosts a fossil magnetic field, which may have been generated by a dynamo in its convective envelope during its pre-main-sequence phase. Additionally, the observed magnetic field strength aligns with predictions from numerical models. The detection of a magnetic field with a radial slope in HD58260 provides further evidence that the dynamo mechanism responsible for generating magnetic fields in rapidly rotating, metal-poor stars produces a fossil field. This finding is particularly significant given that HD58260 is one of the few stars with a magnetic field strength exceeding 1 kG. These results contribute to a better understanding of the magnetic field generation mechanisms in metal-poor stars. We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in NGC 5253, a low-metallicity galaxy ($Z\sim0.3$ Z$_{\odot}$) known for its compact star-forming regions. This line serves as a direct tracer of ionized gas, allowing us to compare the H30$\alpha$-derived gas mass with estimates from the H2 molecular line and dust continuum. Our findings indicate that the H30$\alpha$ emission is dominated by the star-forming regions identified in H2 maps, yet it is not fully captured by the H2 emission within these specific regions. Instead, H30$\alpha$ emission is detected in a broader area, including H2-dark regions that coincide with H81$\alpha$ emission. The H30$\alpha$ emission is optically thick, and its intensity is primarily driven by the electron density ($n_e$) rather than the electron temperature ($T_e$). We derived the H30$\alpha$-based star formation rate (SFR) using a method that accounts for these effects, which yielded a value consistent with SFRs estimated via the H81$\alpha$ line and the H87$\alpha$/H30$\alpha$ ratio. Furthermore, the H30$\alpha$-based SFR correlates with the H2-based SFR, though the correlation is weaker than that observed between H81$\alpha$ and H87$\alpha$/H30$\alpha$ ratios. This discrepancy arises because the H30$\alpha$ line is optically thick, whereas H81$\alpha$ is optically thin. Additionally, the H30$\alpha$-based SFR is lower than the SFR derived from the H87$\alpha$/H30$\alpha$ ratio, a difference attributed to the H30$\alpha$ line's sensitivity to $n_e$ and $T_e$. Finally, we observed a correlation between the H30$\alpha$/H81$\alpha$ ratio and the H87$\alpha$/H30$\alpha$ ratio, which can be utilized to determine the $n_e$-$T_e$ relation in star-forming galaxies. These results suggest that H30$\alpha$ emission is a promising tool for studying the physical conditions of ionized gas in low-metallicity star-forming galaxies. We demonstrate that a broad category of topologically free, minimal actions by virtually cyclic groups on Hausdorff spaces, which are not conjugate to their continuous conjugate, lacks a continuous orbit equivalence to any such action on a space where the conjugating homeomorphism is minimally groupoid equivalent to the identity. This result establishes the first instances of a wide class of dynamical systems being "inflexible" under continuous orbit equivalence. Furthermore, we present a novel construction of topologically free minimal actions on compact spaces that are not conjugate to any of their continuous conjugates. Additionally, we prove that any topologically free action of a virtually cyclic group on a Hausdorff space, which is not conjugate to a free action, is not continuously orbit equivalent to a free action. These findings rely on a general theorem concerning the continuity of the orbit equivalence relation between topologically free actions of virtually cyclic groups. Finally, we examine various extensions of our results to more general settings. The paper concludes with an extensive discussion of open questions regarding both the flexibility and rigidity of virtually cyclic group actions within the realm of topological dynamics. Notably, we establish that any topologically free action of a virtually cyclic group on a Hausdorff space is continuously orbit equivalent to a minimal action of a virtually cyclic group on a compact space. This result also extends to free actions on Hausdorff spaces that are not necessarily minimal. These conclusions are derived from a general theorem applicable to topologically free actions of any amenable group on Hausdorff spaces, which asserts that such an action is continuously orbit equivalent to a minimal action on a compact space via a homeomorphism that is minimally groupoid equivalent to the identity. This finding also generalizes to minimal actions on compact spaces that are not necessarily topologically free. The proof of this theorem utilizes the concept of almost equicontinuous transformations, a tool from classical topological dynamics. We also provide an alternative proof of this theorem using symbolic dynamics. The primary motivation for this work stems from the necessity to construct topologically free actions on compact spaces that are not conjugate to any of their continuous conjugates. This paper serves as the sequel to our previous study, where we constructed topologically free actions on compact spaces that are not minimal and are not conjugate to any of their continuous conjugates. In that earlier work, we also proved that any topologically free action of a virtually cyclic group on a Hausdorff space is continuously orbit equivalent to a topologically free minimal action on a compact space.

The proposed observer ensures that the estimation error converges exponentially to zero, even in the presence of measurement noise. A key advantage of this approach is that it relies exclusively on the final state variable as the sole measured output, eliminating the need for parameter estimation. These results demonstrate that reduced-order observers are effective for epidemic models where only limited state variables can be observed. Furthermore, the findings indicate that utilizing such observers can enhance the accuracy of predictions regarding final epidemic states. This accuracy surpasses the performance of a basic simulation that relies solely on the available measurement data. Consequently, this confirms the potential of reduced-order observers to improve the estimation of final states, specifically the ultimate number of recovered individuals. Temporal Knowledge Graphs (KGs) capture both factual relationships and their temporal validity, offering a structured approach to reasoning about real-world events. However, learning from temporal data presents significant challenges, particularly regarding the vast number of time intervals and the scarcity of unique timestamps. This study investigates whether models trained on timestamped data can generalize to a broader time domain. We introduce TempRM, a novel temporal knowledge base completion task designed to evaluate model generalization to unseen time intervals. To address this, we develop two transformer-based architectures, Temporal Transformer and Temporal TimeTransformer, which integrate time embeddings into transformer layers. Furthermore, we propose a new data generation method that synthesizes training data by sampling time intervals from a test dataset, ensuring a distribution aligned with the test set. Experimental results demonstrate that both the proposed transformer models and the synthetic training data significantly enhance performance on TempRM compared to baselines. Additionally, we find that transformers surpass state-of-the-art methods in standard KG completion tasks when temporal information is included. Finally, we observe that temporal data generation is more effective for temporal transitivity than for other temporal properties. This research investigates Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLM) within the framework of self-consistent Gaussian resonators. By employing a geometrical approach, we derive the essential resonator parameters required to sustain a self-consistent Gaussian pulse in an ultrafast Kerr-lens oscillator. We establish the conditions for the existence of a real spot size and determine the corresponding cavity length. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of the Gaussian mode and identify the parameter ranges that allow for the coexistence of two distinct self-consistent Gaussian spots. Finally, we calculate the fundamental cavity eigenmode and its associated loss, and we discuss the potential of this method for Gaussian resonators containing a Kerr nonlinearity. These findings are supported by the ultrafast Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillator experimentally examined in this study. Additionally, we present a novel technique for measuring the angular dispersion of the ultra-broadband spectrum generated by this oscillator. This method utilizes a spectrometer equipped with a rotating diffraction grating to compensate for group delay dispersion, thereby achieving high spectral resolution. We demonstrate that this approach can accurately determine the grating's rotation speed and the oscillator's angular dispersion. The paper concludes with a discussion on the method's applicability to other resonators and oscillators exhibiting KLM. Ultimately, this study offers a new perspective on the fundamental principles governing KLM resonators and oscillators. The developed theory and analysis tools can aid in the design of ultrafast Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators and the interpretation of their experimental results. This work is anticipated to foster further research into the principles of KLM. This paper introduces a new asynchronous online federated learning framework designed to address nonlinear regression problems, specifically tailored to handle the heterogeneous nature of data sources. The core objective is to minimize a global nonlinear least-squares function derived from distributed datasets. To achieve this, we propose a distributed, data-driven method that utilizes the asynchronous Kaczmarz algorithm. This approach enables distributed nonlinear least-squares solvers to exchange information and iteratively refine their solutions. We further develop two variants of this method: one that accounts for the statistical characteristics of data sources and another that incorporates computational constraints, such as varying numbers of measurements per data source. The method is proven to converge with a rate comparable to existing batch and online approaches. Numerical simulations demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform current batch and online techniques in terms of computational efficiency, while also exhibiting superior performance against other asynchronous online methods from recent literature. Finally, the method is applied to a real-world dataset to estimate the parameters of a nonlinear pharmacokinetic model. The results indicate that the asynchronous online federated methods yield more accurate parameter estimates than both batch and other online solutions. Additionally, the study reveals that these methods are robust to the presence of outliers in individual datasets. Finally, we discuss the method's applicability to other problems, such as distributed parameter estimation in dynamical systems. Key words: Asynchronous online, federated learning, nonlinear regression, distributed parameter estimation. Furthermore, we explore the behavior of the solution as the base $a$ approaches $b$ from above, deriving an asymptotic solution in this limit as well. The study investigates the magnetic properties of the centered honeycomb lattice antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$ through both experimental measurements and theoretical modeling. Experimental results indicate that GdInO$_3$ exhibits a three-sublattice antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering with a Néel temperature of $T_\mathrm{N}=4.5$ K. At temperatures below $T_\mathrm{N}$, the experimental exchange interactions are derived using the Bonner-Fisher method and the equal-time spin correlation technique. Theoretical analysis employs a Heisenberg AFM model incorporating both nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) exchange interactions. By fitting the exchange-coupling parameters to the experimentally derived values, the ratio $J_2/J_1$ is determined to be $0.15\pm0.01$. This ratio aligns with the theoretical prediction of $0.167$ for a three-sublattice AFM state in a centered honeycomb lattice. Furthermore, the theoretical exchange interactions and the corresponding magnetic structure are illustrated. The magnetic ground state is identified as a non-collinear AFM state, consistent with the experimental data. Finally, the magnetic phase diagram is constructed, and the temperature dependence of the magnetization is calculated. The theoretical findings regarding the temperature dependence of the magnetization show good agreement with the experimental observations. These results provide a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$. Additionally, the research demonstrates that the Bonner-Fisher method is effective for extracting exchange interactions in a centered honeycomb lattice. The findings are also applicable to other two-dimensional centered honeycomb antiferromagnets, such as the recently discovered EuInO$_3$. The accompanying data repository contains the raw experimental data, including magnetization curves and the temperature dependence of the exchange interaction parameter $J_1$. The source code used for the theoretical analysis is also provided. Graph representation learning has gained significant traction recently, with node embedding techniques transforming network analysis by converting graphs into low-dimensional vector spaces. These embeddings facilitate the application of machine learning models to graph data. However, most existing methods are tailored for dense graphs, often neglecting the sparse networks that are prevalent in real-world scenarios. This study introduces a novel and streamlined node embedding model designed specifically for sparse graphs, enabling efficient link prediction. The proposed model employs a non-stationary diffusion process to generate node representations. We assess its efficacy through link prediction tasks on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that this model surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in sparse network link prediction. Furthermore, we find that our model predicts links with fewer edges than those present in the original graph. We demonstrate the fabrication of atomic vapor cells containing a silicon chip-on-cell design, which houses a micro-fabricated depth-sensitive interferometer. These cells are produced using standard micro-fabrication techniques and can be scaled to any size. We successfully fabricated and characterized a 10 mm × 10 mm cell, achieving an aluminum atom density of 10^14 cm^-3 at a temperature of 400 K. This design offers a versatile platform for micro-fabricated quantum devices, enabling the study of individual atoms and their ensembles. Additionally, we outline a strategy for integrating such a cell into a silicon photonic circuit. This approach could facilitate the creation of hybrid atomic-photon entangled states, advancing the field of quantum information processing. The proposed method for achieving atomic-photon entanglement is particularly relevant for quantum communication and computing applications utilizing photonic quantum circuits. Furthermore, the experimental techniques employed are broadly applicable to other atomic species and vapor cell dimensions. This paper introduces a model for nonlinear distortion power in dual-polarization four-dimensional formats. By treating the multiplexed carriers in both dimensions as a common resource, the model accounts for the coupling between dimensions, a factor often overlooked in traditional single-dimensional approaches. Validation using a digital back-to-back system demonstrates that the model accurately predicts received signal power and constellation points. Furthermore, it confirms that a linear amplifier can achieve a performance gain of up to 1 dB compared to a Doherty amplifier. Finally, the model is applied to a dual-polarization quadrature quadrature format, yielding a power spectral density that closely matches both theoretical calculations and experimental results. This format proves to be an effective solution for mitigating bandwidth constraints in optical transmission systems. (Corresponds to Paper ID 10011-10)

Detecting wildfires using Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) is crucial for fire management, yet the low contrast of flames against the sky often hinders detection. While combining infrared (IR) and visible (VIS) imagery can enhance performance, current methods struggle with the distinct physical properties of these modalities. This paper introduces a deep learning-based infrared-visible integration approach that generates synthetic IR images from VIS inputs to improve detector performance. By utilizing a generator network, the method creates IR-like images that are more consistent with the actual data distribution, thereby aiding the classification of fire pixels. The system employs a dual-network architecture where a discriminator evaluates both the synthetic IR images and the original IR/VIS pairs to ensure higher fidelity in the generated outputs. Experimental results using real-world IR and VIS infrared integrating spheres (IRIS) datasets demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing IRIS integration techniques. Furthermore, applying this method to a dataset collected in a wildfire-prone region of Portugal yielded superior fire detection outcomes compared to using either IR or VIS imagery alone. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/JoaoPereira1999/FIRe-GAN. This study introduces a new stochastic compartmental model designed to simulate the spatial dissemination of COVID-19. The framework incorporates two compartments for infected individuals: isolated and non-isolated. For each compartment, the system tracks both isolated and non-isolated healthy individuals, alongside isolated and non-isolated infected individuals, as well as isolated and non-isolated susceptible individuals. The analysis focuses on isolated and non-isolated regions, examining both the existence and uniqueness of the stationary distribution and the local stability of the unique positive solution. Furthermore, simulation results are presented to validate the proposed methodology. The findings indicate that increasing the isolation rate of both healthy and infected individuals in non-isolated areas significantly reduces the population count in both zones. Additionally, the model demonstrates that a higher transmission rate in non-isolated areas leads to a higher population of both healthy and infected individuals in isolated areas. Finally, it is observed that a higher isolation rate for both healthy and infected individuals in isolated areas results in a lower population of both healthy and susceptible individuals in non-isolated areas. These outcomes suggest that implementing isolation measures in non-isolated regions can effectively mitigate the spread of COVID-19. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. This study investigates the influence of the isoscalar quadrupole ($\lambda$ = 2) component on isoscalar monopole ($\lambda$ = 0) excitations within $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. By utilizing the relativistic random-phase approximation (RRPA) and coupling monopole and quadrupole modes, we calculate the isoscalar giant monopole resonance (ISGMR) energy and energy-weighted sum rule (EWSR) strength for these nuclei. Our findings indicate that the quadrupole component significantly impacts the ISGMR energy in $^{24}$Mg, resulting in a 1.5% reduction compared to RRPA calculations excluding quadrupole modes. Conversely, in $^{28}$Si, quadrupole coupling has a negligible effect on the ISGMR energy but substantially enhances the EWSR strength. These results are compared against experimental data and other theoretical studies. Furthermore, we observe that the coupling between monopole and quadrupole modes induces a three-peaked structure in the monopole strength distribution for $^{28}$Si, a feature absent in $^{24}$Mg. This suggests that the coupling between monopole and higher-order multipole modes (such as quadrupole, hexapole, etc.) is essential for explaining the ISGMR strength distribution in nuclei with neutron numbers N = 13 and 14. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the evolution of the ISGMR in nuclei near the N = 20 shell gap. Our analysis reveals that the monopole energy in $^{28}$Si is approximately 100 keV lower than in $^{42}$Ca, a trend that aligns with the observed experimental evolution of the ISGMR energy across this region. Additionally, the EWSR strength in $^{28}$Si is found to be about 10% greater than in $^{42}$Ca, a difference that may be attributed to the significant contribution from the three-peaked structure in $^{28}$Si. These results suggest that the evolution of ISGMR strength in the N = 13–20 region is primarily driven by the coupling between monopole and quadrupole modes. Overall, this work demonstrates that incorporating quadrupole coupling into RRPA calculations is crucial for accurately describing the ISGMR in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si

This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled motion systems subject to Coulomb friction, a model prevalent in robotics and mechatronics. The closed-loop system is represented as a hybrid system, analyzed using hybrid Lyapunov functions to establish stability, sliding intervals, and convergence. These findings are demonstrated through a one-link robot arm equipped with dry friction at the joint, where theoretical results are validated via numerical simulations. Furthermore, the study extends its analysis to higher-dimensional systems, illustrating convergence through simulations of a two-link robot arm and a three-link robot arm. Notably, the convergence proofs for these multi-dimensional systems rely on a specific property of the friction cone's normal vector, which is demonstrated in the simulations. The paper concludes by discussing the extension of these results to systems with state-dependent friction. Additionally, the authors address the necessity of a dwell condition to prevent Zeno behavior in the closed-loop system, a topic that also informs the design of hybrid controllers. Finally, the paper presents a hybrid controller design that leverages the inherent stick-slip behavior of the closed-loop system to achieve finite-time convergence. The associated numerical simulations confirm the efficacy of this proposed controller. The work concludes by outlining potential future research directions. This paper introduces the Deep Bellman Insurance (DBI) algorithm, a model-based reinforcement learning approach designed to solve Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with non-linear dynamics. DBI operates by modeling the value function as a deep neural network and utilizing its gradients to determine optimal policy parameters. The method is evaluated across three scenarios: a continuous control task involving a linear dynamical system, a discrete action scenario with a quadratic dynamical system, and a discrete action problem featuring a non-linear dynamical system. The results demonstrate that DBI successfully learns optimal policies in all three cases. Furthermore, a comprehensive ablation study reveals that the algorithm's performance is highly sensitive to the selection of hyperparameters. Finally, extensive experiments conducted on the Deep Mind Control suite assess DBI's efficacy in model-free settings. These findings indicate that, despite its model-based foundation, DBI can achieve competitive performance against state-of-the-art model-free methods. Additionally, the study confirms that DBI's performance is significantly influenced by hyperparameter choices, underscoring the necessity for rigorous hyperparameter optimization. The code and data required to replicate these experiments are publicly accessible. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01001. Sequential recommenders are prevalent in real-world applications due to their ability to deliver personalized suggestions by leveraging historical user behavior. However, these models often overlook the underlying reasons for a user's interactions, leading to a lack of interpretability. To address this, we introduce a new interpretable sequential recommender that captures the latent purposes driving user interactions. By modeling these latent purposes as first-order Markov chains, the model predicts the next item based on both the user's current purpose and their interaction history. We evaluate our approach using the Alibaba Movie Recommender Dataset and Yandex.Chimp datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy while offering valuable insights into the latent purposes of user interactions. Furthermore, an online A/B test on Taobao confirms that the model enhances click-through rates in a live production environment. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/leeyy123/seqrec_interpretability. This work is presented as an extended abstract.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation (DCHE) exhibits a resonance condition where its formal solution becomes reducible; in this scenario, the series solution for the indicial equation $-s$ merges with the logarithmic solution for the indicial value $s$. This article demonstrates that under these resonant circumstances, the DCHE can be derived from a symmetric equation featuring a specific singularity structure. Furthermore, it is shown that the DCHE emerges as a symmetric unfolding of a general symmetric equation that includes an additional singularity at $z=0$. This unfolding is facilitated by a symmetric extension of a Möbius transformation, which maps the punctured unit disk onto itself. The study provides the series solution for the DCHE and offers a symmetric formulation of the corresponding monodromy matrix. Additionally, the paper presents a symmetric interpretation of the connection formula applicable to the reducible case. These findings are supported by explicit examples, with several others left for future exploration. This study addresses the estimation of a low-rank matrix from noisy observations, where each entry faces groupwise heteroskedastic noise. We demonstrate that the minimum mean-squared error (MMSE) achievable by any estimator is governed by the heteroskedasticity structure and the signal's rank. Leveraging these insights, we construct a maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) and prove that, asymptotically, it achieves the derived MMSE bound. These findings are applicable to various models, including those involving groupwise subgaussian noise and specific cases of groupwise spiking noise. Furthermore, our analysis yields a novel lower bound for matrix completion problems involving groupwise subgaussian noise, a result that may hold independent significance. Finally, we validate our theoretical contributions through numerical simulations. Notably, in the context of matrix completion, we observe that the MLE's performance is nearly optimal even with a relatively small number of unobserved entries. Additionally, in a spiking noise model, the number of unobserved entries required for the MLE to reach the MMSE is significantly lower than in subgaussian noise scenarios. These outcomes highlight the distinct advantages of utilizing groupwise spiking noise models. The paper concludes with a discussion of several open questions. Our findings are situated within a broader literature on low-rank matrix estimation, with a specific focus on heteroskedastic noise models. We further demonstrate the relevance of our results to diverse applications, such as image denoising and multi-armed bandits. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and significant loss of life, prompting numerous nations to implement strict lockdowns. However, these measures impose a heavy economic burden, necessitating a strategy that balances health and economic interests. This paper introduces a novel two-stage categorization model designed to classify individuals into high-risk, low-risk, and essential worker groups. By leveraging BERT features, the model analyzes textual data such as age, gender, and comorbidities to determine risk categories. The proposed approach employs a neural network to extract contextual features from text data, which are then processed by a regression model to predict risk categories. Experimental results demonstrate that the two-stage model outperforms the single-stage baseline, achieving an F1 score of 0.81 compared to 0.79. Furthermore, the model's predictions align with the risk categorization guidelines established by the World Health Organization. Given its accuracy, the model offers valuable insights for policymakers to make informed decisions when managing the pandemic. Eco-evolutionary dynamics describe how ecological and evolutionary processes interact across time and space. While historical ecology has traditionally focused on long-term interactions spanning centuries or millennia, the field is increasingly incorporating short-term dynamics occurring over days to years. This perspective is essential for comprehending both rapid adaptations and immediate ecological shifts driven by those adaptations. Conversely, evolutionary theory has historically prioritized long-term changes, often overlooking short-term dynamics. This review examines the relationship between ecological and evolutionary timescales, emphasizing the critical role of eco-evolutionary feedbacks. We explore how these dynamics are influenced by factors such as population size, generation time, and environmental variability. Furthermore, we address the necessity of integrating both long and short-term dynamics to establish a more holistic understanding of evolution and its timescales. Finally, we outline future research directions aimed at synthesizing these diverse components into a unified framework. (This article is part of the theme issue 'Evolution in a changing world: timescales and timescales').

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a cornerstone of modern machine learning, enabling models to derive valuable representations from unlabeled data. This study investigates the adversarial vulnerabilities of speech models trained using SSL. Our findings indicate that self-supervised classifiers are more resilient to adversarial attacks than supervised ones, yet they remain susceptible to attacks that degrade self-supervision objectives and hinder representation learning. We introduce novel gradient-based attacks targeting these non-decision-layer objectives, demonstrating that our method is more potent than existing state-of-the-art attacks for attacking these specific objectives. Furthermore, we offer fresh insights into the susceptibility of various objectives by analyzing how adversarial attacks impact their outputs. Finally, we explore strategies for enhancing the robustness of speech SSL models against such attacks. The code and pre-trained models referenced in this paper are available at: https://github.com/Chenchen2019/Speech-SUS-SSL. The paper itself can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01007. This study examines the conditions under which a blockchain-enabled exchange (BCX) can successfully attract users from a traditional exchange (TX). We construct a model featuring a BCX and a TX, analyzing two market entry scenarios: one where the BCX is established first, and another where both platforms launch simultaneously. Our findings indicate that when the BCX enters the market alone, its ability to poach users from the TX hinges on transaction fees; specifically, lower fees increase adoption, whereas higher fees hinder it. In contrast, a simultaneous market entry results in the BCX capturing a portion of the TX's user base regardless of the fee structure. Furthermore, we observe that while BCX adoption reduces the TX's profits, it can still be economically viable for the BCX under certain conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate that a BCX is more likely to be adopted when transaction volumes are high, as these scenarios offer greater profit potential. Finally, we explore the broader economic implications of these results. JEL Classification: L13, L15, L86. Keywords: Blockchain, Decentralized Exchange, Centralized Exchange, Market Entry.

Sensitivity analysis is essential for addressing missing data, particularly when the missingness mechanism is Non-MAR (Missing At Random). The E-value serves as a metric to quantify the maximum strength of an assumption required to render study results statistically significant. This study introduces a novel E-value specifically for sensitivity analysis in missing data contexts. We derive the likelihood function for Non-MAR assumptions and utilize it to calculate the study probability under various scenarios. Furthermore, we develop a method to determine the strength of the MAR assumption, enabling the computation of the E-value. A simulation study was conducted to evaluate the E-value's performance, and the practical application of this approach is demonstrated using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). The findings indicate that the E-value effectively captures the strength of the MAR assumption. Additionally, the results highlight the critical necessity of conducting sensitivity analysis when dealing with missing data. The E-value method is implemented in the R package 'sensitivityanalysis'. Keywords: Missing data; Sensitivity analysis; E-value; Missing at Random; MAR.

The convergence of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) and Machine Learning (ML) has created new avenues for research and innovation. However, IoV's inherent challenges, such as limited resources, high mobility, and security vulnerabilities, hinder the deployment of ML models. Federated Learning (FL) offers a solution by enabling distributed training across multiple vehicles while safeguarding data privacy and security. Nevertheless, FL faces issues like data imbalance, model poisoning, and resource constraints. To address these, Blockchain (BCN) technology has been integrated with FL to create a robust IoV-FL framework. This paper presents a systematic literature review of blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks for IoV, analyzing 30 studies. The review evaluates these frameworks based on their contributions, methodologies, and results, while also identifying key research gaps and proposing future directions. Ultimately, this survey aims to inspire further research and innovation in the field. This study reports measurements of the nuclear modification factor ($R_{AA}$) for non-prompt and prompt D mesons, utilizing data from the CMS experiment at the LHC collected during the 2015 LHC Run 2 at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV. The analysis covers transverse momentum intervals of $2<p_T<7$ GeV/$c$ for non-prompt D mesons and $2<p_T<15$ GeV/$c$ for prompt D mesons, within the pseudorapidity range $|y|<2.4$. For non-prompt D mesons, the $R_{AA}$ is determined to be $0.70\pm0.06\pm0.06$ (stat.) $\pm$ 0.04 (syst.) at $p_T=4$ GeV/$c$, while for prompt D mesons, the value is $0.75\pm0.05\pm0.05$ (stat.) $\pm$ 0.05 (syst.) at $p_T=8$ GeV/$c$. These findings align with previous measurements from the same experiment at $\sqrt{s}=2.76$ TeV and $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. The results indicate that both non-prompt and prompt D mesons exhibit similar suppression patterns in heavy-ion collisions, with a slight trend toward greater suppression observed at higher $p_T$. Furthermore, the study confirms that non-prompt and prompt D mesons follow similar suppression trends as a function of $p_T$ in the $2<p_T<7$ GeV/$c$ range. The $p_T$ dependence of the $R_{AA}$ for both categories is interpreted using a perturbative QCD framework combined with a hydrodynamic model. Additionally, the $p_T$ dependence of the $R_{AA}$ for prompt D mesons in heavy-ion collisions is compared against those of prompt electrons, charged pions, and jets. The analysis reveals that non-prompt D mesons experience slightly stronger suppression than prompt D mesons at $p_T<7$ GeV/$c$, whereas the suppression is nearly identical at $p_T>7$ GeV/$c$. This suggests that the suppression of D mesons in heavy-ion collisions is primarily driven by charm quark energy loss during their propagation through the quark-gluon plasma

Superconducting quantum processors are anticipated to require cooling systems capable of reaching millikelvin temperatures with substantial thermal power. This study presents the design and performance of a 10-liter dilution refrigerator, designated as the Large Millikelvin System (LMS), currently under installation at Fermilab. The system is engineered to achieve a base temperature of 5 mK, supporting a computational stack comprising up to 100 qubits. This paper details the LMS's thermal design, cryogenic architecture, and achieved temperature profiles. Furthermore, we outline plans for utilizing the LMS to facilitate co-design initiatives between quantum hardware developers and cryogenic engineers. These initiatives aim to optimize both the thermal management of the quantum stack and the overall system performance. We expect the LMS to be fully operational by the end of 2022. Its availability will enable the development of next-generation quantum processors featuring hundreds of qubits, thereby advancing the path toward large-scale quantum computing. Additionally, the LMS will support diverse scientific research across multiple disciplines. The system is owned and operated by Fermilab, which has dedicated resources to its design, construction, and scientific utilization. This study examines the deployment of cryptographic components within Python applications. By analyzing a collection of 1,000 Python projects, we identify the specific crypto modules utilized and evaluate their usage patterns. Our analysis reveals that 60% of the applications are either misconfigured or employ inappropriate crypto modules for their intended tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that 25% of the codebases are susceptible to the crypto abuse vulnerability, with 10% potentially exposed to the SMT attack. Additionally, we illustrate how the PyCryptodome module can be leveraged to execute the SMT attack on Python applications. To assist developers in mitigating these risks, we propose a static analysis tool designed to detect misconfigurations and inapplicable crypto modules. We have integrated this tool into the PyCryptoCheck repository and validated its efficacy through a case study. The source code for the crypto module analyzer is hosted on PyCryptoCheck. The comprehensive source code for this paper is available at: https://github.com/PyCryptoCheck/CryptoCheck/tree/master/paper. PyCryptodome: https://github.com/PyCryptoCheck/CryptoCheck. This paper introduces a voting-based automatic tagging framework designed for urban environments. The system operates by generating multiple tagging hypotheses from diverse models trained on distinct data modalities and feature representations. These hypotheses are aggregated into a unified tag distribution using a straightforward, scalable voting mechanism. We further extend this framework to support multi-label classification. Extensive experiments conducted on two large-scale datasets, PASCAL-51 and GTech, demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robinljy/VALUE. Given its simplicity and modularity, VALUE serves as an effective baseline for large-scale automatic image tagging. Additionally, the framework is highly extensible, allowing for the seamless integration of new models and data sources. We anticipate that VALUE will facilitate the development of more sophisticated tagging systems and offer a robust baseline for researchers in the field. The value of VALUE is evident in its performance, extensibility, and utility as a foundational tool for advancing automatic image tagging technologies.

This paper introduces NuSPAN, a proximal average network designed for sparse priors that operates under the NUTCM (non-uniform, non-negative, and translation-invariant compressible measure) framework. We demonstrate that the gradient of the NuSPAN prior can be expressed as the proximal average of gradients derived from two uniform priors: one assuming a non-negative and translation-invariant process, and the other assuming a non-negative and non-negative-variance process. By employing a proximal average formulation, NuSPAN effectively mitigates the limitations inherent in uniform priors. We apply this prior to seismic reflectivity inversion, proving that it yields superior results compared to conventional uniform priors. Furthermore, we establish the Lipschitz continuity of the NuSPAN gradient, a critical property for the convergence of gradient descent methods. Finally, we examine the dual representation of NuSPAN, which facilitates the development of a proximal average operator network. Numerical experiments confirm that this learned operator network successfully performs seismic reflectivity inversion. The source code for NuSPAN is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/NuSPAN. Additionally, we have released a Jupyter notebook that details the operator learning process for seismic reflectivity inversion, available at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/NuSPAN/blob/master/OperatorLearning/OperatorLearning.ipynb. The corresponding trained model can be downloaded from https://github.com/ChenYi1996/NuSPAN/tree/master/OperatorLearning/TrainedModel. Future research will explore the application of NuSPAN to other inverse problems. The Python implementation is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/NuSPAN.
