This study investigates the Hofstadter model featuring time-reversal symmetry breaking, achieved through complex hopping phases. Our findings indicate that the Chern numbers for the resulting Hofstadter bands are uniformly distributed across all rational flux values. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Hofstadter spectrum within the Chern number regime exhibits a self-similar structure characterized by a fractal dimension of approximately 1.5. Additionally, the wave functions associated with the lowest Landau level display a fractal dimension of roughly 2.5. Finally, we analyze the field-induced localization of Landau levels in this Hofstadter regime, revealing that the resulting localization length is also fractal in nature. These results are corroborated by numerical simulations. Our work offers a theoretical framework for investigating Hofstadter physics in systems where time-reversal symmetry is broken. Specifically, this model is applicable to various platforms, including artificial lattice systems such as circuit lattices and photonic circuits, as well as electronic band structures in time-reversal-broken materials like the quantum Hall regime of graphene and time-reversal-broken topological insulators. Moreover, the Hofstadter model can be realized in ultracold atom setups via optical lattices subjected to synthetic magnetic fields. Our findings suggest that the Hofstadter spectrum in this time-reversal-broken context exhibits a more complex structure than previously observed in time-reversal-symmetric scenarios. This complexity arises from the presence of Weyl points in momentum space, which serve as sources for the non-zero Chern numbers of the Hofstadter bands. Consequently, these results provide a foundation for exploring the Hofstadter spectrum and its associated physical phenomena in time-reversal-broken environments. Notably, the field-induced localization of Landau levels in this regime displays unique characteristics, including the existence of a critical field that differs from that observed in time-reversal-symmetric systems. These distinct features offer a promising avenue for investigating the field-induced localization of Landau levels in ultracold atoms situated within a synthetic magnetic field. Finally, our results may contribute to the experimental realization of Hofstadter physics in time-reversal-broken settings. The interplay between gravity and friction in granular matter generates complex behaviors that diverge significantly from standard theories. A notable example is the "anomalous screening" effect, where gravitational fields are effectively screened within the granular structure, resulting in a uniform pressure gradient that mirrors the behavior of fluids or gases. This phenomenon was first identified in 2008 during a gas discharge experiment involving a granular bed. In this study, we provide a comprehensive explanation of this previously unexplained mechanism. We conducted a systematic experimental investigation using a granular bed situated between two parallel plates, where one plate was driven to induce shear. Our experimental results align closely with numerical simulations based on the Discrete Element Method (DEM). These findings support a theoretical framework that incorporates grain-scale fluctuations in both velocity and force, alongside the influence of shear on pressure gradients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this theoretical model successfully explains the screening effect observed in gas-discharge experiments. Consequently, this work offers a robust explanation for the anomalous screening of gravity in granular matter. The proposed theory is also applicable to other granular systems, such as those involving flowing grains or those subjected to external loads. Ultimately, this research advances our understanding of granular matter by revealing its fundamental similarity to fluids and gases. The theoretical model is implemented in the open-source Python package `anomalous_screening`, which is available at https://github.com/JanoschKlein/AnomalousScreening. This study investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) through first-principles calculations. Specifically, we examine how Mn decoration influences these characteristics. Our results indicate that while pristine silicene on hBN exhibits a negligible band gap of 0.0001 eV, Mn decoration induces a substantial direct band gap of 0.55 eV at the Gamma point. Furthermore, the decoration alters the magnetic configuration from antiferromagnetic (AFA) to ferromagnetic (FM), with the magnetic moment increasing from 2 Bohr magnetons ($\mu_B$) to 4.5 $\mu_B$. Additionally, the system demonstrates stability across various temperatures, as confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations. These findings suggest that Mn-decorated silicene on hBN is a promising candidate for spintronic applications. Finally, the presence of a direct band gap and FM ordering makes this material suitable for both optoelectronics and spintronics. The computational details are provided in Appendix A. Sgr A East, situated in the Galactic Center, is a supernova remnant that exploded approximately 2.5 million years ago. Its progenitor was a massive star with a mass exceeding 20 solar masses. This study aims to determine the explosion site and the nature of the event that birthed Sgr A East. We developed a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulation of the Galactic Center, incorporating a supernova explosion at various locations. By analyzing the resulting radio emission, we compared our simulations with observations to identify the explosion site. Our findings indicate that Sgr A East originated from a supernova detonating roughly 1.5 parsecs from Sgr A*. Furthermore, the supernova likely occurred within a dense molecular cloud, which may have influenced the explosion's characteristics. This research underscores the necessity of investigating the specific sites of supernova explosions within the Galactic Center. Additionally, our simulations reveal that supernova explosions in the Galactic Center can trigger radio flares in Sgr A*, suggesting that supernovae in the past few thousand years could be responsible for these events. This offers a novel perspective on the connection between supernovae and galactic nuclei. Finally, our results suggest that the past few thousand years have been a particularly active era for supernova explosions in the Galactic Center. This conclusion is supported by the presence of multiple young supernova remnants in the region, including Sgr A East, G0.9+0.0, G0.5+0.0, and G0.2+0.0. Multi-label text classification involves assigning multiple categories to a single document, a task that often becomes challenging when specific categories are underrepresented in the training data. This study evaluates four over_sampling techniques—OS-ADASYN, OS-SYN, OS-PORESYN, and OS-POIRESYN—applied to multi-class text classification. The research utilizes a real-world dataset derived from the 2016 US Presidential Election, where the "Rural" label was significantly underrepresented. The findings indicate that all four methods effectively improved the classifier's recall for the "Rural" category. Furthermore, the OS-ADASYN approach demonstrated superior overall performance compared to the other techniques. Finally, the study confirms that over_sampling is a viable strategy for enhancing multi-class text classification, even in scenarios with severe label imbalance. This study examines the interrelationships between local news coverage, COVID-19 metrics (cases, deaths, and audience), and local news consumption. Utilizing data from the COVID-19 News Coverage Database, the study analyzes how various forms of coverage—specifically volume, tone, and focus—correlate with pandemic data and audience figures. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that local news coverage is linked to local COVID-19 cases and deaths, though this relationship is not entirely causal. Finally, the study explores the role of local news in disseminating information regarding the pandemic. These results offer valuable insights for local news organizations aiming to enhance their coverage and reach, thereby supporting communities during the COVID-19 crisis. This study examines the polarization transfer from an initial proton to a final proton within the elastic $e \vec{p} \to e \vec{p}$ scattering process, where a longitudinally polarized electron beam strikes a longitudinally polarized, at-rest proton target. The analysis focuses on scenarios where the scattered electron is detected in a specific channel, while the final proton's polarization is observed in two distinct kinematic regimes: one where it is detected in a different channel, and another where it is measured in the same channel as the scattered electron. Furthermore, the research explores the potential for enhancing sensitivity to new physics by comparing these predictions with results from a similar experiment conducted at a fixed-target facility using a polarized neutron target. Such an experiment could be realized at the European Spallation Source (ESS) by directing the proton beam onto a polarized neutron target. The findings indicate that the predicted polarization transfer is highly sensitive to the electron scattering angle, particularly at large angles, and exhibits a strong dependence on the final proton's scattering angle, which is expected to be significantly larger in the proton-based fixed-target setup than in the neutron-based one. The predicted polarization transfer is also sensitive to the final proton's momentum direction relative to the initial proton's momentum direction. This sensitivity arises from the spin-dependent part of the elastic scattering cross section, which is proportional to the product of the initial and final proton spins. The study demonstrates that this spin-dependent term can be maximized when the final proton's momentum is antiparallel to the initial proton's spin. Experts are a fundamental component of many human-machine collaborative systems, where they are typically trained on data annotated by human experts. However, the high cost of such annotations often restricts the scope of their training datasets. This paper introduces a method to augment training data by synthesoting expert annotations from base data using a generative model of expert behavior. This approach enables the efficient training of high-quality experts even when labeled data is scarce. We validate the efficacy of this method by training diagnostic experts for two tasks: a clinical decision support system for diagnosing sepsis and a diagnostic expert for triaging emergency department patients. In both scenarios, we successfully trained high-quality experts despite having access to only a small portion of the available labeled data. Furthermore, our evaluation demonstrates that the trained experts achieve diagnostic accuracy comparable to human experts. Additionally, we show that our trained experts can collaborate with other agents to deliver superior outcomes compared to those produced by other trained experts. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed method facilitates the training of experts that are more robust to variations in input data. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of generative models for training domain experts. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/medicalml/parametric_experts. This study investigates the exclusive double Higgs boson production process, denoted as $VVHH$, where $V$ represents a vector boson and $H$ stands for the Higgs boson. The analysis covers a proton-proton collision dataset with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the ATLAS detector at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=$ 13 TeV. The data were gathered during the LHC Run 2 period at an instantaneous luminosity of approximately 200 fb$^{-1}$. The event sample is categorized into three groups based on the decay modes of the two Higgs bosons: $b\bar{b}b\bar{b}$, $b\bar{b}\gamma\gamma$, and $b\bar{b}l^+l^-$ (where $l$ is an electron or muon). No significant deviation from the Standard Model background predictions was observed. Consequently, upper limits on the cross section times signal efficiency were established at 95% confidence level for various signal models, ranging from 0.01 to 0.1 times the Standard Model cross section. These findings are presented in three formats: as a single combined limit, and separately for the $b\bar{b}b\bar{b}$, $b\bar{b}\gamma\gamma$, and $b\bar{b}l^+l^-$ channels. Furthermore, the results are utilized to set upper limits on the signal cross section for a simplified production model featuring a single production coupling and two decay couplings. The most stringent constraint achieved is 0.01 times the Standard Model cross section. This represents an improvement of a factor of 1.5 compared to the previous best result from Run 2. The combined limit is more than an order of magnitude tighter than the best result from Run 1. We introduce a platform digital spin laser that operates by detecting the precession of an optically pumped $^{87}$Rb spin. The laser's gain mechanism is driven by the coupling between this precession and the pump's phase modulation. This concept is realized through a compact, all-passive circuit that directly converts the weak $^{87}$Rb$-$radiofrequency (RF) precession coupling into significant microwave (MW) amplitude modulation. This approach establishes a new class of hybrid quantum-classical digital sensors, leveraging the high sensitivity of quantum systems to weak interactions and the robustness of classical circuits in signal processing. Furthermore, we demonstrate the digital spin laser on an $^{87}$Rb$-$Al$ atom-circuit platform, achieving a record narrow linewidth of 1.2 kHz at 5.2 GHz. The device functions as a compact, self-powered, all-passive RF oscillator, offering potential applications in quantum radar, magnetometry, and magnetometry-in-the-loop control. Additionally, it serves as a novel platform for studying many-body physics in strongly driven open quantum systems. Our work highlights the synergistic potential of combining atom-circuit quantum electromagnetism with alkali metal vapor magnetometry. We investigate the stability of a neutralino dark matter candidate within a supersymmetric framework featuring a complex scalar triplet. In this model, the neutralino decays into a pair of right-handed neutrinos, which subsequently decay into Standard Model particles. We demonstrate that the resulting gamma-ray spectrum from these neutralino decays can align with the observed excess in the dwarf galaxy data reported by the Fermi-LAT collaboration. This suggests that a neutralino with a lifetime of approximately $10^{26}$ seconds serves as a viable dark matter candidate. This lifetime is notably shorter than that of supersymmetric neutralinos in other well-known models. Furthermore, we show that the parameter space allowing for this gamma-ray signature is not entirely excluded by current experimental constraints. We also examine the implications of this scenario for future experiments, such as LUX, and discuss how these projections can be utilized to establish a lower limit on the neutralino's lifetime. Finally, we note that the predicted lifetime is significantly longer than that of the recently proposed self-interacting dark matter neutralino, for which a lifetime of roughly $10^{28}$ seconds was suggested. We demonstrate the existence of a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the genus problem in dense graphs. Within this scheme, the objective is to determine the minimum genus $g$ for a dense graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and edge count $m$, achieving an approximation ratio of $(1+\varepsilon)g + O(\varepsilon m)$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$. This result implies that for dense graphs, the genus can be approximated within a $(1+\varepsilon)$ factor up to an additive term that is sublinear relative to the number of edges. Furthermore, our approach yields a PTAS for the edge-addition variant of the genus problem, where the goal is to find the minimum number of edges to add to a graph $G$ to achieve a genus of $g$. This specific PTAS provides an approximation ratio of $(1+\varepsilon)g + O(\varepsilon m + \sqrt{gm})$. These findings extend the work of Marx and Skowron, who previously established a PTAS for the edge-deletion version of the genus problem. Additionally, our results offer an alternative proof for the fact that the genus of dense graphs is an $o(n)$ parameter. Finally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{gn})$ for the edge-addition problem, which complements the upper bound provided by our PTAS. In contrast, Marx and Skowron demonstrated a lower bound of $\Omega(gn^{1/2-\varepsilon})$ for the edge-deletion problem, highlighting a distinct separation between the two problems. Our lower bound for edge addition is nearly tight, as it aligns with the approximation guarantee of the PTAS for edge addition. The primary instrument for our PTAS is a novel algorithm designed for $\varepsilon$-subdivisions of graphs, which we term the \emph{local genus algorithm}. This algorithm operates in polynomial time and, given an $\varepsilon$-subdivision $H$ of a graph $G$, computes a genus embedding of $H$ within a genus of $2\operatorname{genus}(G) + O(\varepsilon |E(H)|)$. We anticipate that this algorithm will prove valuable in addressing a range of geometric graph problems. This paper introduces a stochastic Newton approach designed for large-scale convex optimization problems where data is distributed across multiple machines. The primary challenge in this setting is the communication bottleneck between machines and a central coordinator, which becomes increasingly severe as the number of machines grows. To address this, we propose a framework that eliminates the need to pull data to the coordinator, instead having each machine pull data and push the resulting updates back. Specifically, we develop a distributed algorithm that combines two techniques: a machine-level averaging strategy and a data-level sampling strategy. We demonstrate that this method achieves an optimal convergence rate for both biased and unbiased Newton approaches, matching the performance of centralized algorithms. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to scenarios with stochastic noise in the objective function, stochastic constraints, and inexact data. Finally, we validate our findings through numerical experiments. Our results indicate that the proposed distributed Newton method outperforms existing state-of-the-art distributed solvers. Notably, when compared to a distributed biased Newton method, our approach yields a $10\times$ speedup. Against a distributed data sampling method, we observe a $2\times$ speedup. Most significantly, our method surpasses all other state-of-the-art distributed techniques, including unbiased Newton and data sampling methods, by achieving up to a $10\times$ speedup. These superior performance gains are particularly evident in large-scale problems. Additionally, we show that our approach outperforms all other methods, including centralized ones, by up to $10\times$. This outcome is highly significant, as it confirms that distributed Newton methods can indeed outperform their centralized counterparts. Finally, we discuss the potential of our framework for other distributed optimization problems. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into detecting hate speech within Hindi and Bengali social media contexts. We introduce a novel dataset comprising 10,000 labeled instances of Hindi and Bengali collected from Twitter. Utilizing a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model pre-trained on Hindi and Bengali Wikipedia, we achieve state-of-the-art performance for both languages. Furthermore, we examine the efficacy of transfer learning by pre-training the model on an English dataset and subsequently fine-tuning it on the Hindi and Bengali datasets. Our findings indicate that pre-training on the Hindi and Bengali datasets yields superior results compared to using the English dataset. Additionally, we demonstrate that an English pre-trained BERT model outperforms models trained solely on the Hindi and Bengali datasets, thereby highlighting the significant potential of English pre-trained models for social media-based NLP tasks in Hindi and Bengali. Finally, we compare various neural architectures, including BERT, FastText, and LSTM, to evaluate their performance in hate speech detection. The code and data associated with this study can be accessed at: https://github.com/abhishekgupta1234/BERT-Hate-Speech-Detection.

A Time Projection Chamber (TPC) utilizing a gas detector offers exceptional spatial resolution and a vast active volume, making it ideal for particle physics experiments. By combining two-dimensional hits from gas detectors with three-dimensional particle tracking from beam-dump experiments, we can achieve comprehensive three-dimensional reconstruction of particle interactions. This study introduces a novel method to extract ionization and scintillation yields from high-resolution light curves generated by charged particle tracks in a gas TPC. The technique relies on a two-component model of the TPC signal, which incorporates both the direct ionization detected within the TPC and the scintillation light produced by the ionization of the drift gas in the surrounding photodetector. We demonstrate that this approach is effective for identifying nuclear recoil events in gas TPCs designed for dark matter searches. Furthermore, we show that the energy resolution for 2.5 keV neon recoils in such a detector can reach 10% or better. This framework is applicable to any gas TPC equipped with an external scintillation detection system. The methodology was developed and validated using data from the SAGEEN testbed, a compact, scalable architecture for gas TPCs in beam-dump environments. SAGEEN was tested using a beam of 10 GeV protons at the Fermilab Test Beam Facility. The results presented here demonstrate the viability of gas detectors as a medium for direct dark matter detection within beam-dump facilities. The techniques described in this work are expected to be applicable to future experiments, including the proposed dark matter search at Fermilab's NuSTORM facility. The commercial trucking sector is a vast, diverse industry where human experts evaluate driver performance to determine employment eligibility. This study examines the effectiveness of expert assessments in predicting future driving outcomes, specifically violations and crashes. Utilizing data from over 1.5 million drivers, we analyze how experts make decisions and how those decisions correlate with subsequent crashes and violations. Our findings indicate that while future outcomes are only weakly predicted by outcomes from other drivers, they are strongly predicted by the same outcomes from the same expert. This suggests that expert evaluations possess significant validity and that individual experts hold distinct views on performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining machine learning outputs with contextual information regarding specific experts and companies enhances the prediction of future crashes and violations. These results offer new insights into expert decision-making and underscore the necessity of expert moderation when interpreting machine learning results for individual cases. This paper addresses the Out-of-Categories (OOC) challenge, which aims to develop models capable of detecting images belonging to categories absent from the training dataset. The task involves two components: OOC identification for novel categories and fine-tuning for open-set categories. Our approach utilizes a two-stage framework: first, we train a OOC detector using OOC knowledge distillation, followed by the training of a OOC-aware model. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses the baseline by 1.5% in OOC accuracy and 1.2% in open-set accuracy. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ai-heart/OOC.

This study examines the statistical characteristics of geodesic paths within random field manifolds, with a specific focus on their curvature distributions. We derive the general form of the probability density function (PDF) for geodesic curvature and demonstrate that, under specific conditions, this PDF simplifies to a Gaussian form. Furthermore, we analyze the scaling behavior of the PDF at large curvature values, revealing that it follows a power-law decay. These findings are validated through numerical simulations, which also confirm that the calculated PDFs remain consistent across different manifold dimensions. Our results suggest that these statistical properties are universal and independent of the specific random field model employed. Finally, we explore the potential applications of these insights in the context of cosmic topology research. Our analysis indicates that while the number of geodesic loops is generally low, it may become significant in scenarios involving high background density or when observing distant objects. Additionally, we demonstrate that the cosmic void field can serve as an effective probe for identifying these geodesic loops. We conclude that the cosmic void field is not merely a random superposition of voids but exhibits a more complex structure, characterized by the presence of geodesic loops. This insight could prove valuable for future investigations into the topology of the universe. Our conclusions are supported by a comprehensive analysis of the void field, utilizing both void catalogs derived from the SDSS survey and mock catalogs generated via the VOSSES void simulation code. The paper also includes a detailed discussion of the VOSSES code. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1990/VOSSES. The L-functions associated with modular forms serve as powerful tools for investigating the multiplicative properties of these forms. By utilizing the analytic characteristics of L-functions, researchers can derive significant insights into the multiplicative structure of the coefficients of modular forms. This paper demonstrates that the distinct values of the $n$-th normalized coefficients of the L-functions for all cuspidal Hecke eigenforms with a fixed level $N$ share a common denominator within any given subset of the integers. Furthermore, we establish that the bounding polynomial for this denominator is independent of the level $N$. These findings are achieved by combining the theory of modular forms with the analytic properties of L-functions. The techniques employed here are also applicable to other related problems. Additionally, we provide a brief overview of the connection between L-functions and the Sato-Tate conjecture. Finally, we present a conjecture regarding the behavior of the denominators of distinctive values of the $n$-th normalized L-series coefficients for modular forms with varying levels. The examples used to illustrate this conjecture were generated using the computational software Magma. We hope these observations will inspire further research into the extended denominators of distinctive L-function values across different levels. This work establishes analogues of the Korovkin theorem for weakly nonlinear and monotone operators acting on Banach lattices of multivariate functions, thereby extending the classical Korovki theorem. The findings are applied to create sequential approximation theorems for multivariate functions based on one-sided linear positive and monotone operators, as well as multivariate progressive and periodic fuzzy sets. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that various existing results within the field of multivariate fuzzy logic follow directly from the main theorems and propositions presented in this paper. This includes a multivariate extension of a theorem by Castaño and Godina, a result by Li and Li, and a contribution by Li and Liu. Additionally, the findings offer an alternative proof for the work of Castaño and Godina. Finally, an analogue of the Korovkin theorem for multivariate fuzzy sets is derived, and it is shown that the study by Castaño and Godina constitutes a specific instance of this broader result. The paper concludes with an appendix containing a generalization of the Stone-Weierstrass theorem tailored to multivariate fuzzy sets. This appendix establishes that the set of all fuzzy sets exhibiting a specific continuity property forms a subalgebra within the space of all multivariate fuzzy sets, providing a multivariate extension of a result by Castaño and Godina. A graph $G$ is defined as $\alpha(G)$-pancyclic if, for every independence number $\alpha < \alpha(G)$, the graph $G$ contains a cycle of length $2\alpha$. This study demonstrates that if a $2k$-connected, $\alpha(G)$-pancyclic graph has a maximum degree of $2k+1$, its Hamiltonian complement is bipartite. Furthermore, we establish that if a $2k+1$-connected, $\alpha(G)$-pancyclic graph possesses a maximum degree of $2k+2$, then both the Hamiltonian complement and the independent complement of the graph are bipartite. We also examine the conditions under which $\alpha(G)$-pancyclic graphs are Hamiltonian. Additionally, we present several sufficient conditions for $\alpha(G)$-pancyclicity, which generalize findings by Chvátal and Sch\"{a}fer, as well as those by Broersma, Veldman, and Vizing. Finally, we derive sufficient conditions for a graph to be independent pancyclic by combining our findings with a theorem by Chvátal and Sch\"{a}fer. These results extend and complement the work of Chvátal and Sch\"{a}fer, Broersma, Veldman, and Veldman. In the concluding section, we explore the relationship between Hamiltonicity and bipartiteness in the Hamiltonian complement of $\alpha(G)$-pancyclic graphs. Specifically, we prove that if $G$ is a $2k$-connected $\alpha(G)$-pancyclic graph with a maximum degree of $2k+1$ and is not Hamiltonian, then the Hamiltonian complement is bipartite. We also note that this result does not hold for graphs with a maximum degree of $2k+2$. Finally, we provide a counterexample to the conjecture proposed by Chvátal and Sch\"{a}fer. Our findings also offer a partial answer to a conjecture by Chvátal and Sch\"{a}fer. Additionally, we address a conjecture by Chvátal and Sch\"{a}fer regarding the pancyclicity of graphs with a Hamiltonian complement. This study examines the directed flow of forward hadrons in Au+Au and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV, utilizing data from the PHENIX experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Measurements were conducted at rapidity $y_{\rm lab} \in [2.5,4]$ across centralities from 0–10% to 40–60% for charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons. The directed flow amplitude, $a_1(y_{\rm lab}=3)$, exhibits a weak centrality dependence for pions and kaons, whereas protons display a stronger centrality dependence. Furthermore, the directed flow of forward protons is notably larger than that of pions and kaons, a finding that contrasts with the behavior of midrapidity protons at the same collision energy. These results are compared with directed forward rapidity neutron data from the ALICE experiment at 200 GeV. The observed directed flow of forward hadrons is compared with event-by-event hydrodynamic simulations incorporating both soft and pQCD parton scattering. These simulations successfully describe the centrality dependence of the directed flow amplitude for pions, kaons, and protons. Additionally, the data indicate that the directed flow of forward neutrons is approximately 20% larger than that of charged hadrons, a trend that is also consistent with hydrodynamic model predictions. This suggests that the asymmetry in directed forward neutron and charged hadron flow arises from the asymmetric production of neutrons and charged hadrons. Finally, the data demonstrate that the directed flow of forward hadrons in Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV is significantly larger than that observed in Xe+Xe and Sn+Sn collisions at the same energy. The magnitude of this directed flow is also compared with hydrodynamic model results. The analysis confirms that the directed flow of forward hadrons is primarily driven by the initial conditions of the quark-gluon plasma, with contributions from the quark-gluon plasma and hadron resonance gas phases, as well as hadronization processes. The study concludes that the directed flow of forward hadrons is a sensitive probe of the initial conditions of the quark-gluon plasma. This study introduces a sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral (SSAM) framework designed to enhance the efficiency of the Adaptive Spectral Koopman Method (ASKM). The primary goal of this approach is to minimize the computational expense of applying spectral operators to finite-dimensional approximations of functions. This is accomplished by substituting high-dimensional tensor-product bases with efficiently constructed multivariate orthogonal polynomials. The efficacy of SSAM is validated through numerical experiments involving the analysis of finite-dimensional function representations derived from a chaotic dynamical system and a high-dimensional function arising in the Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness is demonstrated by applying it to the ASKM variant of ASKM, which utilizes adaptive sparse grids to optimize the application of finite-dimensional approximations within the ASKM algorithm. These findings indicate that SSAM substantially lowers computational costs while maintaining high accuracy. Additionally, the implementation of SSAM within the ASKM algorithm proves robust, even when dealing with highly nonlinear functions represented by finite-dimensional approximations generated from high-dimensional data. The core strength of ASKM lies in its ability to automatically identify the most relevant features of the underlying data, thereby eliminating the need for manual selection of model complexity. This capability is crucial for managing the curse of dimensionality, as it allows the method to adaptively concentrate computational resources on the most significant dimensions. Consequently, ASKM offers a promising avenue for advancing the analysis of high-dimensional dynamical systems. The source code for the method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andrewjg/SSAM. The accompanying supplementary material includes additional code and datasets. Specifically, Supplementary Code 1 provides a Python implementation of SSAM, Supplementary Code 2 offers a Python implementation of ASKM, Supplementary Dataset 1 contains the Lorenz-63 dataset, and Supplementary Dataset 2 includes the Navier-Stokes dataset. The strong DC-field outer scaling (SDCFS) is a technique used to analyze the interaction of intense DC electric fields with atoms and molecules. This approach relies on the outer scaling concept, which posits that the behavior of atoms and molecules under strong electric fields is primarily governed by their outermost electrons. We have developed the SDCFS within the framework of the time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) method, enabling its application to both atoms and molecules. The resulting SDCFS-generated orbitals and wave functions are constructed using a basis set composed of complex Gaussian functions. These functions feature exponents that depend on the field strength and are derived from the outer electron configuration of the neutral system in the absence of an electric field. Additionally, the center positions of these basis functions are optimized using the SDCFS self-consistent field (SCF) method. To our knowledge, this represents the first implementation of complex scaling for DCFS. We have applied SDCFS to water, ammonia, and methane molecules across a range of DC field strengths. Our findings indicate that SDCFS-generated orbitals and wave functions remain stable and converge rapidly. Furthermore, the calculated ionization potentials align well with experimental data. We also demonstrate that SDCFS can accurately describe molecular alignment within strong DC electric fields. Finally, we show that the SDCFS method successfully captures the dynamics of electron loss from ammonia molecules in a DC electric field. These results suggest that SDCFS is a highly effective tool for investigating the dynamics of atoms and molecules exposed to DC electric fields. The SDCFS code is accessible at https://github.com/taekyungkim/SDCFS. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a classical iterative method designed to solve the Schrödinger problem, which involves finding a joint distribution with specified marginals that minimizes KL-divergence from a given matrix. This study examines the algorithm's convergence when a solution to the Schrödinger problem does not exist, a scenario that occurs frequently in practical applications. Specifically, we analyze the case where the matrix possesses infinitely many perfect matchings, resulting in a non-unique optimal solution. Under these conditions, we demonstrate that the Sinkhorn iterates converge to the set of optimal solutions for the corresponding optimization problem, provided that certain moments of these matchings are uniformly integrable. These theoretical findings are validated through several examples, including a model of a branching random walk. Furthermore, we establish that the convergence rate is $O(1/\log n)$, where $n$ represents the number of iterations. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's behavior in a setting with unique solutions but with a sequence of matrices approaching the limit, showing that the convergence speed can vary depending on the specific problem parameters. This result is also supported by an example. Additionally, we provide an example of a bipartite graph where the Sinkhorn iterates diverge. Throughout this work, we employ a novel approach to perfect matchings on the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ to derive our results. Specifically, we establish a criterion for the uniform integrability of matchings based on the uniform integrability of matchings with a fixed number of steps, a result that may be of independent interest. We also present a criterion for the finiteness of the free energy of the matchings. Our proofs rely on a novel application of the theory of subadditive ergodic processes. Specifically, we construct a subadditive ergodic process linked to the free energy of matchings and prove its convergence to a constant, which is subsequently used to derive the aforementioned results. This approach may also have independent interest. Finally, we demonstrate that the convergence of Sinkhorn iterates can be characterized by the convergence of free energies, which are defined as the log-determinant of the joint distribution generated by the iterates. This convergence is established using the theory of subadditive ergodic processes. The proof also utilizes a recent result by the authors regarding the asymptotic behavior of free energy. In this paper, we extend that result to establish a criterion for the uniform integrability of matchings. The proof of this criterion employs a technique involving a "shifted" version of the original problem

This study presents a measurement of the top-quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis relies on events where both top quarks decay hadronically. A data sample collected between May and December 2017, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 13.6 fb$^{-1}$, is examined. The measured cross-section is $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 62.8 \pm 1.4 \pm 2.0$ pb, where the first uncertainty represents the statistical error and the second is the systematic uncertainty. This result aligns with the theoretical predictions generated by MADGRAPH5_AMC@NLO and POWHEG-BOPTOP. The measurement is also consistent with the result obtained at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV from the same experiment. Furthermore, the cross-section is compared against predictions from various Monte Carlo event generators, showing good agreement with MADGRAPH5_AMC@NLO and POWHEG-BOPTOP at next-to-leading order (NLO) and leading order (LO) respectively. Additionally, the differential distributions for the invariant mass of the $t\bar{t}$ system and the transverse momentum of the $Z$ boson are compared with NLO predictions from MADGRAPH5_AMC@NLO, POWHEG-BOPTOP, and HERWIG7. The analysis was conducted under the ATLAS Collaboration. Keywords: Top Quark Production, Top Quark Pair, Cross Section, Distributions, ATLAS, LHC, Proton Proton Collisions, Standard Model. Although Anderson localization is typically associated with off-diagonal disorder, systems featuring only diagonal disorder can also exhibit localization under specific conditions. This study examines the impact of introducing a small amount of off-diagonal disorder into a system that was previously governed solely by diagonal disorder. We observe that the resulting system does not immediately transition to delocalized states; instead, it undergoes a localization length transition after a threshold of off-diagonal disorder is exceeded. This unexpected behavior is attributed to the central coupling mechanism within the system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon can be modeled using a two-level system with central coupling, where the localization length is governed by the coupling strength between the two levels. Finally, we validate this theoretical framework by applying it to a molecular chain where molecules are connected at their core. These findings suggest that such systems could be valuable for developing functional materials. Additionally, we note that this central coupling effect has been experimentally observed in both classical and quantum systems. To further explore this topic, we have included a supplementary section in this manuscript. We anticipate that the material presented here will be beneficial for researchers in the field. Urban environments are renowned for their social and cultural variety, yet the pandemic's behavioral shifts may have diminished these interactions. This study examines changes in income diversity within urban encounters across 1,000 U.S. cities from March 2020 to May 2021. Utilizing anonymized mobile phone data, we discovered that the diversity of incomes met in person declined by 10% during the pandemic. This decline was more pronounced in areas with stricter lockdowns and was driven by reduced diversity among younger individuals. Our findings indicate that pandemic-induced behavioral changes significantly altered income diversity in urban settings, a shift that could exacerbate existing social inequalities. Consequently, this underscores the necessity for new urban policies aimed at preserving the diverse interactions that define city life. By applying a high-resolution, privacy-preserving data collection method, our approach offers a framework for monitoring urban diversity and understanding the impacts of future global crises. Additionally, it provides a means to assess the efficacy of various interventions designed to foster diverse urban encounters. Finally, this research advances our understanding of how pandemics influence urban diversity and equips us to better anticipate the effects of future crises on city environments.

This study evaluates various nonlinear field-splitting techniques for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media within the open-source multiphase flow library MFEM. We analyze the convergence characteristics of a standard Picard iteration alongside several nonlinear field-splitting methods, including the semi-implicit method, a fractional-step approach, and a newly developed nonlinear fractional-step variant. By examining convergence rates and computational costs, we recommend implementing a field-splitting scheme in practical applications. Furthermore, we outline a strategy for selecting an appropriate splitting method based on specific problem parameters. Finally, we assess the efficacy of these schemes across a broad spectrum of scenarios, ranging from single-layer to multi-layer heterogeneous domains. The research findings are accessible at https://github.com/mfem/two-phase-flow. Supplementary materials can be found at https://github.com/mfem/two-phase-flow/tree/compare-splitting-methods. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/mfem/two-phase-flow/tree/compare-splitting-methods. The chiral response of optical resonators is typically weak, driven by the small change in parity between even- and odd-parity modes. This limitation can be overcome by designing a resonator with a single-handedness structure, where the parity-breaking is minimal. We demonstrate this approach using a spiral array of dielectric cylinders, which is modeled as a chain of spiral circuits. This framework allows us to derive a compact expression for the quality factor associated with chiral resonances. Furthermore, we identify a class of single-handedness structures that exhibit exceptionally strong chiral responses. These findings are expected to facilitate the design of highly efficient chiral photonic devices. Additionally, we outline potential applications for these devices within chiral quantum optics. Finally, we provide a Python-based open-source code that models the single-handedness structure and calculates its chiral response. This tool is intended to assist researchers in designing their own single-handedness structures and is available at https://github.com/ChiralSpiral. The accompanying paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01007. This work investigates the AdS$_2$ limit of a matrix model that corresponds to the 2D conformal field theory (CFT) defined on the upper half-plane with Liouville CFT boundary conditions. We demonstrate that, in the AdS$_2$ limit, the Liouville CFT reduces to a theory comprising two non-interacting sectors: one describing a free boson and the other a free fermion. This finding aligns with the expectation that the Liouville CFT in the AdS$_2$ limit is dual to 2D Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity. Furthermore, we show that the partition function of the proposed matrix model can be derived from the well-known result for a single Hermitian matrix and the boundary condition of the Liouville CFT on the upper half-plane. Additionally, the Liouville CFT partition function on a genus $h$ surface is equivalent to that on a surface with a boundary of length $L$ in the limit where $h \to 0$ and $L \to \infty$, provided the ratio $h/L^2$ remains fixed. Consequently, the matrix model also captures the large $L$ limit of JT gravity on a genus $h$ surface under the same limit conditions. Finally, we examine the boundary contribution to the JT gravity path integral and establish its correspondence with the boundary term of the Liouville CFT partition function within the AdS$_2$ limit. This correspondence holds specifically when the boundary contribution is treated as a function of $L$ rather than the central charge $c$. In this context, the boundary term of the Liouville CFT partition function in the AdS$_2$ limit successfully reproduces the boundary term of the JT gravity partition function on a genus $h$ surface in the same $h \to 0$ and $L \to \infty$ limit, with $h/L^2$ held constant. This result corroborates the conjecture that JT gravity on a genus $h$ surface exhibits a boundary contribution proportional to $h/L^2$ in the aforementioned limit. Finally, we note that the boundary term of the Liouville CFT partition function in the AdS$_2$ limit can be interpreted as the boundary contribution of the associated matrix model. The warping of spacetime is a fundamental mechanism for generating ideal warp drives, yet the influence of the cosmological constant on this process remains unexplored. This study examines how the cosmological constant affects ideal fluid warp drive solutions, revealing that positive values can enhance field uniformity and reduce energy requirements. Furthermore, a novel class of circular warped spacetimes has been identified, characterized by a metric function dependent on both radial and angular coordinates. These space circular drives are particularly well-suited for applications such as space exploration and planetary observation. Additionally, the paper introduces a new family of planar warped spacetimes featuring nontrivial Killing vectors, which exhibit improved field uniformity. The various warp drive metrics derived in this work are anticipated to serve as viable models for future theoretical and experimental investigations. Finally, the study explores the potential of warp drives in cosmology, specifically regarding the formation of cosmic structures. These findings suggest that the creation of wormholes and other cosmic structures could be facilitated by the generation of warp drives. Consequently, this research may offer valuable insights for future space missions, including the exploration of the solar system, the development of space elevators, and the colonization of other planets. The results are expected to significantly advance our understanding of warp drives and their practical applications. Furthermore, the proposed metrics may contribute to the development of new theories of gravity and the resolution of longstanding problems in cosmology. Cities are increasingly adopting digital technologies to enhance urban management, improve service delivery, and foster sustainable development. However, the widespread implementation of these solutions is often hindered by fragmented data governance, inconsistent data standards, and a lack of interoperability. To address these challenges, we introduce GUIDES (Geospatial Urban Infrastructure Information Engineering Solutions), a reference framework designed to facilitate the deployment of digital city solutions. This framework provides a unified approach to data governance, governance processes, and data modeling, alongside a set of data engineering tools that enable the automatic generation of data pipelines and the integration of city information systems. GUIDES has been successfully applied to multiple digital city initiatives, demonstrating its efficacy in delivering data engineering solutions for city information systems. Furthermore, it offers a scalable and adaptable foundation for implementing digital services, such as those found in smart city applications. This paper details the GUIDES framework and illustrates its application within various digital city projects. Additionally, we provide a user-friendly graphical interface for GUIDES to support the modeling of city information systems and the construction of data pipelines. The GUI is available at https://github.com/SmartCityAnalytics/GUIDES. We anticipate that GUIDES will serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners engaged in developing digital city solutions. We introduce a spin-dephasing method to investigate thermal and non-thermal collective excitations within a two-dimensional Paul trap. This method is highly sensitive to the distribution of vibrational mode amplitudes, allowing for the differentiation between thermal and non-thermal sources. By measuring the dephasing of spin states coupled to a single center-of-mass vibrational mode, we can determine the vibrational temperature of the remaining $2d-1$ modes. This approach enables the characterization of both thermal and non-thermal motional state distributions and the measurement of heating rates. We demonstrate these capabilities by analyzing heating caused by blackbody radiation and by studying the dephasing dynamics of a single vibrational mode excited by a laser push. Furthermore, we establish that the heating rate from blackbody radiation scales with the square of the trap frequency and linearly with the ambient temperature. These findings are compared against blackbody heating rates predicted by theory. Additionally, our analysis of laser-induced heating reveals a strong dependence on the laser pulse duration and a weaker dependence on its focal spot size. Finally, we show that the spin-dephasing technique is effective for extracting the full set of Laguerre polynomials describing the distribution of vibrational mode occupation numbers. These techniques are applicable to any trapped ion system, including those with multiple ions and those confined in traps of arbitrary dimensionality. Our results provide a quantitative assessment of blackbody heating, offering guidance for designing experiments that avoid heating effects. This work also offers a pathway to characterize the motional state of a trapped ion using a single laser beam. Our findings are relevant for quantum information processing, quantum simulation, and the study of many-body physics in trapped ion systems. Specifically, they facilitate the preparation of specific vibrational mode occupation numbers and the analysis of the Paul trap environment, such as blackbody heating, as a critical step toward large-scale quantum information processing. Additionally, our analysis of laser-induced heating serves as a valuable tool for designing quantum information processing experiments. The experimental data presented were collected using the trapped ion system at the University of Innsbruck, Austria. This study presents a systematic investigation into the chemical and electromagnetic contributions to tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS). We employ a fully parameter-free, comprehensive quantum mechanical framework to model the electronic properties of a Au(111) surface, a SiO$_2$-terminated 4-mercaptopyridine (4-MP) monolayer, and a 4-MP bilayer, along with a SiO$_2$-capped 4-MP dimer. This approach integrates density functional theory (DFT) with the embedded cluster method (ECM) to incorporate periodicity, leveraging the latter's ability to accurately describe the electronic structure of extended systems. Furthermore, time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) calculations are utilized to determine the transition dipole moments of the 4-MP species. By combining these quantum mechanical findings with the finite difference time domain (FDTD) method, we calculate the electric field enhancement factors for the various 4-MP configurations. Our results indicate that the electromagnetic mechanism is the primary driver of the observed enhancement in TERS. Additionally, we demonstrate that the quantum mechanical approach is capable of modeling the complex electronic structure of 4-MP dimers, thereby accounting for the experimentally observed charge transfer resonance in TERS. These findings underscore the critical role of quantum mechanical modeling in advancing our understanding of the TERS technique. Finally, the computational methodology developed here is applicable to a broad spectrum of TERS scenarios. The Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT) recently conducted a deep K-band survey of the nearby galaxy group (z=0.01-0.03) to investigate the origin of the microwave background anomaly. This study presents the initial findings, specifically the identification of 11 previously unknown radio galaxies and a significant sample of 1,000 star-forming galaxies (SFGs) with flux densities exceeding 1 mJy. The analysis of these 1,111 SFGs reveals a strong correlation between K-band flux and infrared luminosity, which aligns with findings from other surveys. Furthermore, the SRT data indicate that the star formation rate (SFR) in these galaxies is driven by the radio flux density, with a derived proportionality constant of 1.2 M_sun yr^-1 mJy^-1. This result is consistent with the SFR estimates derived from the SRT's 21 cm data. Additionally, the study confirms the existence of a radio-loud galaxy population within the SFG sample, characterized by a radio flux density greater than 10 mJy and an X-ray luminosity exceeding 10^42 erg s^-1. The SRT data also identify a population of radio galaxies with flux densities above 10 mJy and redshifts greater than 0.01, which are likely to be radio-loud quasars. Ammonium sulfate ((NH$_4$)$_2$(SO$_4$)) exhibits a substantial entropy change near its phase transition, a phenomenon that has sparked significant debate. In this study, we demonstrate that the entropy variation is primarily driven by the extensive nature of the entropy associated with the disordering ammonium ions, which outnumber the ordered ions involved in the primary structural transition. This conclusion is supported by a combination of experimental data and computational modeling. Our findings indicate that the entropy density at the transition is notably lower than that of other extensive molecular solids, such as methylammonium halides, thereby offering a potential explanation for why (NH$_4$)$_2$(SO$_4$) does not display giant electrocaloric effects. Furthermore, we show that the entropy density can be accurately predicted using a simple statistical model. These results provide a framework for understanding the magnitude of entropy changes in molecular solids and for identifying candidates for giant electrocaloric materials. Humans and other animals learn to navigate environments by associating cues with outcomes, yet they do not optimize this process. Instead, they employ various strategies to acquire information and guide behavior, the selection of which often depends on the task's statistical properties. This study investigates the relationship between the deployment of these strategies and neural mechanisms. We recruited 36 participants to perform a probabilistic learning task, collecting both behavioral data and fMRI scans. Our analysis revealed that midbrain regions, including the substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area, encode reward prediction errors in a manner consistent with optimal theories. Furthermore, we identified specific behavioral traits—such as optimism and impulsivity—that influence strategy use and learning efficiency. Notably, the activation of the substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area during the encoding of reward prediction errors varies according to these individual differences. These findings offer new insights into the behavioral and neural underpinnings of probabilistic learning. More broadly, they highlight the significance of suboptimal tactics in learning and their link to individual traits, while also advancing our understanding of the midbrain's role in probabilistic learning and the interplay between individual traits and brain function. These results have significant implications for understanding individual differences in learning and their connection to psychiatric disorders. This study addresses the task of identifying the nearest neighbor to a query within a dataset under the Fréchet distance, which measures the minimum distance between two polygonal curves of equal length. The standard close-neighbor search problem is intractable in the input-restricted setting under fine-grained complexity assumptions. However, recent research has demonstrated that approximate close-neighbor search is feasible under this model. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for constructing a data structure for this task with the same number of parameters as prior work, achieving superior query and update times. We further establish matching lower bounds on the number of parameters and prove that any algorithm with the same parameter count must incur quadratic query and update complexities, thereby closing the gap between upper and lower bounds. Additionally, we propose a new data structure for polygonal curve matching under the Fréchet distance that operates in subquadratic time. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through extensive experiments on real-world datasets. Our results indicate that this structure is competitive with the state-of-the-art for polygonal curve matching, while our parameter counts for the close-neighbor search data structure are more favorable than existing solutions. This paper is the result of a collaboration with researchers from the fields of machine learning and computer vision. Consequently, we have included a concise overview of the underlying applications and their relationship to our contributions. This study examines how electron spill-out and nonlocality influence gap-plasmons in the limit of vanishing separations between two metallic surfaces. We contrast a local response model, which neglects electron spill-out, with a nonlocal response derived from the linearized time-dependent density functional theory. Our findings indicate that while both models predict identical long-wavelength gap-plasmon modes, the frequency in the nonlocal framework is lower. Furthermore, the amplitude of the induced charge density within the gap diminishes as the gap closes, a phenomenon absent in the local approximation. These results are validated using jellium slabs and corroborated by time-dependent density functional tight-binding calculations on metallic clusters. Finally, we demonstrate that electron spill-out into the gap can be precisely tuned by adjusting the aspect ratio of the metallic objects. These insights are applicable to understanding electromagnetic fields near metallic nanostructures. Additionally, we show that electron spill-out can be harnessed to control the distance between two metallic nanoparticles, a capability that could be valuable for nanomechanical devices. To facilitate future investigations, we provide an open-source Python package implementing the nonlocal response for two-dimensional and three-dimensional metallic nanoparticles. The widespread adoption of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has created a substantial repository of heterogeneous clinical data, encompassing both structured and unstructured information. This digital archive offers immense potential for advancing medical research and enhancing patient care. However, effectively mining this data remains challenging due to its complex structure and the scarcity of labeled cases. To address these hurdles, we introduce the Heterogeneous Resemblance Graph Neural Network (HRGNN), a deep learning framework designed to analyze heterogeneous data and identify resemblances among individuals. HRGNN constructs a graph where each node represents a person, utilizing a deep neural network to extract features from both structured and unstructured EHR data. The model generates personalized node embeddings that capture the inherent relationships between individuals, which are then employed for downstream tasks such as disease prediction and patient clustering. We evaluated HRGNN on two real-world datasets comprising over 100,000 individuals, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict diseases and identify patient groups with similar characteristics. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the model's performance, interpretability, and robustness. The results indicate that HRGNN achieves state-of-the-art performance in disease prediction and patient clustering while maintaining strong interpretability. Additionally, the model exhibits resilience to missing data and noise, underscoring its practical utility for real-world applications. Our findings suggest that HRGNN can serve as a powerful tool for medical research and patient care, with potential applications in disease prediction, patient clustering, and treatment recommendation. Software requirements serve as the foundation for the development lifecycle, yet the manual extraction of these requirements from source code remains a challenging task. This difficulty stems from the structured and abstract nature of code, which necessitates domain expertise to interpret. Conversely, source code documentation, such as comments, is often neglected during development, leading to incomplete requirements that hinder subsequent phases. This paper introduces DocSpec, a novel document-driven approach that leverages unstructured documents to automatically extract software specifications. DocSpec employs a hybrid strategy combining data-driven and knowledge-driven techniques to generate specifications from the text of unstructured documents. We validated DocSpec across various scenarios using a dataset comprising multiple open-source projects. The experimental results demonstrate that the method is effective and scalable, achieving an F1 score of 0.72. Furthermore, we conducted a case study on the TensorFlow project to illustrate how DocSpec can identify potential issues within source code. Ultimately, our findings indicate that unstructured documents are a valuable resource for automatically generating software specifications. Additionally, we present practical applications of DocSpec, including its utility for document-driven bug fixing and bug localization. To support future research, we have made the DocSpec tool and its underlying data available at https://github.com/DocSpec/DocSpec. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into document-driven software engineering. Specifically, we propose that future efforts should explore (1) utilizing documents for software understanding and maintenance, (2) leveraging documents for software design, and (3) applying documents to software testing. This study presents a theoretical investigation into the formation of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states by magnetic adatoms and clusters on superconducting Nb(110) surfaces, utilizing a fully relativistic, first-principles approach. The analysis covers both non-Resonant Anderson Model (RAM) and Resonant Anderson Model (RM) scenarios, specifically examining a magnetic Mn adatom and Mn$_3$ clusters on Nb(110). Spin-polarized photoemission spectra are computed to assess the impact of the superconducting environment on the Mn 3$d$ orbitals. The results indicate that the superconducting background significantly influences the position and energy of the Mn 3$d$ $d_{xy}$, $d_{x^2-y^2}$, and $d_{z^2}$ orbitals, which are primarily responsible for YSR state formation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that YSR states can be tuned by adjusting the distance between the Mn adatom and the Nb(110) surface. Finally, the findings suggest that clusters on Nb(110) offer greater potential for generating YSR states compared to isolated magnetic adatoms. However, biases stemming from systematic errors in sensor measurements can lead to inaccurate results. While some methods attempt to correct these biases, they often introduce new challenges, such as high computational costs or the need for external information. This paper introduces a D2D scan matching algorithm grounded in distribution-to-distribution matching, utilizing a deep neural network to mitigate bias. The proposed method is computationally efficient, eliminating the need for additional information, and demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Experimental results validate the method's effectiveness, and its applicability has been demonstrated in a mobile robot scenario. Detecting object boundaries in satellite imagery is a critical task for numerous remote sensing applications. While deep learning approaches have become the standard for this problem, they depend on extensive labeled datasets and powerful computational resources. This paper introduces a new edge detection method that operates without deep networks, eliminating the need for training data. Our approach demonstrates competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods on the MS-UCMerced and PUCS-Chicagoland datasets. The proposed technique is organized into two main components: first, we develop a self-adaptive strategy to generate a reliable edge map from the input image, and second, we refine this result using a series of post-processing operations. Experimental findings indicate that the significant performance gains stem primarily from the post-processing stage. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Self-adaptive.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance in automatic modulation classification (AMC), achieving state-of-the-art accuracy. However, these DNNs are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where minute, carefully designed perturbations added to input signals can cause misclassification with near-zero probability error rates. This study introduces a novel defense mechanism utilizing a blend GAN to generate adversarial examples. By incorporating a discriminator within the generator, the proposed method effectively eliminates adversarial artifacts, resulting in cleaner examples that enhance robustness against adversarial attacks in AMC tasks. Experimental results indicate that the proposed blend GAN surpasses existing methods, reducing the average adversarial error rate from 99.9% to 3.5%. Furthermore, the approach is robust to variations in blend factor, adversarial noise scale, and the number of adversarial examples. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological condition characterized by demyelination, which can result in significant disability. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) serves as a primary diagnostic tool, where lesions appear as hyperintense areas on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences. Although MS lesions are typically small, they vary in shape and are scattered throughout the brain. While numerous deep learning models have been developed to automate MS lesion segmentation, most are trained on datasets from a single institution, limiting their generalizability to scanners used by other hospitals. This study evaluates the impact of domain shift across four external hospital datasets: MSSEG, MSRI, MICCAI2018, and MSSEG-2020. We compare two training strategies: (1) training each model from scratch on every dataset, and (2) continuously training a single model across all datasets. Our findings indicate that the second approach yields superior performance. We also assess the segmentation capabilities of various state-of-the-art models, including U-Net, Attention U-Net, and ResNet-based architectures. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1234/MS-Lesion-Segmentation. This work is supported by the EPSRC grant EP/R018226/1. The corresponding author is Abhishek Kumar.

We introduce a novel method for the contrast step in representation learning, which extends the well-known contrastive loss to accommodate both positive and negative biases, thereby enhancing performance in unsupervised settings. Drawing inspiration from the cognitive science concept of bipolar contrast, this approach leverages the intuitive human capability to distinguish objects more effectively when they are framed within a range of bipolar contrasts rather than in isolation. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through its application to image segmentation and classification tasks. The evaluation results indicate that our technique achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised methods while offering a significant advantage over unsupervised alternatives. Furthermore, the code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexeykolesnikov/bipolar-contrast.

We present findings from a study of the Dragon infrared dark cloud (IRDC) conducted with the Submillimeter Array (SMA) at 1.3 mm, utilizing a resolution of 0.9 arcsec. Our data reveal a dense core within the Dragon cloud exhibiting a distinct size-temperature relation characteristic of core expansion. This expansion is driven by the formation of a massive star at the cloud's center, which is generating an outflow. The core's expansion is primarily caused by the outflow's momentum transfer to the surrounding gas. Furthermore, we identified a large, elongated structure in the cloud's center with a size of 0.15 arcsec that shows no signs of expansion. This structure is likely a shock front resulting from the interaction between the outflow and the ambient medium. Our results indicate that the Dragon IRDC core is expanding due to the outflow from its central massive protostar, providing strong evidence that outflows are the primary mechanism for core expansion in this region. This aligns with recent observations of core expansion in other IRDCs, suggesting that core expansion induced by outflows is a common phenomenon in star-forming regions. Additionally, we observed a large, elongated structure in the center of the Dragon IRDC that appears to be a shock front created by the outflow's interaction with the surrounding environment. This structure exhibits a velocity of 10 km/s, consistent with the outflow's velocity, and is likely a bow shock. The presence of this bow shock supports the theory that outflows decelerate upon interacting with the ambient medium. Primordial black holes (PBHs) are a promising dark matter candidate, with their formation driven by enhanced density fluctuations in the early universe. This formation is closely linked to inflationary models, particularly those featuring non-Gaussianity and features within the power spectrum. We introduce PopSyCLE, a novel code that integrates the established PBH formation framework from the "Critical density of primordial black holes" (CMBPH) code with the PopSyCLE population synthesis code. This new tool enables the calculation of PBH abundance as a function of mass for any specified primordial power spectrum. By utilizing PopSyCLE, researchers can investigate the relationship between PBH properties and dark matter models, as well as determine the initial black hole mass distributions required to replicate observed stellar and black hole populations. We demonstrate the code's capabilities by generating PBH abundance curves from various non-Gaussian and feature-containing power spectra, and we illustrate how to apply PopSyCLE to construct initial black hole mass distributions consistent with observational data. This will be followed by an analysis of how PBHs influence stellar evolution and black hole formation. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/PopSyCLE/PopSyCLE_PBH. We examine a system of hard, spherical wedges. When the half-angle of the wedge is $\alpha = 15^{\circ}$, our findings indicate the coexistence of two nematic phases: one featuring uniform density and another displaying modulated density with a periodicity of approximately 1.5 times the particle diameter. Both phases exhibit nematic order, though the modulated phase demonstrates significantly stronger orientational order. For smaller half-angles ($\alpha = 5^{\circ}$ and $\alpha = 10^{\circ}$), a third phase with chiral order emerges; this phase also possesses modulated density but breaks both nematic and translational symmetry. We attribute the density modulation in all observed phases to nematic splay. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the density profile of this modulation can be accurately modeled using a combination of Bessel functions. Finally, we show that the free energy of the modulated phases can be expressed as a Landau-de Gennes expansion, where the expansion coefficients are determined by the density profile. This enables us to derive the free energy of the system as a function of macroscopic order parameters. The resulting phase diagram aligns with the phases identified through particle simulations. Additionally, we note that wedges with a half-angle of $\alpha = 20^{\circ}$ have previously been shown to form smectic phases. We confirm this finding and provide a corresponding phase diagram. Our results suggest that phases with density modulation and broken nematic symmetry may also exist for these larger wedges. Overall, our findings indicate that phases with modulated density are generically present in systems of hard wedges. These phases are likely to occur in systems of anisotropic hard particles that are nearly spherical. This conclusion is supported by the fact that Landau theory predicts phases with modulated order for all anisotropic hard particles with small half-angles. Parameter-efficient methods have gained significant traction for enhancing pre-trained models, primarily by fine-tuning specific components like attention outputs or input embeddings. This paper introduces SETA, a novel approach that introduces a trainable token to each input embedding, enabling the model to learn the representation of a special token. We demonstrate that this specialized token is highly effective for various NLP tasks, including text classification, question answering, and natural language inference. Notably, we find that the trainable token excels at capturing task-specific information, whereas the original embeddings are better suited for retaining general knowledge. Additionally, we explore the application of this method to pre-trained multi-modal models for visual question answering, showing promising results. Our code and model files are available at https://github.com/ChenRex1990/SETA. The model files can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/chenspace1990/seta. Our source code is also accessible at https://github.com/ChenRex1990/SETA.

This study addresses the challenge of identifying the most preferred set within a given family of sets, where the objective is to determine which element to add to the current most preferred set. We evaluate the performance of non-contextual versus contextual single-item addition, demonstrating that contextual preference questions can significantly reduce the count of queries needed. Furthermore, we present new findings regarding both non-contextual and non-adaptive algorithms, establishing several upper and lower bounds on the number of preference queries required. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the broader set addition problem. Our research was conducted under the assumption of strict preferences, though we also extend several of these results to scenarios involving weak preferences. Additionally, we note that all results hold true in both online and offline settings. We believe this work offers a fresh perspective on online set optimization and may inspire further investigation into this area.

Keywords: set optimization, online set optimization, preference queries, set addition.
