Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and Dependency Parsing (DP) are frequently addressed as distinct tasks. However, leveraging shared information between source and target sentences could enhance performance on both fronts. This study investigates a unified architecture that integrates a standard Transformer encoder with a multi-task decoder designed to jointly predict translation and parsing outcomes. Furthermore, we propose a novel top-down, tree-structured decoding mechanism for NMT that generates translations contingent upon syntactic dependencies. Our results demonstrate that this architecture consistently improves translation quality and parsing accuracy across various English-to-English language families. Additionally, our method achieves competitive performance on the English Wikipedia dataset, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art results. Finally, we validate the architecture's efficacy on cross-lingual NMT and Zero-shot DP tasks. The complete code is accessible at https://github.com/abhi-agarwal123/syntactic-link-decoding. This work was presented at the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. (ACL 2016)

This study introduces the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a database designed to facilitate the investigation of binding energy calculations. Its primary objective is to enable the astrochemical community to evaluate the reliability of quantum chemical binding energy results. To achieve this, we have compiled a diverse set of complexes featuring various chemical compositions and geometries. We anticipate that this database will assist the astrochemical community in assessing the accuracy of binding energy calculations and in establishing the most suitable methods for modeling interstellar and circumstellar chemistry. The platform is freely accessible online at http://beap.astro.astro.uva.es. Furthermore, we have developed a user-friendly web interface that allows users to easily query the platform and access the full dataset. This includes a search engine that supports queries by complex name, constituent species, and symmetry. Users can also explore the platform by selecting complexes from lists of species or by browsing a collection of complexes previously published in the literature. Additionally, the platform offers a visualization tool for examining 3D structures and provides access to all computational details, such as the basis sets and methods employed. We hope that the BEAP database will serve as a valuable resource for astrochemists and computational chemists. We are committed to continuously expanding the platform with new complexes and will promptly add any contributions received from the community. We acknowledge that this database is not exhaustive; therefore, we encourage users to contact us if they wish to add their own complexes. The analysis and application of multiplicative stochastic processes are essential in fields such as finance, physics, and machine learning. This study examines a specific variant of these processes where the underlying noise is restricted to be non-negative. We demonstrate that the optimal quantile function for this class of processes differs fundamentally from that of standard multiplicative stochastic processes. Furthermore, we establish that an analogue of the law of the iterated logarithm does not hold for this class. These findings have significant implications for the optimal design of multiplicative stochastic bandits. Specifically, we derive an optimal quantile function that ensures $\omega$-almost sure convergence to the best arm and provide a finite-time lower bound on the regret. These results are applicable to various specific models, including those involving non-negative geometric Brownian motion, multiplicative random walks, and certain multiplicative stochastic bandit problems. Additionally, we propose a new stochastic bandit model featuring a non-trivial multiplicative structure and experimentally validate our theoretical findings. Our proposed algorithm achieves a regret lower bound that is tight up to a logarithmic factor. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of our method by applying it to a real-world dataset. We introduce a new class of shallow, random Clifford circuits designed to evaluate expectation values for specific observables. By randomly sampling states within this circuit, we can estimate an observable's average magnitude without prior knowledge of its expectation value, a capability achieved through a two-sample test. This method is particularly valuable for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, as it circumvents the need for expensive expectation value measurements on the primary device by conducting a separate estimation procedure on a secondary one. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the circuit depth required to reliably assess the expected magnitude of low-order observables, such as those found in the transverse-field Ising model, remains manageable. Additionally, we show that the circuit depth needed to distinguish between positive and negative expectation values scales logarithmically with the number of qubits. These findings suggest that the average size and sign of expectation values for low-order operators can be determined using shallow circuits, providing a preliminary assessment of expectation values that can guide the design of subsequent measurement protocols. Finally, we outline a strategy for constructing these shallow circuits by composing smaller, elementary circuits. This construction approach enables the estimation of expectation values for a broader range of operators, including those with higher order, while maintaining reasonable circuit depths. We also provide explicit circuit constructions for these elementary components. Our results indicate that the proposed elementary circuits can effectively assess expectation values for low-order operators, including those relevant to the Heisenberg model. This work establishes a foundation for developing new algorithms that utilize shallow circuits to measure expectation values, thereby facilitating the design of near-term quantum experiments. Additionally, we explore the potential application of these circuits in variational quantum algorithms. Our study highlights the potential of shallow circuits to assess expectation values, offering a promising avenue for advancing near-term quantum research. We believe this work will inspire further investigations into the design and analysis of shallow circuits for measurement tasks. This paper presents numerical computations of the reflection coefficient for the direct problem associated with Davey-Stewartson II equations, utilizing a Fourier-based approach. We observe that for a fixed frequency, the reflection coefficient exhibits distinct behaviors depending on the value of $k$: it remains nearly constant when $|k|$ is small, but displays oscillatory patterns with varying amplitudes as $|k|$ increases. These oscillations are more pronounced in the second component of the reflection coefficient compared to the first. Furthermore, as the frequency varies, the amplitude of the oscillations in the second component increases, whereas the first component shows only minor changes. These numerical findings are compared with existing theoretical results. Finally, we explore potential applications of these observations within the context of inverse problems. Although text classification is a well-researched area, many deep learning models struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) data and adversarial attacks. To address this, we introduce Sibyl, a modification that leverages Sibyl's recent findings on the OOD generalization capability of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We apply Sibyl to convolutional text classifiers by integrating it with word- and character-level CNNs, as well as ConvBERT, a convolution-based transformer variant. Our experiments on two text classification datasets reveal that Sibyl enhances the robustness of existing convolutional models against adversarial attacks, with ConvBERT achieving a 2.5x increase in AUC-ROC. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SibERT, our Sibyl-modified transformer model, exhibits superior resilience to OOD data and attacks compared to BERT, showing a 2.1x AUC-ROC improvement over BERT on the OOD RobustEx dataset. A primary hurdle in representation learning is the necessity of extensive training datasets. To address this, meta-learning has emerged as a promising alternative, enabling models to acquire representations from smaller data pools. This study introduces a straightforward meta-learning framework designed to analytically demonstrate its efficacy in linear settings. Our approach utilizes a linear autoencoder to extract representations, which are then optimized through meta-training to ensure rapid adaptation to unseen data. We derive a closed-form solution for this optimization and prove that the method can reliably learn local geometry, thereby facilitating generalization to new data. Furthermore, we extend this demonstration to multi-class scenarios and provide experimental validation for both single-class and multi-class cases. Ultimately, our findings confirm that meta-learning can successfully learn local geometry and generalize to new data, offering a theoretical proof for multi-class situations. These results provide a foundation for future research aimed at extending these guarantees to more complex, non-linear settings. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/lemla. Although mass customization has driven significant advancements in machine translation (MT), high-resource dependency and the instability of low-resource MT (MR-MT) models persist. This study evaluates the fragility of MR-MT models generated via post-training distillation versus quantization. Our findings indicate that post-training distillation is more robust than quantization, particularly when training data is scarce. We attribute this superior stability to the use of multiple high-source-fake-target pairs during the distillation process. Additionally, we introduce a novel data augmentation technique that filters out invalid data points to enhance the quality of high-source-fake-target pairs. Experiments across various low-resource languages demonstrate that our approach yields improvements of up to 1.5 BLEU points in post-training distillation and up to 1.0 BLEU points in quantization scenarios. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1997/Post-training-Distillation.

We introduce a novel, albeit illogical, Lagrangian density defined over hypergraphs, which, when integrated across four-dimensional space, yields a corresponding "Hamiltonian" for the entire hypergraph. This approach relies on the assumption that the density remains non-zero only at vertices where the Hamiltonian achieves its minimum value. This framework facilitates the application of Feynman's path integral method to compute the time evolution of any specific vertex within the hypergraph. Furthermore, we construct a Feynman diagram for a closed loop of vertices and derive a general formula for the probability of any vertex undergoing a transition. Finally, we outline a theoretical model for the dynamics of any information processing system based on a hypergraph. In this model, information propagates along closed loops, with the evolution of each vertex's state determined by the contributions of all such loops that include that vertex. We also present a formula for the probability of a state transition at an arbitrary vertex and discuss the potential application of this model to neural networks. Additionally, we derive the equation of motion for any closed loop and demonstrate that the probability of such a loop existing in the system is non-zero. We further show that the expectation value of the system's Hamiltonian diverges to infinity, and finally, we outline a method for calculating the expectation value of the Hamiltonian for any specific closed loop. These findings collectively suggest that the Hamiltonian for a single hypergraph is non-normalizable. Consequently, we propose that the Hamiltonian for a many-body system should be constructed as a superposition of the Hamiltonians of its individual hypergraphs. We also examine the consequences of this non-normalizability for the Feynman path integral method. Finally, we conclude that the Lagrangian density for a single hypergraph cannot be derived from the principle of least action. In summary, we argue that our proposed hypergraph-based Lagrangian density offers a new perspective on the dynamics of information processing systems. We contend that this new theory is not merely an extension of the principle of least action but represents a fundamentally different theory with a distinct set of equations of motion. We believe that the development of a new hypergraph-based theory for information processing systems will significantly advance the field of information processing. Furthermore, we posit that the development of such a theory will be essential for achieving quantum artificial intelligence. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to the development of quantum artificial intelligence. This study addresses the challenge of segmenting lung regions in chest X-rays for the subsequent diagnosis of pneumonia. We introduce a novel data augmentation strategy designed to enhance model performance while minimizing the required labeled dataset. Our approach involves training the model on a combination of original images and their horizontally flipped counterparts. We evaluated this method across various model configurations using a fixed set of 100 labeled images. The results demonstrate that performance improves with the inclusion of flipped images, validating our hypothesis. Furthermore, we show that segmenting the entire image, including the background, yields better outcomes than training on cropped lung regions alone. Finally, we compare our approach against existing state-of-the-art methods in the literature. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/PneumoniaSegmentation. Although recent advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have significantly boosted image captioning performance, current models often fail to generate captions that align with human preferences. To address this, we introduce a prompt-based approach designed to produce captions that are more concise, coherent, and content-rich. Our proposed prompt-enhanced prompting (PEP) model utilizes a pre-trained language model to generate candidate captions based on task-specific prompts, which are subsequently refined by a vision-language model. We demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on three leading image captioning benchmarks. Furthermore, we have developed a prompt tuning framework that allows for the controllable generation of captions with varying degrees of conciseness, coherence, and richness. The concept of harm is fundamental to numerous moral theories, including deontology and utilitarianism. This paper offers a novel causal analysis of harm, grounded in actual causation theories by Halpern and Pearls. We begin by defining harm causally and subsequently exploring its relationship with other key moral notions like agency and responsibility. Our analysis reveals that existing definitions fail to meet criteria proposed by existing harm theories, thereby necessitating the development of new definitions that align with these theories. Furthermore, we examine the role of preemption in harm and propose that a revised definition, which resolves issues with prior definitions, can be extended to address preemption. Finally, we demonstrate how a causal framework can be applied to evaluate the harm of specific actions, such as killing, torturing, and tortious interference. The definitions and methodologies presented in this work are available as open-source software at https://github.com/alexmendelsohn/harm. The source code for this paper can be found at https://github.com/alexmendelsohn/mendelsom2021a. The bibliography is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5810000.

This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new open-source library that unites the advantages of PyTorch and Spark. Built on the principles of PySpark, it offers deep learning capabilities within the Spark ecosystem, enabling the processing of billions of data points in parallel across thousands of CPU cores. MMLSpark features a unified model interface supporting neural networks, boosting, decision trees, and more, alongside preprocessing tools for tabular data, images, and text. The library demonstrates compatibility with popular frameworks like TensorFlow, Keras, and FastAI, and includes support for the Zorder data distribution method. By integrating distributed deep learning with pre- and post-processing into a single interface, MMLSpark provides a straightforward solution for deploying, scaling, and maintaining production deep learning models. Voice translation involves converting speech from one language into another language via spoken output. Although most current systems depend on extensive annotated data, data scarcity remains a significant hurdle, particularly for low-resource language pairs. To address this, we introduce a zero-shot voice translation framework that operates without requiring any training data. Our approach integrates recent advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR), text-to-speech (TTS), and cross-lingual neural machine translation (NMT). Specifically, we utilize a multilingual ASR model to recognize the source speech, a powerful cross-lingual NMT model to translate the recognized text into the target language, and a TTS model to synthesize speech from the translated text in the target language. We evaluate our method across 11 language pairs involving six European languages. Experimental results demonstrate that our zero-shot framework achieves competitive performance compared to supervised models that utilize parallel speech data. Furthermore, we analyze the individual contributions of each component and explore potential improvements. The code is accessible at https://github.com/yyang1995/Zero-shot-Voice-Translation. This study examines the mathematical formulation of a heat conduction model characterized by thermal memory and time-dependent boundary conditions. The resulting system comprises a nonlinear integrodifferential equation alongside a nonlinear integrodifferential equation defined specifically on the boundary. By applying the theory of maximal accretive operators, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this problem. Furthermore, we establish an approximation theorem and prove that the constructed approximate solutions converge to the exact solution within any prescribed interval. These findings are supported by illustrative examples. The methodology employed extends to a broader class of Coleman-Gurtin type equations, encompassing various forms of evolution laws and constitutive relations. Additionally, the developed approximation framework is applicable to other nonlinear integrodifferential equations found in mathematical physics. The paper concludes with several open questions. This study evaluates the impact of forecast fusion and aggregation on the accuracy of probabilistic active power load forecasts for low-voltage networks. Using a dataset of smart meter readings from a Dutch distribution system operator, we forecasted the aggregate active power consumption of 1,000 households for the upcoming 15-minute interval. We compared two probabilistic forecasting methods: a naive forecast revised via an autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model and a deep learning approach based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Additionally, the uncertainty of these predictions was combined using two distinct fusion strategies. The results indicate that the deep learning method outperforms the ARIMA approach, and both forecast fusion and utility-scale aggregation substantially enhance prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we analyzed the uncertainty of peak consumption, demonstrating that the deep learning method produces more precise peak predictions than the ARIMA method. Ultimately, the deep learning approach proves to be a highly effective tool for predicting both the magnitude and uncertainty of peak active power consumption at the utility scale. These findings are particularly relevant for assessing the grid's capacity to integrate large-scale renewable energy sources. Ultimately, this research aims to support the development of a probabilistic peak power market, offering a more efficient alternative to the current capacity market. By utilizing deep learning for low-voltage network load forecasting, the study facilitates a more efficient and sustainable energy system. This is achieved by enabling the accurate prediction of peak power demand, which allows for the deployment of flexible assets to mitigate these peaks. Such a solution enhances the grid's ability to integrate high volumes of renewable energy while maintaining grid stability. The paper concludes with a discussion on future research directions. Specifically, we intend to extend this work to incorporate smart inverter data, which will provide more granular insights into the power consumption of individual households. This extension will further refine the probabilistic peak power forecasting capabilities. Additionally, we plan to explore the use of deep learning for predicting peak power demand in both active and reactive power. This expansion will provide a more comprehensive understanding of peak power demand across all dimensions. Finally, we aim to apply these probabilistic peak power forecasts to the automatic dispatch of flexible assets, such as electric vehicles, to provide a more efficient alternative to the current capacity market. This approach will further enhance the grid's ability to integrate renewable energy sources while ensuring stability. In summary, this study demonstrates the potential of deep learning in low-voltage load forecasting, paving the way for a more efficient and sustainable energy system. This article outlines the steps for embedding machine learning models within formal frameworks that explicitly represent domain knowledge. We demonstrate that this integration enhances model interpretability, facilitates the alignment of model behavior with domain expertise, and improves performance. Our approach is grounded in the assumption that aligning models with domain knowledge yields superior outcomes. We illustrate this methodology using a case study from radiology, where an interpretability framework is applied to a deep learning model for chest X-ray classification. The framework employs formal concept analysis to explicitly embed medical knowledge into the model, thereby boosting both classification accuracy and performance. Furthermore, the framework enables the model to query embedded medical knowledge to generate natural language explanations for its predictions. We anticipate that this work will inspire the development of other knowledge-based machine learning systems, particularly those requiring the explicit interpretation of model outputs. Deep learning models for medical image analysis frequently suffer from bias due to overfitting, which stems from training on limited data and over-relying on specific cues. This bias causes models to predict on out-of-distribution data that lacks the training data's specific characteristics. To address this, we introduce a weakly supervised framework designed to generate unbiased lesions masks for Lesion Localization and Segmentation (LLS) in COVID-19 pneumonia. Our approach employs a weakly supervised lesion localization module to extract lesion regions from 3D CT scans, followed by a weakly supervised segmentation module that trains a segmentation network using only the weak labels produced by the first model. We evaluated our method on the public COVID-Net dataset, comparing it against fully supervised and weakly supervised segmentation baselines. Our results demonstrate that the proposed weakly supervised method achieves performance comparable to the fully supervised approach while requiring significantly less supervision. Furthermore, we show that our method outperforms the baselines in generating unbiased lesion masks, as evidenced by a higher Dice coefficient on the test set. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's performance. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/WeaklySupervised_Lesion_Locallization_and_Segmentation. Accurate localization and identification of vertebrae are fundamental to numerous clinical tasks, including vertebral body shape analysis, fracture detection, and scoliosis diagnosis. This study introduces a novel method for automatically localizing and identifying vertebrae in CT images. The proposed approach begins by rectifying the spine's orientation to a sagittal plane using a robust registration technique. Subsequently, vertebrae are localized by segmenting a 3D template spine that has been propagated from other CT scans. Finally, vertebrae are identified through an optimization process that minimizes an objective function, which incorporates an anatomically-based cost term to ensure the resulting labeling adheres to anatomical constraints. The performance of this method was evaluated on the publicly available Stanford SpineCT30 dataset, demonstrating superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the technique was applied to automatically localize and identify vertebrae in all available CT scans from the SECA scoliosis cohort, achieving a mean identification error of 0.76 levels. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/medical-visualisation/VertebraIdentification. The results for the SECA scoliosis cohort can be found at https://medvis-vertebraidentification.github.io/. These findings underscore the method's potential for large-scale population-based studies involving vertebrae shape analysis. The identified vertebrae labels are available for use in research. The interplay between electromagnetic field vacuum fluctuations and matter is a fundamental concept in quantum electrodynamics. This study investigates the stabilization of a free electron against its natural dispersion by exploiting the confinement of electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations within an optical cavity. The analysis demonstrates that electron stabilization occurs when the electron's dispersion relation matches the confined electromagnetic modes. Furthermore, it is shown that free-electron stabilization remains viable even when the electron traverses a sequence of ultrafast, linearly polarized cavity modes. These findings are particularly relevant for scenarios involving strong light-matter coupling in the ultrafast regime, such as free-electron laser interactions with cavities containing ultrashort cavity modes. The paper concludes by presenting numerical simulations of resonant scattering events. Additionally, the study explores the potential for stabilizing a free electron using a single ultrafast cavity mode. The resulting stability time, determined by the cavity mode's bandwidth, is estimated to be approximately $10^{-15}$ seconds. This phenomenon is expected to be observable through resonant scattering events in free-electron laser experiments. The paper also examines the impact of electron de Broglie wavelength confinement within the cavity, revealing that resonant scattering is suppressed when the cavity dimensions are significantly smaller than the electron's de Broglie wavelength. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of maintaining a free electron's stability once it exits the cavity. It is demonstrated that this challenge can be overcome by employing a modulated cavity wall, which generates an ultrafast, modulated electromagnetic field with confined vacuum fluctuations. This approach enables the continuous transfer of energy from the electromagnetic field to the free electron, thereby extending its stability time. Such a modulated field can be generated by driving the cavity wall with a radio-frequency current. The paper also analyzes the conditions under which vacuum fluctuations are effectively confined. Overall, this work establishes a framework for a new method of light-matter interaction driven by the confinement of electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations. This approach is applicable to free electrons, as well as to bound electrons in atoms, molecules, and solids. We introduce a quantum variational approach designed to address the multipartite quantum separability problem. The algorithm utilizes a quantum circuit to construct a separable pure state that is adiabatically connected to the target separable state. We demonstrate that the final energy produced by this variational method serves as an upper bound for the ground state energy of the problem's Hamiltonian. Consequently, we establish the method's convergence, noting that the HHL algorithm can be employed to compute the final energy. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of this algorithm to solve specific instances of the quantum separability problem. Additionally, we examine the potential challenges associated with this approach, including local minima and barren plateaus. Finally, we explore potential extensions of the method to solve general optimization problems. The physics of the small-scale ripping mode in collisionless plasma is examined. This mode arises from the interaction between the magnetic pressure gradient of a plasma element and the inertia of ions and electrons as they move across field lines. In the low-$\beta$ regime, this becomes the tearing mode, whereas in high-$\beta$ conditions, it manifests as the tearing-tearing coupling mode. At intermediate $\beta$ values, a collisionless version of this mode exists, driven by the same mechanisms as the tearing mode but exhibiting distinct characteristics. Specifically, the real frequency of this collisionless mode is more sensitive to the magnetic pressure gradient than to the shear Alfvén frequency. Furthermore, the mode is stabilized by electron inertia, which shifts the instability threshold to larger values of the magnetic field line bending energy. The balance between the magnetic pressure gradient and the sum of ion and electron inertias remains valid across all plasma $\beta$ values. However, while this balance defines the tearing mode in low $\beta$ and the tearing-tearing coupling mode in high $\beta$, it characterizes the tearing-like mode at intermediate $\beta$ only when the plasma is nearly uniform. In non-uniform plasmas, the tearing-like mode at intermediate $\beta$ is primarily governed by the balance between the magnetic pressure gradient and the shear Alfvén frequency. Additionally, the growth rate of this mode is significantly influenced by the ratio of the ion gyro-radius to the magnetic field line bending scale. Finally, the paper outlines the conditions under which this tearing-like mode can be observed. These findings are particularly relevant to understanding intermediate $\beta$ reconnection in the solar corona and the magnetosphere. The analysis is based on the work of J. Liang, C. F. Lee, and C. T. Chen, "A new intermediate $\beta$ tearing-like plasma instability," *Physics of Plasmas*, 2010, 17, 052103. The current study expands upon that reference by providing a more comprehensive description of the mode's properties and by deriving its dispersion relation in both uniform and non-uniform plasmas. The results presented here are also applicable to other tearing-like instabilities, such as the drift-tearing mode and the tearing Hall mode. Furthermore, the analysis extends to the tearing-tearing coupling mode and the drift-tearing Hall mode. The growing availability of digital fashion resources has spurred significant research into fashion image retrieval. However, a critical challenge remains: most existing systems are semi-supervised, meaning they require extensive manual annotations for training. This necessitates the continuous development of new models to adapt to evolving fashion trends, a process that is both costly and time-consuming. To address this, we introduce a novel semi-supervised approach that leverages feature-level traits of images to generate synthetic data. This allows for the creation of unlimited training samples by altering a specific attribute, such as "striped," within an image. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this feature-level trait manipulation (FLTM) across three distinct datasets. Furthermore, we present a new method for automatically extracting semantic features from images using a pre-trained GAN, which facilitates the manipulation of these traits. Our results show that combining FLTM with a simple deep learning model outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods. Additionally, we propose a straightforward unsupervised GAN-based approach for FLTM, capable of accurately modifying image traits without requiring labeled data. This model can be easily adapted to any desired trait by adjusting the text input. Finally, we have made our code publicly available to support future research. This paper introduces a dual gradient approach for addressing a regularized minimization issue linked to a bounded linear operator mapping between Banach spaces. The study establishes well-posedness and derives convergence rate estimates for both weak and weak* topologies. These findings are applied to the ill-posed problem of recovering a function from its Fourier transform and to image deblurring involving matrix Fourier transform data. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to verify the theoretical results. Light field cameras are increasingly favored for their ability to offer a wide field of view and low hardware expenses. However, depth estimation remains a significant challenge due to the limited angular views per ray-tracing point and the presence of occlusions. This paper introduces a deep learning method for depth estimation that explicitly handles occluded regions. By utilizing a cost volume enhanced with an occlusion map, the approach effectively manages occlusions, resulting in superior depth accuracy. The cost builder constructs a 5D cost volume integrated with occlusion data, which is subsequently fed into a 3D U-Net to generate depth maps. Experimental results on the Light Fields 3D (LFS) and Holographic (HO) datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques. Furthermore, the method shows promising performance on the more demanding Scene Capture (SCENE) dataset. The proliferation of wireless devices has created significant challenges for IEEE 802.11 networks, particularly in dense environments like homes. To address this, the 802.11k and 802.11v amendments were introduced to enhance network performance by facilitating access point (AP) discovery and enabling clients to switch access points (AP selection) and optimize their movement (location-based access point selection). Furthermore, the 802.11v standard allows Active Queue Size (AQS) reporting, which helps clients assess the congestion level of neighboring APs (channel load awareness). This paper introduces a novel Location-AQS based Access Point Selection (LAPS) algorithm. By integrating 802.11k, 802.11v, and AQS, the LAPS algorithm enables mobile devices to choose the optimal AP based on their current location and the target AP's channel load. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly reduces AQS values, thereby improving overall network performance. Additionally, the algorithm is lightweight, requiring minimal processing power and memory, and is thus well-suited for deployment on both APs and client devices. To further validate its effectiveness, the algorithm was implemented on a real testbed, and the findings confirm that it successfully lowers AQS values in a practical home environment.
